Corporate and Other Laws — Essential Summary

Study notes distilled from the ICAI Intermediate Paper 2 (Corporate and Other Laws) Board of Studies material — 15 chapters extracted to core concepts, definitions, statutory logic, worked examples and application.

15 chapters Companies Act, 2013 LLP Act, 2008 General Clauses Act & FEMA Source: 15 BoS PDFs

Chapter 1 — Preliminary

Source: 87769bos-aps2160-ch1.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • What the Companies Act, 2013 is: An Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to companies, enacted to meet changes in the national and international economic environment and to support expansion and growth of the economy.
  • Assent and notification dates: Received the assent of the President of India on 29th August 2013; notified in the Official Gazette on 30th August 2013, stating that different dates may be appointed for enforcement of different provisions through notifications.
  • Staggered commencement (actual figures): Section 1 came into force on 30th August 2013; 98 sections came into force on 12th September 2013; 143 sections were enforced from 1st April 2014, and so on.
  • Size and structure of the Act: It is a rule-based legislation with 470 sections and seven schedules, divided into 29 chapters, and each chapter has at least one set of Rules. Its stated aims are to improve corporate governance, simplify regulations and strengthen the interests of investors.
  • Why the definition clause matters: Section 2 is the definition section. Definitional sections/clauses are ‘internal aids to construction’ — when a word is defined as having a particular meaning in the enactment, that meaning alone must be given to it while interpreting a section, unless there is anything repugnant in the context.
  • Borrowed definitions — section 2(95): Words and expressions used but not defined in the Companies Act, 2013 but defined in the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, the SEBI Act, 1992 or the Depositories Act, 1996 carry the meanings assigned to them in those Acts.
  • Numbering convention: The number in brackets at the start of each definition, e.g. (85), denotes the clause of section 2 — so "small company" is section 2(85).

Section 1 — Short Title, Extent, Commencement and Application

  • Short title: The Act may be called the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Extent: It extends to the whole of India.
  • Commencement: Section 1 came into force at once; the remaining provisions come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint, and different dates may be appointed for different provisions. Any reference to "commencement of this Act" in a provision is construed as a reference to the coming into force of that provision.

Application — the Act applies to:

ClauseEntity coveredCarve-out
1(4)(a)Companies incorporated under this Act or under any previous company lawNone
1(4)(b)Insurance companiesExcept in so far as the provisions are inconsistent with the Insurance Act, 1938 or the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999
1(4)(c)Banking companiesExcept in so far as inconsistent with the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
1(4)(d)Companies engaged in generation or supply of electricityExcept in so far as inconsistent with the Electricity Act, 2003
1(4)(e)Any other company governed by any special Act for the time being in forceExcept in so far as inconsistent with that special Act
1(4)(f)Such body corporate incorporated by any Act, as the Central Government may by notification specifySubject to such exceptions, modifications or adaptations as specified in the notification

Meaning of "except in so far as": it means excluding to the extent of — i.e. if any provision of the Companies Act is inconsistent with a provision of the other Act (Insurance Act, Banking Regulation Act, Electricity Act, etc.) governing that company, the company shall comply with the provisions of the respective Act by which it is governed and regulated.

Key Definitions / Terms (Section 2)

Abridged prospectus — 2(1)
A memorandum containing such salient features of a prospectus as may be specified by SEBI by making regulations in this behalf.
Accounting standards — 2(2)
The standards of accounting or any addendum thereto for companies or class of companies referred to in section 133. Under section 133, the Central Government may prescribe standards as recommended by the ICAI (constituted under section 3 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949), in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations of the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA). Read with Rule 7 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014: (i) standards specified under the Companies Act, 1956 are deemed to be the accounting standards until standards are specified by the Central Government under section 133; (ii) till NFRA was constituted under section 132, the Central Government could prescribe standards as recommended by ICAI in consultation with the National Advisory Committee on Accounting Standards constituted under section 210A of the Companies Act, 1956. The Central Government prescribed that the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006 and the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015 may be followed. NFRA's date of constitution: 1st October 2018.
Alter / Alteration — 2(3)
Includes the making of additions, omissions and substitutions.
Articles — 2(5)
The articles of association of a company as originally framed, or as altered from time to time, or applied in pursuance of any previous company law, or applied in pursuance of this Act.
Associate company — 2(6)
In relation to another company, a company in which that other company has significant influence, but which is not a subsidiary of the company having such influence, and includes a joint venture company. "Significant influence" = control of at least 20% of total voting power, or control of or participation in business decisions under an agreement. "Joint venture" = a joint arrangement whereby the parties that have joint control of the arrangement have rights to the net assets of the arrangement. Per Circular dated 25/06/2014, shares held by a company in another company in a fiduciary capacity are not counted for determining the associate-company relationship (a fiduciary holds a legal or ethical relationship of trust and prudently takes care of money or other assets for another person).
Auditing standards — 2(7)
Standards of auditing or any addendum thereto for companies or class of companies referred to in sub-section (10) of section 143. Under section 143(10) the Central Government may prescribe them as recommended by ICAI in consultation with and after examination of NFRA's recommendations; proviso — until auditing standards are notified, the standards of auditing specified by ICAI are deemed to be the auditing standards.
Authorised capital / Nominal capital — 2(8)
Such capital as is authorised by the memorandum to be the maximum amount of share capital of the company.
Board of Directors / Board — 2(10)
In relation to a company, the collective body of the directors of the company.
Body corporate / Corporation — 2(11)
Includes a company incorporated outside India, but does not include (i) a co-operative society registered under any law relating to co-operative societies; and (ii) any other body corporate (not being a company as defined in this Act) which the Central Government may, by notification, specify.
Book and Paper / Book or Paper — 2(12)
Include books of account, deeds, vouchers, writings, documents, minutes and registers maintained on paper or in electronic form.
Books of account — 2(13)
Includes records maintained in respect of: (i) all sums of money received and expended by the company and the matters in relation to which the receipts and expenditure take place; (ii) all sales and purchases of goods and services; (iii) the assets and liabilities of the company; and (iv) the items of cost as may be prescribed under section 148 in the case of a company belonging to any class specified under that section. So: companies specified under section 148 maintain (i)+(ii)+(iii) plus cost items; other companies maintain only (i), (ii) and (iii). Section 148 authorises the Central Government to specify audit of items of cost in respect of certain companies.
Branch office — 2(14)
In relation to a company, any establishment described as such by the company.
Called-up capital — 2(15)
Such part of the capital which has been called for payment.
Charge — 2(16)
An interest or lien created on the property or assets of a company or any of its undertakings or both as security, and includes a mortgage.
Chartered Accountant — 2(17)
A chartered accountant as defined in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 who holds a valid certificate of practice under sub-section (1) of section 6 of that Act.
Chief Executive Officer — 2(18)
An officer of a company who has been designated as such by it. (Read with sections 2(51) and 203 on KMP.)
Chief Financial Officer — 2(19)
A person appointed as the Chief Financial Officer of a company. (Read with sections 2(51) and 203.)
Company — 2(20)
A company incorporated under this Act or under any previous company law.
Company limited by guarantee — 2(21)
A company having the liability of its members limited by the memorandum to such amount as the members may respectively undertake to contribute to the assets of the company in the event of its being wound up.
Company limited by shares — 2(22)
A company having the liability of its members limited by the memorandum to the amount, if any, unpaid on the shares respectively held by them.
Contributory — 2(26)
A person liable to contribute towards the assets of the company in the event of its being wound up. Explanation: a person holding fully paid-up shares shall also be considered a contributory.
Control — 2(27)
Includes the right to appoint a majority of the directors or to control the management or policy decisions, exercisable by a person or persons acting individually or in concert, directly or indirectly, including by virtue of shareholding, management rights, shareholders agreements, voting agreements or in any other manner. It is an inclusive definition and is relevant for the provisions relating to subsidiary and holding companies.
Debenture — 2(30)
Includes debenture stock, bonds or any other instrument of a company evidencing a debt, whether constituting a charge on the assets of the company or not. Proviso: (a) instruments referred to in Chapter III-D of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and (b) such other instrument as may be prescribed by the Central Government in consultation with the RBI, shall not be treated as debenture.
Director — 2(34)
A director appointed to the Board of a company.
Dividend — 2(35)
Includes any interim dividend.
Document — 2(36)
Includes summons, notice, requisition, order, declaration, form and register, whether issued, sent or kept in pursuance of this Act or any other law in force or otherwise, maintained on paper or in electronic form.
Employees' stock option — 2(37)
The option given to the directors, officers or employees of a company or of its holding company or subsidiary company or companies, giving them the benefit or right to purchase or subscribe for the shares of the company at a future date at a pre-determined price.
Expert — 2(38)
Includes an engineer, a valuer, a Chartered Accountant, a Company Secretary, a Cost Accountant and any other person who has the power or authority to issue a certificate in pursuance of any law in force.
Financial statement — 2(40)
In relation to a company, includes: (i) a balance sheet as at the end of the financial year; (ii) a profit and loss account, or in the case of a company carrying on any activity not for profit, an income and expenditure account for the financial year; (iii) cash flow statement for the financial year; (iv) a statement of changes in equity, if applicable; and (v) any explanatory note annexed to or forming part of any document referred to in (i) to (iv). Proviso: the financial statement of a One Person Company, small company and dormant company may not include the cash flow statement.
Financial year — 2(41)
In relation to any company or body corporate, the period ending on 31st March every year; and where it has been incorporated on or after 1st January of a year, the period ending on 31st March of the following year, in respect whereof the financial statement is made up. Proviso: where a company/body corporate is a holding, subsidiary or associate company of a company incorporated outside India and is required to follow a different financial year for consolidation of accounts outside India, the Central Government may, on an application in the prescribed form and manner, allow any period as its financial year, whether or not that period is a year. "Company incorporated outside India" refers to a foreign company incorporated under laws applicable outside India.
Free reserves — 2(43)
Such reserves which, as per the latest audited balance sheet, are available for distribution as dividend. Excluded by proviso: (i) any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets, whether shown as a reserve or otherwise; (ii) any change in the carrying amount of an asset or a liability recognised in equity, including surplus in the profit and loss account on measurement of the asset or liability at fair value.
Global Depository Receipt — 2(44)
Any instrument in the form of a depository receipt, by whatever name called, created by a foreign depository outside India and authorised by a company making an issue of such depository receipts.
Government company — 2(45)
Any company in which not less than 51% of the paid-up share capital is held by the Central Government, or by any State Government or Governments, or partly by the Central Government and partly by one or more State Governments, and includes a company which is a subsidiary company of such a Government company. Explanation (inserted by the notification dated 02.03.2020 under section 462, effective 3rd March 2020): where shares with differential voting rights have been issued, "paid-up share capital" shall be construed as "total voting power".
Holding company — 2(46)
In relation to one or more other companies, a company of which such companies are subsidiary companies. Explanation: the expression "company" here includes any body corporate.
Issued capital — 2(50)
Such capital as the company issues from time to time for subscription.
Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) — 2(51)
In relation to a company, means: (i) the Chief Executive Officer or the managing director or the manager; (ii) the company secretary; (iii) the whole-time director; (iv) the Chief Financial Officer; (v) such other officer, not more than one level below the directors, who is in whole-time employment and designated as KMP by the Board; and (vi) such other officer as may be prescribed. Note: till now no other officer has been prescribed.
Listed company — 2(52)
A company which has any of its securities listed on any recognised stock exchange. Proviso: such class of companies which have listed or intend to list such class of securities, as may be prescribed in consultation with SEBI, shall not be considered listed companies.
Manager — 2(53)
An individual who, subject to the superintendence, control and direction of the Board, has the management of the whole, or substantially the whole, of the affairs of a company, and includes a director or any other person occupying the position of a manager, by whatever name called, whether under a contract of service or not.
Managing Director — 2(54)
A director who, by virtue of the articles, or an agreement with the company, or a resolution passed in general meeting, or by the Board, is entrusted with substantial powers of management, and includes a director occupying the position of managing director by whatever name called. Explanation 1 — powers NOT deemed "substantial": administrative acts of a routine nature when authorised by the Board, such as affixing the common seal to any document; drawing and endorsing any cheque on the company's bank account; drawing and endorsing any negotiable instrument; signing any share certificate or directing registration of transfer of any share. Explanation 2: an individual must first be a director duly appointed under the Act — a person who is not a director cannot be appointed Managing Director.
Member — 2(55)
(i) the subscriber to the memorandum, deemed to have agreed to become a member and, on registration, entered as member in the register of members; (ii) every other person who agrees in writing to become a member and whose name is entered in the register of members; (iii) every person holding shares whose name is entered as beneficial owner in the records of a depository.
Memorandum — 2(56)
The memorandum of association of a company as originally framed or as altered from time to time in pursuance of any previous company law or of this Act.
Net worth — 2(57)
The aggregate value of paid-up share capital + all reserves created out of profits + securities premium account + debit or credit balance of profit and loss account, less the aggregate value of accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not written off, as per the audited balance sheet; but does not include reserves created out of revaluation of assets, write-back of depreciation and amalgamation.
Notification — 2(58)
A notification published in the Official Gazette; the expression "notify" is construed accordingly.
Officer — 2(59)
Includes any director, manager or key managerial personnel or any person in accordance with whose directions or instructions the Board or any one or more of the directors is or are accustomed to act.
Officer who is in default — 2(60)
For any provision that makes an officer in default liable to penalty or punishment by imprisonment, fine or otherwise, means: (i) whole-time director; (ii) KMP; (iii) where there is no KMP, such director(s) as specified by the Board who have given written consent to such specification, or all the directors if no director is so specified; (iv) any person who, under the immediate authority of the Board or any KMP, is charged with any responsibility including maintenance, filing or distribution of accounts or records, who authorises, actively participates in, knowingly permits, or knowingly fails to take active steps to prevent, any default; (v) any person in accordance with whose advice, directions or instructions the Board is accustomed to act, other than a person giving advice in a professional capacity; (vi) every director who is aware of the contravention by virtue of receipt of Board proceedings or participation in such proceedings without objecting, or where the contravention took place with his consent or connivance; (vii) in respect of the issue or transfer of shares, the share transfer agents, registrars and merchant bankers to the issue or transfer.
One Person Company (OPC) — 2(62)
A company which has only one person as a member.
Ordinary or special resolution — 2(63)
An ordinary resolution or, as the case may be, a special resolution referred to in section 114.
Paid-up share capital / share capital paid-up — 2(64)
Such aggregate amount of money credited as paid-up as is equivalent to the amount received as paid-up in respect of shares issued, and also includes any amount credited as paid-up in respect of shares, but does not include any other amount received in respect of such shares, by whatever name called.
Postal ballot — 2(65)
Voting by post or through any electronic mode. Related to section 110 read with Rule 22 of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014, which specifies the procedure and lists the items of business that must be transacted only by voting through postal ballot.
Prescribed — 2(66)
Prescribed by rules made under this Act.
Private company — 2(68)
A company having a minimum paid-up share capital as may be prescribed, and which by its articles: (i) restricts the right to transfer its shares; (ii) except in the case of an OPC, limits the number of its members to two hundred — where two or more persons hold one or more shares jointly they are treated as a single member; and persons in the employment of the company, and persons who were formerly employees and were members while in that employment and have continued to be members after the employment ceased, are not included in the number of members; and (iii) prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe for any securities of the company. Since nothing has been prescribed so far, there is no minimum paid-up share capital to form a private company.
Promoter — 2(69)
A person (a) named as such in a prospectus or identified by the company in the annual return referred to in section 92; or (b) who has control over the affairs of the company, directly or indirectly, whether as a shareholder, director or otherwise; or (c) in accordance with whose advice, directions or instructions the Board is accustomed to act. Proviso: sub-clause (c) does not apply to a person acting merely in a professional capacity.
Prospectus — 2(70)
Any document described or issued as a prospectus and includes a red herring prospectus or shelf prospectus or any notice, circular, advertisement or other document inviting offers from the public for the subscription or purchase of any securities of a body corporate.
Public company — 2(71)
A company which (a) is not a private company; and (b) has a minimum paid-up share capital as may be prescribed. Deeming proviso: a company which is a subsidiary of a company that is not a private company shall be deemed to be a public company for the purposes of this Act, even where such subsidiary continues to be a private company in its articles. Nothing has been prescribed, so there is no minimum paid-up share capital to form a public company.
Register of companies — 2(74)
The register of companies maintained by the Registrar on paper or in any electronic mode under this Act.
Registrar — 2(75)
A Registrar, an Additional Registrar, a Joint Registrar, a Deputy Registrar or an Assistant Registrar, having the duty of registering companies and discharging various functions under this Act.
Related party — 2(76)
With reference to a company: (i) a director or his relative; (ii) a KMP or his relative; (iii) a firm in which a director, manager or his relative is a partner; (iv) a private company in which a director or manager or his relative is a member or director; (v) a public company in which a director or manager is a director and holds along with his relatives more than 2% of its paid-up share capital; (vi) any body corporate whose Board, managing director or manager is accustomed to act in accordance with the advice, directions or instructions of a director or manager; (vii) any person on whose advice, directions or instructions a director or manager is accustomed to act — proviso: (vi) and (vii) do not apply to advice/directions/instructions given in a professional capacity; (viii) any body corporate which is (A) a holding, subsidiary or associate company of such company, (B) a subsidiary of a holding company to which it is also a subsidiary (i.e. a fellow subsidiary), or (C) an investing company or the venturer of the company — "investing company or venturer" means a body corporate whose investment in the company would result in the company becoming an associate company of that body corporate; (ix) such other person as may be prescribed. Rule 3 of the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, 2014: for sub-clause (ix), a director (other than an independent director) or KMP of the holding company, or his relative, is deemed to be a related party.
Relative — 2(77)
Anyone related to another if (i) they are members of a Hindu Undivided Family; (ii) they are husband and wife; or (iii) one person is related to the other in such manner as may be prescribed. Rule 4 of the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, 2014 lists the relatives: (1) Father (includes step-father), (2) Mother (includes step-mother), (3) Son (includes step-son), (4) Son's wife, (5) Daughter, (6) Daughter's husband, (7) Brother (includes step-brother), (8) Sister (includes step-sister).
Remuneration — 2(78)
Any money or its equivalent given or passed to any person for services rendered by him, and includes perquisites as defined under the Income Tax Act, 1961.
Share — 2(84)
A share in the share capital of a company and includes stock.
Small company — 2(85)
A company, other than a public company, whose (i) paid-up share capital does not exceed ₹50 lakh or such higher amount as may be prescribed, which shall not be more than ₹10 crore; and (ii) turnover as per the profit and loss account for the immediately preceding financial year does not exceed ₹2 crore or such higher amount as may be prescribed, which shall not be more than ₹100 crore. Proviso — does NOT apply to: (A) a holding company or a subsidiary company; (B) a company registered under section 8; (C) a company or body corporate governed by any special Act. Actually prescribed limits under the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, 2014: paid-up capital ₹4 crore and turnover ₹40 crore.
Subscribed capital — 2(86)
Such part of the capital which is for the time being subscribed by the members of a company.
Subsidiary company / Subsidiary — 2(87)
In relation to any other company (the holding company), a company in which the holding company (i) controls the composition of the Board of Directors; or (ii) exercises or controls more than one-half of the total voting power, either on its own or together with one or more of its subsidiary companies. Proviso: such class or classes of holding companies as may be prescribed shall not have layers of subsidiaries beyond such numbers as may be prescribed. Explanation: (a) a company is deemed a subsidiary even if the control in (i) or (ii) is of another subsidiary of the holding company; (b) the composition of the Board is deemed to be controlled by another company if that other company, by exercise of some power exercisable at its discretion, can appoint or remove all or a majority of the directors; (c) "company" includes any body corporate; (d) "layer" in relation to a holding company means its subsidiary or subsidiaries. Per notification dated 27th December 2013, shares held or power exercisable by a company in another company in a fiduciary capacity shall not be counted for determining the holding–subsidiary relationship under section 2(87).
Sweat equity shares — 2(88)
Such equity shares as are issued by a company to its directors or employees at a discount or for consideration other than cash, for providing their know-how or making available rights in the nature of intellectual property rights or value additions, by whatever name called.
Total voting power — 2(89)
In relation to any matter, the total number of votes which may be cast in regard to that matter on a poll at a meeting of a company if all the members or their proxies having a right to vote on that matter are present and cast their votes.
Tribunal — 2(90)
The National Company Law Tribunal constituted under section 408.
Turnover — 2(91)
The gross amount of revenue recognised in the profit and loss account from the sale, supply or distribution of goods or on account of services rendered, or both, by a company during a financial year.
Unlimited company — 2(92)
A company not having any limit on the liability of its members.
Voting right — 2(93)
The right of a member of a company to vote in any meeting of the company or by means of postal ballot.

How It Works / Logic

  • Financial-year rule of thumb: the period always ends on 31st March. If incorporated on or after 1st January of a year, the first financial year runs to 31st March of the following year (so it can be up to 15 months). Only a holding/subsidiary/associate of a foreign company needing overseas consolidation can seek a different financial year, and only by application to the Central Government, which may allow any period, whether or not it is a year.
  • Small company is a two-limb, cumulative test: both the paid-up capital limit (₹4 crore prescribed) and the turnover limit (₹40 crore prescribed) must be satisfied. Failing either one disqualifies the company. On top of that, the entity must not be a public company, a holding company, a subsidiary company, a section 8 company, or governed by a special Act.
  • Holding–subsidiary is a control test, not merely a shareholding test: either control of Board composition or control/exercise of more than one-half of total voting power (including through other subsidiaries) makes a company a subsidiary. Shares held in a fiduciary capacity are excluded from the computation (notification dated 27th December 2013).
  • Associate vs subsidiary: at least 20% of total voting power (or participation in business decisions under an agreement) gives significant influence → associate. But if the relationship crosses into control under section 2(87), it becomes a subsidiary and is expressly excluded from the associate definition. Fiduciary holdings are again excluded (Circular dated 25/06/2014).
  • Private company deemed public: a private company that is a subsidiary of a non-private company is deemed public under the proviso to section 2(71) — which knocks out its access to the private-company exemptions even though its articles still contain the private-company restrictions.
  • Counting members for the 200 limit (section 2(68)): joint holders count as one member; present employees who are members and ex-employees who became members while employed and continued after employment ceased are excluded entirely.
  • Layers of share capital (sections 2(8), 2(86), 2(50), 2(15), 2(64)): Authorised (maximum permitted by memorandum) → Subscribed (subscribed by members) → Issued (actually issued) → Called-up (called for payment) → Paid-up (actually received).
  • Officer in default cascade (section 2(60)): WTD and KMP first; if there is no KMP, the Board-specified directors who have consented in writing; if no director is specified, all directors are in default.

Not to be treated as "listed companies" — Rule 2A

Under Rule 2A of the Companies (Specification of definitions details) Rules, 2014, the following classes are not considered listed companies:

ClauseClass of company
(a)Public companies which have not listed their equity shares on a recognised stock exchange but have listed — (i) non-convertible debt securities issued on private placement basis under the SEBI (Issue and Listing of Debt Securities) Regulations, 2008; or (ii) non-convertible redeemable preference shares issued on private placement basis under the SEBI (Issue and Listing of Non-Convertible Redeemable Preference Shares) Regulations, 2013; or (iii) both categories (i) and (ii)
(b)Private companies which have listed their non-convertible debt securities on private placement basis on a recognised stock exchange under the SEBI (Issue and Listing of Debt Securities) Regulations, 2008
(c)Public companies which have not listed their equity shares on a recognised stock exchange but whose equity shares are listed on a stock exchange in a jurisdiction specified under sub-section (3) of section 23 of the Act

Examples

  • Example 1 — Act applies to older companies: ABC Ltd. was incorporated on 1.1.1972 under the Companies Act, 1956. Since section 1(4)(a) covers companies incorporated under any previous company law, the Companies Act, 2013 shall also be applicable to ABC Ltd.
  • Example 2 — bodies corporate notified under section 1(4)(f): Food Corporation of India (FCI) and National Highway Authority of India (NHAI).
  • Example 3 — "company" includes companies under previous law [2(20)]: Reliance Industries Limited (incorporated 1973), Tata Steel Limited (incorporated 1907), Infosys Limited (incorporated 1981). Companies incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 (previous company law) are also included in the definition and are treated as a "Company".
  • Example 4 — company limited by shares [2(22)]: A shareholder who has paid ₹75 on a share of face value ₹100 can be called upon to pay only the balance of ₹25.
  • Example 5 — Government company test fails [2(45)]: X Industries Ltd. has 25% shareholding held by the Central Government, 10% by the Government of Maharashtra, and 15% by the Central Government and the Government of Rajasthan. Conclusion: X Industries Ltd. is not a government company, because the minimum holding of at least 51% of the paid-up share capital by the Central Government, or any State Government(s), or partly by the Central Government and partly by one or more State Governments, is not complied with.
  • Example 6 — net worth and fair valuation [2(57)]: The statutory auditors of a company were required to certify the net worth as on 30th September 2024 computed as per section 2(57). The company had fair valued its property, plant and equipment in the current year and this was mistakenly taken into retained earnings. Answer: under section 2(57), reserves created out of revaluation of assets do not form part of net worth. Even though the company routed the fair valuation through retained earnings, the resultant credit in reserves (by whatever name called) falls in the category of "reserves created out of revaluation of assets", which is specifically excluded from net worth, and hence should be excluded. The auditors should also separately consider the accounting of this reserve at the time of audit of the books.
  • Example 7 — all directors as officers in default [2(60)]: A company committed a default in relation to allotment of shares. The company had no managing director, no whole-time director, no manager, no secretary, no person charged by the Board with the responsibility of complying with the Act, and no director/directors specified by the Board. Conclusion: in such a situation all the directors of the company may be treated as officers in default.
  • Example 8 — private company deemed public [2(71)]: A Pvt. Ltd. is a wholly owned subsidiary of AB Ltd., a public company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013. A Pvt. Ltd. wanted to avail exemptions available to private companies. Conclusion: since A Pvt. Ltd. is a subsidiary of a public company, it will be deemed to be a public company and will not be allowed to avail the exemptions provided to a private company.
  • Example 9 — fellow subsidiaries of a private holding company [2(76)]: XYZ Pvt. Ltd. has two subsidiaries, Y Pvt. Ltd. and Z Pvt. Ltd. Under section 2(76)(viii)(B), Y Pvt. Ltd. and Z Pvt. Ltd. are related parties. However, under Notification No. G.S.R. 464(E) dated 5th June 2015, clause (viii) shall not apply with respect to section 188 to a private company — therefore Y Pvt. Ltd. and Z Pvt. Ltd. are not related parties for the purpose of section 188. But if Y Pvt. Ltd. and Z Pvt. Ltd. have common directors, they will be deemed related parties by virtue of section 2(76)(iv).
  • Example 10 — fellow subsidiaries of a public holding company [2(76) with 2(71)]: XYZ Ltd., a public company, has two subsidiaries, Y Pvt. Ltd. and Z Pvt. Ltd. Under section 2(71), a private company which is a subsidiary of a public company is deemed to be a public company, so Y Pvt. Ltd. and Z Pvt. Ltd. are not eligible for the exemption under Notification No. G.S.R. 464(E) dated 5th June 2015. Therefore, under section 2(76)(viii)(B), Y Pvt. Ltd. and Z Pvt. Ltd. are related parties; in addition, XYZ Ltd. will also be a related party to Y Pvt. Ltd. and Z Pvt. Ltd.
  • Example 11 — subsidiary cannot be a small company [2(85) proviso]: H Ltd. is the holding company of S Pvt. Ltd. As per S Pvt. Ltd.'s last profit and loss account for the year ending 31st March 2024, its turnover was ₹1.50 crore and its paid-up share capital was ₹40 lakh. Although S Pvt. Ltd. meets the turnover and paid-up share capital norms and wants to be categorised as a small company, it cannot be categorised as a "small company" because it is the subsidiary of another company (H Ltd.) — proviso to section 2(85).
  • Example 12 — computing the five layers of share capital: ABC Ltd. was registered with an authorised capital of ₹2,00,00,000, each share of ₹10. Applications were received for 10,00,000 shares, but the company actually issued 7,00,000 shares on which it called ₹8 per share. All calls were met in full except three shareholders who still owe on 6,000 shares in total. Answer: Authorised share capital = ₹2,00,00,000 (2 crore); Subscribed capital = 10,00,000 × 10 = ₹1,00,00,000 (1 crore); Issued capital = 7,00,000 × 10 = ₹70,00,000; Called-up capital = 7,00,000 × 8 = ₹56,00,000; Paid-up capital = 56,00,000 − (6,000 × ₹8) = ₹55,52,000.

Test Your Knowledge — MCQs with Answers

  • MCQ 1 — first financial year: Green Ltd. is incorporated on 3rd January 2023. What will be the financial year for the company? Options: (a) 31st March 2023; (b) 31st December 2023; (c) 31st March 2024; (d) 30th September 2024. Answer: (c) 31st March 2024 — because it was incorporated on or after 1st January, section 2(41) pushes the first financial year to 31st March of the following year.
  • MCQ 2 — public company cannot be a small company: Roma along with her six friends incorporated Roma Trading Ltd. in May 2023; paid-up share capital ₹2 crore; in April 2024 she noted that the last financial year's turnover was well below ₹40 crore. Answer: (b) — the concept of "small company" is applicable only in the case of a private limited company/OPC and therefore, despite meeting the criteria of a small company, being a public limited company it cannot enjoy the benefits of a small company. (Rejected options: (a) it is definitely a small company since capital is below ₹4 crore and turnover below ₹40 crore; (c) a public company must maintain the small-company norms continuously for two years; (d) an undertaking by all shareholders to the ROC not to exceed the limits for two years would suffice.)
  • MCQ 3 — section 8 company cannot be a small company: Abhilasha and Amrita incorporated a ‘not for profit’ private limited company registered under Section 8. A friend said it can be categorised as a small company because, as per the last profit and loss account for the year ending 31st March 2024, turnover was less than ₹40 crore and paid-up share capital less than ₹4 crore. Answer: (c) — the status of "small company" cannot be bestowed upon a ‘not for profit’ company registered under Section 8. (Rejected options involved acquiring at least a 5% stake in another small company in the immediately following financial year, or in the second financial year with the written permission of the concerned ROC, or availing the status with the ROC's permission if incorporated as a private limited company.)
  • MCQ 4 — meaning of significant influence: "Associate company", in relation to another company, means a company in which that other company has a significant influence, but which is not a subsidiary of the company having such influence, and includes a joint venture company. "Significant influence" means: (a) control of at least 10% of total voting power; (b) at least 15%; (c) at least 20%; (d) at least 25%. Answer: (c) Control of at least 20% of total voting power.

Test Your Knowledge — Descriptive Questions with Answers

  • Descriptive Q1 — MNP Private Ltd. and small-company status: MNP Private Ltd. is registered under the Companies Act, 2013 with a paid-up share capital of ₹2 crore and turnover of ₹60 crore. Law: section 2(85) — a small company is a company other than a public company whose (1) paid-up share capital does not exceed ₹50 lakh or such higher prescribed amount not more than ₹10 crore, and (2) turnover as per its last profit and loss account does not exceed ₹2 crore or such higher prescribed amount not more than ₹100 crore; and the clause does not apply to (A) a holding or subsidiary company, (B) a section 8 company, or (C) a company/body corporate governed by a special Act. The Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, 2014 prescribe ₹4 crore paid-up capital and ₹40 crore turnover. (i) Answer: only the capital criterion (not exceeding ₹4 crore) is met; the turnover criterion (not exceeding ₹40 crore) is not met, and both criteria must be met — so MNP Ltd. cannot avail the status of a small company. (ii) Answer: if turnover were ₹30 crore, both criteria would be fulfilled and MNP Ltd. can avail the status of a small company.
  • Descriptive Q2 — Flora Fauna Limited, counting members for conversion to a private company: Flora Fauna Limited was registered as a public company with 230 members: (a) Directors and their relatives 50; (b) Employees 15; (c) Ex-employees (shares allotted when they were employees) 10; (d) 5 couples holding shares jointly in the name of husband and wife = 10 (5 × 2); (e) Others 145. Law: section 2(68) — a private company limits its members to 200 (except an OPC); joint holders of one or more shares are treated as a single member; and present employees and ex-employees who were members while in employment and continued after it ceased are excluded from the count. Answer: countable members = Directors and their relatives 50 + 5 couples counted as 5 × 1 = 5 + Others 145 = 200. The 15 employees and 10 ex-employees are excluded. Since the existing number of members is 200, which does not exceed the maximum limit of 200, no reduction in the number of members is necessary and the company may be converted into a private company. (The provisions on conversion of a public company into a private company are covered in Chapter 2 — Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto.)

Why It Matters / Application

Section 2 is the switch that turns every other provision of the Companies Act, 2013 on or off for a given entity. Whether a company must file a cash flow statement (section 2(40) proviso), whether it may keep a non-March financial year (section 2(41) proviso), how much it may pay as dividend or buy back (free reserves, section 2(43)), whether a transaction needs section 188 related-party approval (section 2(76) read with the private-company exemption in G.S.R. 464(E)), whether it must consolidate accounts and appoint KMP under section 203 — all of these turn on a status determination made purely from these definitions. The small-company, OPC, private, public, holding, subsidiary and associate labels also determine which of the hundreds of compliance concessions under the Act apply, which is why the numeric thresholds (20% voting power for significant influence, more than one-half of total voting power for subsidiary, 51% for a government company, 200 members for a private company, more than 2% paid-up capital for a related-party public company, ₹4 crore / ₹40 crore for a small company) must be memorised exactly.

Note — Exceptions, Provisos and Exam Traps

  • Private-company exemption to section 2(40): for private companies, the proviso reads — "the financial statement, with respect to one person company, small company, dormant company and private company (if such private company is a start-up) may not include the cash flow statement". "Start-up" / "start-up company" means a private company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 or the Companies Act, 1956 and recognised as a start-up in accordance with the notification issued by the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, Ministry of Commerce and Industry. These exceptions, modifications and adaptations apply only to a private company which has not committed a default in filing its financial statements under section 137 or its annual return under section 92 with the Registrar.
  • Section 8 companies and minimum paid-up capital: the requirement of having a minimum paid-up share capital does not apply to a section 8 company (formation of companies with charitable objects, etc.) vide notification dated 5th June 2015 — this exemption applies to both section 2(68) (private) and section 2(71) (public). The exemption is available only to a section 8 company which has not defaulted in filing financial statements under section 137 or annual return under section 92 [vide amendment notification G.S.R. 584(E) dated 13th June 2017].
  • Nothing prescribed for minimum capital: footnotes to sections 2(68) and 2(71) confirm that since nothing has been prescribed so far, there is no minimum paid-up share capital to form either a private or a public company.
  • Associate company definition differs from accounting standards: the definition under AS 23 / Ind AS 28 (Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements / Investment in Associates and Joint Ventures) is slightly different from the section 2(6) definition — do not mix them.
  • Related-party carve-outs: clause 2(76)(viii) shall not apply with respect to section 188 (Related Party Transactions) to a private company vide Notification No. G.S.R. 464(E) dated 5th June 2015; and it shall not apply with respect to section 188 to a Specified IFSC Public company vide Notification No. G.S.R. 08(E) dated 4th January 2017.
  • IFSC financial-year relaxation: for a specified IFSC public company and specified IFSC private company, a proviso inserted vide notification dated 5th January 2017 allows a company that is a subsidiary of a foreign company to keep the same financial year as its holding company, and approval of the Tribunal is not required.
  • Financial-year transitional provisos: any application pending before the Tribunal as on the date of commencement of the Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019 shall be disposed of by the Tribunal in accordance with the provisions applicable before such commencement; and a company or body corporate existing at the commencement of the Act was required to align its financial year within two years of such commencement (this provision is no longer relevant but still forms part of the Act).
  • Fiduciary holdings are ignored twice: once for the associate relationship (Circular dated 25/06/2014) and once for the holding–subsidiary relationship (notification dated 27th December 2013).
  • KMP trap: no "other officer" has been prescribed under section 2(51)(vi) so far; and the officer under 2(51)(v) must satisfy all three tests — not more than one level below the directors, in whole-time employment, and designated as KMP by the Board.
  • Managing Director trap: routine administrative powers (affixing the common seal, drawing/endorsing cheques and negotiable instruments, signing share certificates, directing registration of share transfers) are not "substantial powers of management"; and a non-director can never be appointed Managing Director.
  • Terminology note: "Profit and Loss Account" may also be referred to as "Statement of Profit and Loss" at some places under the Act.

Chapter 2 — Incorporation of Company and Matters Incidental Thereto

Source: 87770bos-aps2160-ch2.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Scope of Chapter II: Sections 3 to 22 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014 — covering formation (Sec 3, 3A), MOA (Sec 4), AOA (Sec 5), Act overriding MOA/AOA (Sec 6), incorporation procedure (Sec 7), Section 8 charitable companies, effect of registration (Sec 9), effect of MOA/AOA (Sec 10), commencement of business (Sec 10A), registered office (Sec 12), alteration of MOA (Sec 13), alteration of AOA (Sec 14), noting alterations in every copy (Sec 15), rectification of name (Sec 16), copies to members (Sec 17), conversion (Sec 18), subsidiary holding shares in holding company (Sec 19), service of documents (Sec 20), authentication (Sec 21) and execution of bills of exchange (Sec 22).
  • Promoter as a fiduciary: Section 2(69) defines promoter as a person named as promoter in a prospectus, or identified as promoter in the annual return, or who controls the affairs of the company directly/indirectly as shareholder, director or otherwise, or on whose advice/directions/instructions the Board is accustomed to act — but excluding a person acting merely in a professional capacity (attorney, technical or functional expert). Judicially, a promoter is one who undertakes to form a company with reference to a given project and to set it going (Twycross v. Grant), need not be associated with the initial formation — one who later arranges the floating of its capital is equally a promoter (Lagunas Nitrate Co. v. Lagunas Syndicate), and stands in a fiduciary position (Erlanger v. New Sombrero Phosphate Co.). Promotion itself was described in Whaley Bridge Printing Co. v. Green.
  • Three modes of incorporation: An incorporated company may be a Chartered Company (royal charter, pre-independence), a Statutory Company (special Act of the legislature) or a Registered Company. Section 3 deals only with registered companies.
  • MOA is the charter; AOA is the internal rulebook: The memorandum defines the company's relationship with outsiders — its powers and permitted activities. The articles contain internal regulations and create a contract between the company and members and between the members inter se (Naresh Chandra Sanyal v. Calcutta Stock Exchange Association Ltd., AIR 1971 SC 422).
  • Doctrine of ultra vires: Any act beyond the objects stated in the memorandum is ultra vires and void, and cannot be ratified even by the assent of the whole body of shareholders. The doctrine exists to protect shareholders and creditors. Widening the objects by alteration operates prospectively only — an act once ultra vires remains so forever.
  • Doctrine of constructive notice vs doctrine of indoor management: These are counter-doctrines. Constructive notice puts the onus on the outsider to know what the MOA and AOA say; indoor management protects that outsider from the company's internal irregularities. Constructive notice protects the company against outsiders; indoor management protects outsiders against the company.
  • Certificate of incorporation is NOT conclusive proof: Under the Companies Act, 2013 the certificate is evidence of registration (separate legal entity with perpetual succession) but not conclusive proof that everything prior to incorporation was in order — sub-sections (6) and (7) of section 7 make this clear.

Key Definitions / Terms

One Person Company (OPC) — Sec 3(1)(c)
A company formed by one person, treated as a private company. Only a natural person, other than a minor, who is an Indian citizen — whether resident in India or otherwise — is eligible to incorporate an OPC (Rule 3(1)).
Resident in India (for OPC)
A person who has stayed in India for a period of not less than 120 days during the immediately preceding financial year.
Corporate Identity Number (CIN)
A 21 alpha-numeric digit unique identification number allotted by the Registrar from the date mentioned in the certificate of incorporation, included in that certificate.
Entrenchment — Sec 5(3)
A provision in the articles stating that specified provisions may be altered only if conditions more restrictive and harder than those applicable to a special resolution are met — i.e. deliberately making alteration of the articles more difficult in order to enhance protection.
Ultra vires
An act done beyond or outside the objects stated in the memorandum; it is void and unratifiable. Doctrine first enunciated by the House of Lords in Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche (1878) L.R. 7 H.L. 653.
Courier — Sec 20
A person or agency which delivers the document and provides proof of its delivery.
Electronic transmission — Sec 20
A communication that creates a record capable of retention, retrieval (recovery) and review, and which may thereafter be rendered into clearly legible tangible form — by fax or email provided by the company/officer, by posting on an electronic message board or network designated by the Registrar or the member (validly delivered upon posting), or by other electronic means where reasonable systems verify the sender.
Tribunal
The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), constituted on 1st June, 2016 under section 408 — a quasi-judicial body adjudicating company matters.
IFSC Company
A company licensed to set up business in any International Financial Services Centre in India (e.g. Gujarat International Finance Tec-City). Specified IFSC Public/Private Companies may be formed only as companies limited by shares, and must suffix "International Financial Service Company" or "IFSC" to the name.
SPICe+ (Form INC-32)
Simplified Proforma for Incorporating Company Electronically Plus — an integrated web form offering 10 services by 3 Central Government Ministries/Departments (Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Ministry of Labour, and Department of Revenue in the Ministry of Finance).
List 'A' and List 'B' contributories
List 'A' = shareholders who are members at the time of winding-up; they are primarily liable. List 'B' = persons who were members during the 12 months preceding the date of winding-up; they contribute only if amounts realised from List 'A' are insufficient.

Formation of Company [Section 3] and Minimum Members

  • For a lawful purpose, by subscribing their names to a memorandum and complying with the Act: a public company — by 7 or more persons; a private company — by 2 or more persons; a One Person Company (as a private company) — by 1 person.
  • Section 3(2): a company so formed may be incorporated as (a) limited by shares, (b) limited by guarantee, or (c) unlimited liability. A limited liability company may be limited by guarantee as well as by shares.
  • Section 3A — members severally liable: Members become severally liable and may be severally sued for payment of the whole debts of the company contracted after the elapse of six months where (i) membership falls below 7 (public) or 2 (private); (ii) the company carries on business for more than six months with the reduced number; and (iii) the person carrying on business after those six months is cognizant of that fact.

One Person Company — Nominee Rules

  • The MOA of an OPC must name a natural person, other than a minor, an Indian citizen (resident or otherwise) as nominee, with prior written consent, who becomes the member on the subscriber's death or incapacity to contract — this secures perpetual succession.
  • Nominee's name is filed in Form INC-32 (SPICe+) with consent in Form INC-4 at the time of incorporation, along with the memorandum and articles.
  • Rule 3(2): a natural person shall not be a member of more than one OPC at any time, and shall not be a nominee of more than one OPC. If a member of one OPC becomes a member of another by virtue of being its nominee, he must meet the one-OPC criterion within 180 days.
  • Withdrawal of consent: the nominee may withdraw by written notice to the sole member and to the OPC; the sole member must nominate another person within 15 days of receipt of the notice of withdrawal, intimating the company in writing with the new nominee's consent in Form INC-4.
  • Replacement of nominee: the member may change the nominee at any time for any reason (including death or incapacity of the nominee) after obtaining the new nominee's prior consent, by written intimation to the company. The Act/rules do not state whether intimation is prior or subsequent; on reasonable construction it should be prior intimation.
  • Nominee becoming member: where the sole member ceases to be a member and the nominee becomes the new member, that new member must nominate a fresh nominee within fifteen days of becoming member.
  • In all three cases (withdrawal, replacement, cessation) the company shall file notice with the Registrar in Form INC-4 within 30 days of receipt of the notice/intimation/cessation.
  • Any such change in the name of the nominated person is not deemed to be an alteration of the memorandum.
  • An OPC cannot be incorporated or converted into a Section 8 company (Rule 3(5)), and cannot carry out Non-Banking Financial Investment activities including investment in securities of any body corporate.

Relaxations for an OPC (additional reading)

  • Not required to prepare a cash-flow statement — effect of section 2(40).
  • Annual return under section 92 may be signed by the Director, not necessarily a Company Secretary; an abridged annual return may be prescribed.
  • Section 134 — one director signing the audited financial statements suffices; an abridged director's report may be prescribed.
  • Holding an AGM under section 96 is not necessary; sections 100 to 111 on general/extraordinary general meetings may not apply.
  • Section 173 requires only one Board meeting in each half of a calendar year.
  • Section 137 — financial statements may be filed within six months from the close of the financial year (against 30 days).

Incorporation Procedure [Section 7]

  • Nine steps: (1) determine the nature of company (private or public); (2) reservation of name by filing an application; (3) drafting and signing of MOA & AOA; (4) submission of MOA and AOA to ROC; (5) consent of persons nominated as directors; (6) submission of statutory declaration of compliance; (7) pay fees and stamp duty; (8) obtain certificate of incorporation; (9) file declaration about address of registered office.
  • Application is filed with the Registrar within whose jurisdiction the registered office is proposed to be situated, in SPICe+ (INC-32). e-MOA is Form INC-33; e-AOA is Form INC-34.
  • Rule 13 signing requirements: each subscriber adds name, address, description and occupation in the presence of at least one witness who attests the signature and adds his own particulars. An illiterate subscriber affixes a thumb impression/mark, described as such by the person writing for him, who places the subscriber's name against/below the mark, authenticates it with his own signature, and writes against the name the number of shares taken. Typewritten or printed particulars are allowed so long as the signature or thumb impression is appended.
  • A body corporate subscriber signs through a director, officer or employee authorised by a board resolution; an LLP subscriber signs through a partner authorised by a resolution approved by all the partners. In either case the authorised person shall not himself be a subscriber to the MOA and AOA.
  • A foreign national residing outside India must have signatures, address and proof of identity notarized by a Notary (Public) with a certificate; if he resides in a country outside the Commonwealth and not a party to the Hague Apostille Convention, 1961, the Notary's certificate must be authenticated by a Diplomatic or Consular Officer. A foreign national visiting India to incorporate must hold a valid Business Visa — not required for a Person of Indian Origin or an Overseas Citizen of India.
  • Declarations: Form INC-8 — declaration of compliance by an advocate/CA/cost accountant/CS in practice engaged in the formation, and by a person named in the articles as director, manager or secretary. Form INC-9 — declaration from every subscriber and every first director that documents filed are correct, complete and true, that he is not convicted of any offence in connection with the promotion, formation or management of any company, and has not been found guilty of fraud, misfeasance or breach of duty to any company during the last five years.
  • First directors: particulars (name, DIN, residential address, nationality, proof of identity, interest in other firms/bodies corporate) with consent in Form DIR-2, filed in Form DIR-12.
  • Subscriber particulars required: name with recent photograph; father's/mother's name; nationality (with proof if foreign national); date and place of birth (district and state); educational qualification and occupation; PAN; email and phone; permanent and present residential address; residential proof (bank statement, electricity bill, telephone/mobile bill — not more than two months old); proof of identity (Indian nationals: voter's identity card, passport copy, driving licence copy, UIN; foreign nationals and NRIs: passport); and if already a director/promoter elsewhere, the company name, CIN and whether interested as director or promoter.
  • Body corporate subscriber particulars: name and CIN/registration number; GLN if any; registered office address or principal place of business; email id; certified true copy of board resolution authorising subscription to the MOA (or resolution agreed by all partners if an LLP/partnership firm); for foreign bodies corporate, copy of certificate of incorporation and registered office address.
  • Rule 12: where any object requires registration or approval from sectoral regulators such as RBI and SEBI, that approval must be obtained before pursuing those objects and a declaration submitted at the stage of incorporation. A company incorporated as a Nidhi must obtain the Central Government declaration under section 406 before commencing business, with a declaration submitted at incorporation.
  • Certificate of incorporation is issued in Form INC-11, mentioning the PAN of the company where issued by the Income-tax Department. It contains the company name, date of issue, CIN and the signature of the Registrar with his seal.
  • The company shall maintain and preserve copies of all documents and information as originally filed at its registered office till its dissolution.
  • Fraud at incorporation: a person furnishing false/incorrect particulars or suppressing material information of which he is aware is liable for action for fraud under section 447. Post-incorporation, if the company is proved to have been incorporated by false information/representation, suppression of material fact, or any fraudulent action, the promoters, the persons named as first directors, and the persons making declarations are each liable under section 447.
  • Tribunal's powers on such fraud: NCLT, on application, may (a) regulate the management including changes in the MOA/AOA in public interest or in the interest of the company, members and creditors; (b) direct that the liability of members shall be unlimited; (c) direct removal of the company's name from the register; or (d) order winding up — provided the company is given a reasonable opportunity of being heard and the Tribunal takes into consideration transactions entered into, obligations contracted and payment of liabilities.

Memorandum of Association [Section 4] — Clauses

  • Name clause [4(1)(a)]: last word "Limited" for a public limited company, "Private Limited" for a private limited company. Not applicable to section 8 companies. IFSC companies suffix "International Financial Service Company" or "IFSC".
  • Name reservation [4(4)]: for a proposed company — application in SPICe+ (INC-32); for a change of name of an existing company — application through the web service RUN (Reserve Unique Name). In both cases resubmission for rectification of defect is allowed within 15 days.
  • Prohibited names [4(2)]: a name identical with or resembling too nearly the name of an existing company registered under this Act or any previous company law; a name whose use would constitute an offence under any law in force; or a name undesirable in the opinion of the Central Government (delegated to ROC vide S.O. 1353(E) dated 21st May, 2014).
  • Names needing previous Central Government approval [4(3)]: names giving the impression of connection with, or patronage of, the Central Government, any State Government, any local authority, corporation or body constituted by them; and names including Board; Commission; Authority; Undertaking; National; Union; Central; Federal; Republic; President; Rashtrapati; Small Scale Industries; Khadi and Village Industries Corporation; Financial Corporation and the like; Municipal; Development Authority; Prime Minister or Chief Minister; Minister; Nation; Forest corporation; Development Scheme; Statute or Statutory; Court or Judiciary; Governor; Bureau; and the use of the word Scheme with the name of Government(s), State, India, Bharat or any Government authority.
  • Reservation period [4(5)]: 20 days from the date of approval for a new company; 60 days from the date of approval where an existing company applies for reservation or change of its name.
  • Extension of reservation (Rule 9A) — application before expiry of 20 days: (a) another 20 days (total 40) with fee of ₹1000, further extendable by another 20 days (total 60) with fee of ₹2000; or (b) another 40 days (total 60) with fee of ₹3000.
  • Registrars must ensure names do not contravene the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950 (General Circular No. 29/2014 dated 11th July, 2014). Rule 8A of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules 2014 lists 23 instances amounting to "undesirable names".
  • Cancellation of reserved name [4(5)] where the name was obtained by wrong or incorrect information: if the company is not yet incorporated, the reserved name is cancelled and the applicant is liable to a penalty up to one lakh rupees; if the company has been incorporated, the Registrar, after opportunity of being heard, may direct a change of name within 3 months after passing an ordinary resolution, or take action for striking off the name, or petition for winding up.
  • Situation clause [4(1)(b)]: the MOA states only the name of the State where the registered office is proposed to be situated. It fixes the company's domicile for jurisdiction (ROC, RD, NCLT bench, High Court), fiscal matters, the place where statutory books are kept (a public company's general meeting must be held at the registered office or in the city where it is situated), and the address for notices.
  • Objects clause [4(1)(c)]: states the objects for which the company is proposed to be incorporated and any matter considered necessary in furtherance thereof. IFSC companies must state objects to do financial services activities permitted under the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 read with SEZ Rules, 2006, per the licence granted by RBI, SEBI or IRDA.
  • Liability clause [4(1)(d)]: company limited by shares — liability limited to the amount unpaid on shares held. Company limited by guarantee — the amount each member undertakes to contribute to the assets on winding-up while he is a member or within one year after he ceases to be a member, for debts and liabilities contracted before he ceased to be a member, and to the costs, charges and expenses of winding-up and adjustment of the rights of contributories among themselves.
  • Capital clause [4(1)(e)(i)]: the amount of share capital with which the company is registered (authorised/nominal capital), its division into shares of a fixed amount (face value and number), and the number of shares subscribers agree to subscribe — not less than one share.
  • Subscription clause [4(1)(e)(ii)]: the number of shares each subscriber intends to take, indicated opposite his name.
  • Nomination clause [4(1)(f)]: only for an OPC — the name of the person who, on the death of the subscriber, becomes the member.
  • Section 4(7): in a company limited by guarantee and not having a share capital, any provision in the MOA or AOA giving a person a right to participate in the divisible profits otherwise than as a member is void. Section 13(11) extends the same to any alteration of the memorandum.
