Articles of Association [Section 5]

  • The articles contain the regulations for management of the company and such matters as may be prescribed (Rule 11 refers to the matters in the model forms in Schedule I). A company may include additional matters considered necessary for its management.
  • Entrenchment timing [5(4)]: only (a) on formation of the company, or (b) by amendment agreed to by all the members in a private company, and by special resolution in a public company.
  • Notice of entrenchment [5(5) + Rule 10]: at incorporation, in SPICe+ (INC-32); for existing companies, in Form MGT-14 within thirty days from the date of entrenchment of the articles.
  • Section 5(8): for a company registered after commencement of this Act, in so far as its registered articles do not expressly exclude or modify the model regulations applicable to it, those model regulations apply as if contained in the duly registered articles.
  • Section 5(9): section 5 applies only to articles registered or amended under this Act — it does not apply to articles registered under a previous company law provided they have not been amended under this Act.

MOA vs AOA

BasisMemorandumArticles
ContentFundamental conditions as the basis of incorporation; defines the relation of the company with outsidersInternal regulations; regulates the company–member relationship and members inter se
SupremacyCannot include any clause contrary to law; on conflict between the two, MOA prevailsSubordinate to both the law and the memorandum
Scope / ratificationActs beyond the memorandum are ultra vires and void; cannot be ratified even by all shareholdersActs beyond the articles can be ratified by shareholders provided they are not beyond the memorandum

Registered Office [Section 12] and Change of Place

  • A company shall, within thirty days of incorporation and at all times thereafter, have a registered office capable of receiving and acknowledging all communications and notices; verification of the registered office must be furnished to the Registrar within thirty days of incorporation [12(1) & 12(2)]. It must be a physical location where someone is present during normal business hours — not a P.O. Box — and may differ from the head office or corporate office. For specified IFSC public and private companies, "thirty days" reads as "sixty days" (G.S.R. 08(E) dated 4th January, 2017), and the registered office must be in the IFSC in the approved multi-service SEZ.
  • Labelling [12(3)]: paint or affix the name and registered office address outside every office/place of business in a conspicuous position in legible letters (and in the characters of the local language where different); have the name engraved on its seal, if any; print name, registered office address, CIN, telephone number, fax number if any, email and website addresses in all business letters, billheads, letter papers, notices and other official publications; and print the name on hundies, promissory notes and bills of exchange. Where the name has been changed during the last two years, both/all names must be shown. An OPC must mention the words "One Person Company" in brackets below its name wherever printed, affixed or engraved.
  • Notice of change [12(4)]: verified in Form INC-22 and given to the Registrar within 30 days of the change (60 days for IFSC companies).
  • Confirmation route [12(6)]: for a shift from the jurisdiction of one Registrar to another within the same State — the Regional Director's confirmation shall be communicated within 30 days from the date of receipt of the application; the company shall file the confirmation with the Registrar within 60 days of the date of confirmation; the Registrar shall certify the registration within thirty days from the date of filing. The certificate is conclusive evidence that all requirements regarding change of registered office have been complied with, and the change takes effect from the date of the certificate.
  • If the Registrar has reasonable cause to believe the company is not carrying on any business or operations, he may cause a physical verification of the registered office and, on default under sub-section (1), initiate action for removal of the name from the register under Chapter XVIII.
  • Penalty [12(8)]: the company and every officer in default is liable to a penalty of ₹1,000 for every day during which the default continues, not exceeding ₹1,00,000.
Type of changeApproval requiredFurther step
Within the same city, town or villageBoard resolutionNotice to ROC in 30 days
Within a State, one city to another (same ROC)Special resolutionNotice to ROC in 30 days
Within a State, one ROC to another ROCSpecial resolutionPermission of Regional Director in Form INC-23; RD communicates in 30 days / company files in 60 days / Registrar certifies in 30 days — conclusive evidence
From one State to another (alters situation clause)Special resolutionApproval of Central Government (delegated to RD) in Form INC-23, disposed of within 60 days; certified copy of order filed in Form INC-28 with ROC of each State within 30 days; fresh certificate of incorporation issued

Alteration of Memorandum [Section 13]

  • "Alteration" includes additions, omissions and substitutions. Governed by section 13 with Rules 29 to 32. Alteration requires a special resolution [13(1)], and the special resolution must be filed with the Registrar [13(6)(a)].
  • Name change [13(2), 13(3)]: requires approval of the Central Government (delegated to ROC vide S.O. 1353(E) dated 21st May, 2014) in writing in Form INC-24. No approval is needed where the change is only the addition or deletion of the word "Private" on conversion of one class of company to another. Change of name is not allowed to a company which has not filed annual returns or financial statements due for filing, or has failed to pay/repay matured deposits or debentures or interest thereon — once filed/paid, the change is allowed. The Registrar enters the new name in the register and issues a fresh certificate of incorporation in Form INC-25; the change is complete and effective only on issue of such certificate.
  • Registered office from one State to another [13(4), 13(5), 13(7)]: application in Form INC-23 to the Central Government (delegated to RD vide S.O. 4090(E) dated 19th December, 2016), accompanied by: copy of MOA with proposed alterations; copy of the minutes of the general meeting at which the resolution was passed, giving the number of votes cast for and against; copy of Board Resolution or Power of Attorney or executed vakalatnama; list of creditors and debenture holders; and acknowledgment of service of a copy of the application with annexures on the Registrar and the Chief Secretary of the State/UT. Advertisement in Form INC-26 must be published not more than thirty days before the date of filing, in a vernacular newspaper in the principal vernacular language of the district and in an English newspaper with wide circulation in the State. The Central Government disposes of the application within 60 days, after satisfying itself that the alteration has the consent of creditors, debenture-holders and other persons concerned, or that sufficient provision has been made for due discharge of all debts and obligations, or that adequate security has been provided.
  • Change of objects where money was raised from the public [13(8)]: where a company has raised money from the public through a prospectus and has any un-utilised amount, it may change the objects only by a special resolution through postal ballot. The notice must state: total money received; total money utilised for the objects stated in the prospectus; un-utilised amount; particulars of the proposed alteration; justification for the change; amount proposed to be utilised for the new objects; estimated financial impact on earnings and cash flow; other relevant information for an informed decision; and the place from which any interested person may obtain a copy of the notice. Details of each resolution must be advertised simultaneously with dispatch of the postal ballot notices in newspapers (one English, one vernacular) circulating where the registered office is situated, and hosted on the company's website, if any. Dissenting shareholders shall be given an exit opportunity by the promoters and shareholders having control, in accordance with SEBI regulations.
  • Registration of object alteration [13(9)]: the Registrar shall register the alteration and certify the registration within 30 days from the date of filing of the special resolution. Section 13(10): no alteration takes effect unless registered.

Rectification of Name [Section 16]

  • Where the Central Government (power conferred on Regional Directors under section 458, S.O. 4090(E) dated 19th December, 2016) is of the opinion that a company's name (original or new) is identical with or too nearly resembles the name of an existing company — on its own motion, or on an application by the proprietor of a trade mark registered under the Trade Marks Act, 1999 — it may direct a change of name.
  • The company must change its name within three months of the direction, after adopting an ordinary resolution.
  • An application by a proprietor of a registered trade mark must be made within three years of incorporation or registration or change of name of the company.
  • Notice of the change, with the Central Government (RD) order, must be given to the Registrar within fifteen days of the change; the Registrar makes the necessary changes in the certificate of incorporation and the memorandum.
  • On default, the Central Government shall allot a new name; the Registrar enters it in the register and issues a fresh certificate of incorporation, which the company must use thereafter. Proviso: nothing prevents the company from subsequently changing its name under section 13.

Alteration of Articles [Section 14] and Section 15

  • A company may alter its articles by special resolution, subject to the Act and the conditions contained in its memorandum. A company cannot divest itself of this power (Andrews v. Gas Meter Co. (1897) 1 Ch. 161). Matters on which the memorandum is silent can be dealt with by altering the articles.
  • Alteration includes conversion of a private company into a public company or vice-versa. Conversion of a public company into a private company is not valid unless approved by an order of the Central Government on an application made within sixty days from the date of passing the special resolution, filed with the Regional Director in e-Form RD-1, accompanied by: draft MOA and AOA with proposed alterations; copy of the minutes of the general meeting with details of votes cast for and against and names of dissenters; copy of Board resolution or Power of Attorney dated not earlier than thirty days; and a declaration by a key managerial personnel regarding compliance.
  • Where, after alteration, a private company's articles no longer include the restrictions and limitations required for a private company, it ceases to be a private company from the date of such alteration.
  • Filing [14(2)]: every alteration of the articles and a copy of the Central Government order approving it, together with a printed copy of the altered articles, must be filed with the Registrar within fifteen days in Form INC-27. Section 14(3): the registered alteration is valid and has effect as if it were originally contained in the articles.
  • Section 15: every alteration made in the MOA and AOA must be noted in every copy, whether issued in electronic form or otherwise. Default attracts a penalty on the company and every officer in default of ₹1,000 for every copy of the articles issued without the alteration.
  • Section 17: on payment of the prescribed fee the company must send a member a copy of the memorandum, the articles, and every agreement and resolution referred to in section 117(1) not embodied in them, within seven days of the request. Default makes the company and every officer in default liable to a fine of ₹1,000 for each day during which the default continues, or ₹1,00,000, whichever is less.

Section 8 — Companies with Charitable Objects

  • Licence conditions [8(1)]: the Central Government may grant a licence where a person or association proposed to be registered as a limited company (a) has in its objects the promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, protection of environment or any such other object; (b) intends to apply its profits, if any, or other income in promoting its objects; and (c) intends to prohibit the payment of any dividend to its members.
  • Delegation: to ROCs (S.O. 1353(E) dated 21st May, 2014) for sub-section (1), clause (i) of sub-section (4) except alteration of memorandum on conversion into another kind of company, and sub-section (5); to Regional Directors (S.O. 4090(E) dated 19th December 2016) for clause (i) of sub-section (4) for alteration of memorandum on conversion, and sub-section (6).
  • The words "Limited" or "Private Limited" are not added to the name, yet on registration the company enjoys the same privileges and obligations as a limited company. An OPC cannot be incorporated or converted into a section 8 company (Rule 3(5)); a small company under section 2(85) cannot be incorporated or converted into a section 8 company; a firm may be a member of a section 8 company.
  • Application (Rule 19): in Form SPICe+ (INC-32), accompanied by (a) the MOA and AOA of the proposed company; (b) a declaration by an advocate, CA, cost accountant or CS in practice that the MOA and AOA conform to section 8 and that all requirements have been complied with; (c) an estimate of future annual income and expenditure for the next three years, specifying sources of income and objects of expenditure; and (d) a declaration by each applicant.
  • Alteration: prior permission of the Central Government (delegated to Regional Directors) for alteration of the memorandum, and of the Central Government (delegated to ROCs) for alteration of the articles.
  • Conversion into another kind of company (Rules 21 & 22): pass a special resolution at a general meeting; the explanatory statement to the notice must set out the reasons; file Form INC-18 with the Regional Director with a certified true copy of the special resolution and the notice with explanatory statement; attach proof of service of notice by registered post or hand delivery on the Chief Commissioner of Income Tax having jurisdiction, the Income Tax Officer having jurisdiction, the Charity Commissioner, the Chief Secretary of the State in which the registered office is situated, and any organisation or Department of the Central/State Government or authority under whose jurisdiction the company operates — such authorities may make representations to the RD within sixty days of receipt of the notice, after giving the company an opportunity. Intimation with a copy of the INC-18 application also goes to the Registrar through the MCA system.
  • Publication: within a week from the date of submitting the application to the RD, publish a notice in Form INC-19 at the company's own expense — at least once in a vernacular newspaper in the principal vernacular language of the district where the registered office is situated with wide circulation, and at least once in English in an English newspaper with wide circulation in that district — and on the company's website, if any; a copy as published is sent forthwith to the RD.
  • Filings: the company must have filed all financial statements and annual returns up to the financial year preceding the application, and all other returns up to the date of the application. If the application is made after expiry of three months from the date of the preceding financial year for which the financial statement was filed, a statement of financial position certified by a chartered accountant made up to a date not preceding thirty days of filing must be attached.
  • On satisfaction the RD issues an order approving conversion, subject to terms and conditions; before imposing conditions or rejecting the application the company must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. On approval, the company convenes a general meeting to pass a special resolution amending the MOA and AOA, files these with the Registrar (with a declaration to adhere to RD conditions), and the Registrar registers them and issues a fresh Certificate of Incorporation.
  • Revocation of licence: the Central Government (delegated to RD) may revoke where the company contravenes the requirements or licence conditions, or where the affairs are conducted fraudulently, or in violation of the objects, or prejudicially to the public interest — after written notice and opportunity to be heard. On revocation, the Registrar puts "Limited" or "Private Limited" against the company's name in the register.
  • After revocation, if satisfied it is essential in the public interest, and after a reasonable opportunity of being heard, the Central Government may order that the company be wound up — excess assets after satisfaction of debts and liabilities may be transferred to another section 8 company with similar objects on conditions the Tribunal may impose, or sold and the proceeds credited to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Fund formed under section 224 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 — or that the company be amalgamated with another section 8 company having similar objects, the Central Government being empowered with overriding effect to specify the constitution, properties, powers, rights, interests, authorities, privileges, liabilities, duties and obligations of the single entity.
  • Relaxations for a Section 8 company: may call a general meeting by giving a clear 14 days' notice instead of 21 days; requirements as to minimum number of directors and independent directors do not apply; need not constitute a Nomination and Remuneration Committee or a Shareholders Relationship Committee.
Offence under Section 8Penalty
Company defaults in complying with any requirement of section 8Company punishable with fine from ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore
Same default — directors and every officer in defaultFine from ₹25,000 to ₹25 lakh
Affairs of the company conducted fraudulentlyEvery officer in default liable for action under section 447

Other Provisions — Sections 6, 9, 10, 10A, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22

  • Section 9 — effect of registration: from the date of incorporation specified in the certificate, the subscribers to the memorandum and all other persons who may become members are a body corporate by the name in the memorandum, capable of exercising all the functions of an incorporated company, having perpetual succession, with power to acquire, hold and dispose of property both movable and immovable, tangible and intangible, and to contract and to sue and be sued.
  • Section 6 — Act overrides: the Act has overriding effect over the memorandum, articles, any agreement executed by the company, and any resolution passed in general meeting or by the Board, whether registered/executed/passed before or after commencement of the Act; anything in conflict is void. Section 6 opens with a saving clause ("Save as otherwise…") — if another section of the Act makes the MOA/AOA/agreement/resolution superior, that prevails.
  • Section 10(1) — effect of MOA and AOA: once registered, they bind (a) members to the company, (b) the company to the members, and (c) members to the members, to observe all provisions as if signed by each. Section 10(2): all monies payable by any member under the MOA or AOA are a debt due from him to the company. But neither the company nor the members are bound to an outsider — "No Article can constitute a contract between the company and a third person."
  • Section 10A — commencement of business: a company incorporated after the commencement of the Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019 and having a share capital shall not commence business or exercise borrowing powers unless (a) it has filed verification of its registered office under section 12(2), and (b) a director has filed with the Registrar a declaration in Form INC-20A within 180 days of the date of incorporation, duly verified by a CS/CA/Cost Accountant in practice, that every subscriber has paid the value of the shares agreed to be taken by him as on the date of the declaration. Where objects require sectoral registration/approval (RBI, SEBI etc.), that approval must be obtained and attached with the declaration.
  • Section 18 — conversion of companies already registered: a company of any class may convert into another class by alteration of its memorandum and articles. On an application, the Registrar, after satisfying himself that the provisions applicable for registration have been complied with, shall close the former registration and, after registering the required documents, issue a certificate of incorporation in the same manner as its first registration. Conversion does not affect any debts, liabilities, obligations or contracts incurred or entered into before conversion — these may be enforced as if the registration had not been done. Reference: Rules 6, 7, 7A and 20 to 22 of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, Rules 37 and 38 of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2016, Forms INC-5 and INC-6, and INC-27.
  • Section 19 — subsidiary cannot hold shares in holding company: the prohibition extends to the subsidiary's nominees; any allotment or transfer of shares in a holding company to its subsidiary is void. If the holding company is a guarantee or unlimited company without share capital, the restriction applies to holding the interest in whatever form. Exceptions: (a) subsidiary concerned as legal representative of a deceased member of the holding company; (b) subsidiary holds shares as a trustee; (c) subsidiary was a shareholder before it became a subsidiary. The subsidiary has the right to vote at a meeting of the holding company only in respect of shares held as legal representative or trustee. The prohibition also does not apply where the subsidiary already had shares in its holding company at the commencement of the Act, and a subsidiary can buy shares in its holding company as part of a scheme of amalgamation sanctioned by the court/tribunal (Himachal Telematics Ltd v Himachal Futuristic Communications Ltd, (1996) 37 DRJ 476).
  • Section 20 — service of documents: on a company or its officer, by sending it to the registered office by registered post, speed post, courier service, leaving it at the registered office, or prescribed electronic or other mode; where securities are held with a depository, records of beneficial ownership may be served by the depository on the company electronically. On the Registrar or any member, by post, registered post, speed post, courier, delivering at his office or address, or prescribed electronic or other mode; a member may request delivery through a particular mode on paying such fees as determined by the company in its annual general meeting. Section 20(2) deemed service by post: a notice of a meeting is deemed served at the expiration of 48 hours after posting; in any other case, at the time the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post. For a Nidhi, section 20(2) applies with modification — documents may be served only on members holding shares of more than ₹1,000 in face value or more than 1% of the total paid-up share capital, whichever is less; for other shareholders, service is by public notice in a newspaper circulated in the district of the registered office plus publication on the Nidhi's notice board.
  • Section 21 — authentication: a document or proceeding requiring authentication by a company, or contracts made by or on behalf of a company, may be signed by any key managerial personnel (section 2(51)) or an officer or employee duly authorised by the Board. For specified IFSC public and private companies, "An officer" reads as "An officer or any other person" (G.S.R. 08(E) dated 4th January, 2017).
  • Section 22 — execution of bills of exchange and deeds: a bill of exchange, hundi or promissory note is deemed made, accepted, drawn or endorsed on behalf of the company if done in the name of, or on behalf of, or on account of the company by any person acting under its authority — express or implied. A company may, by writing under its common seal, if any, or — where it has no common seal — authorised by 2 directors, or by a director and the Company Secretary where a CS has been appointed, authorise any person, generally or for specified matters, as its attorney to execute deeds on its behalf, in or outside India; a deed signed by such attorney under his seal binds the company. Section 22 applies when a person seeks to enforce obligations against a company and the company denies the contract or disputes liability — it cannot be used where the proceeding is by the company.

Doctrine of Constructive Notice and Doctrine of Indoor Management

  • Constructive notice: the MOA and AOA, when registered, become public documents (section 399) open to inspection by anyone by electronic means on payment of the prescribed fee. Laid down first in Ernest v Nicholls (1857) 6 HL Cas 401 — any person dealing with the company is deemed familiar with the contents of all its public documents; it is his duty to inspect them and ensure his contract conforms. Per Lord Hatherley, whether a person actually reads them or not, he is in the same position as if he had read them. Absence of notice of the MOA and AOA is no excuse for relief (Kotla Venkataswamy v. Chinta Ramamurthy, AIR (1934) Mad 579).
  • Criticism: it is an unreal doctrine — people know a company through its officers, not through its documents; it ignores the realities of business life and is inconvenient for business transactions, since an outsider cannot ascertain whether prior approvals or sanctions of shareholders required by the articles have in fact been obtained. It was abrogated in Europe by section 9 of the Europe Communities Act, 1972; in India the Calcutta High Court in Charnock Collieries Co Ltd v. Bholanath Dhar, ILR (1912) 39 Cal 810, enforced a security not signed in accordance with the company's articles.
  • Indoor management (Turquand's Rule): persons dealing with the company are entitled to presume that internal proceedings and requirements have been duly complied with — they need not enquire whether the necessary meeting was convened and held properly or the necessary resolution passed properly. Rationale: what happens internally is not a matter of public knowledge; without the doctrine a company could escape creditors by denying the authority of its officials.
  • Exceptions to indoor management (i.e. where constructive notice applies): (a) Knowledge of irregularity — an outsider with actual knowledge gets no benefit and may well be considered part of the irregularity; (b) Negligence — where the irregularity could be discovered with a minimum of effort, or where circumstances are so suspicious as to invite inquiry and the outsider makes no proper inquiry; (c) Forgery — nothing can validate forgery, and a company can never be bound by forgeries committed by its officers; (d) where the question concerns the very existence of an agency; (e) where a pre-condition must be fulfilled before the company itself can exercise a particular power — i.e. the act is ultra vires the company, not merely ultra vires the directors/officers.
  • Effects of ultra vires: (a) any member may obtain an injunction to restrain an ultra vires act that has been or is about to be undertaken (Attorney-General v. Great Eastern Rly Co (1880) 5 AC 473); (b) neither party — even an outsider — can sue for enforcement or specific performance of such an agreement. Acts merely incidental to and consequential upon the stated objects are not ultra vires (same case) — e.g. renting or owning a building, issuing invoices, making and receiving payments. Acts ultra vires the authority of directors may be ratified by the company (Rajendra Nath Dutta v. Shilendra Nath Mukherjee, (1982) 52 Com Cases 293 (Cal.)).

Examples

  • Promoter (True/False): "To be a promoter one necessarily be associated with the initial formation of the company." False — one who subsequently helps the company to keep going, raise funds and advise the board (other than in a professional capacity) will equally be regarded as a promoter.
  • OPC — nominee becomes member (Ms. Madhu): Ms. Madhu formed an OPC with Mr. Sudan as nominee, his name specified in the MOA along with his consent. Ms. Madhu is declared insolvent and, pending discharge of insolvency, becomes incompetent to contract. Mr. Sudan therefore becomes the member of the OPC.
  • OPC — change of nominee (Rajesh): Rajesh formed an OPC with his wife Roopali as nominee. Roopali has suffered a terminal illness for the last two years and he wants to replace her. His options are his trusted friend Ramnivas or his son Rakshak, aged seventeen. Rajesh can appoint Ramnivas but not Rakshak, because Rakshak is a minor.
  • OPC — NRI (True/False): "Even a Non-Resident Indian can form and become member of OPC." True — per Rule 3(1), only a natural person, other than a minor, who is an Indian citizen, whether resident in India or otherwise, is eligible to incorporate an OPC.
  • Section 3A — Harmony Limited: Amar, Akbar and Anthony along with five friends were members of Harmony Limited (8 members). Amar and Akbar died on 18th August 2022, reducing the count to 6, and everyone was aware of it. Harmony Limited continued operations without increasing members. In March 2023 the company took a loan and defaulted in repayment. The lender can sue the company, or Anthony, or any of the remaining five friends — members are severally liable for the loan.
  • Section 3A (True/False): "Members who knowingly operate the company for more than six months with less than the minimum number of members specified in Section 3(1) are severally liable for the payment of all debts contracted by the company during the period since the number of members was first reduced." False — such members are liable severally for the whole debts contracted during that time, i.e. after the elapse of six months.
  • Decoding a CIN — Infosys Limited, L85110KA1981PLC013115: first character L = listing status (L for listed, U for unlisted); next five digits 85110; next two letters KA = the Indian State of registration (Karnataka); next four digits 1981 = year of incorporation; next three characters PLC = classification (PLC public, PTC private, FTC foreign, GOI government); last six digits 013115 = registration number with the concerned ROC.
  • Practical insight — MOA extract: extracts from the Memorandum of Association of XYZ Limited, Corporate Identification Number L85XXXKA1981PLC01XX15.
  • Certificate of incorporation not conclusive as to legality of objects: if a company has been registered whose objects are illegal, incorporation does not validate the illegal objects; the only remedy available is to wind up the company.
  • Name obtained by wrong information — Mr. Anil Desai: he applied to reserve a company name with the prefix "Sanwariya", claiming it was a registered trademark in his name. It was later found the prefix was not registered to him, and he had formed the company by giving incorrect documents/information while applying for the name. The Registrar shall take action under the Act after giving an opportunity of being heard.
  • When names "resemble" (Rule illustrations): plural/singular — Green Technology Ltd. is the same as Greens Technology Ltd. and Greens Technologies Ltd.; type/case/spacing/punctuation — ABC Ltd. is the same as A.B.C. Ltd. and A B C Ltd.; tenses — Ascend Solutions Ltd. is the same as Ascended Solutions Ltd. and Ascending Solutions Ltd.; slight spelling variation — Disc Solutions Ltd. is the same as Disk Solutions Ltd. but not Disco Solutions Ltd.; phonetic spellings — Bee Kay Ltd is the same as BK Ltd, Be Kay Ltd., B Kay Ltd., Bee K Ltd., B.K. Ltd. and Beee Kay Ltd; complete translation/transliteration — National Electricity Corporation Ltd. is the same as Rashtriya Vidyut Nigam Ltd.; host name/domain extension — Ultra Solutions Ltd. is the same as Ultrasolutions.com Ltd., but Supreme Ultra Solutions Ltd. is not the same as Ultrasolutions.com Ltd.; order of words — Ravi Builders and Contractors Ltd. is the same as Ravi Contractors and Builders Ltd.; definite/indefinite article — Congenial Tours Ltd. is the same as A Congenial Tours Ltd. and The Congenial Tours Ltd., but Isha Industries Limited is not the same as Anisha Industries Limited; addition of a place name — if Salvage Technologies Ltd. exists, Salvage Technologies Delhi Ltd. is the same, but Retro Pharmaceuticals Ranchi Ltd. is not the same as Retro Pharmaceuticals Chennai Ltd.; numerals — Thunder Services Ltd is the same as Thunder 11 Services Ltd and One Thunder Services Ltd (unless the numeral represents a brand).
  • Ratification of an act ultra vires the directors: a director is authorised to issue a cheque of ₹10,000 but issues one for ₹12,000 — the company can ratify this, because it is beyond the directors' authority but within the memorandum.
  • Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche (1878) L.R. 7 H.L. 653: the memorandum stated the objects as "to make and sell, or lend or hire, railway plants to carry on the business of mechanical engineers and general contractors…". The company contracted with M/s. Riche, a firm of railway contractors, to finance the construction of a railway line in Belgium. The company repudiated the contract as ultra vires; Riche sued for damages for breach, arguing "general contractors" empowered the company and that the contract had been ratified by a majority of shareholders. Held (House of Lords): the contract was ultra vires and null and void. "General contractor" was read as the making generally of such contracts as are connected with the business of mechanical engineers. Even if every shareholder had been in the room and said "That is a contract which we desire to make, which we authorise the directors to make", it would still be ultra vires — shareholders cannot ratify what the Act of Parliament prohibited them from doing.
  • Liability clause — Modern Furniture Limited: a company limited by shares, share capital divided into shares of face value ₹10 each, of which ₹8 is called up. Mr. Singh holds 200 shares and has paid all ₹8 per share; Ms. Sarla owns 100 shares and has paid ₹10 per share (₹2 in advance); Mr. Sanju owns 250 shares and has paid ₹6 per share (₹2 in arrear per share). Maximum liability: Mr. Singh ₹400, Ms. Sarla Nil, and Mr. Sanju ₹1,000 respectively.
  • Constructive notice — Modern Furniture Limited cheque: one of the articles of Modern Furniture Limited provides that a cheque below ₹1 lakh may be signed by a single director, but a cheque above ₹1 lakh must be signed by at least two directors; similar instructions were issued to the bank. M/s Sagwan Wood Works, a vendor, accepts a cheque of ₹2.20 lakh signed by only one director. Applying the doctrine of constructive notice, M/s Sagwan Wood Works (payee) has no right to claim when the cheque is returned unpaid by the bank.
  • Royal British Bank v. Turquand (1856) 6 E & B 327: the directors were authorised by the articles to borrow on bonds such sums as should from time to time be authorised by a resolution of the company in general meeting. The directors gave a bond to Turquand without any such resolution. Held: the company was liable on the bond, as Turquand was entitled to assume that the resolution in general meeting had been passed.
  • Illustration (MCQ): "The doctrine of indoor management is considered to be ______ to the doctrine of constructive notice." Options: (a) Exception (b) Extension (c) Alternative (d) Not related. Answer — (a) Exception.
  • Section 6 — dividend out of profits: Section 123 declares that no dividend shall be paid except out of profits. This cannot be undone by any provision in the articles, because the articles cannot sanction something forbidden by the Act; any such attempt is void.
  • Section 6 — saving clause in action: Section 47 deals with the voting power of members. A notification dated 5th June, 2015 says section 47 applies to a private company subject to its Articles of Association. If the AOA of a private company says section 47 is not applicable to it, then the AOA becomes superior and section 47 will not apply.
  • Member bound to the company — Borland's Trustee v Steel Bros & Co Ltd (1901) 1 Ch 279: the articles provided that on the bankruptcy of a member his shares would be sold to a person and at a price fixed by the directors. Borland, a shareholder, was adjudicated bankrupt; his trustee in bankruptcy claimed he was not bound and should be at liberty to sell at true value. Held: the contract contained in the articles is one of the original incidents of the shares; having purchased on those terms, it is impossible to say those terms are not to be observed.
  • Company bound to the member — Wood v Odessa Waterworks Co (1889) 42 Ch D 636: the articles provided that "the directors may, with the sanction of the company at general meeting, declare a dividend to be paid to the members". Instead of paying dividend in cash, a resolution was passed to give shareholders debenture bonds. Mr. Wood, a member, sued to restrain the directors. Held: "Prima facie that means to be paid in cash. The debenture bonds proposed to be issued are not a payment in cash."
  • Member bound to member — Rayfield v Hands (1958) 2 WLR 851: Clause 11 of the articles required Mr. Rayfield, a shareholder, to inform the directors of his intention to transfer his shares, and provided that the directors would take those shares equally between them at a fair value. He so notified the directors (who were themselves members), who contended the articles could not impose such an obligation on them in their capacity as directors. Held: their argument was set aside by treating those directors as members, and they were compelled to take Mr. Rayfield's shares at a fair value.
  • No contract with an outsider — Browne v La Trinidad (1887) 37 Ch D 1: the articles of La Trinidad contained a clause that Browne should be a director and should not be removable till after 1888. He was removed earlier and sued to restrain the company from excluding him. Held: there was no contract between Browne and the company; no outsider can enforce the articles against the company even if they purport to give him certain rights.
  • Section 10(2) — monies payable are a debt: a company can recover calls in arrear from a member as forcefully as it recovers a loan due.
  • Name change — Tata Sky: Tata Sky Limited changed its name to Tata Play Limited (CIN U92120MH2001PLC130365).
  • Industrial insight — ITC: on 24 August 1910 a company was registered in India as Imperial Tobacco Company of India Limited. As ownership progressively Indianised, the name changed to India Tobacco Company Limited in 1970 and then to I.T.C. Limited in 1974. The full stops were removed effective 18 September 2001, making it 'ITC Limited', where 'ITC' is no longer an acronym or initialised form.
  • Section 8 CIN examples: Prem Foundation (CIN U85191MH2014NPL253514) and Azim Lalji Foundation (CIN U93980KA2001NPL028740) — the 5th data section "NPL" signifies a Not-for-Profit Licence company.
  • Section 19 — RPIP Ltd and SSP Pvt. Ltd.: RPIP Ltd. invested 51% in the shares of SSP Pvt. Ltd. on 31st March 2023. SSP Pvt. Ltd. has been holding 2% equity of RPIP Ltd. since 2013. SSP Pvt. Ltd. cannot increase its equity beyond that 2% on or after 31st March 2023, but it can continue to hold or reduce its initial 2% stake.
  • Section 20(2) — deemed service, Modern Furniture: a notice of general meeting sent by postal mail is deemed served 48 hours after posting. Read with the requirement of 21 clear days' notice under section 101, Modern Furniture Limited should have posted the letter containing the notice 23 days prior to the meeting day (48 hours of post-delivery + 21 clear days).

MCQs from the Chapter (with answers)

  • MCQ 1 — Entrenchment by an existing private company: Modern Furniture Limited, an existing private company, wishes to insert provisions for entrenchment. Options: (a) ordinary resolution (b) special resolution (c) agreed by all the members (d) cannot amend articles to make entrenchment provisions. Answer — (c) Can amend the article agreed by all the members.
  • MCQ 2 — OPC eligibility (Mr. Nilanjan Chattopadhyay): It is July 2024. Mr. Nilanjan Chattopadhyay, a 24-year-old Indian, returned to India in January 2024 after completing his education in bio-nutrient, and wants to form an OPC. He concludes: (i) OPC can be formed by an Indian citizen only; (ii) he cannot form an OPC because in the immediately previous year he was not resident in India. Options: (a) both valid (b) none valid (c) first invalid (d) second invalid. Answer — (d) Second conclusion is invalid.
  • MCQ 3 — Name reservation for an existing company: the Registrar may reserve the name for a period of ______ from the date of approval. Options: (a) 90 days (b) 60 days (c) 30 days (d) 20 days. Answer — (b) 60 days.
  • MCQ 4 — Section 10A penalty (Modern Furniture): incorporated 30th June 2022, its directors filed the declaration under section 10A(1)(a) regarding receipt of the value of shares with the Registrar on 18th April 2023. Options: (a) ₹1,11,000 and ₹1,11,000 (b) ₹50,000 and ₹1,11,000 (c) ₹1,11,000 and ₹50,000 (d) ₹50,000 and ₹1,00,000. Answer — (d) ₹50,000 and ₹1,00,000 respectively (the officer's daily penalty of ₹1,000 is capped at ₹1,00,000).
  • MCQ 5 — Section 15 (I.T.C. Limited to ITC Limited): the company and officers defaulted by failing to make the alteration in every issued copy of the memorandum and articles. Pick the incorrect statements from: (i) alteration must be made to every copy because these are public documents; (ii) alteration must be made to every copy, be it in electronic form or otherwise; (iii) penalty is ₹1,000 for every copy of the articles issued without such alteration. Options: (a) (ii) only (b) (iii) only (c) (ii) and (iii) only (d) None of (i), (ii) and (iii). Answer — (d) None of (i), (ii) and (iii) — all three are correct statements.

Descriptive Questions from the Chapter (with answers)

  • Q1 — Yadav Dairy Products Private Limited (entrenchment): the company registered its articles with the memorandum in December 2019. The directors want the provisions on forfeiture of shares to be changeable only by a resolution of 90% majority, while section 14 allows alteration by special resolution; one director says they cannot make a provision against the Act. Advice: section 5 permits entrenchment — specified provisions may be altered only if conditions more restrictive than a special resolution are met. Entrenchment may only be made on formation or by amendment agreed to by all the members in a private company (special resolution in a public company), and notice must be given to the Registrar. Since Yadav Dairy Products is a private company, entrenchment is allowed, but it must pass a resolution with the permission of all the members and give notice to the ROC.
  • Q2 — 'Budding Pilots Flying Club' (Section 8 feasibility): a group wants a limited liability company under section 8 to impart classroom teaching and aircraft flight training to trainee pilots, for ten years, after which the club will be dissolved and the surplus of assets over liabilities distributed amongst the members. Answer: section 8(1) requires that the company intends to apply its profits or other income only in promoting its objects and to prohibit payment of dividend to members. Distribution of surplus among members violates this, and section 8(9) further restricts the application of surplus assets on winding up or dissolution. The proposal is not feasible.
  • Q3 — Alfa School (revocation powers of Central Government): Alfa School began imparting education on 1st April 2010, with the sole objective of providing education to children of weaker society free of cost or at a very nominal fee depending on parents' financial condition. On 30th March 2024 the Central Government learnt it was operating in violation of its objects clause, on the basis of which it had been granted section 8 status. Powers of the Central Government: (i) revoke the licence where the company contravenes the requirements/conditions of section 8 or where affairs are conducted fraudulently, in violation of the objects, or prejudicial to public interest — on revocation the Registrar puts 'Limited' or 'Private Limited' against the company's name; but before revocation, written notice of intention and an opportunity of being heard must be given; (ii) after revocation, if satisfied it is essential in the public interest, direct that the company be wound up or amalgamated with another section 8 company, no such order to be made unless the company is given a reasonable opportunity of being heard; (iii) where amalgamation with another section 8 company having similar objects is essential in the public interest, order such amalgamation to form a single company with such constitution, properties, powers, rights, interest, authorities, privileges, liabilities, duties and obligations as specified in the order, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Act.
  • Q4 — XY Ltd. (Mumbai to Pune): XY Ltd. has its registered office at Mumbai, Maharashtra, and wants to shift to Pune (within Maharashtra, but from Mumbai ROC to Pune ROC). Answer: since the situation clause in the memorandum names only the State, a change from Mumbai to Pune does not alter the memorandum, so section 13 and its sub-sections do not apply. Under section 12(5), a change of registered office from one town or city to another within the same State must be approved by a special resolution; and since the office is shifted from one ROC to another, the company must also seek approval of the Regional Director.
  • Q5 — Anushka Security Equipments Limited (change of objects): a manufacturer of CCTV cameras raised ₹100 crore through a public issue of equity shares for a new manufacturing unit. It utilised ₹10 crore and then realised the existing business has no expansion potential because the government reduced customs duty on imported CCTV cameras, making Chinese imports cheaper. It now wants to use the remaining amount in mobile app development by adding a new object. Answer: under section 13, a company that has raised money from the public through a prospectus and still has an unutilised amount shall not change the objects unless a special resolution is passed, and (i) details of the resolution are published in newspapers (one English, one vernacular) circulating where the registered office is situated and placed on the company's website, if any, indicating the justification for the change; and (ii) dissenting shareholders are given an exit opportunity by the promoters and shareholders having control in accordance with SEBI regulations. The company must file the special resolution with the ROC, who will certify the registration within thirty days; the alteration is effective only after that certificate. Yes — the company can add the mobile app development object and divert the public money, subject to these requirements.
  • Q6 — Vivek Industries Limited (real-estate to food processing): the objects clause empowers real-estate business and any allied business. Due to a downward trend, management decided to take up food processing and wants to alter the memorandum. Answer: under section 13(1) a company may alter its memorandum by special resolution after complying with the section. For the objects clause, section 13(6) requires filing of the special resolution with the Registrar; section 13(9) requires the Registrar to register the alteration and certify the registration within thirty days of filing; section 13(10) provides that no alteration takes effect unless so registered. Vivek Industries Limited can make the change.
  • Q7 — Indoor management and constructive notice: persons dealing with the company need not inquire whether internal proceedings relating to the contract were followed correctly, once satisfied that the transaction accords with the MOA and AOA; they need not enquire whether the necessary meeting was convened and held properly or whether the necessary resolution was passed properly, and are entitled to take it for granted that the company went through those proceedings regularly. The doctrine of indoor management is opposite to the doctrine of constructive notice — constructive notice protects a company against outsiders, while indoor management protects outsiders against the actions of a company, and safeguards against the possibility of abusing the doctrine of constructive notice. Constructive notice applies (i.e. indoor management fails) in cases of knowledge of irregularity, negligence, and forgery.
  • Q8 — Taxmann Advisory Private Limited (Section 16): Manglu and friends registered a company named Taxmann Advisory Private Limited; Taxmann is a registered trademark. After 5 years the trademark owner learned of it and filed an application with the relevant authority. Answer: under section 16, where the name is identical with the name of a previously registered company the Central Government may direct a change and the company must change it by ordinary resolution within 3 months; where the name is identical with a registered trade mark and the owner applies to the Central Government within three years of incorporation/registration of the company, it may direct a change, and the company shall change its name by ordinary resolution within 6 months. Notice to ROC with the Central Government order must be given within 15 days of the change; default makes the company and defaulting officer punishable. Here the trademark owner objected after 5 years when it should have applied within 3 years, so the company cannot be compelled to change its name. However, under section 13 a company may at any time change its name by special resolution and approval of the Central Government — so if the trademark owner requests and the company accepts, it can change its name voluntarily.
  • Q9 — When a subsidiary can become a member of its holding company: under section 19 a subsidiary cannot, by itself or through nominees, hold shares in its holding company, and no holding company shall allot or transfer its shares to a subsidiary — any such allotment or transfer is void. Exceptions: (1) the subsidiary holds shares as the legal representative of a deceased member of the holding company; (2) the subsidiary holds such shares as a trustee; (3) the subsidiary was a shareholder in the holding company before it became its subsidiary.
  • Q10 — Shri Laxmi Electricals Ltd. (S) and Hanuman Power Suppliers Limited (H): H holds 60% of S's paid-up share capital. A shareholder of H created a charitable trust and donated his 10% shares in H and ₹50 crore to the trust, appointing S as the trustee; all trust assets are held in S's name. Answer: although a subsidiary shall not hold shares in its holding company, one of the exceptions is where the subsidiary holds such shares as a trustee. Here the subsidiary will hold shares in the holding company in the capacity of a trustee — therefore S can hold shares in H. (Note: where the exception is that the subsidiary was a shareholder before becoming a subsidiary, it will not have a right to vote at the meeting of the holding company.)
  • Q11 — Service of documents: under section 20 a document may be served on a company or its officer by sending it to the registered office by registered post, speed post, courier service, by leaving it at the registered office, or by prescribed electronic or other mode; where securities are held with a depository, records of beneficial ownership may be served by the depository on the company electronically. Under section 20(2), a document may be served on the Registrar or any member by post, registered post, speed post, courier, delivery at his office or address, or prescribed electronic or other mode; a member may request delivery through a particular mode on paying such fees as determined by the company in its annual general meeting.
  • Q12 — Parag Constructions Limited (Section 22): Mr. Parag, a director, had signed all construction contracts on behalf of the company for many years and all parties dealing with the company knew him well. The company obtained an important construction contract from a renowned software company and would build the site in partnership with a local contractor, Firozbhai. Mr. Parag signed the partnership deed with Firozbhai on behalf of the company claiming implied authority. Later, in a dispute, the company denied liability as a partner. Answer: under section 22 a company may authorise any person as its attorney to execute deeds on its behalf in or outside India, but the common seal must be affixed on the authority letter, or the authority letter must be signed by two directors, or by one director and the secretary; the authority may be general or for a specific deed, and a deed signed by such attorney under his seal binds the company as if made under its common seal. Here the company neither gave written authority nor affixed the common seal to any authority letter, so Mr. Parag was not legally entitled to execute deeds on behalf of the company; the deed does not bind it, and the company can deny its liability as a partner.
