Why It Matters / Application

Chapter II decides three practical questions that arise in every corporate engagement. First, can this entity legally do this act? — answered by the objects clause and the doctrine of ultra vires: an act beyond the memorandum is void and unratifiable even by unanimous shareholder consent (Ashbury v. Riche), so a lender or contractor must read the objects clause before financing a project, and a company like Anushka Security Equipments must formally alter the objects by postal-ballot special resolution with a SEBI-compliant exit for dissenters before diverting ₹90 crore of unutilised public issue money into mobile app development. Second, can an outsider rely on what a company officer does? — answered by the twin doctrines: the outsider is fixed with constructive notice of the MOA and AOA (so M/s Sagwan Wood Works cannot recover on a ₹2.20 lakh cheque signed by a single director where the articles demand two), but is protected by Turquand's rule for purely internal irregularities, unless he knew of the irregularity, was negligent, relied on a forgery, or the act was ultra vires the company itself. Third, what formalities attach to a change? — the correct instrument (Board resolution, ordinary resolution, special resolution, all-member consent for entrenchment in a private company), the correct approver (ROC, Regional Director, Central Government, NCLT), the correct form (INC-22, INC-23, INC-24, INC-25, INC-26, INC-27, INC-28, INC-20A, MGT-14, RD-1) and the correct clock (30 days, 60 days, 180 days, three months). Getting the registered office, name rectification, commencement-of-business declaration or nominee-change filings wrong exposes both the company and every officer in default to daily-accruing penalties and, in the worst case, to striking off under Chapter XVIII.

Note

Exam traps and provisos. (1) A change of registered office within the same State from one city to another does not alter the memorandum — the situation clause names only the State — so section 13 does not apply; only section 12(5) (special resolution) and, if the ROC changes, Regional Director approval. (2) Under section 10A the officer's penalty is ₹1,000 per day capped at ₹1,00,000, which is why MCQ 4's answer is ₹50,000 and ₹1,00,000, not ₹1,11,000. (3) Section 3A liability attaches only to debts contracted after the six-month period elapses, not from the date membership first fell below the minimum. (4) Entrenchment in an existing private company requires the agreement of all members, not a special resolution — that is the public-company route. (5) A section 16 application by a registered trade mark proprietor must come within three years; a company like Taxmann Advisory Private Limited cannot be compelled after 5 years, though it may still change its name voluntarily under section 13. (6) No Central Government approval is needed for a name change that is only the addition or deletion of the word "Private" on conversion of class; and a name change is barred outright while annual returns/financial statements are unfiled or matured deposits/debentures or interest remain unpaid. (7) An OPC cannot be incorporated or converted into a section 8 company, cannot carry on Non-Banking Financial Investment activities, and its nominee changes are not alterations of the memorandum. (8) A small company under section 2(85) also cannot be incorporated or converted into a section 8 company, but a firm may be a member of one. (9) The certificate of incorporation is not conclusive proof that pre-incorporation matters were in order — illegal objects are not validated by registration; the only remedy is winding up. (10) Section 22 protects a person suing the company; it cannot be invoked where the proceeding is by the company. (11) In a company limited by guarantee without share capital, any MOA/AOA provision — or any later alteration — giving a person a right to share divisible profits otherwise than as a member is void (sections 4(7) and 13(11)). (12) For a Nidhi, section 20(2) service is limited to members holding shares of more than ₹1,000 face value or more than 1% of total paid-up capital, whichever is less. (13) For specified IFSC companies, "thirty days" in section 12 reads as "sixty days", a Board resolution suffices for a change of registered office (but never outside the IFSC), and "An officer" in section 21 reads as "An officer or any other person".

Chapter 3 — Prospectus and Allotment of Securities

Source: 87771bos-aps2160-ch3.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Scope of Chapter III: Sections 23 to 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, supplemented by the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, split into Part I — Public offer (Sections 23–41) and Part II — Private placement (Section 42).
  • Two routes to capital: capital raised from the public at large goes through a Public Offer (advertisement in accordance with the applicable provisions, to protect prospective investors from fraud); capital raised from a selected group of identified persons goes through Private Placement.
  • Public offer is closed to private companies: under Section 23(2) a private company may issue securities only by rights issue, bonus issue, or private placement under Section 42. It can never make a public offer.
  • Public offer is a family of three: it includes an initial public offer (IPO), a further public offer (FPO, also called follow-on public offer) by the company, and an offer for sale (OFS) of securities to the public by an existing shareholder — OFS is sometimes called a deemed public offer.
  • Uberrimae fides: a contract of shares is a contract of "utmost good faith" — all parties must make a full declaration of all material facts, and intending purchasers of shares are entitled to true and correct disclosure of all facts in the prospectus. This is the doctrinal root of Sections 34, 35 and 36.
  • The criminal / civil split: Section 34 punishes every person who authorises the issue of a misleading prospectus under Section 447 (loss to any investor is not required, and liability is strict); Section 35 makes the company, directors, proposed directors, promoters, persons authorising issue, and the expert under Section 26(5) liable to pay compensation to persons who sustained loss or damage.
  • Doctrine of ultra vires applied to issue proceeds: once funds are raised through a given prospectus the company must use them strictly in accordance with the prospectus; deviations need pre-approval of investors under Section 27 and a recall/exit option for dissenting investors.
  • Allotment: offers for shares are made on the company's application forms; acceptance of that offer by the company is an allotment. Technically, it is an appropriation out of the previously unappropriated capital of the company. Re-issue of forfeited shares is not an allotment.

Key Definitions / Terms

Prospectus [Section 2(70)]
Any document described or issued as a prospectus, and includes a red herring prospectus (Section 32), a shelf prospectus (Section 31), or any notice, circular, advertisement or other document inviting offers from the public for subscription or purchase of any securities of a body corporate. Four constituents in all — the "means" limb plus three "includes" items; the fourth (document inviting offer from the public) is the deemed prospectus / prospectus by implication.
Securities [Section 2(81)]
Securities as defined in Section 2(h) of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 — shares, scrips, stocks, bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other marketable securities of a like nature; derivatives; units issued by a collective investment scheme; security receipts under Section 2(zg) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002; units under any mutual fund scheme; certificates issued by a special purpose distinct entity acknowledging beneficial interest in debt/receivables including mortgage debt; Government securities; instruments declared securities by the Central Government; and rights or interests in securities. Excludes any unit linked insurance policy or similar instrument combining life risk benefit and investment issued by an insurer under Section 2(9) of the Insurance Act, 1938.
Deemed prospectus [Section 25(1)]
Where a company allots or agrees to allot securities with a view to those securities (all or any part) being offered for sale to the public, any document by which the offer is made is deemed to be a prospectus issued by the company for all purposes — all enactments and rules of law on prospectus contents and liability for misstatement apply, subject to Sections 25(3) and 25(4).
Shelf prospectus [Explanation to Section 31]
A prospectus in respect of which the securities or class of securities included therein are issued for subscription in one or more issues over a certain period without the issue of a further prospectus.
Red herring prospectus [Explanation to Section 32]
A prospectus which does not include complete particulars of the quantum or price of the securities — used for book building, where price per security and number of securities are left open to be decided post closure of the issue.
Abridged prospectus [Section 2(1)]
A memorandum containing such salient features of a prospectus as may be specified by SEBI by regulations — a summarised form of the actual prospectus, used to cut the cost of publishing large numbers of full prospectuses to accompany application forms.
Expert [Section 2(38)]
Includes an engineer, a valuer, a Chartered Accountant, a Company Secretary, a Cost Accountant and any other person who has the power or authority to issue a certificate in pursuance of any law for the time being in force.
Global Depository Receipt [Section 2(44)]
Any instrument in the form of a depository receipt, by whatever name called, created by a foreign depository outside India and authorised by a company making an issue of such depository receipts. Generically, a certificate issued by a depository bank which purchases shares of foreign companies and creates a security on a local exchange backed by those shares.
Private placement [Explanation I to Section 42(3)]
Any offer or invitation to subscribe or issue of securities to a select group of persons by a company (other than by way of public offer) through a private placement offer-cum-application, satisfying the conditions in Section 42.
Identified persons [Section 42(2)]
The select group of not more than 200 persons in a financial year identified by the Board, to whom alone the private placement offer may be made after passing a special resolution.
Qualified institutional buyer [Explanation II to Section 42(3)]
A QIB as defined in the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2009 — excluded from the count of 200.
Fraud [Explanation (i) to Section 447]
In relation to the affairs of a company or body corporate, includes any act, omission, concealment of any fact or abuse of position committed by any person or any other person with connivance in any manner, with intent to deceive, to gain undue advantage from, or to injure the interests of, the company or its shareholders or its creditors or any other person, whether or not there is any wrongful gain or wrongful loss.
Wrongful gain / wrongful loss [Explanations (ii) and (iii) to Section 447]
Wrongful gain is the gain by unlawful means of property to which the person gaining is not legally entitled; wrongful loss is the loss by unlawful means of property to which the person losing is legally entitled.
Untrue statement [Section 34]
A statement in a prospectus is deemed untrue if (a) it is misleading in the form and context in which it is included, or (b) where any inclusion or omission of any matter is likely to mislead.

Modes of Issue — Public vs Private Company [Section 23]

Mode of IssuePublic CompanyPrivate Company
Public Offer (including IPO, FPO or OFS)YesNo
Private PlacementYesYes
Rights issue / Bonus issueYesYes
Compliance with SEBI rules & regulationsYes*No

*For a listed company or a company proposed to be listed.

  • Section 23(3) — overseas direct listing: such class of public companies may issue such class of securities for listing on permitted stock exchanges in permissible foreign jurisdictions or such other jurisdictions as may be prescribed. Before this, Indian companies could access overseas equity markets only through depository receipts (ADRs/GDRs) or by listing debt securities such as foreign currency convertible bonds and masala bonds.
  • How direct listing differs from ADRs/GDRs: in a direct listing a domestic company enlists with foreign stock exchanges without an intermediary — it offers its shares directly instead of giving them to a foreign depository bank; this excludes intermediaries, decreases overall transaction cost, and increases transparency.
  • Section 23(4) — exemption power: the Central Government may by notification exempt any class or classes of public companies referred to in Section 23(3) from any provision of Chapter III, Chapter IV, Section 89 (declaration of beneficial interest), Section 90 (register of significant beneficial owners) or Section 127 (punishment for failure to distribute dividends); a copy of every such notification must be laid before both Houses of Parliament.
  • Section 24 — who administers what: SEBI administers those provisions of Chapters III and IV relating to issue and transfer of securities and non-payment of dividend by listed companies or companies intending to list. All other matters — including matters relating to prospectus, return of allotment and redemption of preference shares — are administered by the Central Government, the Tribunal or the Registrar. SEBI's power flows from Sections 11, 11A, 11B and 11D of the SEBI Act, 1992.

How It Works / Logic — Prospectus Requirements

  • Deemed prospectus presumption [Section 25(2)]: the allotment is presumed to have been made with a view to offering the securities to the public if either (a) securities are offered to the public within six months of allotment, or (b) the full consideration had not been received by the company at the date of the offer to the public. Sections 25(1) and (2) are not exhaustive — other situations may also amount to a deemed prospectus.
  • Extra contents of a deemed prospectus [Section 25(3)] — in addition to (not in substitution of) Section 26: (a) a statement of the net amount received or to be received as consideration for the securities to which the offer relates; (b) the time and place at which the underlying contract for allotment may be inspected; (c) that the persons making the offer were named in the prospectus as directors of the company.
  • Signing of a deemed prospectus [Section 25(4)]: it is sufficient if the document is signed on behalf of the company by two directors.
  • Meaning of "public": not restricted to the public at large — it includes any section of the public, howsoever selected. Public connotes persons not personally known to the promoter, as distinguished from his own friends, relatives, connections and acquaintances. "Issued" means issued to the public, and the term "issue" is not satisfied by a single private communication — there must be some measure of publicity, however modest.
  • Section 26(1) contents: the prospectus shall be dated and signed, shall state such information and set out such reports on financial information as may be specified by SEBI in consultation with the Central Government; must carry a declaration affirming compliance with the Companies Act, 2013 and a statement that nothing in the prospectus is contrary to (a) the Companies Act, 2013, (b) the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, (c) the SEBI Act, 1992 and (d) the rules and regulations made under those three statutes. Proviso: until SEBI specifies the financial information, the existing SEBI regulations apply.
  • Section 26(1) does not apply [Section 26(2)] where the prospectus is issued (a) to existing members or debenture-holders of a company, or (b) in relation to shares or debentures which are in all respects uniform with shares or debentures previously issued and for the time being dealt in or quoted on a recognised stock exchange.
  • Date of publication [Explanation to Section 26(3)]: the date indicated in the prospectus is deemed to be the date of its publication.
  • Filing with Registrar [Section 26(4)]: a prospectus shall not be issued unless a signed copy has been delivered to the Registrar for filing, signed by every person named as director or proposed director in it; a duly authorised attorney may sign in a representative capacity.
  • Expert's statement conditions [Section 26(5)]: a prospectus shall not include a statement purporting to be made by an expert if (a) he is engaged or interested in the formation, promotion or management of the company, or (b) the expert has not given written consent to the issue of the prospectus, or (c) he has withdrawn his consent before delivery of a copy of the prospectus to the Registrar for filing. A statement that these conditions do not exist must be included. The purpose is to ensure the expert's independence, protecting investors who rely on his statement.
  • Face of the prospectus [Section 26(6)]: must state that a copy has been delivered for filing to the Registrar under Section 26(4), and the documents required to be attached to the copy so delivered (or refer to statements in the prospectus specifying those documents). Section 26(7) was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2019, w.e.f. 15-8-2019.
  • Validity for issue [Section 26(8)]: a prospectus is valid for issue only if 90 days have not lapsed from the date a copy was delivered to the Registrar. If 90 days have expired, a fresh copy should be filed to avoid the Section 26(9) penalty.
  • Penalty [Section 26(9)]: the company and every person knowingly a party to the issue of a prospectus in contravention of Section 26 is punishable with fine of ₹50,000 to ₹3,00,000.
  • Section 27 — variation of contract terms or objects: permitted only with the authority of the company in general meeting by special resolution. First proviso: prescribed details of the notice to shareholders must be published in newspapers (one English, one vernacular) circulating in the city of the registered office, clearly indicating the justification for the variation. Second proviso: the company shall not use any amount raised through the prospectus for buying, trading or otherwise dealing in equity shares of any other listed company. Section 27(2): dissenting shareholders must be given an exit offer by promoters or controlling shareholders at such exit price, manner and conditions as SEBI specifies.
  • Rule 7 procedure for Section 27: sub-rule (1) — the special resolution must be passed through postal ballot, with prescribed contents in the notice; sub-rule (2) — the advertisement of the notice shall be in Form PAS-1, published simultaneously with dispatch of the postal ballot notices; sub-rule (3) — the notice shall also be placed on the company's website, if any.
  • Section 28 — offer for sale by members: members, in consultation with the Board, may offer whole or part of their holding of shares to the public; the offer document is treated as a prospectus issued by the company [28(2)]; the members (individuals or bodies corporate or both) shall collectively authorise the company to take all actions on their behalf and shall reimburse the company for all expenses [28(3)].
  • Rule 8 for Section 28: Sections 23 to 41 and the rules apply to an offer for sale except provisions on (a) minimum subscription, (b) minimum application value, (c) any statement by the Board on utilisation of money, and (d) information which cannot be compiled or gathered by the offeror, with detailed justification for non-compliance. Rule 8(2): the prospectus must disclose the name of the person/entity bearing the cost of making the offer for sale, along with reasons.
  • Section 29 — dematerialised form: Section 29(1) has overriding effect — every company making a public offer, and such other prescribed classes, shall issue securities only in dematerialised form under the Depositories Act, 1996. Section 29(1A) (inserted 2019): for prescribed classes of unlisted companies, securities shall be held or transferred only in dematerialised form. Section 29(2): any other company may convert its securities into dematerialised form, or issue in physical form under this Act, or issue in dematerialised form under the Depositories Act, 1996. Rules 9 and 9A of the 2014 Rules govern the procedure.
  • Section 30 — advertisement of prospectus: must specify the contents of the memorandum as to (a) objects, (b) liability of members and the amount of share capital, (c) names of the signatories to the memorandum, (d) number of shares subscribed for by the signatories, and (e) capital structure of the company.
  • Section 31 — shelf prospectus: may be filed with the Registrar at the stage of the first offer of securities by classes of companies specified by SEBI regulations; must indicate a validity period not exceeding one year, commencing from the date of opening of the first offer; no further prospectus is required for any second or subsequent offer during validity. Section 31(2): an information memorandum must be filed with the Registrar prior to the second or subsequent offer, containing all material facts of new charges created, changes in financial position between the first/previous offer and the succeeding offer, and such other prescribed changes. Proviso: where applications with advance payments were received before the change, the company must intimate the changes, and on a desire to withdraw, refund all monies received as subscription within fifteen days. Section 31(3): the information memorandum together with the shelf prospectus is deemed to be a prospectus. Rule 10: information memorandum in Form PAS-2, filed with fee under the Companies (Registration Offices and Fees) Rules, 2014, within one month prior to the second or subsequent offer.
  • Section 32 — red herring prospectus: may be issued prior to the issue of a prospectus [32(1)]; must be filed with the Registrar at least three days before the opening of the subscription list and the offer [32(2)]; carries the same obligations as a prospectus, and any variation between the RHP and the prospectus must be highlighted as variations in the prospectus [32(3)]; on closing of the offer, the prospectus stating the total capital raised (whether by debt or share capital), the closing price of the securities and any other details not in the RHP must be filed with the Registrar and SEBI [32(4)]. Book building is a price discovery method — the company gives a price range rather than a fixed price, and an underwriter builds a book by accepting orders from fund managers indicating the number of shares desired and the price they will pay.
  • Section 33 — abridged prospectus: every application form for shares or debentures must be accompanied by an abridged prospectus [33(1)]. Proviso exceptions: (a) an application form issued with a bona fide invitation to a person to enter into an underwriting agreement; (b) shares or debentures not offered to the public; (c) an offer made only to existing members. Section 33(2): the full prospectus must be furnished to any person who requests it before the closing of the subscription list and the offer. Section 33(3): penalty of ₹50,000 for each default.

Misstatement — Remedies, Civil and Criminal Liability

  • Available remedies: against the company — rescission and damages; against the company and others — civil liability (compensation) under Section 35 and criminal liability under Section 34; against persons authorised to issue the prospectus — damages for deceit. Rescission, damages and deceit are not under this Act — they arise under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 read with the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
  • Remedies are alternative, not cumulative: not all are available simultaneously, though an appropriate combination may be claimed. A claim for compensation under Section 35 (a special statute, jurisdiction with the NCLT) cannot be moved simultaneously with a claim for damages under the general provisions.
  • Right of rescission: a person who purchased shares from the company on the basis of a prospectus containing untrue and misleading statements of material facts may apply to the court to rescind. The agreement to take shares is voidable at the option of the subscriber and remains valid until he actually rescinds. On repudiation the company removes his name from the register of members and returns his money with interest and other incidental cost. Compensation for damages sustained through non-fulfilment of the contract arises under Section 75 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
  • Rescission not available: (a) to subsequent purchasers of shares from the market; (b) to a subscriber to the Memorandum of Association — the company was not in existence when he signed the memorandum, so he cannot be said to have been influenced by any statement in the prospectus.
  • Right of action for damages arises where the misstatement amounts to fraud, and is available even after the company has gone into liquidation. Pre-requisites: (a) fraudulent misrepresentation of a material fact in the prospectus, (b) the person was intended to act upon it, (c) he suffered damages as a consequence of acting upon it.
  • Damages for deceit lie under general law, Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and survive even where rescission against the company is lost through laches or negligence or the company goes into liquidation. Pre-requisites: (a) fraudulent misstatement relating to some existing material facts; (b) the claimant is the original allottee and had seen the prospectus; (c) he has been actually deceived.
  • Section 35 — who is liable: the company, and every person who (i) is a director at the time of issue of the prospectus; (ii) has authorised himself to be named and is named in the prospectus as a director, or has agreed to become such director immediately or after an interval; (iii) is a promoter of the company; (iv) has authorised the issue of the prospectus; and (v) is an expert referred to in Section 26(5). Liability: in addition to any punishment under Section 36, to pay compensation to every person who sustained loss or damage.
  • Section 35(2) defences: the person proves that (a) he withdrew his consent to be a director and the prospectus was issued without his consent and authority; (b) he gave reasonable public notice that the prospectus was issued without his knowledge and consent; (c) he made the statement on the authority of an expert whom he believed competent and who had given and not withdrawn consent; (d) he had reasonable ground for believing the statement to be true and did believe it to be true up to the time of allotment; (e) the statement was a correct copy or extract from an official document and he in fact believed it.
  • Section 35(3) — personal liability without limit: where it is proved that the prospectus was issued with intent to defraud the applicants or any other person, or for any fraudulent purpose, every person referred to in Section 35(1) is personally responsible, without any limitation of liability, for all losses or damages incurred by any person who subscribed on the basis of that prospectus.
  • Section 34 — criminal liability: triggered where a prospectus is issued, circulated or distributed which includes any statement untrue or misleading in the form or context in which it is included, or where any inclusion or omission of any matter is likely to mislead. Liable: every person who authorises the issue. Punishment: under Section 447. Proviso defences: he proves the misstatement or omission was immaterial, or that he had reasonable grounds to believe, and did up to the time of issue believe, that the statement was true or that the inclusion or omission was necessary.
  • Two traps under Section 34: (a) actual loss from the misstatement is not essential to hold a person guilty; (b) liability is strict — it is immaterial whether the omission was intentional or unintentional.
  • Section 36 — fraudulently inducing investment: any person who knowingly or recklessly makes a statement, promise or forecast which is false, deceptive or misleading, or deliberately conceals material facts, to induce another to enter into (or offer to enter into) (a) any agreement for acquiring, disposing of, subscribing for or underwriting securities; or (b) any agreement whose purpose or pretended purpose is to secure a profit to any party from the yield of securities or by reference to fluctuations in the value of securities; or (c) any agreement for obtaining credit facilities from any bank or financial institution — is liable for action under Section 447.
  • Section 37 — action by affected persons: a suit or any other action under Section 34, 35 or 36 may be brought by any person, group of persons, or any association of persons affected by the misleading statement or the inclusion or omission. This has paved the way for class action — the class need not be present in court and may be represented by one petitioner, so injured persons need not each file separately.
  • Section 38 — personation: punishable under Section 447 where a person (a) makes or abets an application in a fictitious name for acquiring or subscribing for securities; (b) makes or abets multiple applications in different names or different combinations of his name or surname; or (c) otherwise induces, directly or indirectly, a company to allot or register any transfer of securities to him or any other person in a fictitious name. Section 38(2): every company issuing a prospectus must reproduce Section 38(1) prominently in the prospectus and in every application form. Section 38(3): on conviction the court may order disgorgement of any gain, and seizure and disposal of securities in his possession. Section 38(4): the amount received through disgorgement or disposal is credited to the Investor Education and Protection Fund. Note: a person who gets shares allotted in a fictitious name becomes liable as a shareholder — where a person carried on business under an assumed name and took shares in that name, his trustee in bankruptcy could not avoid liability.

Allotment, Listing and Commission [Sections 39–41]

  • Minimum subscription [Section 39(1)]: the amount of minimum subscription must be stated in the prospectus; no shares can be allotted unless at least that amount has been subscribed and the sums payable on application for that amount have been paid to and received by the company by cheque or other instrument at the time of application. Remittances must be cleared and actual cash received before allotment; an application not accompanied by such payment is not a valid offer. Under Regulation 45(1) of the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018, minimum subscription is 90% of the entire issue.
  • Application money [Section 39(2)]: not less than 5% of the nominal amount of the security, or such other percentage/amount as SEBI specifies. Under Regulation 47(4) of the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018, the minimum sum payable on application per specified security is at least 25% of the issue price; and by its proviso, in an offer for sale the full issue price is payable at the time of application.
  • Failure of minimum subscription [Section 39(3)]: if the stated minimum amount has not been subscribed and the sum payable on application is not received within 30 days from the date of issue of the prospectus (or such other period prescribed by SEBI), the amount received must be returned. Rule 11(1): refund within 15 days from the closure of the issue; on default, directors and officers responsible are jointly and severally liable to repay with interest at 15% p.a. Rule 11(2): the refund must be credited only to the bank account from which the subscription was remitted.
  • Return of allotment [Section 39(4)]: Rule 12(1) — file Form PAS-3 with the Registrar within 30 days with the prescribed fee. Rule 12(2) attachments (certified by the signatory for completeness and correctness): a list of allottees with names, address, occupation if any, and the number of securities allotted to each. Rule 12(3), for securities (other than bonus shares) allotted fully or partly paid for consideration other than cash: a copy of the contract duly stamped pursuant to which the securities were allotted, and any contract of sale relating to property or an asset, or a contract for services or other consideration. Rule 12(4): where such a contract is not in writing, the company must furnish complete particulars stamped with the same duty as if reduced to writing, deemed an instrument under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899. Rule 12(5): a registered valuer's report on valuation of the consideration where Rule 12(3) or 12(4) applies. Rule 12(7): where shares are issued under Section 62(1)(c) by a company other than a listed company whose equity shares or convertible preference shares are listed, the registered valuer's valuation report must be attached to Form PAS-3.
  • Penalty [Section 39(5)]: for default under Section 39(3) or 39(4), the company and its officer in default are liable to a penalty, for each default, of ₹1,000 for each day the default continues or ₹1 lakh, whichever is less.
  • Section 40 — listing: before making a public offer, every company shall apply to one or more recognised stock exchanges and obtain permission for the securities to be dealt with [40(1)]; the name(s) of the exchange must be stated in the prospectus [40(2)]; all monies received on application must be kept in a separate bank account in a scheduled bank and used only for adjustment against allotment where dealing permission has been obtained, or for repayment within the time specified by SEBI where the company is unable to allot [40(3)]; any condition requiring an applicant to waive compliance with Section 40 is void [40(4)].
Section 40(5) default — DefaulterMinimum FineMaximum Fine
Company₹5,00,000₹50,00,000
Defaulting Officer₹50,000₹3,00,000
  • Commission [Section 40(6) read with Rule 13]: payment must be authorised in the Articles of Association, and may be paid out of the proceeds of the issue, or the profit of the company, or both. No commission is payable to any underwriter on securities which are not offered to the public for subscription. The prospectus must disclose the name of the underwriters, the rate and amount of commission payable, and the number of securities to be underwritten or subscribed absolutely or conditionally. A copy of the contract for payment of commission must be delivered to the Registrar at the time of delivery of the prospectus for filing.
SecurityMaximum rate of commission
SharesShall not exceed 5% of the price at which the shares are issued, or any less rate/amount authorised by the articles
DebenturesShall not exceed 2.5% of the price at which the debentures are issued, or any less rate/amount authorised by the articles
  • Section 41 — Global Depository Receipts: a company may issue depository receipts in any foreign country after passing a special resolution in general meeting, subject to the conditions prescribed in the Companies (Issue of Global Depository Receipts) Rules, 2014. Depository receipts may be issued by public offering or private placement or any other manner prevalent in the concerned jurisdiction, and may be listed or traded there. They may be issued against issue of new shares or sponsored against shares held by existing shareholders, on conditions the Central Government or the Reserve Bank of India may prescribe. The underlying shares are allotted in the name of the overseas depository bank, and the depository receipts are issued against those shares by that bank.
  • GDR voting rights: a holder of depository receipts may become a member and vote as such only on conversion of the depository receipts into underlying shares following the Scheme and this Act. Until conversion, the overseas depository is entitled to vote on behalf of the holders in accordance with the agreement between the depository, the holders and the company.

Private Placement — Procedure and Limits [Section 42]

  • Ceiling [Section 42(2)]: offer only to a select group of not more than 200 persons in a financial year, identified by the Board, after passing a special resolution. Excluded from the count of 200: (a) qualified institutional buyers, and (b) employees of the company offered securities under an ESOP scheme under Section 62(1)(b). Section 42(2) originally said "fifty (50) or such higher number as may be prescribed"; Rule 14(2) (as amended by the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Second Amendment Rules, 2018) prescribes 200, so the limit reads as 200. The restriction is reckoned individually for each kind of security — equity share, preference share or debenture. NBFCs registered with the RBI and housing finance companies registered with the National Housing Bank need not comply with Rule 14(2) if complying with the RBI's or NHB's regulations on private placement offers.
  • Breach of the 200 limit [Explanation III to Section 42(3) with Section 42(11)]: if a company, listed or unlisted, offers to allot, invites subscription, allots, or agrees to allot securities to more than 200 identified persons — whether or not payment has been received, and whether or not the company intends to list in or outside India — it is deemed to be an offer to the public and Sections 23 to 41 apply, along with all provisions of this Act, the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and the SEBI Act, 1992. The penalties under Sections 42(9) and 42(10) can still be imposed.
  • Special resolution per offer [Rule 14(1)]: prior shareholder approval by special resolution is required for each private placement offer or invitation. The explanatory statement must disclose (a) particulars of the offer including the date of the Board resolution; (b) kinds of securities offered and the price; (c) basis or justification for the price including premium; (d) name and address of the valuer who performed the valuation; (e) the amount the company intends to raise; (f) material terms of raising the securities, proposed time schedule, purposes or objects of the offer, contribution being made by promoters or directors as part of the offer or separately in furtherance of objects, and principal terms of assets charged as securities. Exceptions: a Board resolution under Section 179(3)(c) suffices for non-convertible debentures where the amount to be raised does not exceed the Section 180(1)(c) limit; above that limit, one previous special resolution once a year covers all such debenture offers during the year. For issues to QIBs too, one previous special resolution once a year covers all offers and allotments to such buyers during the year. Copies of these resolutions must be filed with the Registrar prior to issue of the private placement offer-cum-application letter.
  • Land border proviso [Rule 14(1), inserted by the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Amendment Rules, 2022]: no offer or invitation of any securities shall be made to a body corporate incorporated in, or a national of, a country which shares a land border with India, unless that body corporate or national has obtained Government approval under the FEM (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 and attached it with the private placement offer-cum-application letter. The countries sharing a land border with India are China, Bhutan, Nepal, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
  • Offer-cum-application letter [Rule 14(4)]: issued in Form PAS-4; serially numbered; addressed specifically to the person to whom the offer is made; sent in writing or electronic mode; sent within thirty days of recording the name of that person under Section 42(3). No person other than the person so addressed may apply through that form, and any non-conforming application is invalid. The private placement offer and application shall not carry any right of renunciation. Complete records of private placement offers must be maintained in Form PAS-5.
  • Subscription money [Section 42(4) with Rule 14(5)]: payable by cheque, demand draft or other banking channel, not by cash, and from the bank account of the person subscribing; the company must keep a record of that bank account. First proviso: in the case of joint holders, monies shall be paid from the bank account of the person whose name appears first in the application. Monies raised through private placement cannot be utilised unless allotment is made and the return of allotment is filed with the Registrar under Section 42(8).
  • Limit on fresh offer [Section 42(5)]: no fresh offer or invitation may be made unless the allotments with respect to any earlier offer or invitation have been completed, or that offer has been withdrawn or abandoned. Proviso: subject to the maximum of 200 identified persons, a company may at any time make more than one issue of securities to such class of identified persons as may be prescribed.
  • Time limit for allotment [Section 42(6)]: allot within sixty days from the date of receipt of application money. On failure, repay the application money within fifteen days from expiry of the sixty days; on further failure to repay, the money is repayable with interest at 12% per annum from the expiry of the sixtieth day. Monies received on application must be kept in a separate bank account in a scheduled bank and used only for adjustment against allotment, or for repayment where the company is unable to allot.
  • No public advertisement [Section 42(7)]: no company shall release any public advertisement or use any media, marketing or distribution channels or agents to inform the public at large about a Section 42 issue.
  • Return of allotment [Section 42(8) with Rule 14(6)]: file Form PAS-3 with fee within fifteen days from the date of allotment, with a complete list of all allottees stating (a) full name, address, Permanent Account Number and E-mail ID of the security holder; (b) class of security held; (c) date of allotment; (d) number of securities held, nominal value and amount paid, and particulars of consideration received where issued for consideration other than cash.
  • Penalty for default in filing return [Section 42(9)]: the company, its promoters and directors are liable to a penalty for each default of ₹1,000 for each day of default, not exceeding ₹25 lakh.

Promoters and DirectorsFineAmount raised through the private placement or ₹2 crore, whichever is lower
