Examples

  • MCQ — what counts as "securities" for Section 23: Which shall be considered securities — (i) Unit linked insurance policy, (ii) Actionable claim regarding mortgaged debt, (iii) Securities issued by National Asset Reconstruction Ltd.? Options: (a) (iii) only; (b) both (i) and (iii); (c) both (ii) and (iii); (d) none. Answer — (c), referring to Section 2(h) of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956.
  • True/False — SEBI and preference share redemption: "The powers to administer matters pertaining to redemption of preference shares by a listed company vest with SEBI." Answer — False (refer Section 24(1)(a)) — redemption of preference shares is administered by the Central Government / Tribunal / Registrar.
  • SEBI v Kunnamkulam Paper Mills Ltd (2013) 178 Comp Cas 371 (Ker): where a rights issue is made to existing members with a right to renounce in favour of others, if the number of such others exceeds fifty, it also becomes a deemed prospectus.
  • True/False — Section 25(3) matters: "The matters specified under Section 25(3) need to be stated in substitution of matters stated under Section 26." Answer — False — Section 25(3) prescribes three matters to be stated in addition to those required under Section 26.
  • Re, South of England Natural Gas and Petroleum Co. Ltd (1911) 1 Ch. 573 | 104 LT 378: 3,000 copies of a document offering subscription of shares, headed "For Private Circulation only," were circulated to the members of a certain number of gas companies only. Decision — though the offer was to a limited class, it was no less an offer to the public, because those persons from the limited class were nonetheless the public; the document was a prospectus and had to contain the particulars required by the Act.
  • Nash v. Lynde (1929) AC 158 | 140 LT 146 (HL): Nash applied for shares on the basis of a document sent to him by Lynde, the managing director, marked "strictly private and confidential"; the document did not contain all material facts required by the Act. Nash sued for compensation for loss caused by the omissions. Decision — suit dismissed. Viscount Sumner's dictum: "The public in the definition is of course a general word, no particular number are prescribed. Anything from two to infinity may serve, perhaps even one if he is intended to be the first of a series of subscribers… The point is that the offer is such as to be opened to anyone who brings his money and applies in due form… A private communication is not thus open and does not construe to be a prospectus."
  • Q&A — prospectus forwarded by a solicitor: a company's prospectus was given to the company's solicitor, who forwarded it to one of his clients despite it being marked strictly private; the client applied for shares and later sued for damages. Answer — No, this did not amount to an issue to the public, so the provisions of the Act on liability for omissions are not attracted (refer Nash v. Lynde).
  • Ms. Sarika — signing by an authorised attorney: Ms. Sarika, executive director of a leading Fintech company, had to fly to Davos for the World Economic Forum meet. As the company secretary intended to file a copy of the prospectus with the Registrar, Ms. Sarika authorised Mr. Gautam in writing to sign that copy on her behalf — permissible, since a duly authorised attorney may sign in a representative capacity under Section 26(4).
  • Pharmaceutical Limited — prospectus not filed with the ROC: the Board allotted shares to the public by issuing a prospectus that was not filed with the Registrar. A public company may issue securities to the public only by issuing a prospectus [Section 23(1)(a)], and Section 26(4) requires a duly signed copy to be forwarded to the Registrar for filing before issue. Conclusion — the prospectus was issued in violation of Section 26; the company and every person knowingly a party to it are punishable under Section 26(9).
  • True/False — signing of the filed copy: "The copy of prospectus submitted with the Registrar for filing needs to be duly signed by a majority of directors." Answer — False — under Section 26(4) it must be signed by every person named as director or proposed director; a duly authorised attorney may sign in representative capacity.
  • Ind-swift Pharma Limited — variation of objects: after issue of the prospectus the company wished to vary the objects of the issue due to changes in the industry brought about by covid-19 and other pharma dynamics. Advice — authorise the change by special resolution at a general meeting; publish the notice given to shareholders in the newspapers along with the justification for the variation; and if any shareholder dissents, provide an exit option in accordance with SEBI's guidelines.
  • MCQ — variation in terms of contract or objects; which statements are NOT true: (i) an ordinary resolution shall be passed at a general meeting; (ii) notice given to shareholders shall also be published in two newspapers; (iii) the amount so raised can be invested only in equity shares of a prescribed class of companies. Options: (a) (i) only; (b) both (i) and (ii); (c) both (i) and (iii); (d) both (ii) and (iii). Answer — (c) — a special resolution is required, and the proceeds cannot be used for equity shares of any other listed company.
  • Super-Fix-it Limited — recovery of offer-for-sale expenses: some members offered part of their shareholding to the public in consultation with the Board, and the company took all actions on their behalf, incurring expenses of ₹3.2 lakh. Can the company recover the full amount from those members? Answer — Yes; members offering their holdings must authorise the company to act on their behalf and are bound to reimburse the company for all expenses incurred on the matter [Section 28(3)].
  • MCQ — withdrawal after a change reported in the information memorandum: an applicant who applied with advance payment of subscription expresses a desire to withdraw after the changes reported in the information memorandum come to his knowledge. Options: (a) may refund at the discretion of the Board; (b) shall refund after deducting administrative charges within fifteen days; (c) shall refund all monies received as subscription within fifteen days; (d) shall refund after deducting administrative charges within 30 days. Answer — (c), per the proviso to Section 31(2).
  • Henderson v. Lacon — misleading by a prima facie statement of fact: the prospectus said "the directors and their friends have subscribed a large portion of the capital and they now offer to the public the remaining shares," whereas in fact each director had subscribed only 10 shares. Held — such a statement is misleading.
  • Rex v. Kylsant — misleading by hiding the truth behind a superficially true statement: the prospectus stated that the company had regularly paid dividends, while in fact the company had been incurring substantial losses during all those years and had been writing back past provisions to the credit of the profit and loss account. Held — the prospectus did not disclose the true picture of the company.
  • Smith v. Chadwick (HL, 18 Feb 1884) — misleading by ambiguity: the prospectus of a manufacturing company said "the present value of turnover is £1 million sterling per annum," which was true only if production capacity was meant, and untrue if it meant the present production level (capacity in utilisation). Held — a statement which the directors knew may bear multiple meanings, any of which could be false to their knowledge, amounts to furnishing a misleading statement.
  • Q&A — dividends paid out of realised capital profits: all statements in the prospectus were literally true; it stated that the company had paid dividends for a number of years, but there was no disclosure that the dividends were paid out of realised capital profits and not out of trading profits. An allottee wants to avoid the contract. Answer — non-disclosure of this fact is a concealment of a material fact, since a company is normally required to distribute dividend only from trading or revenue profits and only in exceptional circumstances from capital profits; a material misrepresentation has been made and the allottee can avoid the contract of allotment.
  • Anilesh — the expert who gave public notice: a prospectus contained certain misstatements; on becoming aware of them, Anilesh, an expert who had earlier given his consent, forthwith gave a reasonable public notice that the prospectus was issued without his knowledge and consent. Answer — Section 35(2) protects a person who proves the prospectus was issued without his knowledge or consent and that on becoming aware of its issue he forthwith gave reasonable public notice to that effect. Anilesh is covered by that exception and escapes liability.
  • Director who relied on the promoters: an allottee sued a director over false statements in the prospectus; the director contended the statements were prepared by the promoters and he simply relied on them. Answer — Yes, the director is liable under Sections 34 and 35. Section 34 imposes criminal punishment on every person who authorises the issue of such prospectus, and Section 35 specifically includes a director of the company in the imposition of liability. The exceptions in Section 35(2) do not include reliance on statements prepared by promoters as a valid ground to escape liability.
  • Peek v. Gurney — deceit requires purchase on the faith of the prospectus: Gurney issued a fraudulent prospectus on behalf of a company. Peek purchased no shares at that time; several months afterwards he purchased 2,000 shares from the stock exchange and sued the directors for deceit on the basis of the prospectus. Held — the directors were not liable, as the shares were not purchased on the basis of the prospectus.
  • Section 36 — the "project overview" document: huge sums of money were collected from NRIs under a document described as a "project overview", but shares were not allotted in the proposed joint venture company; instead the money was diverted to some off-shore companies controlled by the accused persons. Conclusion — a prima facie offence under Section 36 is made out.
  • M and N — who may sue under Section 37: M applied for equity shares on the basis of a prospectus containing a misstatement; the shares were allotted to him and he afterwards transferred them to N. Can N bring an action for rescission on the ground of misstatement under Section 37? Answer — No. Under Section 37 a suit or action under Section 34, 35 or 36 may be taken only by any person, group of persons or association of persons affected by the misleading statement or the inclusion or omission in the prospectus. Therefore only M is eligible to file a suit.
  • Mr. Raju and Mr. Angad — fraud without loss: Mr. Raju, a prospective investor, sued under Section 37 the persons who authorised the issue of the prospectus for fraudulent misstatements, and also filed a complaint under Section 420 of the IPC, 1860 and Section 447 of the Act. Mr. Angad, one of the authorised persons, pleaded that Mr. Raju took no shares, bore no loss, and therefore no fraud was committed against him. Answer — the persons who authorised the issue are punishable under Section 447 despite Mr. Raju having borne no loss, because wrongful gain or wrongful loss is not an essential constituent of fraud under Section 447.
  • Application money on nominal value: if a listed company offers shares with a nominal value of ₹10, the application money shall be at least ₹2.5; if the nominal value is ₹100, it shall be at least ₹25.
  • Raksha Detective Instruments Limited — allotment on 80% of minimum subscription: having received only 80% of the minimum subscription stated in the prospectus, and before finalisation of the allotment, the company withdrew 50% of that amount from the bank to purchase certain assets, then started allotting shares. Rashmi, a subscriber, was allotted 1,000 equity shares and refused to accept the allotment. Answer — since the minimum amount was not received in full, the allotment contravenes Section 39(1), which prohibits allotment until the minimum subscription stated in the prospectus is received; under Section 39(3) the company must refund the application money received (the 80%). Rashmi is within her rights to refuse the allotment, which was illegally made.
  • Ind-swift Pharma Labs Limited — commission capped by the Articles: the company issued shares to raise capital; its Articles authorised payment of commission at 2%. Since commission cannot exceed 5% of the issue price of shares or any lesser rate authorised by the articles, the cap for payment of commission under Section 40(6) is 2%.
  • Q&A — Board decides 5% but Articles allow 3%: the Board decided to pay 5% of the issue price of shares as underwriting commission, though the Articles permit only 3%, and to pay it out of the proceeds of the share capital. Answer — under Rule 13 the rate shall not exceed, for shares, 5% of the issue price or the rate authorised by the articles, whichever is less; therefore the decision to pay 5% is invalid. However, the decision to pay the commission out of the proceeds of the share issue is valid, provided it is paid at the rate authorised by the Articles.
  • Ruhi and Sohit — joint holders' subscription money: Ruhi and her brother Sohit were jointly offered 1,000 equity shares of ₹100 each by Soumya Software Private Limited on a private placement basis, the offer-cum-application letter being addressed to both as "Ms. Ruhi, Mr. Sohit". Answer — under the first proviso to Rule 14(5), monies payable on subscription to securities held by joint holders shall be paid from the bank account of the person whose name appears first. Since Ruhi's name appears first, the subscription of ₹1,00,000 is payable by her from her account, and the company is obliged to ensure the money comes from her bank account and not from Sohit's.
  • Late filing of PAS-3 under private placement: an allotment under Section 42 was completed on 9th November 2023 and the return of allotment in Form PAS-3 was filed on 28th November 2023 — beyond the fifteen-day limit. Result — a penalty of ₹4,000 shall be imposed on the company, its promoters and directors.
  • MCQ 1 — Modern Furniture Limited, deemed prospectus contents: which are correct additional requirements — (i) a statement of the net amount received or to be received as consideration for the securities; (ii) the persons making the offer were named in the prospectus as promoters of the company; (iii) the time and place at which the underlying contract for allotment may be inspected? Answer — (b) i or iii only (Section 25(3) refers to persons named as directors, not promoters).
  • MCQ 2 — Madhav Casting Limited, partial listing permission: the company applied to three exchanges, received permission from only a couple of them, and proceeded with the public issue. Answer — (c): penalty on Madhav Casting Limited ranging from ₹5 lakh to ₹50 lakh and on every officer in default ranging from ₹50 thousand to ₹3 lakh.
  • MCQ 3 — Rig Exploration and Refinery Limited (RERL), shelf prospectus: RERL must file an information memorandum with the Registrar within ______ prior to the issue of a second or subsequent offer. Options: (a) 15 days; (b) 21 days; (c) 30 days; (d) 1 month. Answer — (d) 1 month.
  • MCQ 4 — Modern Furniture, signing of prospectus filed with the Registrar: options were (a) any two directors including managing directors; (b) majority of directors; (c) majority of directors including proposed directors; (d) every director or proposed director. Answer — (d) Every director or proposed director.
  • Descriptive Q1 — Irregular allotment: the Act does not define "irregular allotment"; broadly, an allotment is irregular when made in violation of Sections 23, 26, 39 or 40, i.e. (1) where the company does not issue a prospectus in a public offer as required by Section 23; (2) where the prospectus does not include matters required under Section 26(1), or the information given is misleading, faulty and incorrect; (3) where the prospectus has not been filed with the Registrar under Section 26(4); (4) where the minimum subscription specified in the prospectus has not been received under Section 39; (5) where the minimum amount receivable on application is less than 25% of the nominal value of the securities offered or lower than the amount prescribed by SEBI; (6) where, in a public issue, approval for listing has not been obtained from one or more recognised stock exchanges under Section 40.
  • Descriptive Q2 — Shelf prospectus: requires the Explanation to Section 31 definition, plus (1) filing with the Registrar at the stage of the first offer by classes of companies specified by SEBI, validity not exceeding one year from the date of opening of the first offer, with no further prospectus needed for subsequent offers in that period; (2) filing of the information memorandum with new charges, changes in financial position between offers, and other prescribed changes, in Form PAS-2 within one month prior to the subsequent offer; (3) the safeguard of intimation and refund within fifteen days to advance-paying applicants who wish to withdraw; (4) the information memorandum together with the shelf prospectus being deemed to be a prospectus.
  • Descriptive Q3 — Chandra Mechanical Toys Limited, financial reports in the prospectus: under Section 26(1) every prospectus issued by or on behalf of a public company, whether on formation or subsequently, or by or on behalf of any person engaged or interested in its formation, shall be dated and signed and set out such reports on financial information as SEBI specifies in consultation with the Central Government; until SEBI so specifies, its existing regulations under the SEBI Act, 1992 apply. Under Section 26(1)(c) the prospectus must declare compliance with the Companies Act, 2013 and state that nothing in it is contrary to that Act, the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and the SEBI Act, 1992 and the rules and regulations thereunder. The Board must therefore provide the SEBI-specified financial reports and make that declaration.
  • Descriptive Q4 — Unique Builders Limited, commission in flats: the company decided to pay 2.5% of the value of debentures as underwriting commission, but the Articles authorise only 2.0%, and it further decided to pay the commission in the form of flats. Answer — commission must be authorised by the Articles, may be paid out of proceeds of the issue or profits or both, and for debentures shall not exceed 2.5% of the issue price or the rate in the Articles, whichever is less; so paying commission exceeding 2% is invalid. Payment in the form of flats is permissible as there is no prohibition on payment of underwriting commission in kind — in Booth v New Africander Gold Mining Co. it was held that underwriting commission may be paid in cash or in kind, in a lump sum or by way of a percentage.
  • Descriptive Q5 — PQR Bakers Limited, two overlapping private placements: the company issued private placement offer letters for equity shares to 55 persons, of whom four are qualified institutional buyers and the rest individuals; before completing the allotment under that offer, it issued another private placement offer letter to 155 persons in their individual names for debentures. Answer — a public company may use the private placement route. Excluding the 4 QIBs, the first offer was effectively to 51 persons, well within the 200 limit, so on that count it complies. However, the second offer of debentures was made before completing the allotment of the first offer, which breaches Section 42(5) — this restriction applies even where the issue is of a different kind of security — so both offers will be treated as a public offer and governed by the prospectus provisions. If instead the debenture offer had been given after the allotment of equity shares was complete but within the same financial year, both offers could well be treated as valid private placement offers.
  • Descriptive Q6 — minimum amount and application money in a public issue: under Section 39(1) no allotment shall be made unless (i) the amount stated in the prospectus as the minimum amount has been subscribed and (ii) the sums payable on application for that amount have been paid to and received by the company. Under Section 39(2) the amount payable on application on each security shall not be less than 5% of the nominal amount or such amount as SEBI prescribes. Under Section 39(3), if the stated minimum amount is not received within 30 days of the date of issue of the prospectus (or the time prescribed by SEBI), the application money must be refunded; Rule 11(1) fixes repayment within fifteen days from the closure of the issue, failing which the directors who are officers in default are jointly and severally liable to repay with interest at 15% p.a. On any default the company and its officer in default are liable to a penalty, for each default, of ₹1,000 per day of continuing default or ₹1 lakh, whichever is less.
  • Descriptive Q7 — X Limited, 4% in Articles vs 5% decided: the Articles of X Limited allow underwriting commission up to 4% of the issue price of the shares, but the Board decided to pay 5% to Deal & Co., the underwriters. Answer — under Section 40(6) with Rule 13 the rate shall not exceed, for shares, 5% of the issue price or the rate authorised by the articles, whichever is less; the Board's decision to pay 5% is therefore invalid.

Why It Matters / Application

This chapter is the gatekeeping law for how a company touches outside money. Section 23 fixes what a private company may never do (public offer); Section 26 fixes what must be in the document and when it goes stale (90 days from filing with the Registrar); Sections 31, 32 and 33 give the three practical variants used in live issues — shelf prospectus for repeat issuers over a one-year window, red herring filed three days before the subscription list opens for book-built issues, abridged prospectus attached to every application form. Sections 34 to 38 then supply the enforcement teeth: strict criminal liability under Section 34 punished through Section 447, compensation under Section 35 with its five statutory defences, Section 36 for fraudulent inducement to invest, Section 37 for class action, and Section 38 for fictitious-name applications with disgorgement into the Investor Education and Protection Fund. Sections 39 and 40 govern the mechanics of a valid allotment — 90% minimum subscription under SEBI ICDR, 5% application money under the Act and 25% under ICDR, the separate scheduled-bank account, PAS-3 within 30 days, and 5% / 2.5% commission caps read down by the Articles. Section 42 is the parallel regime for the 200-person private route, where the offer-cum-application in PAS-4, the special resolution for each offer, the 60-day allotment window and the PAS-3 filing within 15 days are the compliance spine — and breaching the count or the sequencing converts the whole exercise into a public offer.

Note

  • Exam trap — Section 34 vs Section 35. Section 34 is criminal, attaches only to "every person who authorises the issue", needs no proof of loss, is strict liability, and is punished under Section 447. Section 35 is civil, attaches to a wider list (company, director, proposed director, promoter, person authorising the issue, and the expert under Section 26(5)), requires loss or damage to a subscriber, and results in compensation. Their defences also differ: Section 34's proviso gives only two (immateriality; reasonable grounds to believe up to the time of issue), while Section 35(2) gives five (withdrawal of consent as director; reasonable public notice; reliance on a consenting competent expert; reasonable ground to believe up to the time of allotment; correct copy or extract of an official document).
  • Fraud without loss is still fraud. Explanation (i) to Section 447 expressly covers fraud "whether or not there is any wrongful gain or wrongful loss" — this is what defeats the Angad-type defence that no investor lost money.
  • Section 26(7) has been omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2019, with effect from 15-8-2019 — do not cite it.
  • Two different 200-person consequences. Exceeding 200 identified persons triggers Explanation III to Section 42(3) with Section 42(11) — a deemed public offer attracting Sections 23 to 41, the SCRA, 1956 and the SEBI Act, 1992 — yet the Section 42(9) and 42(10) penalties can still be imposed. The 200 count is per kind of security (equity share, preference share, debenture reckoned separately) and excludes QIBs and Section 62(1)(b) ESOP employees.
  • Section 42(5) sequencing is the commonest trap: a fresh private placement offer cannot be made until the earlier allotment is complete, withdrawn or abandoned — and this holds even where the second offer is of a different kind of security.
  • Two different interest rates and two different windows. Public issue: refund within 15 days of closure of the issue under Rule 11(1), default interest 15% p.a. Private placement: allot within 60 days, repay within 15 days of the expiry of the 60 days, further default interest 12% p.a. from the expiry of the sixtieth day.
  • Two different PAS-3 timelines. Public/general allotment under Section 39(4) with Rule 12(1) — 30 days; private placement under Section 42(8) with Rule 14(6) — 15 days. The Section 39(5) penalty is capped at ₹1 lakh; the Section 42(9) penalty is capped at ₹25 lakh.
  • Commission is doubly capped: the statutory ceiling (5% shares / 2.5% debentures) and the rate in the Articles — whichever is less. Commission may be paid in kind (flats), per Booth v New Africander Gold Mining Co., but no commission at all is payable to an underwriter on securities not offered to the public for subscription.
  • Rights issue with unlimited renunciation is dangerous: per SEBI v Kunnamkulam Paper Mills Ltd, if renouncees exceed fifty, the rights offer document becomes a deemed prospectus.
  • 2022 amendment to Rule 14(1): no private placement offer to a body corporate incorporated in, or a national of, a land-bordering country (China, Bhutan, Nepal, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar) without prior Government approval under the FEM (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, attached to the PAS-4 letter.
  • Rescission is not available to market purchasers or to memorandum subscribers — the same logic underlies Peek v. Gurney (bought later on the exchange, not on the faith of the prospectus) and the Section 37 answer in the M-to-N transfer illustration.
  • Section 40(4) makes any waiver clause void — a company cannot contract out of the listing-permission and separate-bank-account requirements by making applicants waive them.

Chapter 4 — Share Capital and Debentures

Source: 87772bos-aps2160-ch4.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Scope of Chapter IV: Sections 43 to 72 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014. Sections 43–70 deal with shares; Section 71 deals exclusively with debentures.
  • Shares vs debentures: Shares represent an ownership interest carrying entrepreneurial risk and reward; debentures represent a lender's interest with limited risk and limited return. Jointly the Act calls them "securities". Both sit on the liabilities side of the issuer's balance sheet and on the assets side of the investor's/lender's balance sheet.
  • Share [Section 2(84)]: a share in the share capital of a company, and includes stock. Capital is divided into units of a fixed face value; each unit is a share.
  • Judicial meaning of a share: In New London & Brazilian Bank v. Brockle Bank (1882) 21 Ch D 302 (F) a share was held to be "not a sum of money… but an interest measured in a sum of money, and made up of various rights contained in the contract". Nearly two decades later J. Farwell in Borland's Trustee v. Steel Brothers & Co Ltd (1901) 1 Ch 279 held a share to be the interest of a shareholder in the company measured by a sum of money — for liability first and interest second — and also a series of mutual covenants entered into by all shareholders inter se under the Act and the Articles.
  • Stock: where a company aggregates the fully paid-up shares of members at their request and merges them into one fund, that fund is "stock" — a bundle of fully paid-up shares. Stock is stated in a lump sum and has no face value; a share is the smallest unit and has a face value. Stock is never issued originally — it arises only by conversion of fully paid-up shares under Section 61(1)(c), which also allows reconversion of stock into fully paid-up shares of any denomination.
  • Two kinds of share capital [Section 43]: equity share capital and preference share capital. Equity share capital sub-divides into (i) equity shares with voting rights ("plain vanilla") and (ii) equity shares with differential rights as to dividend, voting or otherwise under Rule 4.
  • Capital conservation: the principle underlying Sections 66, 67 and 70 — capital is the fund out of which creditors are paid, so a company may not ordinarily return capital to members or finance the purchase of its own shares except through the fenced routes of reduction (Sec 66) and buy-back (Sec 68).

Key Definitions / Terms

Preference share capital [Explanation (ii) to Section 43]
That part of the issued share capital of a company limited by shares which carries a preferential right as to (a) payment of dividend — an absolute amount or an amount at a fixed rate, free of or subject to income-tax; and (b) repayment of capital on winding up, limited to the amount paid up or deemed paid up, whether or not there is a preferential right to a fixed premium specified in the memorandum or articles, unless agreed otherwise.
Equity share capital [Section 43(a) read with Explanation (i)]
All share capital which is not preference share capital. Also called ordinary shares or common shares.
Voting right [Section 2(93)]
The right of a member of a company to vote in any meeting of the company or by means of postal ballot.
Sweat equity shares [Section 2(88)]
Equity shares issued by a company to its directors or employees at a discount or for consideration other than cash, for providing know-how, or making available rights in the nature of intellectual property rights, or value additions, by whatever name called.
Employees' stock option [Section 2(37)]
The option given to directors, officers or employees of a company or of its holding or subsidiary company, giving them the benefit or right to purchase or subscribe for the shares of the company at a future date at a pre-determined price.
Employee for sweat equity [Explanation I to Rule 8(1)]
(a) a permanent employee of the company working in India or outside India; (b) a director, whether whole-time or not; (c) an employee or director as above of a subsidiary or holding company, in India or outside India.
Value additions [Explanation II to Rule 8(1)]
Actual or anticipated economic benefits derived or to be derived by the company from an expert or professional for providing know-how or making available IPR-type rights, by the person to whom sweat equity is issued, for which consideration is not paid or not included in normal remuneration under the contract of employment.
Authorised / nominal capital [Section 2(8)]
Such capital as is authorised by the memorandum to be the maximum amount of share capital of the company.
Called-up capital [Section 2(15)]
Such part of the capital which has been called for payment.
Debenture [Section 2(30)]
Includes debenture stock, bonds or any other instrument of a company evidencing a debt, whether constituting a charge on the assets of the company or not. Excludes (a) instruments referred to in Chapter III-D of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and (b) such other instrument as may be prescribed by the Central Government in consultation with the RBI.
Transmission
Devolution of title to securities otherwise than by transfer — by death, succession, inheritance, bankruptcy, marriage, etc. Effected by forwarding documents (e.g. a notarised copy of the death certificate) — no instrument of transfer is needed, because a deceased transferor cannot sign a transfer deed.
Specified securities [Explanation I to Section 68]
Includes employees' stock option or other securities as may be notified by the Central Government from time to time.
Free reserves for buy-back [Explanation II to Section 68]
Includes the securities premium account.
Pari passu
Latin for "on equal footing" — sweat equity holders rank pari passu with other equity shareholders [Section 54(2)].
Forged transfer
A transfer registered on an instrument bearing forged signatures of the transferor. It is a nullity, void ab initio; the transferee acquires no ownership, the real owner can force the company to delete the transferee's name and restore his own.

Kinds of Share Capital, Differential Rights and Voting (Sec 43, Rule 4, Sec 47)

  • Rule 4(1) conditions for equity shares with differential rights: (a) the AOA authorises the issue; (b) shareholders approve by ordinary resolution in general meeting — a listed public company must pass it through postal ballot; (c) voting power of differential-rights shares must not exceed 74% of total voting power at any point of time; (d) no default in filing annual accounts and annual returns for the 3 financial years preceding the year of decision; (e) no subsisting default in payment of declared dividend, repayment of matured deposits, redemption of preference shares or debentures due for redemption, or payment of interest on such deposits/debentures; (f) no default in payment of dividend on preference shares, repayment of any term loan from a PFI/State level financial institution/scheduled bank or interest thereon, statutory dues relating to employees, or crediting amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund; (g) not penalised by Court or Tribunal during the last three years for any offence under the RBI Act 1934, SEBI Act 1992, Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act 1956, FEMA 1999 or any other special Act under which the company is regulated by a sectoral regulator.
  • Cure of default: a company may issue equity shares with differential rights upon expiry of five years from the end of the financial year in which the default was made good.
  • Rule 4(3): conversion of existing equity share capital with voting rights into equity share capital carrying differential voting rights, and vice versa, is prohibited.
  • Rule 4(2), (4), (5), (6): the explanatory statement to the notice of the general meeting/postal ballot must state particulars of the issue including size and details of differential rights; the Board's Report for the financial year in which the issue was completed must disclose specified particulars; holders of differential-rights shares enjoy all other rights (bonus shares, rights shares, etc.); the Register of Members under Section 88 must carry all relevant particulars of such shares and shareholders.
  • Section 47(1) — equity voting: subject to Sections 43, 50(2) and 188(1), every member holding equity share capital has a right to vote on every resolution, and his voting right on a poll is in proportion to his share in the paid-up equity share capital. Nidhi company exception: no member may exercise voting rights on poll in excess of 5% of total voting rights of equity shareholders.
  • Section 47(2) — preference voting: a preference shareholder votes only on resolutions which directly affect the rights attached to his preference shares, and on resolutions for winding up or for repayment/reduction of equity or preference share capital; on a poll in proportion to his share in the paid-up preference share capital.
  • Second proviso to Sec 47(2): where dividend on his class of preference shares has not been paid for two years or more, the preference shareholder gets the right to vote on all resolutions placed before the company.
  • First proviso to Sec 47(2): where both classes vote, the proportion of equity voting rights to preference voting rights is the same as the proportion of paid-up equity capital to paid-up preference capital.
  • Section 43 overrides Section 47 — holders of differential-rights equity shares vote as per the AOA/terms of issue, not on a strictly proportional basis. Section 106 separately restricts voting rights.
  • Sections 43 and 47 do not apply to: (1) a Specified IFSC Public Company where its MOA or AOA so provides [GSR 8(E), 4 January 2017]; (2) a private company where its memorandum or articles so provide.

Certificates, Variation of Rights, Calls (Sec 46, 48, 49–51)

  • Section 46(1): a share certificate is prima facie evidence of title if issued (a) under the common seal, if any, or (b) signed by two directors, or (c) signed by a director and the Company Secretary where one is appointed. Since 29-05-2015 (Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015) the common seal is optional. If the composition of the Board permits, at least one of the two directors must be a person other than the managing or whole-time director. A facsimile/printed/digital signature counts, but not a rubber stamp; the director remains personally responsible for permitting affixation and for safe custody of the machine.
  • Section 46(4): where a share is held in depository form, the record of the depository is prima facie evidence of the interest of the beneficial owner. Rule 9A of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 (inserted w.e.f. 2-10-2018) requires every unlisted public company to issue securities only in dematerialised form and to facilitate dematerialisation of existing securities.
  • Renewed certificate [Sec 46(2) + Rule 6]: issued where the original is defaced, mutilated or torn, against surrender of the original. It must state "Issued in lieu of share certificate No..... sub-divided/replaced/on consolidation". Fee as the Board thinks fit but not exceeding ₹50 per certificate; no fee for a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the High Court or Central Government. On sub-division, consolidation, merger, demerger or reconstitution, all existing certificates may be replaced without surrender of the old ones.
  • Duplicate certificate: issued where the original is lost or destroyed, with Board consent on evidence produced. Fee not exceeding ₹50 per certificate. It must prominently state "duplicate issued in lieu of share certificate No......" and the word "duplicate" must be stamped or printed prominently. Time to issue: three months for unlisted companies, 45 days for listed companies, from the date of submission of complete documents.
  • Records: particulars of every renewed and duplicate certificate are kept in a register in Form SH-2, cross-referenced to the Register of Members, at the registered office or where the Register of Members is kept, preserved permanently, in the custody of the company secretary or a person authorised by the Board, and entries authenticated by him.
  • Rule 5 (physical shares): a certificate is issued on surrender of the letter of allotment or fractional coupons of requisite value (except issues against letters of acceptance or renunciation, or bonus issues), pursuant to a Board resolution. It shall be in Form SH-1 and specify the name(s) of the person(s), the shares to which it relates, and the amount paid-up thereon. Particulars go into the Register of Members under Section 88 with the date of issue.
  • Rule 7: blank certificate forms must be printed only on the authority of a Board resolution, be consecutively machine-numbered, and kept in the custody of the secretary or a Board-authorised person. Books relating to share certificates must be preserved not less than thirty years, and permanently in disputed cases. Surrendered certificates must immediately be defaced by stamping/printing "cancelled" in bold and may be destroyed only after three years from surrender, under a Board resolution and in the presence of a person appointed by the Board.
  • A share certificate is not a negotiable instrument. For jointly held shares only one certificate is issued and delivery to any one joint holder amounts to delivery to all.
  • Section 48 — variation of class rights, three cumulative conditions: (1) the memorandum or articles must entitle the company to vary such class rights, or, failing that, the terms of issue of that class must not prohibit variation; (2) holders of at least 75% of the issued shares of that class must consent in writing, or a special resolution must be passed at a separate class meeting; (3) holders of at least 10% of the shares of that class who did not consent or vote in favour may apply to the Tribunal, and the variation does not take effect unless confirmed by the Tribunal. The application must be made within 21 days of the date of the consent or resolution, by one or more persons appointed in writing on behalf of the applicants.
  • Proviso to Sec 48(1): if variation by one class affects the rights of any other class, the consent of three-fourths of that other class must also be obtained and Section 48 applies to that variation too. Sec 48(3): the Tribunal's decision binds all shareholders of the class. Sec 48(4): the company must file a copy of the order with the Registrar within 30 days of the order.
  • What is NOT a variation: a new issue of preference shares ranking pari passu with existing shares does not amount to variation and needs no consent of preference shareholders (White v. Bristol Aeroplane Co Ltd (1953) 2 WLR 144); cancellation of shares and reduction of capital also do not amount to variation of class rights (Essar Steel Ltd, re, (2005) 59 SCL 457 (Guj)). Contrast Cumbrian Newspapers Group Ltd v. Cumberland & Westmorland Herald Newspaper & Printing Co Ltd (1987) 2 Comp LJ 39, where a shareholder with a pre-emptive right to purchase shares was held to form a special class whose right could not be taken away without his consent.
  • Section 10(2): all money payable by any member to the company under the memorandum or articles is a debt due from him — but liability to pay arises only when a valid call is made.
  • Section 49 — uniformity of calls: calls must be made on a uniform basis on all shares falling under the same class. Shares of the same nominal value on which different sums have been paid are not of the same class. A shareholder served with a regular call may choose to pay only part of the sum due — the call debt is not entire and indivisible, so the company may be bound to accept the amount tendered. How much to call on a partly paid share is a Board decision, subject to the Articles and terms of issue.
  • Section 50 — calls in advance: if authorised by its articles a company may accept from any member the whole or part of the amount remaining unpaid on his shares although no part of it has been called up. Advance payment gives no extra voting rights until all members have been called upon to pay. Interest may be paid on the advance if the articles permit; a rate permitted by the articles may be varied by shareholders in general meeting — e.g. 6 percent may be increased to 10% (CIT v. Manipal Industries Ltd, (1997) 12 SCL 15 (ITAT)).
  • Section 51: if authorised by the articles, a company may pay dividends in proportion to the amount paid-up on each share. The Board may pay pro rata where equity shares are not equally paid-up; on preference shares dividend is always at a fixed rate.

Premium, Discount, Sweat Equity, Preference Shares (Sec 52–55)

  • Section 52(1): premium may be received in cash or in kind; it must be carried to a separate Securities Premium Account, maintained with the same sanctity as paid-up share capital, and reducible only in the manner in which paid-up share capital may be reduced. The power to issue at a premium need not be specifically provided in the AOA. It must be shown as a separate item in the Balance Sheet under Schedule III, Part B, with disclosure of how it was disposed of. The DCA opined premium cannot be treated as a free reserve, being in the nature of a capital reserve (Circular No 3/77 of 15-4-1977); a reduction of the premium account was allowed under a scheme experts approved as fair, just and proper (Zee Tele Films Ltd, re, (2005) 124 Comp Cas 102 (Bom)).
  • Section 52(2) — permitted applications: (a) issue of fully paid bonus shares; (b) writing off preliminary expenses; (c) writing off issue expenses including commission paid or discount allowed on any issue of shares or debentures; (d) premium payable on redemption of any preference shares or debentures; (e) buy-back under Section 68.
  • Section 52(3) — restricted applications (overrides 52(1) and (2)) for such class of companies as may be prescribed whose financial statements comply with the accounting standards under Section 133: only (a) issue of fully paid bonus shares; (b) writing off issue expenses/commission/discount on any issue of equity shares; (c) buy-back under Section 68.
  • Section 53: except sweat equity shares under Section 54, a company shall not issue shares at a discount; any share issued at a discount is void [53(2)]. Sub-section 2A (inserted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017, effective 09 February 2018) overrides 53(1) and (2) and permits issue of shares at a discount to creditors on conversion of their debt into shares under (a) a statutory resolution plan or (b) a debt restructuring scheme, in accordance with guidelines/directions/regulations of the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934 or the Banking (Regulation) Act, 1949.
  • Sections 52 and 53 apply only to shares (equity or preference) and not to debt products like bonds or debentures, whose pricing is governed mostly by yield-to-maturity considerations.
  • Section 54(1) — conditions for sweat equity: (a) shares of that class must already have been issued; (b) the issue is authorised by a special resolution; (c) the resolution specifies the number of shares, the current market price, the consideration if any, and the class or classes of directors or employees to whom they are to be issued; (d) the issue complies with SEBI regulations if the company is listed on a recognised stock exchange, otherwise with Rule 8 of the Companies (Share and Debentures) Rules, 2014.
  • Rule 8 limits: the special resolution is valid for allotment within twelve months of passing [sub-rule 3]. In a year the maximum issue is the higher of 15% of existing paid-up equity share capital or shares of issue value ₹5 crore [sub-rule 4]. Cumulative sweat equity (including all previous issues) shall not exceed 25% of paid-up equity capital at any time; for startups the limit is 50% of paid-up capital up to 10 years from the date of incorporation or registration. Lock-in: 3 years from the date of allotment [sub-rule 5]. Valuation of the shares and of the IPR/know-how/value additions must be by a registered valuer with a justified report addressed to the Board [sub-rules 6 and 7]; quoted market prices in an active market are the best evidence of fair value. Non-cash consideration is carried to the balance sheet if it is a depreciable or amortizable asset, otherwise recorded as an expense [sub-rule 9]. Disclosure in the Directors' Report for the year of issue [sub-rule 13]; a Register of Sweat Equity Shares in Form SH-3 is maintained at the registered office or such other place as the Board decides [sub-rule 14].
  • Section 55(1): a company limited by shares shall not issue irredeemable preference shares. The category was abolished by the 1988 amendment to the Companies Act, 1956.
  • Section 55(2): redeemable preference shares may be issued only if authorised by the articles, and must be redeemed within 20 years from the date of issue. Rule 9(1) conditions: a special resolution in general meeting, and no subsisting default at the time of issue in redemption of preference shares or payment of dividend due on any preference shares. Rule 9(4): the Register of Members under Section 88 must contain particulars of preference shareholders. Rule 9(5): listing of preference shares requires compliance with SEBI regulations.
  • Infrastructure exception (first proviso to Sec 55(2) + Explanation + Rule 9): for infrastructure projects specified in Schedule VI, preference shares may be issued for a period exceeding twenty years but not exceeding thirty years, subject to redemption of at least 10% of such preference shares annually from the 21st year onwards or earlier, on a proportionate basis, at the option of the preference shareholders.
  • Second proviso to Sec 55(2) — redemption: redemption only out of (1) profits which would otherwise be available for dividend, or (2) the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of such redemption. Only fully paid shares can be redeemed. Where redeemed out of profits, a sum equal to the nominal amount of the shares redeemed must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR), which is maintained with the sanctity of paid-up share capital and reducible only as paid-up capital may be reduced. Redemption is not a reduction of authorised share capital, and new shares up to the nominal amount redeemed may be issued without the capital being deemed increased.
  • Section 55(3): where a company cannot redeem preference shares or pay dividend on them per the terms of issue ("unredeemed preference shares"), it may issue further redeemable preference shares to those holders equal to the amount due including the dividend, with the consent of holders of three-fourths in value of such unredeemed preference shares and the approval of the Tribunal on a petition; the unredeemed preference shares are then deemed redeemed. The Tribunal, while approving, shall order forthwith redemption of shares held by non-consenting holders.
  • Section 55(4): the CRR account may be applied in paying up unissued shares to be issued to members as fully paid bonus shares.

Premium on Redemption — Source and Timing

CategorySource of premiumTiming
Such class of companies as may be prescribed whose financial statements comply with accounting standards under Section 133Out of the profits of the companyBefore such shares are redeemed
Premium payable on redemption of preference shares issued on or before the commencement of this Act (by such company)Out of the profits of the company or out of the company's securities premium accountBefore such shares are redeemed
Any other caseOut of the profits of the company or out of the company's securities premium accountBefore such shares are redeemed

Transfer, Transmission, Refusal and Rectification (Sec 56–59)

  • Section 56(1) conditions for registering a transfer (not applicable where both transferor and transferee are recorded as beneficial owners with a depository): (a) the instrument of transfer is executed by both transferor and transferee; (b) it specifies the name, address and occupation, if any, of the transferee; (c) it is duly stamped and dated; (d) it is in Form SH-4 [Rule 11(1)] where securities are in physical form; (e) it is delivered to the company with the certificate (or the letter of allotment if no certificate exists) within 60 days from the date of execution.
  • Proviso to Sec 56(1): where the instrument is lost or not delivered within 60 days, the company may register the transfer on such terms as to indemnity as the Board thinks fit.
  • Section 56(3) + Rule 11(3): where the application is by the transferor alone and relates to partly paid shares, the company shall not register the transfer unless it has given notice in Form SH-5 to the transferee and the transferee has raised no objection within two weeks from receipt of the notice.
  • Government company exemptions [Notification GSR 463(E), 5 June 2015] — available to a Government company which has not defaulted in filing financial statements under Section 137 or the annual return under Section 92: full exemption from Sec 56(1) for transfer of securities held by nominees of the Government; partial exemption for transfer of bonds issued by a Government company — only an intimation by the transferee giving name, address and occupation, delivered with the bond certificate (or letter of allotment), is needed; no properly stamped and executed instrument of transfer is required.
  • Section 56(2): the company's power to register a transmission is unaffected by Sec 56(1) — an intimation from the person to whom the right has been transmitted suffices; no instrument of transfer is needed. Illustrative cases of transmission: death (to the legal representative), insolvency (to the Official Receiver), lunacy (to the administrator appointed by the Court).
  • Section 56(5): a transfer of any security or other interest made by the legal representative of a deceased person is valid as if the legal representative were the holder at the time of execution of the instrument, even though he is not a registered holder.
  • Section 56(6) penalty: for default in complying with sub-sections (1) to (5), the company and every officer in default are liable to a penalty of ₹50,000.
  • Section 56(7): a depository or depository participant who, with intent to defraud a person, has transferred shares is liable under Section 447 in addition to liability under the Depositories Act, 1996.
  • Section 57 — personation: a person who deceitfully personates as the owner of any security, or interest in a company, or of any share warrant or coupon, and thereby obtains or attempts to obtain such security/interest/warrant/coupon, or receives or attempts to receive money due to such owner, is punishable with imprisonment of not less than one year up to three years and a fine of not less than ₹1 lakh up to ₹5 lakh. Personation for acquisition of securities is separately an offence under Section 38 punishable under Section 447 (Section 447 being the general provision). Cheating by personation under Section 416 IPC, 1860 is punishable under Section 419 IPC with imprisonment of either description up to three years, or fine, or both.
  • Forged transfer consequences: a subsequent bona fide buyer who takes from the forged transferee cannot be denied his ownership rights, yet the original shareholder's name must also be restored because the forged transfer is void ab initio. The company may be asked to compensate the bona fide buyer and may in turn seek indemnity from the first transferee who used the forged instrument.
  • Section 58(1): a private company limited by shares refusing to register a transfer or transmission must send a notice of refusal stating reasons to both the transferor and the transferee (or to the person giving intimation of transmission) within 30 days of delivery of the instrument or intimation.
  • Section 58(2): securities or other interest of any member in a public company are freely transferable; any contract or arrangement between two or more persons in respect of transfer of securities is enforceable as a contract. A private company must, under Section 2(68)(i), restrict the right to transfer — typically by a pre-emption clause requiring members to offer shares first to existing members. The right to transfer is inherent in ownership and the Articles can never make shares absolutely non-transferable.
  • Section 58(5): the Tribunal may dismiss the appeal or order (a) that the transfer/transmission be registered, the company complying within 10 days of receipt of the order, or (b) rectification of the register and payment of damages sustained by any aggrieved party. Section 58(6): contravention of the Tribunal's order is punishable with imprisonment of not less than one year up to three years and fine of not less than ₹1 lakh up to ₹5 lakh.
  • Section 59(1): an aggrieved person, a member, or the company may appeal to the Tribunal (or to a competent court outside India specified by the Central Government for foreign members or debenture holders residing outside India) for rectification where, without sufficient cause, a name is entered in the register, or a name is omitted after having been entered, or there is default or unnecessary delay in entering the fact of a person having become or ceased to be a member. "Unnecessary delay" is undefined and is a question of evidence; failure to register a transfer within one month of the application, contrary to the listing agreement, was held to be unreasonable delay. Any member may apply without showing injury or prejudice — personal grievance is not necessary for locus standi.
  • Section 59(2): the Tribunal may dismiss the appeal or direct registration within 10 days, or direct rectification of the depository's records or of the register and, in the latter case, direct the company to pay damages.
  • Section 59(3): the right of a holder of securities to transfer them is protected, and a person acquiring such securities is entitled to voting rights unless those rights have been suspended by an order of the Tribunal. Section 59(4): on an application by the depository, depository participant, company, holder of the securities or SEBI, the Tribunal may direct a company or depository to set right a contravention and rectify its register/records where a transfer contravenes the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, the SEBI Act, 1992, the Companies Act, 2013, or any other law in force.

Time Limits for Delivery of Certificates [Section 56(4)]

ParticularsTime period for delivering the certificates

Any allotment of sharesWithin two months from the date of allotment
Transfer of securitiesWithin one month from the date of receipt of the instrument of transfer by the company
Transmission of securitiesWithin one month from the date of receipt of the intimation of transmission by the company
Any allotment of debenturesWithin six months from the date of allotment
All securities — specified IFSC public and private company [GSR 9(E), 4 January 2017]Within sixty days after incorporation, allotment, transfer or transmission

Proviso to Sec 56(4): where securities are dealt with in a depository, the company shall intimate details of allotment to the depository immediately on allotment.
