Alteration, Rights Issue, Bonus, Reduction (Sec 61–66)

  • Section 61(1) — five modes of alteration (if authorised by the articles, by resolution in general meeting): (a) increase authorised capital by such amount as it thinks expedient; (b) consolidate and divide the whole or any part of the share capital into shares of larger amount; (c) convert all or any fully paid-up shares into stock and reconvert stock into fully paid-up shares of any denomination; (d) sub-divide the whole or any part into shares of smaller amount, the proportion between paid and unpaid amounts on each reduced share remaining the same as on the original share; (e) cancel shares not taken up and reduce the capital accordingly. NCLT approval is required only where consolidation and division under (b) results in a change in the voting percentage of shareholders. Section 61(2): cancellation of shares under (e) is not deemed a reduction of share capital (reduction is governed by Section 66).
  • Section 64 + Rule 15: notice in Form SH-7 must be filed with the Registrar along with the altered memorandum within 30 days of the alteration, in the case of (a) alteration under Sec 61(1), (b) a Government order under Sec 62(4) read with 62(6) increasing authorised capital, or (c) redemption of any redeemable preference shares. Penalty [Sec 64(2)]: ₹500 per day of continuing default, subject to a maximum of ₹5 lakh for the company and ₹1 lakh for every officer in default.
  • Which law governs a rights issue: listed companies or companies intending to get securities listed follow the SEBI Act, 1992 and rules/regulations thereunder [Section 23(1)(c)]; other public companies and private companies follow this Act and the rules thereunder [Section 23(2)(a)].
  • Section 62(1)(a) — rights issue: further shares must be offered to existing equity shareholders in proportion to the paid-up capital on their shares, by a letter of offer in the form of a notice which must (i) state the number of shares offered; (ii) state the time within which the offer must be accepted — not less than 15 days (or such lesser number of days as may be prescribed) and not exceeding 30 days from the date of the offer; Rule 12A [inserted by G.S.R. 113(E) dated 11 February 2021] fixes the prescribed lesser period at not less than seven days; (iii) state that if not accepted within the time the offer is deemed declined; (iv) confirm the right of renunciation in favour of another person, unless the articles provide otherwise. If the offer is declined, the Board may dispose of those shares in a manner not disadvantageous to the shareholders and the company. Proportion is applied "as nearly as circumstances admit". A private company and a Specified IFSC public company may adopt a shorter acceptance period if 90% of the members consent in writing or electronically.
  • Section 62(1)(b) — ESOP: offer to employees under a scheme of employees' stock option requires a special resolution plus compliance with Rule 12. An ordinary resolution suffices for (a) a private company which has not defaulted in filing financial statements under Section 137 or the annual return under Section 92, and (b) a Specified IFSC public company. Listed companies must observe the SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefits) Regulations, 2014.
  • Section 62(1)(c) — preferential allotment to any persons: permitted if authorised by special resolution, for cash or for consideration other than cash; where consideration is non-cash, the price must be determined by a valuation report of a registered valuer subject to conditions in Rule 13.
  • Section 62(2): the notice must be dispatched by registered post, speed post, electronic mode, courier or any other mode having proof of delivery to all existing shareholders at least three days before the opening of the issue. A private company may use a shorter notice period if 90% of the members consent in writing or electronically.
  • Section 62(3) — exclusion: Section 62 does not apply to an increase in subscribed capital caused by conversion of debentures (per the conditions of issue) or of a loan (per the conditions of the grant), provided those terms and conditions were approved by special resolution in general meeting before the issue of the debentures or the grant of the loan.
  • Section 62(4), (5), (6) — Government-directed conversion: the Government may, by order, direct conversion of debentures issued to it or loans given by it, wholly or partly, into shares, if it considers it necessary in the public interest, on such terms as appear reasonable, even if the terms of issue do not provide an option to convert. Where the terms are not acceptable, the company may appeal to the Tribunal within sixty days of communication of the order, and the Tribunal, after hearing the company and the Government, passes such order as it deems fit. In fixing terms the Government must consider (a) the financial position of the company, (b) the terms of issue of the debentures or loans, (c) the rate of interest payable, and (d) such other matters as it considers necessary. On such conversion the authorised share capital stands increased by the value of the shares issued and the memorandum stands altered.
  • Section 62 does not apply to a Nidhi company [GSR 465(E), 5 June 2015]; Nidhi companies must nevertheless ensure their shareholders' interests are protected.
  • Section 63 — bonus shares. "Bonus share" is not defined in the Act. Standard Chartered Bank v. Custodian (2000) 6 SCC 427: a bonus share is an accretion, issued when the company capitalises its profits by transferring an amount equal to the face value of the share from its reserve to nominal capital — a distribution of capitalised undivided profit — and is property with an identity and value of its own, capable of being bought and sold.
  • Sources for bonus [Sec 63(1)]: free reserves (other than revaluation reserve), the securities premium account, or the capital redemption reserve account. Proviso: bonus shares shall not be issued by capitalising reserves created by revaluation of assets.
  • Pre-requisites [Sec 63(2)]: (a) authorised by the Articles; (b) authorised in general meeting on the recommendation of the Board; (c) no default in payment of interest or principal on fixed deposits or debt securities issued by it; (d) no default in payment of statutory dues of employees such as provident fund contribution, gratuity and bonus; (e) partly paid-up shares outstanding on the date of allotment are made fully paid-up; (f) compliance with Rule 14 — a company which has once announced its Board's decision recommending a bonus issue shall not subsequently withdraw it.
  • Section 63(3): bonus shares shall not be issued in lieu of dividend. The proviso to Section 123(5) confirms that a company may capitalise profits or reserves to issue fully paid-up bonus shares or to pay up amounts unpaid on shares held by members.
  • Section 66(1) — reduction of capital by a company limited by shares, or limited by guarantee and having a share capital, in any manner and in particular by (a) extinguishing or reducing liability on shares in respect of capital not paid-up; (b) cancelling paid-up share capital which is lost or unrepresented by available assets; (c) paying off paid-up capital in excess of the wants of the company — subject to a special resolution, alteration of the memorandum reducing the amount of its share capital and of its shares accordingly, and the condition that repayment of any deposits accepted, or interest payable thereon, is not in arrear.
  • Section 66(2): the Tribunal shall give notice of every application to (a) the Central Government (power delegated to Regional Directors), (b) the Registrar, (c) SEBI in the case of listed companies, and (d) the creditors, and shall consider representations made within three months from receipt of the notice. Where no representation is received in that period, they are presumed to have no objection. The Tribunal is statutorily required to consider representations, not to admit them in full.
  • Section 66(3): the Tribunal may confirm the reduction on such terms as it deems fit only if satisfied that (a) the debt or claim of every creditor has been discharged, determined, secured, or his consent obtained; and (b) the accounting treatment proposed conforms to the accounting standards under Section 133 — evidenced by a certificate from the company's auditor filed with the Tribunal along with the application.
  • Section 66(4) and (5): the order of confirmation must be published by the company as the Tribunal directs; within 30 days of receiving the copy of the order, the company must deliver to the Registrar a certified copy of the order and the Tribunal-approved minutes showing the amount of share capital, the number of shares into which it is divided, the amount of each share, and the amount deemed paid-up on each share at the date of registration. The Registrar registers these and issues a certificate.
  • Section 66(6): Section 66 does not apply to buy-back under Section 68. Section 66(7): a member, past or present, is liable to pay a call or contribution only up to the difference between the amount deemed to have been paid on his shares and the nominal value of the reduced shares.
  • Section 66(8) — omitted creditor: where a creditor entitled to object was left off the list of creditors because of his ignorance of the proceedings or the nature of his interest, the company commits a default within the meaning of Section 6 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 in respect of his interest. Remedy: if the company is running, every person who was a member on the date of registration of the reduction order by the Registrar is liable to contribute to payment of that debt, but not exceeding the amount he would have been liable to contribute had winding up commenced on the day immediately before that date. If the company is wound up, the Tribunal may, on the creditor's application and proof of his ignorance, settle a list of persons so liable and make and enforce calls and orders on them as if they were ordinary contributories.
  • Section 66(9): nothing in sub-section 8 affects the rights of contributories among themselves. Section 66(10): an officer is liable to punishment under Section 447 if he knowingly conceals the name of any creditor entitled to object, or abets or is privy to such concealment, or knowingly misrepresents the nature or amount of any creditor's debt or claim, or abets or is privy to such misrepresentation. ("Abet" = encourage or incite another to commit a crime; "privy" = a co-participant, one who has an interest in a matter.)

Financial Assistance, Buy-Back and CRR (Sec 67–70)

  • Section 67(1): a company limited by shares, or limited by guarantee and having a share capital, shall not buy its own shares unless the consequent reduction of capital is effected under the provisions of this Act. Section 67(2): a public company shall not give financial assistance — directly or indirectly, by loan, guarantee, provision of security or otherwise — for the purpose of, or in connection with, a purchase or subscription of any shares in the company or in its holding company.
  • Section 67(3) exceptions: (a) lending of money by a banking company in the ordinary course of its business — the phrase is undefined; a bank cannot supervise a borrower's use of funds, so if a borrower uses the money to buy the bank's shares the bank and its officers are protected, but an English court held that where money is given for the very purpose of purchasing the bank's shares that is not lending in the ordinary course of business and the provision would be violated; (b) provision of money for the purchase of fully paid shares in the company or its holding company by trustees for the company's employees under an employee share scheme approved by special resolution and complying with Rule 16; (c) loans by a company to its employees (other than directors or key managerial personnel), not exceeding six months' salary, to enable them to buy or subscribe fully paid shares in the company or its holding company and hold them by way of beneficial ownership.
  • Rule 16 conditions for employee share schemes: if the shares are listed, purchases must be made only through a recognised stock exchange, not by private offers or arrangements; if unlisted, valuation must be by a registered valuer; the aggregate value of shares purchased or subscribed shall not exceed 5% of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves; and the Board's report must disclose, for voting rights not exercised directly by employees — (a) names of employees who did not vote directly, (b) reasons for not voting directly, (c) name of the person exercising such voting rights, (d) number of shares held by or in favour of such employees and their percentage of total paid-up share capital, (e) date of the general meeting where such voting power was exercised, (f) resolutions on which votes were cast, (g) percentage of such voting power to total voting power on each resolution, and (h) whether votes were cast in favour of or against the resolution.
  • Section 67(4): nothing in Section 67 affects a company's right to redeem preference shares issued under this Act or any previous company law.
  • Section 67 exemptions: Section 67 does not apply to private companies (which have not defaulted in filing financial statements under Section 137 and the annual return under Section 92) and Specified IFSC public companies where all three conditions are met — (a) no other body corporate has invested any money in its share capital; (b) borrowings from banks, financial institutions or any body corporate are less than twice its paid-up share capital or ₹50 crore, whichever is lower; and (c) it is not in default in repayment of such borrowings subsisting at the time of the transaction. Section 67(1) does not apply to Nidhi companies where shares are purchased from a member on his ceasing to be a depositor or borrower, and such purchase is not treated as reduction of capital under Section 66 [GSR 465(E), 5 June 2015].
  • Section 68(1) — sources of funds for buy-back: free reserves; or the securities premium account; or the proceeds of the issue of any shares or other specified securities. Buy-back cannot be made out of the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares or specified securities.
  • Section 68(2) — conditions: (a) authorised by the articles; (b) a special resolution in general meeting — not necessary where the buy-back does not exceed 10% of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves and is authorised by a Board resolution passed at its meeting; (c) the amount of buy-back must not exceed 25% of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves, and in the case of buy-back of equity shares the maximum is 25% of total paid-up equity capital in any financial year; (d) after buy-back the ratio of debts (secured and unsecured) owed by the company must not be more than twice the paid-up capital and free reserves (the Central Government may prescribe a higher ratio for a class of companies); (e) the shares/securities must be fully paid-up; (f) compliance with Rule 17, or with SEBI regulations for listed securities. Proviso: no offer of buy-back shall be made within one year reckoned from the date of closure of the preceding buy-back offer.
  • Section 68(3): the notice of the meeting at which the special resolution is proposed must carry an explanatory statement stating (a) full and complete disclosure of all material facts, (b) the necessity for the buy-back, (c) the class of shares or securities intended to be purchased, (d) the amount to be invested, and (e) the time limit for completion. Rule 17(1) lists 14 matters whose particulars must be stated in the explanatory statement.
  • Section 68(5) — sources of securities: from existing shareholders or security holders on a proportionate basis; or from the open market; or from securities issued to employees under a scheme of stock option or sweat equity.
  • Section 68(6) — declaration of solvency: filed before implementing the buy-back resolution, with the Registrar and also with SEBI if the shares are listed. It must be in Form SH-9, verified by affidavit, stating that the Board has made a full inquiry into the affairs of the company and found it capable of meeting all its liabilities and that it will not be rendered insolvent for a period of 12 months from the date of the declaration. It must be signed by at least two directors, one of whom shall be the managing director, if any.
  • Section 68(4): every buy-back must be completed within twelve months from the date of passing the special resolution or Board resolution.
  • Section 68(7): securities bought back must be extinguished and physically destroyed within seven days of the last date of completion of buy-back. Section 68(8) — cooling period: no further issue of the same kind of shares or specified securities within six months; a bonus issue, and discharge of existing obligations such as conversion of warrants, stock option schemes, sweat equity, or conversion of preference shares or debentures into equity shares, are permitted. Other types of security may be freely issued.
  • Section 68(9): a register of shares/securities bought back in Form SH-10 must record (a) the shares or securities bought, (b) the consideration paid, (c) the date of cancellation, (d) the date of extinguishing and physically destroying them, and (e) such other particulars as prescribed. It is kept at the registered office in the custody of the secretary or a Board-authorised person, whose authentication of entries is required.
  • Section 68(10): a return of buy-back in Form SH-11 with fee must be filed with the Registrar (and SEBI if listed) within thirty days of completion, accompanied by a certificate in Form SH-15 signed by two directors including the managing director, if any, certifying compliance with the Act and rules.
  • Section 68(11) penalty: for default under Section 68 or under SEBI regulations made for Sec 68(2)(f), the company is punishable with fine not less than ₹1 lakh up to ₹3 lakh, and every officer in default with fine not less than ₹1 lakh up to ₹3 lakh.
  • Section 69: where a company purchases its own shares out of free reserves or the securities premium account, a sum equal to the nominal value of the shares so purchased must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve account and the details disclosed in the balance sheet. Under Sec 69(2) the CRR may be applied only in paying up unissued shares to be issued to members as fully paid bonus shares — the same use as under Sec 55(4).
  • Section 70(1) — prohibition: no company shall directly or indirectly purchase its own shares or other specified securities (a) through any subsidiary company including its own subsidiary companies; (b) through any investment company or group of investment companies; (c) if a default is made by the company in repayment of deposits or interest thereon, redemption of debentures, redemption of preference shares, payment of dividend to any shareholder, or repayment of any term loan or interest thereon to any financial institution or banking company. Where the default is remedied and a period of three years has lapsed after the default ceased to subsist, buy-back is not prohibited.
  • Section 70(2): buy-back is also prohibited where the company has not complied with Section 92 (Annual Return), Section 123 (Declaration and Payment of Dividend), Section 127 (Punishment for failure to distribute dividends) and Section 129 (Financial Statement).

Debentures (Sec 71 and Rule 18)

  • Features: a debenture is the smallest unit of a sizeable loan; applicants receive certificates for the money lent; the certificate is issued under the common seal, if any, or under the signatures of two directors, or a director and the company secretary if appointed; the company pays periodic interest until redemption; the rate is generally pre-fixed in the name of the instrument; no voting rights [Sec 71(2)]; under Section 44 a debenture is movable property transferable as per the Articles; it may be secured (charge created in favour of the debenture trustee) or unsecured; it may be redeemed at the end of the full term or in instalments; terms may allow conversion into equity at maturity at the holder's option; certificates must be delivered within six months of allotment under Section 56(4)(d) unless prohibited by law or by order of a Court, Tribunal or authority.
  • Types: by security — secured / unsecured; by redeemability — redeemable / irredeemable; by convertibility — convertible (mandatorily or optionally, partially or fully) / non-convertible.
  • Section 71(1): a company may issue debentures with an option to convert them into shares, wholly or partly, at the time of redemption, if authorised by a special resolution in general meeting.
  • Rule 18(1)(a) — tenor of secured debentures: not more than 10 years from the date of issue, except up to 30 years for (i) companies engaged in setting up infrastructure projects; (ii) Infrastructure Finance Companies as defined in clause (viia) of sub-direction (1) of direction 2 of the Non-Banking Financial (Non-deposit accepting or holding) Companies Prudential Norms (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2007; (iii) Infrastructure Debt Fund NBFCs as defined in clause (b) of direction 3 of the Infrastructure Debt Fund Non-Banking Financial Companies (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2011; (iv) companies permitted by a Ministry or Department of the Central Government, the RBI, the National Housing Bank or any other statutory authority to issue debentures for a period exceeding ten years.
  • Rule 18(1)(b)–(d): a debenture trustee must be appointed before the issue of the prospectus or letter of offer; security is created by charge or mortgage in favour of the debenture trustee on specified movables of the company, its subsidiaries, holding or associate companies, or on specified immovable properties wherever situate, or any interest therein — the value of the charged assets must be sufficient for due repayment of the debentures and interest. For NBFCs the charge or mortgage may be created on any movable property. For a Government company whose debentures are fully secured by a guarantee of the Central Government or one or more State Governments or both, the charge-creation requirement of Rule 18(1) does not apply. The debenture trust deed in Form SH-12 must be executed within three months of closure of the issue or offer.
  • Section 71(4) + Rule 18(7) — Debenture Redemption Reserve: the DRR is created out of profits available for payment of dividend and its credit balance shall not be utilised except for redemption of debentures. The relaxations were introduced by the MCA to reduce the cost of borrowings. Other financial institutions covered under Section 2(72) are treated like NBFCs registered with the RBI for DRR purposes. In the case of partly convertible debentures, DRR is created only in respect of the non-convertible portion.
  • Rule 18(7) — investment/deposit requirement: by 30th April of each year, an amount equal to 15% of debentures maturing during the financial year ending on 31st March of the next year must be invested or deposited in (a) deposits with any scheduled bank, free from charge or lien; (b) unencumbered securities of the Central Government or any State Government; (c) unencumbered securities mentioned in sub-clauses (a) to (d) and (ee) of section 20, or unencumbered bonds issued by any other company notified under sub-clause (f) of section 20 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. The amount so invested/deposited shall not at any time fall below 15% of the debentures maturing during the year ending 31st March of that year — i.e. it must be placed by 30th April and maintained thereafter till the end of the financial year (or till maturity if earlier). This applies to listed companies (other than All India Financial Institutions and banking companies) for publicly placed debentures, and to unlisted companies (other than All India Financial Institutions and banking companies) for publicly placed and privately placed debentures — other than privately placed debentures of NBFCs registered with the RBI under section 45IA of the RBI Act and housing finance companies registered with the National Housing Bank.
  • Section 71(5): before issuing a prospectus or making an offer or invitation to the public or to its members exceeding five hundred for subscription of its debentures, the company must appoint one or more debenture trustees. Except for a public offer of debentures, appointment and removal are governed by Rule 18(2): the trustees' names must be stated in offer letters and notices; written consent must be obtained before appointment and a statement to that effect must appear in the letter of offer.
  • Rule 18(2)(b) — who cannot be a debenture trustee: (i) a beneficial holder of shares in the company; (ii) a promoter, director, key managerial personnel, or any other officer or employee of the company or its holding, subsidiary or associate company; (iii) a relative of any promoter, director or key managerial personnel of the company; (iv) a beneficiary entitled to moneys payable by the company otherwise than as remuneration payable to the debenture trustee; (v) a person indebted to the company or its subsidiary, holding or associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company; (vi) a person who has furnished any guarantee in respect of the principal debts secured by the debentures or interest thereon; (vii) a person having a pecuniary relationship with the company amounting to 2% or more of its gross turnover or total income, or ₹50 lakh (or such higher amount as may be prescribed), whichever is lower, during the two immediately preceding financial years or the current financial year.
  • Removal and vacancy: a debenture trustee may be removed before expiry of his term only with the approval of holders of not less than three-fourths in value of the debentures outstanding, at their meeting. A casual vacancy may be filled by the Board itself; a vacancy caused by resignation requires the written consent of the majority of debenture holders. While a vacancy continues the remaining trustee(s), if any, may act until an appointment is made.
  • Section 71(6) + Rule 18(3), 18(4): the debenture trustee must take steps to protect the interests of debenture holders and redress their grievances, and must convene a meeting of all debenture holders on (a) receiving a duly signed written request from debenture holders holding at least one-tenth in value of the debentures, or (b) the happening of any event constituting a breach or default, or which in the trustee's opinion affects the interest of the debenture holders. Rules 18(3) and 18(4) do not apply in the case of a public offer of debentures.
  • Section 71(7): any provision in a trust deed securing the issue of debentures, or in any contract with debenture holders secured by a trust deed, which exempts or indemnifies a debenture trustee from liability for breach of trust where he fails to show the degree of care and due diligence required of him, is void. Exemptions given to a debenture trustee must be agreed to by debenture holders holding at least 75% in value of the debentures at a meeting held for this purpose. The yardstick for "reasonable degree of care and due diligence" is determined with regard to the provisions of the trust deed conferring power, authority or discretion on the trustee.
  • Section 71(8), (9), (10): the company shall pay interest and redeem the debentures per the terms of issue. Where the trustee concludes that the assets of the company are insufficient, or are likely to become insufficient, to discharge the principal amount when due, he may petition the Tribunal, which after hearing the company and any other interested person may impose restrictions on the incurring of further liabilities by the company as it considers necessary in the interests of debenture holders. Where a company fails to redeem debentures on maturity or fails to pay interest when due, the Tribunal may, on the application of any or all of the debenture holders or the debenture trustee and after hearing the parties, direct the company to redeem the debentures forthwith on payment of principal and interest due.
  • Section 71(12): a contract with the company to take up and pay for any debentures may be enforced by a decree for specific performance. The holder may seek relief under the Specific Relief Act, 1963; a decree under section 2(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 may be executed under Order 21 CPC.
  • Section 71(13): the Central Government may prescribe the procedure for securing the issue of debentures, the procedure for debenture holders to inspect the trust deed and obtain copies, the form of the debenture trust deed, the quantum of debenture redemption reserve required to be created, and such other matters.
  • Borrowing limit trigger: for a company other than a private company, the Board must obtain shareholders' approval by special resolution before issuing debentures if the borrowings by such issue together with amounts already borrowed exceed the aggregate of the company's paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium (i.e. a debt-equity ratio above 1). Borrowings exclude short-term or temporary loans.
  • Return of allotment: under Rule 12(1) of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, a company having share capital which allots debentures (debentures being "securities") must file a Return of Allotment in Form PAS-3 within thirty days of allotment with the jurisdictional Registrar.

Debenture Redemption Reserve — Class-wise Applicability [Rule 18(7)]

CategoryPublicly placed debenturesPrivately placed debentures
All India Financial Institutions (regulated by RBI)ExemptedExempted
Banking companiesExemptedExempted
Listed companies (other than AIFIs and banking companies)Exempted, except NBFCs not registered with RBI u/s 45IA of the RBI Act, and housing finance companies not registered with the National Housing BankExempted, except NBFCs not registered with RBI u/s 45IA of the RBI Act, and housing finance companies not registered with the National Housing Bank
Unlisted companies (other than AIFIs and banking companies)DRR equal to 10% of outstanding debenturesDRR equal to 10% of outstanding debentures, except NBFCs registered with RBI u/s 45IA of the RBI Act and housing finance companies registered with the National Housing Bank

SameEvery officer of the company in defaultLiable for action under Section 447
Issue of shares at a discount [Sec 53(3)]Every officer in defaultUp to an amount equal to the amount raised through the issue at a discount, or ₹5 lakh, whichever is less
SameCompanyRefund all monies received with interest at 12% per annum from the date of issue of such shares
Default in complying with Sec 56(1) to (5)Company and every officer in defaultPenalty of ₹50,000
Personation of a shareholder [Sec 57]Any personImprisonment: minimum 1 year, maximum 3 years and fine: minimum ₹1 lakh, maximum ₹5 lakh

SameEvery officer in default₹500 per day of continuing default, maximum ₹1 lakh

SameEvery officer in defaultImprisonment up to 3 years and fine not less than ₹1 lakh extending to ₹25 lakh
