Examples

  • Example 1 — Sun Bakers Limited (meaning of share): authorised share capital ₹50 lakh, face value of each share ₹10. The company therefore has 5 lakh shares of ₹10 each. When these shares, in part or whole, are allotted, the allottees become shareholders on the date of allotment. Note: a company having share capital must quote in its memorandum — "The share capital of the company is _____ rupees, divided into _____ shares of ___ rupees each."
  • Example 2 — Ind-swift Pharma Labs Limited and Panacea Biotec Limited (forms of preferential dividend): Ind-swift Pharma provides that the preferential dividend may be a fixed amount, say ₹5,00,000 in one year, payable to preference shareholders before anything is paid to ordinary shareholders. Panacea Biotec provides that the preferential dividend is calculated at a fixed rate of 8 percent of the nominal value of each share. Both are valid forms under Explanation (ii) to Section 43.
  • Illustration (Q&A) — Can a company have only preference share capital? Answer: a company may have only equity share capital, but it cannot have only preference share capital, because preference shareholders have "preferential rights" over equity shareholders; in the absence of equity share capital there cannot be preference share capital (Bihar State Financial Corporation vs. CIT Bihar (1976)).
  • Example 3 — Golden Apple Transport Limited (duplicate certificates to defraud): duplicate certificates were issued with intent to defraud in respect of nearly 12,00,000 shares of face value ₹10 each. The maximum fine that can be imposed on the company is ₹12,00,00,000 — being ten times the face value (10 × ₹10 × 12,00,000 = ₹12 crore), which is higher than ₹10 crore.
  • Example 4 — Indswift Pharma Labs Limited (preference voting rights): capital of ₹300 crore raised through a single series of 8% preference shares, apart from ₹1200 crore of ordinary shares. Dividend was last paid to preference shareholders for 2021-22. Preference shareholders acquire the right to vote on any resolution placed before the company w.e.f. 1st April 2024; until 31st March 2024 they may vote only on resolutions directly affecting the rights attached to their preference shares, or relating to winding up or repayment/reduction of equity or preference share capital. The proportion of voting rights of equity shareholders to preference shareholders is 4:1 (₹1200 crore : ₹300 crore).
  • Illustration (MCQ) — DBS Chemicals Limited (variation of class rights): a class had only 105 holders; 100 of them own 0.5% of the shares of that class each, and each of the remaining 5 holders holds 10% of that class. The 100 small holders (together 50%) have already signed the consent letter. How many of the 5 large holders must also authorise it? Options: (a) 0, (b) 1, (c) 3, (d) 5. Answer: (c) 3 [Section 48(1)] — consent of holders of at least 75% of the issued shares of that class is required; 50% + 3 × 10% = 80%, whereas 2 would give only 70%. Note the test is 75% of issued shares' holders, not 75% of the number of holders.
  • Example 6 — Prism Glass Limited (uniformity of calls): three series of equity shares, all of nominal value ₹100, with paid-up values of ₹100, ₹80 and ₹55 respectively. All three are treated as different classes. Since the first class is fully paid-up no call can be made on it; calls can be made on the remaining two classes.
  • Illustration (Q&A) — annoyed directors making a call on one member: a shareholder paid the first two calls after great delay and neglected the third; the directors, being annoyed, called upon him to pay the whole amount due. Is the call valid? Answer: No. A call cannot be made on some members only unless they constitute a separate class of shareholders, so such a call is invalid (Galloway v. Halle Concerts Society, (1915) 2 Ch 233).
  • Example 7 — Coriander Masale Limited (calls in advance and voting): 10,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each; ₹6 per share called up till allotment; the first and final call of ₹4 is yet to be made. Reena holds 10,000 shares on which she has paid the whole of ₹10 per share. At the upcoming EGM she wants to vote as the owner of fully paid-up shares. The company cannot permit her — she has no voting right in respect of the ₹4 per share paid in advance, and the restriction continues until that amount is duly called up.
  • Illustration (Q&A) — Moon Star Machineries Limited: its articles authorise acceptance of the whole or part of unpaid calls in advance. Anand, a shareholder, deposits in advance the remaining amount due on his partly paid-up shares without any call being made. Answer: valid. In view of the authorisation in the Articles, Moon Star Machineries Limited is permitted to accept the advance amount from Anand under Section 50.
  • Example 8 — premium: a share of face value ₹10 issued at ₹14; the ₹4 over and above face value is the premium.
  • Practical Insight — XYZ Luxuries IPO: the issue opened 28 September 2022 and closed 30 September 2022; date of listing on NSE SME was 11 October 2022 (Tuesday). The fixed issue price against a face value of ₹10 per share is ₹40 per share — hence the premium is ₹30 per share.
  • Example 9 — discount: a share of face value ₹100 issued at the lower price of ₹95; the differential of ₹5 is the discount allowed by the company (prohibited under Section 53 except for sweat equity).
  • Illustration (True/False) — sweat equity and age of company: "A company incorporated and having commenced business on 9th Nov 2022 can issue sweat equity shares only after 8th Nov 2023." Answer: False. There is currently no condition in Section 54(1) regarding the age of the company — the old clause (c), "not less than one year has, at the date of such issue, elapsed since the date on which the company had commenced business", was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 w.e.f. 7th May 2018.
  • Example 9 (second, on preference shares) — Medanta Healthcare Limited: the company plans to raise capital through an issue of preference shares; its articles are silent on the matter, though the Board believes redeemable shares can be issued. Since the articles do not expressly authorise the issue, Medanta Healthcare Limited cannot issue preference shares; it may first alter its articles of association.
  • Example 10 — Vintee Lifestyles Garments Limited (CRR on redemption): redemption of 20,000 preference shares of ₹100 each at a premium of ₹20 per share, the Accounts Department confirming profits are sufficient. The amount to be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve out of profits otherwise available for dividend is ₹20,00,000 — being the sum equal to the nominal amount of the preference shares redeemed (20,000 × ₹100). No amount paid towards the premium needs to be transferred to CRR.
  • Example 11 — Bell Homes Furnisher Limited (BHFL), Sec 55(3): unable to redeem preference shares as they became due, BHFL decided to issue further preference shares against the unredeemed ones. Holders of 93% in value of such unredeemed preference shares consented, and the Tribunal assented. The 18 holders owning the remaining 7% seek redemption of their shares. While giving approval under Section 55(3), the Tribunal shall order the redemption forthwith of the shares (7% in value) held by the 18 dissenting holders.
  • Example 12 — Himanshu / Chaitanya Progressive Books Private Limited (transfer of partly paid shares): Himanshu received notice on 7th August, 2023 that Shefali had submitted a transfer deed duly signed by her for transfer of 500 partly paid shares (₹6 paid-up out of a face value of ₹10 per share) in his name. As transferee he must raise his objection latest by 21st August, 2023 (two weeks from receipt of the Form SH-5 notice).
  • Example 13 — Richa Daniel / Speed Software Limited (Sec 56(5)): after obtaining a succession certificate Richa Daniel succeeded to 7,000 shares of ₹100 each allotted to her late father Alexender Daniel. To pay off the debt of her cousin Stesley she wants to transfer all 7,000 shares to her on a duly stamped instrument of transfer signed by both. On receipt of the duly stamped instrument, the requisite share certificates and the succession certificate, the company shall transfer the shares in favour of Stesley — the transfer is valid under Section 56(5) even though Richa is not herself on the Register of Members, as if she had been the holder at the time of executing the transfer deed. Alternative: Richa may instead apply to be registered as the holder of the 7,000 shares, submitting the share certificates and succession certificate; no instrument of transfer is needed in transmission because a deceased transferor cannot sign a transfer deed. The company will then enter Richa's name, delete Alexender Daniel's name and issue new certificates in her name.
  • Example 14 — Ind-swift Pharma Labs Limited (delivery on transfer): a request for transfer was received in Form SH-4 along with the instrument of transfer on 25th November 2022. The company shall deliver the certificate by 24th December 2022 (one month).
  • Example 15 — private company, no response: an application for transfer of shares was received by a private company on 25th November 2022; the transferee received no response, so he may appeal to the Tribunal by 24th January 2023 (60 days from delivery, no notice having been sent).
  • Example 16 — public company, no response: an application for transfer was received by a public company on 25th November 2022; with no response, the transferee may appeal to the Tribunal by 23rd February 2023 (90 days from delivery of the instrument).
  • Illustration (True/False) — notice of refusal: "Notice of refusal to register transfer of shares by a private company shall be sent only to the transferee within 30 days, stating reasons of refusal." Answer: False — notice of refusal must be given to both the transferee and the transferor under Section 58(1).
  • Example 17 — rectification with damages: after hearing both parties to an appeal over removal of the applicant's name from the register of members without sufficient cause, the Tribunal ordered reinstatement of the name in the register together with payment of damages to the holder as well as the cost of litigation. The company has to pay the damages as ordered in addition to rectifying the register [Section 59(2)].
  • Example 18 — sub-division under Sec 61(1)(d): a share with face value ₹100 on which ₹80 is paid up can be split into 10 shares of ₹10 nominal value each, with ₹8 being paid up on each — preserving the same paid/unpaid proportion.
  • Example 19 — rights ratio: a "1:10 rights issue" means an existing shareholder can buy one extra share for every ten shares held. The rights price is usually below the prevailing market price to encourage subscription.
  • Practical Insight — Suzlon Energy Limited rights issue (October 2022): to part-finance repayment/prepayment of certain borrowings (₹900.00 crore) and general corporate purposes (₹283.50 crore), SEL offered a rights issue of 240 crore equity shares (face value ₹2) at a price of ₹5 per share (current market price ₹8.47) to mobilise ₹200.00 crore. The ratio was 5 shares for every 21 shares held as of the record date 4 October 2022. Rights entitlements could be renounced up to 14 October 2022 (market price of the rights entitlement was ₹1.32). The issue opened 11 October 2022 and closed 20 October 2022. Only 50% (₹2.50 per share) was payable on application, the balance on one or more calls. Post allotment the shares were to be listed on BSE and NSE. SEL proposed to spend ₹16.50 crore on the rights issue process.
  • Example 20 — further shares to non-members: a company listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange intends to offer further shares to non-members; existing members consider this invalid under Section 62(1)(a). The company is not absolutely prohibited — it can do so after passing a special resolution under Section 62(1)(c). Thus new shares may be issued to non-members in certain circumstances.
  • Illustration (Q&A) — length of the acceptance period: the notice of offer of further shares must specify the time within which the offer must be accepted: not less than 15 days (or such lesser number of days as may be prescribed) and not exceeding 30 days from the date of the offer; Rule 12A prescribes that the period shall be not less than seven days from the date of offer.
  • Example 21 — shorter notice consent (Sec 62(2)): notice of a rights issue was dispatched to holders at their registered e-mail IDs two days in advance of the opening of the issue. Out of 4,230 members, 3,075 members holding 94% of the shares acknowledged the mail and consented to the shorter notice. Although the mode of dispatch and the furnishing of consent are valid, the notice is invalid because at least 90% of the members must consent, whereas here only about 72.70% (3,075 out of 4,230) did. It is the number of members that counts, not their shareholding.
  • Example 23 — bonus ratio: where a bonus issue is in the ratio 1:2 (one for every two shares held), a holder of 100 shares gets 50 bonus shares without payment, so his holding becomes 150 instead of 100.
  • Illustration (True/False) — bonus on partly paid shares: "Bonus shares can be issued on partly paid shares in proportion to paid-up value." Answer: False — bonus shares can only be issued as fully paid; partly paid-up shares outstanding on the date of allotment must first be made fully paid-up [Sec 63(2)(e)].
  • Example 24 — reduction by extinguishing liability: in respect of a share of ₹10, a company has called only ₹7 per share and all shareholders have paid it. The company decides not to call the remaining ₹3 and reduces the shareholders' liability. The company is then said to have reduced its ₹10 share to a ₹7 fully paid-up share [Sec 66(1)(a)].
  • Example 24 (second, on Sec 66(2) timelines): an application for reduction of capital was received by the NCLT on 22nd November 2022 from an unlisted company; the Tribunal sent notice of the application to the concerned Regional Director, the RoC and the creditors on 28th November 2022. The notice to the RD and RoC was sent by registered post and reached them on 1st December 2022. The RD and RoC can make representations till 28th February 2023 (three months from receipt of the notice); if any representation is made thereafter the Tribunal is not bound to consider it.
  • Example 25 — Mr. Nilanjan Iyer / Modern Furniture Limited (omitted creditor): the name and interest of Mr. Iyer, a creditor, were kept outside the list of creditors when the company reduced its capital. On learning of this he wishes to take legal action against the company under the IBC, 2016, the limitation period not having expired. He is entitled to do so — exclusion of his name is construed as an offence under the IBC as well [Sec 66(8) read with Section 6 of the IBC, 2016]. (Limitation is the maximum period set by statute within which a legal action may be brought or a right enforced; the Limitation Act, 1963 governs.)
  • Example 26 — Rainbow Sports Limited (declaration of solvency): a listed company filed Form SH-9 with the Registrar and with SEBI stating that the Board had made a full inquiry into the affairs of the company and found it capable of meeting all its liabilities and that it would not be rendered insolvent for a period of 6 months from the date of the declaration; the declaration was signed by 3 directors, none of them the MD, the MD being out of the country to attend the FIFA World Cup event in Qatar (the company being one of the sponsors). There are two lacunae under Section 68(6): first, the declaration must be for a period of 12 months; second, where a managing director has been appointed, he must sign the declaration of solvency.
  • Illustration (MCQ) — buy-back by Board resolution: "Buy-back with a Board resolution is allowed if the amount involved is:" (a) not exceeding 25% of total paid-up equity capital and free reserves; (b) not exceeding 25% of total paid-up equity capital; (c) not exceeding 10% of total paid-up equity capital and free reserves; (d) not exceeding 10% of total paid-up equity capital. Answer: (c) [Section 68(2)].
  • Illustration (True/False) — resolution for a 10% buy-back: "Passing an ordinary resolution is sufficient where the buy-back does not exceed ten percent of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves." Answer: False — such buy-back has to be authorised by a Board resolution passed at its meeting, not an ordinary resolution.
  • Illustration (True/False) — use of CRR: "CRR can be used to issue partly paid bonus shares or to finance the discount portion of sweat equity shares." Answer: False — the CRR may be applied only in paying up unissued shares of the company to be issued to members as fully paid bonus shares.
  • Example 27 — Sigma Electronic Limited (SEL), Sec 70(1)(c): financially unstable in 2018 due to the economic slowdown, SEL defaulted in June 2020 in repayment of a loan from a public finance corporation on account of the cash crunch caused by the nation-wide lockdown; its account was marked in the defaulters list and classified as NPA. A stimulus package enabled SEL to repay the due amount in December 2020, and in February 2021 the account was removed from the NPA category. SEL won a tender in mid-2021, became a supplier to military retail canteens, accumulated reserves and became cash-surplus. It decided to buy back 10% of its equity shares in December 2022. SEL shall not be allowed to buy back its securities, as 3 years have not elapsed since the default was remedied.
  • Example 28 — naming of debentures: the name "10% Debentures" indicates that the company shall pay interest at the rate of 10% on the outstanding amount till maturity.
  • Example 29 — Sigma Computers Limited (structure of a debenture issue): the company wishes to borrow ₹50,00,000 from the public by issuing 7% debentures, each unit of ₹100. It can therefore issue 50,000 debentures of ₹100 each carrying 7% interest, payable at the end of every quarter. If such debentures (secured by a charge on the company's assets) are issued for a six-year duration, the principal is repaid by the end of the sixth year; alternatively the terms may allow repayment of principal in equal yearly instalments, in which case a portion of the debentures is redeemed yearly and interest is paid only on the outstanding amount. Holders may also be given the option of converting their debentures into equity shares at maturity. Thus the company borrows a large sum from many lenders instead of approaching a single borrower, and debenture holders exert no influence over ownership and working of the company unless their interest is jeopardised.
  • Example 30 — Roshan Bulb Limited (duty to convene a debenture holders' meeting): the company took a bank loan in contravention of the covenant on the permissible debt-equity ratio stated in the offer document issued for subscription of its debentures. The debenture trustee is bound to convene a meeting of all debenture holders, as the decision to take the loan is not only a breach but also a default affecting the interest of the debenture holders [Rule 18(4)].
  • Example 31 — failure of due diligence by a debenture trustee: a debenture trustee fails to keep a close watch on the change in value of the asset against which the debentures are secured — a preliminary responsibility specifically marked upon him. It can be said that the trustee failed to show the degree of care and due diligence required of him as a trustee [Sec 71(7)].
  • Illustration (True/False) — voting by debenture holders: "If interest to debenture holders remains unpaid for two years then they may vote on resolutions affecting their interests." Answer: False — a debenture holder can never assume voting rights unless the debenture is converted into equity as per the terms of issue [Sec 71(2)]. A similar provision does exist for preference shareholders where preference dividend remains unpaid for two years [second proviso to Sec 47(2)].

Test Your Knowledge — MCQs with Answers

  • MCQ 1 — Mr. Bahu / Mahishmati Private Limited: notice received on 2nd March, 2024 that Mr. Bali had submitted a transfer deed duly signed by him for transfer of 1000 partly paid shares (₹8 paid-up out of face value ₹10 per share) in Mr. Bahu's name. Mr. Bahu as transferee must raise his objection latest by — (a) 9th March 2024, (b) 16th March 2024, (c) 17th March 2024, (d) 31st March 2024. Answer: (c) 16th March, 2024 (two weeks from receipt of the Form SH-5 notice; the printed answer key states "(c) 16th March, 2024").
  • MCQ 2 — Star Engineering Limited (Sec 67 contravention): the company, not covered by any exemption, contravened the restriction on giving financial assistance for purchase of its own or its holding company's shares. Every officer in default shall be liable for — (a) fine not less than ₹1 lakh but up to ₹25 lakh; (b) fine not less than ₹1 lakh but up to ₹25 lakh or imprisonment up to three years or both; (c) fine up to ₹25 lakh or imprisonment up to three years or both; (d) fine not less than ₹1 lakh but up to ₹25 lakh and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Answer: (d).
  • MCQ 3 — Modern Furniture (duplicate certificate, unlisted company): complete documents for issue of a duplicate share certificate were submitted on 30th December 2022. The company shall issue the duplicate certificates by — (a) 29th January 2023, (b) 13th February 2023, (c) 28th February 2023, (d) 29th March 2023. Answer: (d) 29th March 2023 — three months for an unlisted company (45 days would apply to a listed company).

Test Your Knowledge — Descriptive Questions with Answers

  • Q1 — VRS Company Ltd. / SV Company Ltd. (exclusion from a rights issue): VRS holds 45% of the total equity of SV Company Ltd. (incorporated 1 January 2019). SV's Board resolved not to offer further equity shares to VRS on the ground that it already held a high percentage, and on 1 March 2019 offered new equity shares to all shareholders except VRS. SV's Articles provided that new shares should first be offered to existing shareholders. Answer: Under Section 62(1)(a), further shares must first be offered to existing equity shareholders as at the date of the offer, in proportion to the paid-up capital on their shares; a company cannot ignore a section of existing shareholders. SV Company Ltd. had no legal authority to exclude VRS. The Board's decision is not valid — it violates Section 62(1)(a) as well as the Articles of the issuing company.
  • Q2 — Mars Motors India Ltd. (alteration of the capital clause): under Section 61(1), a limited company having a share capital may, if authorised by its Articles, alter its memorandum in general meeting to (i) increase its authorised share capital by such amount as it thinks expedient; (ii) consolidate and divide all or any of its share capital into shares of a larger amount — but no consolidation and division which results in changes in the voting percentage of shareholders shall take effect unless approved by the Tribunal on an application made in the prescribed manner; (iii) convert all or any of its paid-up shares into stock and reconvert that stock into fully paid shares of any denomination; (iv) sub-divide its shares into shares of smaller amount than fixed by the memorandum; (v) cancel shares which, at the date of the resolution, have not been taken or agreed to be taken by any person, and diminish the share capital by the amount so cancelled. Under Section 64, notice in Form SH-7 (Rule 15) must be filed with the Registrar with the altered memorandum within thirty days. The capital clause, if authorised by the Articles, is altered by passing an ordinary resolution under Section 61(1).
  • Q3 — Ramesh / Suresh / Ryan Entertainment Private Limited (delay in delivering certificates): Ramesh, a resident of New Delhi, sent a transfer deed duly signed by him as transferee and his brother Suresh as transferor to the company's registered office in Mumbai; he did not receive the transferred share certificates even after four months from dispatch. Answer: Under Section 56(4), the company must deliver certificates of all shares transferred within one month from the date of receipt of the instrument of transfer. Under Section 56(6), for default in complying with sub-sections (1) to (5) the company and every officer in default are liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees.
  • Q4 — Silver Robotics Limited (inability to redeem preference shares): due to insufficient profits the company is unable to redeem existing preference shares of ₹10,00,000 (10,000 preference shares of ₹100 each) though the terms of issue require redemption within the next two months; it has not defaulted in payment of dividend. Answer: Under Section 55(3) it may, with the consent of holders of three-fourths in value of such preference shares and with the approval of the Tribunal on a petition, issue further redeemable preference shares equal to the amount due — i.e. ₹10,00,000 — including dividend thereon, whereupon the unredeemed preference shares are deemed to have been redeemed. Where some preference shareholders have not consented, the Tribunal may order the company to redeem their shares forthwith, so Silver Robotics Limited must keep sufficient funds ready for redeeming the shares of the non-consenting holders.
  • Q5 — Trisha Data Security Limited (sweat equity for a one-year-old company): incorporated just a year ago with paid-up share capital of ₹200 crore, highly profitable and employee-friendly, it wants to issue sweat equity; a friend of the CEO says it cannot, as a minimum of 2 years have not elapsed since commencement of business. Answer: Under Section 54 a company may issue sweat equity shares of a class of shares already issued if (i) the issue is authorised by a special resolution; (ii) the resolution specifies the number of shares, the current market price, the consideration if any, and the class or classes of directors or employees to whom they are to be issued; (iii) where the equity shares are listed on a recognised stock exchange the issue complies with SEBI regulations, and if not listed, with Rule 8 of the Companies (Share and Debentures) Rules, 2014. Sweat equity shares carry the same rights, limitations and restrictions as equity shares and rank pari passu with other equity shareholders. Trisha Data Security Limited can issue sweat equity shares; it makes no difference that it is only about a year old, because there is no age or commencement-of-business requirement under Section 54.
  • Q6 — Walnut Foods Limited (application of securities premium): authorised share capital of 2,00,000 equity shares of ₹100 per share and ₹2 crore in its Securities Premium Account as on 31-3-2024. Answer: Under Section 52, the premium must be transferred to a "securities premium account" and the provisions relating to reduction of share capital apply as if it were paid-up share capital. It may be applied — (a) towards the issue of unissued shares to members as fully paid bonus shares; (b) in writing off preliminary expenses; (c) in writing off the expenses of, or commission paid or discount allowed on, any issue of shares or debentures; (d) in providing for the premium payable on redemption of any redeemable preference shares or debentures; or (e) for the purchase of its own shares or other securities under Section 68. For such class of companies as may be prescribed whose financial statements comply with the accounting standards under Section 133, it may be applied only — (a) in paying up unissued equity shares to be issued as fully paid bonus shares; (b) in writing off expenses/commission/discount on any issue of equity shares; or (c) for purchase of its own shares or other securities under Section 68. Walnut Foods Limited should utilise its Securities Premium Account accordingly.
  • Q7 — OLAF Limited / Mr. Surya Nayan (loan to an employee to buy shares): OLAF Limited, a subsidiary of PQR Limited, decided to give a loan of ₹4,00,000 to its Human Resource Manager Mr. Surya Nayan — who is not Key Managerial Personnel and draws a salary of ₹40,000 per month — to buy 500 partly paid-up equity shares of ₹1000 each in OLAF Limited. Answer: Under Section 67(3) a company may lend to its employees subject to — (a) the employee must not be a director or KMP; (b) the loan shall not exceed six months' salary; (c) the loan must be for subscribing fully paid-up shares. The decision is invalid on two counts: (i) ₹4,00,000 exceeds six months' salary — it should have been restricted to ₹2,40,000 only (6 × ₹40,000); and (ii) the loan is meant for the purchase of partly paid shares.
  • Q8 — Shilpi Developers India Limited / Sunil (shares for consideration other than cash): the company owed Sunil ₹10,000; on the debt becoming payable it offered him 100 shares of ₹100 each in full settlement, and allotted them to him as fully paid-up in lieu of his debt. Answer: Under Section 62(1)(c), where a company proposes to increase its subscribed capital by issue of further shares either for cash or for a consideration other than cash, such shares may be offered to any persons if authorised by a special resolution and if the price is determined by the valuation report of a registered valuer, subject to compliance with the applicable provisions of Chapter III and any other prescribed conditions. For this allotment to be classified as shares issued for consideration other than cash, it must be approved by the members by a special resolution and the valuation must be done by a registered valuer.
  • Q9 — appointment of debenture trustees (three specific persons): Under Section 71(5), no company shall issue a prospectus or make an offer or invitation to the public or to its members exceeding five hundred for subscription of its debentures unless it has, before such issue or offer, appointed one or more debenture trustees. Rule 18(2) requires written consent to be obtained before appointment, with a statement to that effect in the letter of offer, and disqualifies a person who beneficially holds shares in the company; is a promoter, director, KMP, officer or employee of the company or its holding, subsidiary or associate company; is beneficially entitled to moneys payable by the company otherwise than as trustee remuneration; is indebted to the company or its subsidiary, holding or associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company; has furnished any guarantee in respect of the principal debts secured by the debentures or interest thereon; has a pecuniary relationship with the company amounting to two percent or more of gross turnover or total income or ₹50 lakh (or such higher amount as prescribed), whichever is lower, during the two immediately preceding financial years or the current financial year; or is a relative of any promoter or of any person in the employment of the company as a director or KMP. Answers: (i) a shareholder who has no beneficial interest CAN be appointed as a debenture trustee; (ii) a creditor whom the company owes ₹499 CANNOT be appointed — the amount owed is immaterial; (iii) a person who has given a guarantee for repayment of the principal and interest on the debentures CANNOT be appointed.
  • Q10 — Mr. Nilesh / Ms. Mukta / Perfect Vision Private Limited (no notice of refusal): Mr. Nilesh transferred 1000 equity shares to his sister Ms. Mukta; the company neither registered the transfer nor sent a notice of refusal to either of them within the prescribed period. Answer: The company committed the wrongful act of not sending the notice of refusal. Under Section 58(1) a private company limited by shares refusing to register a transfer must send notice of refusal to the transferor and the transferee within thirty days of delivery of the instrument. Under Section 58(3) the transferee may appeal to the Tribunal within thirty days from receipt of the notice, or, where no notice has been sent, within sixty days from the date on which the instrument of transfer was delivered to the company. As no notice of refusal was sent, Ms. Mukta as transferee may appeal to the Tribunal within sixty days from the date the instrument of transfer was delivered.
  • Q11 — Shankar Portland Cement Limited (bonus issue 1:2): Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2024 — Authorised Share Capital 25,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each = ₹2,50,00,000; Issued, subscribed and paid-up capital 10,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully paid-up = ₹1,00,00,000; Free Reserves ₹3,00,00,000. The Board proposes a bonus issue of 1 share for every 2 shares held. Answer: Under Section 63 bonus shares may be issued out of (i) free reserves, (ii) the securities premium account, or (iii) the capital redemption reserve account — but not by capitalising reserves created by revaluation of assets. Conditions: authorised by the Articles; authorised in general meeting on the Board's recommendation; no default in payment of interest or principal on fixed deposits or debt securities; no default in payment of statutory dues of employees such as provident fund contribution, gratuity and bonus; partly paid-up shares outstanding on the date of allotment made fully paid-up; and compliance with Rule 14 — a bonus issue once announced by the Board cannot subsequently be withdrawn. Bonus shares must not be issued in lieu of dividend. Computation: the issue requires reserves of ₹50,00,000 (half of ₹1,00,00,000 paid-up capital), which is readily available out of the free reserves of ₹3,00,00,000. Hence, after complying with the above conditions, the company may proceed with the bonus issue of 1 share for every 2 shares held.
  • Q12 — Declaration of Solvency by an unlisted public company on buy-back: Under Section 68(6), where an unlisted public company has passed a special resolution under Section 68(2)(b), or the Board has passed a resolution under item (ii) of the proviso to Section 68(2)(b), to buy back its own shares, it shall, before making such buy-back, file with the Registrar a Declaration of Solvency in Form SH-9. The declaration must be verified by an affidavit to the effect that the Board has made a full inquiry into the affairs of the company as a result of which it has formed the opinion that the company is capable of meeting its liabilities and will not be rendered insolvent within a period of one year from the date of the declaration of solvency adopted by the Board. It must be signed by at least two directors, one of whom shall be the managing director, if any.

Buy-Back Procedure — Time Check Points [Rule 17]

StepTime limit
File letter of offer with the Registrar in Form SH-8, with feeBefore the buy-back
Dispatch the letter of offer to shareholders/security holdersImmediately after filing with the RoC, but not later than twenty days from its filing
Offer for buy-back to remain openNot less than fifteen days and not exceeding thirty days from the date of dispatch of the letter of offer; where all members of the company agree, the offer may remain open for less than fifteen days
Oversubscription of the offerAcceptance per shareholder on a proportionate basis out of the total shares offered for buy-back
Complete verification of offers receivedWithin fifteen days from the date of closure of the offer; securities lodged are deemed accepted unless a communication of rejection is made within twenty one days from closure
Payment in cash to accepted holders / return of certificates to those not accepted (or the balance on part acceptance)Within seven days of the verification process
Extinguish and physically destroy the securities bought back [Sec 68(7)]Within seven days of the last date of completion of buy-back
Complete the buy-back [Sec 68(4)]Within twelve months from the date of passing the special resolution or Board resolution
File return of buy-back in Form SH-11 with the Registrar (and SEBI, if listed), with a Form SH-15 compliance certificate signed by two directors including the MD, if any [Sec 68(10)]Within thirty days of completion
Cooling period before a further issue of the same kind of securities [Sec 68(8)]Six months (bonus issue and discharge of existing obligations excepted)
Gap between successive buy-back offers [Proviso to Sec 68(2)]One year from the date of closure of the preceding offer

Why It Matters / Application

Chapter IV determines what a company may lawfully do with its own capital structure, and almost every question turns on a threshold, a form or a date. Whether a rights issue can bypass a 45% shareholder (it cannot — Sec 62(1)(a)), whether a ₹4,00,000 loan to an HR manager on ₹40,000 salary is legal (it is not — the cap is six months' salary and the shares must be fully paid — Sec 67(3)), whether a company that cured a loan default in December 2020 can buy back shares in December 2022 (it cannot — Sec 70 requires three clear years), whether a CRR transfer covers the redemption premium (it does not — only the nominal amount, Sec 55(2)(c)) — each answer is a mechanical application of a specific sub-section. The chapter also supplies the arithmetic that valuation and secretarial work depend on: the 25%/10% buy-back tests measured against paid-up capital plus free reserves, the 2:1 post-buy-back debt ratio, the 15%/25%/50% sweat equity ceilings, the 74% differential-voting cap, the 75% class-consent and 10% dissent thresholds under Sec 48, the 90%-of-members consent for shorter rights-issue notice, the 10% DRR for unlisted companies and the 15%-by-30th-April investment requirement. Form numbers (SH-1 to SH-15, PAS-3) and delivery periods (two months on allotment, one month on transfer, six months on debentures) are the operational spine of company secretarial compliance under this chapter.

Note

Exceptions and exemptions to memorise. Sections 43 and 47 do not apply to a Specified IFSC public company or a private company where the MOA/AOA so provides. Section 62 does not apply to a Nidhi company, nor to conversion of debentures or loans into equity where the terms were approved by special resolution before issue/grant [Sec 62(3)]. Section 67 does not apply to qualifying private companies and Specified IFSC public companies meeting all three conditions (no body-corporate investment; borrowings less than twice paid-up capital or ₹50 crore, whichever is lower; no subsisting default), and Sec 67(1) does not apply to Nidhi companies buying shares from a member ceasing to be a depositor or borrower. Section 66 does not apply to buy-back under Section 68 [Sec 66(6)].

Amendments. Common seal became optional w.e.f. 29-05-2015 (Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015). Section 53(2A), permitting issue at a discount to creditors on conversion of debt under a statutory resolution plan or debt restructuring scheme per RBI directions, was inserted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 effective 09 February 2018. The one-year-since-commencement condition in Section 54(1)(c) for sweat equity was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 w.e.f. 7 May 2018. Rule 12A, prescribing a minimum seven-day acceptance period for rights offers, was inserted by G.S.R. 113(E) dated 11 February 2021. Rule 9A of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, requiring every unlisted public company to issue securities only in dematerialised form, was inserted w.e.f. 2-10-2018. Equity shares with differential rights issued under the Companies Act, 1956 continue to be regulated under those provisions [G.S.R. 413(E), w.e.f. 18 June 2014]; before the year 2000 amendment to the 1956 Act, differential voting rights shares could not be issued, though such rights existed before that Act was enacted.

Exam traps. (1) Section 48 counts 75% of the issued shares of a class, not 75% of the number of holders — the DBS Chemicals MCQ answer is 3, not 1. (2) Section 62(2)'s shorter-notice consent counts 90% of members by number, not by shareholding — 3,075 of 4,230 members is 72.70% and fails, even though they hold 94% of shares. (3) The 10% buy-back exemption from a special resolution requires a Board resolution passed at a meeting, not an ordinary resolution. (4) Only the nominal amount of redeemed preference shares goes to CRR — never the premium. (5) A duplicate certificate takes three months for unlisted and 45 days for listed companies — the December 30, 2022 MCQ answer is 29 March 2023. (6) Appeal windows differ by company type: 30/60 days for private companies, 60/90 days for public companies. (7) Notice of refusal under Sec 58(1) must go to both transferor and transferee. (8) Debenture holders never acquire voting rights for unpaid interest — the two-year unpaid-dividend voting right belongs only to preference shareholders. (9) Bonus shares can never be issued in lieu of dividend, never out of revaluation reserve, and never on shares that remain partly paid on the date of allotment. (10) A bonus issue once announced by the Board cannot be withdrawn [Rule 14].

Note on source numbering. The chapter's own example numbering skips Example 5 and Example 22, and repeats the numbers "Example 9" (discount; and Medanta Healthcare) and "Example 24" (reduction to ₹7 fully paid; and the NCLT three-month representation timeline). All items appearing in the source are reproduced above.

Chapter 5 — Acceptance of Deposits by Companies

Source: 87773bos-aps2160-ch5.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Statutory scope: Chapter V of the Companies Act, 2013 consists of Sections 73 to 76A read with the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014. Section 73 = prohibition & acceptance from members; Section 74 = repayment of pre-1-4-2014 deposits; Section 76 = acceptance from public by eligible companies; Section 76A = punishment for contravention of Section 73 or 76.
  • Why deposits are regulated: deposits from members and the public are an important source of finance for the corporate sector, so the law controls the companies inviting them to safeguard persons who part with their precious savings.
  • Inclusive definition: ‘deposit’ under Section 2(31) is an inclusive definition — any receipt of money by way of deposit, or loan, or in any other form, minus the prescribed exclusions notified in consultation with the RBI. So the starting presumption is that money received is a deposit unless it fits an exclusion in Rule 2(1)(c).
  • Who may take deposits from whom: a private company can accept deposits from its members only; a public company can accept from its members, and additionally from the public only if it is an ‘eligible company’ (net worth ≥ ₹100 crore or turnover ≥ ₹500 crore).
  • Deposit provisions regulate non-banking non-financial companies: banking companies, NBFCs and housing finance companies are outside the net, so the rules effectively bite on manufacturing companies, trading companies etc.
  • Secured vs unsecured deposits: secured deposits are fully secured by creating a charge on tangible assets; where security is partial or absent, the deposits are unsecured deposits and must be so described in every circular, form, advertisement or document relating to invitation/acceptance.

Key Definitions / Terms

Deposit [Section 2(31)]
Includes any receipt of money by way of deposit or loan or in any other form, by a company, but does not include such categories of amount as may be prescribed in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India. Features: repayment is time-bound; it may be secured or unsecured; it may be accepted in joint names not exceeding three persons; a depositor may nominate any person at any time; every deposit shall be repaid with interest; premature repayment is permitted.
Depositor [Rule 2(1)(d)]
(i) any member of the company who has made a deposit with the company under Section 73(2); or (ii) any person who has made a deposit with a public company under Section 76. Hence any member of a private or public company who deposits money is a depositor, and any person even if not a member is a depositor if he deposits with a public (eligible) company.
Eligible company [Rule 2(1)(e) / Section 76(1)]
A public company having net worth of not less than ₹100 crore or turnover of not less than ₹500 crore, which has obtained prior consent in general meeting by special resolution and has filed that resolution with the Registrar before making any invitation to the public. Proviso: an eligible company accepting deposits within the limits specified under Section 180(1)(c) may accept deposits by an ordinary resolution.
Start-up company [Explanation to Rule 2(1)(c)(xvii)]
A private company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 or the Companies Act, 1956 and recognised as a start-up in accordance with Notification No. G.S.R. 127(E), dated 19-02-2019 issued by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade.
Convertible note [Explanation to Rule 2(1)(c)(xvii)]
An instrument evidencing receipt of money initially as a debt, repayable at the option of the holder, or convertible into such number of equity shares of the start-up company upon occurrence of specified events and as per the other terms indicated in the instrument.
Specified IFSC public company
An unlisted public company licensed to operate by the RBI or SEBI or IRDAI from the International Financial Services Centre located in an approved multi-services Special Economic Zone set up under the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 read with the SEZ Rules, 2006.
Deposit Repayment Reserve Account [Section 73(2)(c), Rule 13]
A separate account with a scheduled bank in which, on or before 30th April each year, the company deposits at least 20% of the amount of its deposits maturing during the following financial year; the balance shall not at any time fall below 20% of deposits maturing during the financial year and the money cannot be used for any purpose other than repayment of deposits.

Amounts NOT Considered as Deposit [Rule 2(1)(c)]

Sub-clauseAmount receivedCondition / proviso attached
(i)From the Central Government; a State Government; any source whose repayment is guaranteed by the Central or a State Government; a local authority; a statutory authority constituted under an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature—
(ii)From foreign Governments; foreign or international banks; multilateral financial institutions (including but not limited to International Finance Corporation, Asian Development Bank, Commonwealth Development Corporation, International Bank for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction); foreign Government-owned development financial institutions; foreign export credit agencies; foreign collaborators; foreign bodies corporate and foreign citizens; foreign authorities or persons resident outside IndiaReceipt of funds is subject to the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 and rules/regulations made thereunder
(iii)As a loan or facility from any banking company; SBI or its subsidiary banks; a notified banking institution; a corresponding new bank as defined in the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts of 1970 and 1980; any co-operative bank—
(iv)As a loan or financial assistance from Public Financial Institutions (as notified by the Central Government in consultation with the RBI); any regional financial institutions; insurance companies; scheduled banks as defined in the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934—
(v)Against issue of commercial paper or any other instrument issued per RBI guidelines/notification—
(vi)By a company from any other company — Inter Company Deposit (ICD)—
(vii)Held towards subscription to any securities, including share application money or advance towards allotment pending allotmentOnly so long as appropriated against the amount due on allotment. If securities cannot be allotted within 60 days of receipt and the money is not refunded within 15 days from the completion of those 60 days, it becomes a deposit. Any adjustment of the amount for any other purpose is not a refund.
(viii)From a person who at the time of receipt was a director of the company, or a relative of the director of a private companyThe giver must furnish, at the time of giving the money, a written declaration that the amount is not being given out of funds acquired by him by borrowing or accepting loans/deposits from others; and the company must disclose the details in the Board's report
(ix)Raised by issue of bonds/debentures secured by a first charge or a charge ranking pari passu with the first charge on assets referred to in Schedule III (excluding intangible assets); or bonds/debentures compulsorily convertible into shares within 10 yearsWhere secured by a charge on Schedule III assets (excluding intangibles), the amount of such bonds/debentures shall not exceed the market value of such assets as assessed by a registered valuer
(ixa)Raised by issue of non-convertible debentures not constituting a charge on the assets of the company and listed on a recognised stock exchange as per applicable SEBI regulations—
(x)From an employee, not exceeding his annual salary, under a contract of employment, in the nature of a non-interest bearing security depositAny excess over annual salary makes the whole amount a deposit
(xi)Any non-interest bearing amount received and held in trust—
(xii)Received in the course of, or for the purposes of, the business of the company — (a) advance for supply of goods or provision of services; (b) advance towards consideration for an immovable property under an agreement/arrangement; (c) security deposit for performance of a contract for supply of goods or provision of services; (d) advance under long-term projects for supply of capital goods (other than (b)); (e) advance towards future services as a warranty or maintenance contract; (f) advance allowed by any sectoral regulator or per directions of the Central/State Government; (g) advance for subscription towards publication, print or electronic(a) must be appropriated against supply within 365 days of acceptance — the 365-day limit does not apply where the advance is the subject matter of legal proceedings before any court; (b) must be adjusted against the property per the terms of the agreement; (e) service period must not exceed common business practice or five years from acceptance, whichever is less; (g) adjusted against receipt of publications. Deeming rule: amounts under (a), (b) and (d) that become refundable (with or without interest) because the company lacks the necessary permission/approval to deal in those goods, properties or services are deemed deposits, and are deemed deposits on expiry of 15 days from the date they become due for refund.
(xiii)Brought in by promoters by way of unsecured loan in pursuance of a stipulation of a lending financial institution or bankAll three must hold: (a) the loan is brought because of a stipulation imposed by the lending institution on the promoters to contribute such finance; (b) the loan is provided by the promoters themselves or their relatives or both; (c) the exemption is available only till the loans of the financial institution or bank are repaid and not thereafter
(xiv)Accepted by a Nidhi company in accordance with rules made under Section 406—
(xv)By way of subscription in respect of a chit under the Chit Fund Act, 1982—
(xvi)Under any collective investment scheme in compliance with SEBI regulations—
(xvii)₹25 lakh or more received by a start-up company by way of a convertible note (convertible into equity shares, or repayable within a period not exceeding 10 years from the date of issue) in a single tranche, from a personFails the exemption if the ₹25 lakh is built up over more than one tranche, or if repayment tenure exceeds 10 years
(xviii)From Alternate Investment Funds, Domestic Venture Capital Funds, Infrastructure Investment Trusts, Real Estate Investment Trusts and Mutual Funds registered with SEBI, in accordance with SEBI regulations‘Real Estate Investment Trusts’ inserted by the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Amendment Rules, 2019 w.e.f. 22-01-2019

Pre-1-4-2014 receipts by private companies [General Circular No. 5/2015, dated 30-03-2015]: amounts received by private companies from their members, directors or their relatives before 1st April, 2014 are not to be treated as deposits, provided the private company discloses in the notes to its financial statement the figure of such amounts and the accounting head under which they are shown. Any renewal, or acceptance of fresh deposits, on or after 1st April, 2014 must comply with the Act and Rules.

Prohibition and Exempted Companies

  • Section 73(1): on and after commencement of the Act, no company shall invite, accept or renew deposits from the public except in the manner provided in Chapter V.
  • Proviso to Section 73(1) + Rule 1(3) — deposit provisions do not apply to: (i) any banking company; (ii) any Non-Banking Financial Company as defined in the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934; (iii) any Housing Finance Company registered with the National Housing Bank established under the National Housing Bank Act, 1987; (iv) such other company as the Central Government may specify after consultation with the RBI.
  • Rule 18 — Power of Central Government: if any question arises as to the applicability of these Rules to a particular company, that question is decided by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India.

How It Works — Deposits from Members [Section 73(2) & Rules]

  • (1) Resolution: a resolution must be passed in general meeting for acceptance of deposits from members [Section 73(2)].
  • (2) Circular in Form DPT-1 [Section 73(2)(a), Rule 4]: a circular to all members showing the financial position of the company, the credit rating obtained, the total number of depositors and the amount due towards deposits in respect of previous deposits. Sent by registered post with acknowledgement due, or speed post, or electronic mode, in Form DPT-1. It may additionally be published in English in an English newspaper and in the vernacular in a vernacular newspaper having wide circulation in the State where the registered office is situated. It is issued on the authority and in the name of the Board of Directors.
  • Statutory auditor's certificate in DPT-1: stating no default has been committed in repayment of deposits or payment of interest, whether accepted before or after commencement of the Act. If a default had occurred, the certificate must state that the company made good the default and that a period of five years has lapsed since the date of making good the default.
  • Validity of circular: valid till the earliest of — (a) six months from the closure of the financial year in which it is issued; or (b) the date on which the financial statements are laid before the company at the AGM, or where no AGM was held, the latest day on which the AGM should have been held. A fresh circular must be issued in each succeeding financial year.
  • (3) Filing of circular [Section 73(2)(b)]: a copy of the circular with the statement must be filed with the Registrar within 30 days before the date of issue of the circular.
  • (4) Deposit Repayment Reserve [Section 73(2)(c), Rule 13]: on or before 30th April each year deposit at least 20% of deposits maturing during the following financial year in a separate account with a scheduled bank; the balance shall not at any time fall below 20% of deposits maturing during the financial year.
  • (5) Certification of no default [Section 73(2)(e)]: as above, with the five-year cooling period after making good any earlier default. Note: clause (d) relating to deposit insurance was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 w.e.f. 15th August, 2018.
  • (6) Security [Section 73(2)(f)]: security is optional; if provided, the company must take steps to create a charge on its property or assets. If deposits are not secured, or only partially secured, they are unsecured deposits and must be described as such in every circular, form, advertisement or document.
  • (7) Repayment [Section 73(3)]: every deposit shall be repaid with interest per the terms of the agreement.
  • (8) NCLT [Section 73(4)]: on failure to repay deposit or interest, the depositor may apply to the National Company Law Tribunal for an order directing payment of the sum due or for loss or damage incurred, and such other orders as the NCLT deems fit.
  • (9) Use of DRR [Section 73(5), Rule 13]: the Deposit Repayment Reserve Account cannot be used for any purpose other than repayment of deposits.
  • (14) Interest and brokerage [Rule 3(6)]: any rate of interest or brokerage is permissible but it shall not exceed the maximum rate of interest or brokerage prescribed by the RBI for NBFCs. No brokerage is payable except to a person authorised in writing by the company to solicit deposits and through whom deposits are actually procured; payment to anyone else is deemed a violation of the deposit rules.
  • (15) Application form [Rule 10]: deposits (secured or unsecured) are accepted or renewed only on an application submitted by the intending depositor, containing a declaration that the deposit is not being made out of any money borrowed by him from any other person.
  • (16) Joint names [Rule 3(2)]: deposits may be accepted in joint names not exceeding three, with or without the clauses “Jointly”, “Either or Survivor”, “First named or Survivor”, “Anyone or Survivor”. These clauses operate on maturity.
  • (17) Nomination [Rule 11]: every depositor may nominate any person at any time; the deposit vests in the nominee on the depositor's death.
  • (18) Deposit receipt [Rule 12]: to be furnished to the depositor or his agent within 21 days from the date of receipt of money, or realisation of cheque, or date of renewal — signed by an officer duly authorised by the Board and stating date of deposit, name and address of the depositor, amount, rate of interest and maturity date.
  • (21) Return of deposits [Rule 16]: a duly audited return in Form DPT-3 with particulars as on 31st March of every year, filed with the Registrar with fee on or before 30th June of that year, with the auditor's declaration in Form DPT-3 (inserted by the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Amendment Rules, 2022). DPT-3 covers particulars of deposits, or of transactions not considered deposits, or both, by every company other than a Government company.
  • (22) No alteration [Rule 3(7)]: after the circular/advertisement is issued and deposits accepted, the company cannot alter, directly or indirectly, any terms of the deposit, deposit trust deed or deposit insurance contract to the disadvantage of depositors.
  • (23) Disclosure [Rule 16A]: a public company discloses in its financial statements by note the money received from its directors; a private company discloses money received from its directors or relatives of directors. As a one-time measure under Rule 16A(3), every company (other than a Government company) had to file a one-time return in Form DPT-3 of outstanding receipts of money or loan not considered deposits from 1st April 2014 till 31st March 2019, within ninety days from 31st March 2019.
  • (24) Penal interest [Rule 17]: on failure to repay deposits (secured or unsecured) on maturity after they are claimed, the company pays penal interest of 18% per annum for the overdue period.
