Exemption to Certain Private Companies from Section 73(2)(a) to (e)

In terms of Notification No. GSR 464(E), dated 05-06-2015 as amended, clauses (a) to (e) of Section 73(2) — issue of circular, filing the copy with the Registrar, depositing the DRR amount and certification as to no default — shall not apply to a private company:

  • (A) which accepts from its members monies not exceeding 100% of aggregate of the paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium account; or
  • (B) which is a start-up, for five years from the date of its incorporation; or
  • (C) which fulfils all of the following: (a) it is not an associate or a subsidiary company of any other company; (b) its borrowings from banks or financial institutions or any body corporate are less than twice its paid-up share capital or ₹50 crore, whichever is lower; and (c) it has not defaulted in the repayment of such borrowings subsisting at the time of accepting deposits under this section.
  • Such a company must nevertheless file the details of monies accepted with the Registrar in Form DPT-3.
  • By Notification No. GSR 8(E), dated 04-01-2017, clauses (a) to (e) of Section 73(2) also do not apply to a Specified IFSC public company accepting from its members monies not exceeding 100% of aggregate of paid-up share capital and free reserves, subject to filing in Form DPT-3.

Deposits from the Public by Eligible Companies [Section 76]

  • Only eligible companies may access the public; acceptance is subject to compliance with Section 73(2) and the prescribed Rules. Under Rule 19 and Section 76(2), Sections 73 and 74 (indeed the whole of Chapter V) apply mutatis mutandis to deposits accepted from the public under Section 76.
  • Credit rating [first proviso to Section 76(1), Rule 3(8)]: the rating (covering net worth, liquidity and ability to pay deposits on the due date) must be obtained from a recognised credit rating agency, informed to the public at the time of invitation, and obtained every year during the tenure of the deposits. A copy obtained at least once a year is sent to the Registrar along with the Return of Deposits in Form DPT-3. The rating shall not be below the minimum investment grade rating or other specified rating for fixed deposits, from one of the agencies approved for NBFCs under the Non-Banking Financial Companies Acceptance of Public Deposits (Reserve Bank) Directions, 1998.
  • Charge for secured deposits [second proviso to Section 76(1), Rule 6]: a company accepting secured public deposits must create a charge on its assets within thirty days of acceptance, of an amount not less than the deposits accepted, in favour of the deposit holders. Security may be created on tangible assets only — not on intangible assets such as goodwill or trademarks. Total value of security must not be less than the deposits accepted and interest payable thereon; market value of the charged assets is assessed by a registered valuer; the security is created in favour of a trustee for the depositors on specific movable and immovable property.
  • Circular in the form of advertisement [Rule 4]: issued in Form DPT-1, published in English in an English newspaper and in the vernacular in a vernacular newspaper, both with wide circulation in the State of the registered office, and also placed on the company's website if it has one; issued on the authority and in the name of the Board. A copy signed by a majority of the directors who approved it (or by their duly authorised agents) must be delivered to the Registrar for registration at least thirty days before its issue. Validity is the same as for the members' circular. The date of issue of an advertisement is the date it appeared in the newspaper; the effective date of issue of a circular is the date the circular was dispatched. A fresh advertisement is required in each succeeding financial year.
  • Premature repayment [Rule 15]: where a depositor requests premature repayment after the expiry of six months but before the maturity date, the interest rate payable is 1% less than the rate payable for the period the deposit has actually run. In computing the period run, a part of a year that is less than six months is excluded; a part that is six months or more is taken as one year. The 1% reduction does not apply where the deposit is prematurely repaid (i) to comply with Rule 3, i.e. to bring the total deposits within the permissible limits, or (ii) to provide for war risk or other related benefits to personnel of the naval, military or air forces or their families during an emergency declared under Article 352 of the Constitution.
  • Premature closure to earn a higher rate [second proviso to Rule 15]: where a depositor renews his deposit before the actual maturity date to avail a higher rate of interest, the company pays the higher rate only if the deposit is renewed for a period longer than the unexpired period of the original deposit.

Trustee for Depositors [Rule 7] and Meetings [Rule 9]

  • No circular or advertisement inviting secured deposits may be issued unless one or more trustees for depositors are appointed for creating security.
  • Written consent must be obtained from the trustees before appointment, and a statement to the effect that the trustees have given their consent must appear in the circular/advertisement with reasonable prominence.
  • A Deposit Trust Deed in Form DPT-2 must be executed at least seven days before issuing the circular or circular in the form of advertisement.
  • Disqualifications: no person — including a company in the business of providing trusteeship services — may be appointed trustee if he (a) is a director, key managerial personnel or any other officer or employee of the company or of its holding, subsidiary or associate company, or a depositor in the company; (b) is indebted to the company, or its subsidiary, holding or associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company; (c) has any material pecuniary relationship with the company; (d) has entered into any guarantee arrangement in respect of principal debts secured by the deposits or interest thereon; (e) is related to any person specified in clause (a).
  • Removal: after issue of the circular/advertisement and before expiry of his term, a trustee may be removed only with the consent of all the directors present at a Board meeting; where the company is required to have independent directors, at least one independent director must be present at that meeting.
  • Trustee to call a meeting of depositors [Rule 9]: (a) on receipt of a requisition in writing signed by at least one-tenth of the depositors in value for the time being outstanding; or (b) on the happening of any event which constitutes a default or which, in the trustee's opinion, affects the interest of depositors.

Register of Deposits [Rule 14]

  • Every company accepting deposits maintains one or more separate registers at its registered office, with the following entered separately for each depositor: (a) name, address and PAN; (b) particulars of the guardian, in case of a minor; (c) particulars of the nominee; (d) deposit receipt number; (e) date and amount of each deposit; (f) duration of the deposit and the date on which each deposit is repayable; (g) rate of interest payable; (h) due date for payment of interest; (i) mandate and instructions for payment of interest and for non-deduction of tax at source, if any; (j) date or dates on which interest shall be paid; (l) particulars of security or charge created for repayment of deposits; (m) any other relevant particulars.
  • Entries must be made within seven days from the date of issuance of the receipt, duly authenticated by a director or secretary or any other officer authorised by the Board.
  • The register must be preserved in good order for not less than eight years from the financial year in which the latest entry is made. Clause (k), relating to details of deposit insurance, was omitted by the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Amendment Rules, 2018 [Notification No. G.S.R. 612(E), dated 5th July 2018] w.e.f. 15-08-2018.

Punishment / Penalties

DefaultCompanyOfficer-in-default
Section 76A — accepting/inviting deposits, or allowing another to do so on its behalf, in contravention of the manner or conditions under Section 73 or 76 or the Rules; or failing to repay deposit/part/interest within the time specified under Section 73 or 76 or the Rules or such further time allowed by the Tribunal under Section 73In addition to repaying the deposit or part thereof and the interest due — fine not less than ₹1 crore or twice the amount of deposit accepted, whichever is lower, extendable to ₹10 croreImprisonment which may extend to seven years and fine not less than ₹25 lakh, extendable to ₹2 crore. If it is proved that he contravened knowingly or wilfully with intent to deceive the company, its shareholders, depositors, creditors or tax authorities, he is liable for action under Section 447 (punishment for fraud)
Section 74(3) — failure to repay pre-commencement deposits within the time in Section 74(1) or the extended time allowed by the Tribunal under Section 74(2)In addition to repayment of deposit and interest due — fine minimum ₹1 crore, maximum ₹10 croreImprisonment extendable to seven years, or fine minimum ₹25 lakh and maximum ₹2 crore, or both
Rule 21 — contravention of any deposit rule by a company inviting deposits (including an eligible company) or any other person, where no punishment is provided in the ActFine extendable to ₹5,000; if continuing, further fine up to ₹500 for every day after the first day during which the contravention continuesSame as company (company and every officer-in-default)

Repayment of Pre-2013-Act Deposits [Section 74]

  • Section 74(1): where a deposit was accepted before commencement of the Act (i.e. before 1-4-2014) and the deposit or interest remains unpaid as on 1-4-2014 or becomes due thereafter, the company must — (a) file with the Registrar within 3 months from such commencement or from the date on which such payments are due, a statement of all deposits accepted, sums remaining unpaid with interest payable thereon, and the arrangements made for repayment (notwithstanding anything in any other law in force, or in the terms on which the deposit was accepted, or any scheme framed under any law); and (b) repay within three years from such commencement, or on or before expiry of the period for which the deposits were accepted, whichever is earlier.
  • Note 1 (Explanation to Rule 19): if the company has been repaying such deposits and interest without default on due dates for the remaining period of the deposit in accordance with the terms and conditions, requirement (b) is deemed complied with.
  • Note 2: renewal of any such deposit must be done in accordance with Chapter V and the rules made thereunder.
  • Section 74(2): the Tribunal may, on application by the company and after considering its financial condition, the amount of deposit and interest payable and other matters, allow further time as it considers reasonable to repay the deposit.

Examples

  • Example 1 — Soorya Ltd., listed NCDs: raised ₹20,00,000 through issue of non-convertible debentures (20,000 NCDs of ₹100 each) not constituting a charge on the company's assets, listed on a recognised stock exchange as per applicable SEBI regulations. Not a deposit, under sub-clause (ixa).
  • Example 2 — Ratnakar / Siddhi Transporters and Logistics Limited: Ratnakar was appointed Supervisor on an annual salary of ₹6,00,000 and required to deposit ₹6,50,000 under the contract of employment as a non-interest bearing security deposit. Since the amount exceeds his annual salary, it will be considered a deposit under sub-clause (x). Had the security deposit been limited to ₹6,00,000 or less, it would not have been a deposit.
  • Example 3 — Greedwood Limited, start-up convertible note: the company received ₹20 lakh and ₹10 lakh on different dates by way of convertible note. Although the aggregate is ₹25 lakh or more, it was not received in a single tranche, so the amount will be considered a deposit under sub-clause (xvii).
  • Example 4 — Ray Pharmaceuticals Limited, validity of circular: circular inviting deposits from members issued on 14-02-2023; AGM held on 07-09-2023. Six months from the closure of FY 2022-23 ends on 30-09-2023, but the AGM date is earlier, so the circular remains valid only till 07-09-2023. A fresh circular is needed thereafter to invite further deposits.
  • Example 5 — Arpit / Swapnil Traders Private Limited, tenure: Arpit, a member, deposited ₹1,00,000 on 1st April 2024. Earliest repayment date is 30th September 2024 (6 months) and latest is 31st March 2027 (36 months); the tenure must lie between six and thirty-six months per company policy.
  • Example 6 — Swapnil Traders Private Limited, short-term deposits: assuming aggregate of paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium account is ₹2,00,00,000, to meet short-term fund requirements it can raise a maximum of ₹20,00,000 (10% of ₹2,00,00,000) with a repayment tenure of less than six months, but such deposits must be repayable only on or after three months from the date of deposit.
  • Example 7 — A, B and C, joint deposit of ₹3,00,000: under a “Jointly” clause, repayment on maturity is made to all three together (A, B and C) or the survivors; under “Either or Survivor”, to either A or B or C or the survivor; under “First named or Survivor”, to the first named person, i.e. A, or the survivor; under “Anyone or Survivor”, as in ‘Either or Survivor’.
  • MCQ 1 — Varsha Limited: raises deposits of ₹20 lakh from members but secures them only partially, offering security worth ₹15 lakh. Answer: (b) Unsecured deposits — partial security means the deposits are unsecured for the purpose of the Rules.
  • MCQ 2 — Maximum tenure for which a company can accept or renew deposits from members as well as public. Answer: (c) 36 months.
  • MCQ 3 — Fin Limited, Register of Deposits: minimum period for which the complete register at its registered office must be preserved. Answer: (c) Eight years from the financial year in which the latest entry is made in the Register.
  • MCQ 4 — Penal rate of interest per annum for the overdue period on deposits, secured or unsecured, matured and claimed but remaining unpaid. Answer: (c) 18%.
  • MCQ 5 — Eligible company tenure blanks: not repayable on demand or in less than ___ months; maximum period cannot exceed ___ months; for short-term requirements may be repayable earlier than ___ months. Answer: (a) six, thirty six, six.
  • Case Study 5(i) — Zarr Technology Private Limited (start-up): director Samit's friend Ritesh lent ₹30 lakh in a single tranche by convertible note repayable within six years of issue. Rule 2(1)(c)(xvii) requires ₹25 lakh or more, single tranche, and repayment within ten years — all satisfied. ₹30 lakh is NOT a deposit.
  • Case Study 5(ii) — Polestar Traders Limited / Rachna: loan of ₹30 lakh received from Rachna, one of its directors. Under Rule 2(1)(c)(viii) this is not a deposit, assuming she was a director at the time of giving the loan, she furnished a written declaration that the money was not out of funds acquired by borrowing or accepting loans/deposits from others, and the company disclosed the details in the Board's report.
  • Case Study 5(iii) — City Bakers Limited / Swati: failed to repay deposits of ₹50 crore and interest due even after the extended time granted by the Tribunal — a contravention of Section 73. Company: in addition to repaying the deposit and interest, fine not less than ₹1 crore or twice the deposit accepted, whichever is lower, extendable to ₹10 crore. Swati (officer-in-default): imprisonment up to seven years and fine not less than ₹25 lakh extendable to ₹2 crore; and if she contravened knowingly or wilfully with intent to deceive the company, shareholders, depositors, creditors or tax authorities, she is liable under Section 447.
  • Case Study 5(iv) — Shringaar Readymade Garments Limited: wants deposits of ₹50 lakh from members for a tenure of less than six months. Possible only if justified as meeting short-term requirements of funds, provided such deposits do not exceed 10% of the aggregate of paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium account and are repayable only on or after three months from the date of deposit.
  • Case Study 5(v) — Diamond Housing Finance Limited: assuming it is registered with the National Housing Bank, the Acceptance of Deposits Rules do not apply to it under Rule 1(3)(iii), and it is an exempted company under the proviso to Section 73(1). It can accept and renew public deposits from time to time without following the prescribed manner.
  • Question 6 — ABC Limited, net worth ₹120 crore: since net worth exceeds ₹100 crore it falls within ‘eligible company’. Special care: when accepting deposits from its members, the amount together with member deposits outstanding on the date of acceptance or renewal must not exceed 10% of the aggregate of paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium account [Rule 4(a)/Rule 3(4)]. It must also have obtained prior consent by special resolution (ordinary resolution if within Section 180(1)(c) limits) and filed it with the Registrar.
  • Question 7(i) — Rishi Confectionaries Limited: ₹5,00,000 raised through NCDs not constituting a charge on the company's assets and listed on a recognised stock exchange per SEBI regulations. Not a deposit — sub-clause (ixa) of Rule 2(1)(c).
  • Question 7(ii) — Raja Yarns Limited / Mr. Tarun: ₹2,00,000 received as a non-interest bearing security deposit under a contract of employment from an employee whose annual salary is ₹1,50,000. Since the amount received exceeds his annual salary, it IS a deposit — sub-clause (x).
  • Question 7(iii) — Private company / relative of a director: ₹3,00,000 received from a relative of a director who furnishes a declaration that the amount was received by him from his mother as a gift (hence not out of borrowed funds). Not a deposit — sub-clause (viii). The company must still disclose the details in the Board's report and, per Rule 16A(2), disclose in its financial statements by way of notes the money received from directors or relatives of directors.
  • Question 8(i) — ABC Private Limited (True/False): may it accept deposits from members of ₹50 lakh where the aggregate of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium account is ₹50 lakh? The general limit is 35% under Rule 3(3), but a private company may accept up to 100% of that aggregate and file details in Form DPT-3. ₹50 lakh = 100% of ₹50 lakh. Statement is TRUE.
  • Question 8(ii) — Government company (True/False): statement says an eligible Government company cannot accept public deposits exceeding 25% of the aggregate of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium account. Under Rule 3(5) the applicable ceiling is 35%, not 25%. Statement is FALSE.
  • Question 9(a) — Prayas Electricals Limited: paid-up capital ₹1 crore; availed a term loan of ₹10,00,000 from Beta Bank Limited to purchase electrical items. Director Mr. Sambhav says it is a deposit. Under Rule 2(1)(c)(iii) any amount received as a loan or facility from a banking company is not a deposit — Mr. Sambhav's contention is not correct.
  • Question 9(b) — Eklavya Publishing Company Limited: facing a cash crunch, wants to use part of the Deposit Repayment Reserve Account to pay short-term creditors pressing for ₹20,00,000. Rule 13 prohibits use of that account for any purpose other than repayment of deposits — the company is not permitted to do so.
  • Question 9(c) — Sanjiv / Utsah Textiles Private Limited: Sanjiv holds 10,000 shares of ₹10 each; his wife Sneha and three sons Aayush, Pranav and Himanshu hold 1,000 shares each. He wants to deposit ₹1,00,000 for 36 months jointly in five names. Rule 3(2) permits joint deposits not exceeding three names, so Sanjiv can deposit ₹1,00,000 jointly with two other persons only, irrespective of the fact that all five are members of the company.
  • Question 10 — Shubhra Chemicals Private Limited (not a start-up): wants to accept deposits from members of 200% of aggregate paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium account. The first proviso to Rule 3(3) caps a private company at 100%; but the second proviso removes the limit if the company (a) is not an associate or subsidiary of any other company; (b) has borrowings from banks/financial institutions/any body corporate less than twice its paid-up share capital or ₹50 crore, whichever is less; and (c) has not defaulted in repayment of such subsisting borrowings at the time of accepting deposits under Section 73. If all three are satisfied, it can accept 200%, and must file the details of monies accepted with the Registrar in Form DPT-3 (third proviso).

Forms Used in This Chapter

FormPurposeTiming
DPT-1Circular to members / circular in the form of advertisement inviting deposits, with the statutory auditor's certificate attachedFiled with the Registrar 30 days before issue; valid till the earlier of six months from FY closure or the AGM date
DPT-2Deposit Trust Deed for secured depositsExecuted at least seven days before issuing the circular/advertisement
DPT-3Audited Return of Deposits (particulars as on 31st March); also used for particulars of transactions not considered deposits; also used by exempted private companies and Specified IFSC public companies to report monies accepted; credit rating copy sent with itOn or before 30th June each year, with fee; one-time return under Rule 16A(3) was due within 90 days from 31-03-2019

Why It Matters / Application

The line between a ‘deposit’ and an excluded receipt decides whether a company must pass a general-meeting resolution, issue DPT-1, park 20% in a Deposit Repayment Reserve Account, and expose its officers to seven years' imprisonment under Section 76A. Because Section 2(31) is inclusive — deposit, loan, or money "in any other form" — routine commercial receipts such as customer advances, employee security deposits, promoter contributions and share application money fall inside the definition unless they satisfy a specific limb of Rule 2(1)(c) together with its time limit or declaration requirement. Each exclusion is therefore conditional, not absolute: a customer advance turns into a deposit on day 366; share application money turns into a deposit if allotment does not happen within 60 days and refund is not made within a further 15 days; a director's loan is exempt only if the written declaration was furnished at the time of giving the money; a promoter's unsecured loan is exempt only while the bank's stipulated loan remains outstanding. The chapter also fixes the financing architecture available to each type of company — a private company is confined to its own members (100% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium, unlimited if it is a start-up for ten years or meets the three-condition test), while public deposits are available only to the ₹100 crore net worth / ₹500 crore turnover eligible company, subject to annual credit rating, trustee appointment, DPT-2 trust deed and charge on tangible assets within thirty days.

Note

Amendments and omissions: Section 73(2)(d), which mandated deposit insurance, was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 w.e.f. 15-08-2018 — do not list deposit insurance as a live requirement. Correspondingly, clause (k) of the Register of Deposits (details of deposit insurance) was omitted by the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Amendment Rules, 2018 [G.S.R. 612(E), dated 05-07-2018] w.e.f. 15-08-2018, which is why Rule 14 runs (a)–(j) then (l), (m). ‘Real Estate Investment Trusts’ was inserted in sub-clause (xviii) by the 2019 Amendment Rules w.e.f. 22-01-2019. The auditor's declaration in Form DPT-3 was inserted by the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Amendment Rules, 2022.

Exam traps: (1) The 35% ceiling is for deposits from members of a company generally and for an eligible Government company's total deposits; 10%/25% is the members/non-members split for an ordinary eligible company; 100% is the private company / Specified IFSC public company member ceiling — a very common mix-up (see Question 8(ii), where 25% for a Government company is false). (2) The 10% figure also appears as the short-term deposit cap under the proviso to Rule 3(1) — a different rule with a three-month floor. (3) The circular's validity is the earliest of the two dates, so an AGM held before six months from FY closure cuts the circular short (Example 4). (4) The private-company start-up exemption from Section 73(2)(a)–(e) runs for five years from incorporation, but the exemption from the maximum deposit limit under the second proviso to Rule 3(3) runs for ten years — two different periods. (5) The three-condition test appears twice with different wording: borrowings less than twice paid-up share capital or ₹50 crore, “whichever is lower” in the GSR 464(E) exemption and “whichever is less” in the second proviso to Rule 3(3). (6) A convertible note fails the exclusion if the ₹25 lakh is not in a single tranche (Example 3) even though the ten-year test is met, whereas a six-year tenure is comfortably within the ten-year test (Case Study 5(i)). (7) The employee security deposit exclusion is breached the moment the amount exceeds annual salary — ₹6,50,000 against ₹6,00,000 salary, and ₹2,00,000 against ₹1,50,000 salary, both become deposits. (8) Joint deposits are capped at three names regardless of how many joint holders are members (Question 9(c)). (9) Rule 21's ₹5,000 / ₹500 per day fine applies only where no punishment is provided in the Act; where Section 73 or 76 is contravened, Section 76A's ₹1 crore–₹10 crore and ₹25 lakh–₹2 crore penalties apply instead.

Chapter 6 — Registration of Charges

Source: 87774bos-aps2160-ch6.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Scope of Chapter VI: Sections 77 to 87 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Registration of Charges) Rules, 2014 govern creation, modification, satisfaction and rectification of charges.
  • Charge as security, not as debt: A charge is the security interest attached to the company's property when it borrows. Registration protects the security; the underlying debt survives independently even if registration fails (Section 77(4)).
  • Registration is mandatory and time-bound: The duty falls first on the company creating the charge (Section 77), and only on failure does it shift to the charge-holder (Section 78) or to a purchaser of charged property (Section 79).
  • Charge can be created inside or outside India: The property, assets or undertaking charged may be situated within India or outside India, and may be tangible (land and building, machinery, investment in shares or debentures) or otherwise — i.e. intangible such as patent, copyright or trademark. The word "otherwise" in a section widens the scope and operation of the provision.
  • Charge by deposit of title deeds: Banks often accept an equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds instead of a proper mortgage (Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882). Such a charge is equally registrable by the borrowing company.
  • Public document / constructive notice: Every registered charge is a public document on the MCA Portal, so registration also operates as a fraud-prevention device — it stops a company from offering the same asset as security to a different lender.
  • Certificate is conclusive evidence: The Registrar's certificate of registration or modification is conclusive evidence that the requirements of Chapter VI and the Rules as to registration have been complied with.

Key Definitions / Terms

Charge [Section 2(16)]
"An interest or lien created on the property or assets of a company or any of its undertakings or both as security and includes a mortgage."
Fixed Charge
A charge on specific, identified assets of a permanent nature — land and building, machinery, office premises. The assets are identified at the time of creation of the charge, usually by mortgage or deposit of title deeds. The company may use the asset but cannot sell it during the charge period without the charge-holder's permission or consent. It is vacated when the borrowed money is repaid in full.
Floating Charge
A charge on assets or a class of assets of fluctuating or changing nature — raw material, stock-in-trade, debtors — covering both present and future assets. It "floats above ever-changing assets"; the company may deal with them in the ordinary course of business and the buyer takes them free of charge.
Crystallisation of a Floating Charge
The conversion of a floating charge into a fixed charge on all the assets available on that date. A floating charge remains dormant until it crystallises; on crystallisation the security becomes fixed and available for realisation by the lender.
Constructive notice / Deemed notice [Section 80]
"Constructive" means implied or deemed; "notice" means knowledge. Where a charge is registered under Section 77, any person acquiring such property, assets, undertakings or part thereof or any share or interest therein shall be deemed to have notice of the charge from the date of such registration — even if he never actually looked at the public record, because the deeming provision creates a legal fiction.
Ad valorem fee
Fee "in proportion to the estimated value of the transaction concerned" — here, based on the value of the charge, i.e. the amount of loan advanced against security of the property.
Pari passu charge
A pari passu charge-holder is entitled to a proportionate share in the mortgaged property. On ceding it, that holder becomes a second charge-holder, and his entitlement becomes subject to full satisfaction of the first charge-holder's claim. Ceding a pari passu charge is a modification.
Modification of charge [Section 79(b)]
Variation in any term or condition of the agreement, including change in rate of interest, whether by mutual agreement or by operation of law; variation in the extent or operation of any charge; and even assignment of a charge-holder's rights to a third party.
Satisfaction of charge
Beyond simple repayment, satisfaction also happens where the amount is not repaid but an asset of equal value is offered in place of the property being released from the charge.

How It Works / Logic

  • Filing (Section 77(1) and Rule 3(1)): Particulars of the charge in the prescribed form together with a copy of the instrument creating the charge, duly signed by the company and the charge-holder, must be filed with the Registrar within 30 days of creation, with the prescribed fee.
  • Forms for filing (Rule 3): Form CHG-1 for charges other than debentures; Form CHG-9 where the charge relates to debentures.
  • Verification of the instrument (Rule 3(4)): Where the deed relates solely to property outside India, the copy may be verified by a certificate issued under the seal (if any) of the company, or under the hand of any director or company secretary of the company or an authorised officer of the charge-holder, or under the hand of some person other than the company who is interested in the mortgage or charge. Where the deed relates to property in India, wholly or partly, verification is limited to a certificate under the hand of a director or company secretary of the company or an authorised officer of the charge-holder — the third (outsider) mode is not available.
  • Application for extension (Rule 4): The company applies to the Registrar in Form CHG-1 (or CHG-9 for debentures), supported by a declaration signed by its company secretary or a director that the belated filing shall not adversely affect the rights of any other intervening creditors. The Registrar must be satisfied that the company had sufficient cause for not filing within the original 30 days, and the additional fee or ad valorem fee must be paid.
  • Certificates issued (Section 77(2) and Rule 6): Form CHG-2 for fresh registration of a charge (registered under Section 77(1) or Section 78); Form CHG-3 for modification of charge; Form CHG-5 for registration of satisfaction of charge.
  • Charges outside Section 77 (Fourth Proviso to Section 77(1), inserted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 w.e.f. 7th May 2018): Certain charges prescribed in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India are outside Section 77. Rule 3(5): Rule 3 does not apply to a charge required to be created or modified by a banking company in favour of the RBI where a loan or advance has been made to it under sub-clause (d) of clause (4) of Section 17 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.
  • Registration by the charge-holder (Section 78): If the company fails to register within 30 days, the person in whose favour the charge is created may apply to the Registrar with the instrument of charge. The Registrar gives notice to the company and, if no objection is received, allows registration on payment of prescribed fees within a period of 14 days after giving the notice. The Registrar shall not allow registration by the charge-holder if the company itself registers the charge, or shows sufficient cause why the charge should not be registered.
  • Recovery of fees (Section 78): Where registration is effected on the charge-holder's application, he is entitled to recover from the company the fees or additional fees paid by him to the Registrar.
  • Acquisition of charged property (Section 79(a)): Where property already carrying a registered charge is sold with the charge-holder's permission, the acquiring company must get the charge registered under Section 77 — the earlier charge is vacated and a new charge registered in the name of the acquirer, in place of the seller, in the ROC records.
  • Register of Charges kept by the Registrar (Section 81): The Registrar shall, in respect of every company, keep a register containing particulars of charges registered under Chapter VI in the prescribed form and manner. Rule 7(1): particulars maintained on the MCA portal (www.mca.gov.in/MCA21) are deemed to be the register of charges for Section 81. Section 81(2) and Rule 7(2): the register is open to inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fee for each inspection.
  • Register of Charges kept by the company (Section 85 and Rule 10): Every company shall keep a Register of Charges in Form CHG-7 at its registered office, covering all charges and floating charges affecting any property, assets or undertakings, with the prescribed particulars. Proviso to Section 85(1): a copy of the instrument creating the charge must also be kept at the registered office along with the Register.
  • Rule 10 mechanics: Rule 10(1) — entries cover all charges registered with the Registrar, property acquired subject to a charge, and every modification and satisfaction. Rule 10(2) — entries must be made forthwith after creation, modification or satisfaction. Rule 10(3) — entries must be authenticated by a director or the secretary or any other person authorised by the Board.
  • Inspection of the company's register (Section 85(2) and Rule 11): Open during business hours — (a) to any member or creditor without any fee; (b) to any other person on payment of prescribed fee — subject to reasonable restrictions the company may impose by its articles.
  • Preservation (Rule 10(4)): The Register of Charges is preserved permanently; the instrument creating a charge or modification thereon is preserved for eight years from the date of satisfaction of charge.
  • Satisfaction — intimation (Section 82 and Rule 8): Intimation of payment or satisfaction in full of a registered charge is given to the Registrar in Form CHG-4 within 30 days of such payment or satisfaction. Proviso to Section 82(1): on an application by the company or the charge-holder, the Registrar may allow the intimation within 300 days on payment of prescribed additional fees. (Rule 8(1) was substituted by the Companies (Registration of Charges) Amendment Rules, 2018, w.e.f. 05-07-2018, to allow 300 days instead of 30.)
  • Satisfaction — show cause (Section 82(2)): On receipt of intimation the Registrar sends a notice to the holder of the charge to show cause within the time specified, not exceeding 14 days, why satisfaction in full should not be recorded. If no cause is shown, he orders entry of a memorandum of satisfaction and informs the company. If cause is shown, he records a note to that effect in the register of charges and informs the company. No notice is required at all where the intimation is in Form CHG-4 and is signed by the holder of the charge.
  • Registrar's suo motu power (Section 83): Even without intimation from the company — typically where charged property is sold to a third party and neither the company nor the charge-holder informs the Registrar — if evidence is shown to his satisfaction that the debt has been paid or satisfied wholly or in part, or that part of the charged property has been released or has ceased to form part of the company's property or undertaking, he may enter a memorandum of satisfaction to that effect. Section 82(4) preserves this power. Section 83(2): the Registrar shall inform the affected parties within 30 days of making the entry.
  • Receiver or manager (Section 84 and Rule 9): A person who obtains an order for appointment of a receiver or manager of charged property, or who appoints one under a power in an instrument, must give notice to the company and the Registrar with a copy of the order or instrument within 30 days of the passing of the order or making of the appointment, in Form CHG-6. The Registrar registers the particulars in the register of charges on payment of the prescribed fee. On ceasing to hold the appointment, the person must again notify the company and Registrar (also Form CHG-6), and the Registrar registers that notice.
  • Rectification (Section 87 and Rule 12): Application in Form CHG-8 by the company or any interested person; powers of the Central Government under Section 87 stand delegated to the Regional Directors vide Notification No. S.O. 4090(E) dated 19-12-2016.
