Fixed Charge vs Floating Charge

BasisFixed ChargeFloating Charge
Subject matterSpecific, identified assets of permanent nature — land and building, machinery, office premisesAssets or a class of assets of fluctuating nature — raw material, stock-in-trade, debtors
IdentificationAssets identified at the time of creation of chargeAssets keep changing; covers present and future assets
Mode of creationUsually by mortgage or by deposit of title deedsCharge on a shifting class of assets that "floats" above them
Right to deal with the assetCompany may use but not sell during the charge period; sale only with permission or consent of the charge-holderCompany may sell or otherwise deal in the ordinary course of business; the buyer gets the asset free of charge
End of chargeVacated when the money borrowed against those assets is repaid in fullRemains dormant until it crystallises into a fixed charge

Consequences of Non-Registration [Section 77(3) and (4)]

  • Void against liquidator and creditors: No charge shall be taken into account by the liquidator appointed under the Companies Act, 2013 or the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, or by any other creditor, unless it is duly registered and a certificate of registration is given by the Registrar (Section 77(3)). At winding up, the holder of an unregistered charge is reduced to the level of an unsecured creditor.
  • Debt survives, security is lost: Section 77(4) — non-registration shall not prejudice any contract or obligation for repayment of the money secured. The debt remains valid and enforceable against the company by filing a suit; only the security is lost.
  • No immunity from penalty: Failure to register does not absolve the company from liability in respect of any offence under Chapter VI.
  • Loss of priority (Third Proviso to Section 77(1)): Any subsequent registration — even registration within an extended period rather than the original 30 days — shall not prejudice any right acquired in respect of the property before the charge was actually registered. A later-created but earlier-registered charge therefore ranks ahead.

Penalties [Section 86]

DefaultPerson liablePenalty / punishment
Default in complying with any provision of Chapter VI [Section 86(1)]The companyPenalty of ₹5,00,000 (five lakh rupees)
Default in complying with any provision of Chapter VI [Section 86(1)]Every officer of the company who is in defaultPenalty of ₹50,000 (fifty thousand rupees)
Wilfully furnishing false or incorrect information, or knowingly suppressing material information, required to be registered under Section 77 [Section 86(2), inserted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2019 w.r.e.f. 02-11-2018]Any personLiable for action under Section 447 — punishment for fraud

Rectification by the Central Government [Section 87]

  • Section 87 (as substituted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2019 w.r.e.f. 02-11-2018) read with Rule 12 empowers the Central Government to order rectification where: (i) there was omission in giving intimation to the Registrar of payment or satisfaction of charge within the specified time; or (ii) there was omission or mis-statement of any particulars in any filing previously made to the Registrar relating to any charge, any modification of charge, or any memorandum of satisfaction or other entry made under Section 82 or Section 83.
  • Before directing that the time for giving intimation be extended, or that the omission or mis-statement be rectified, the Central Government must be satisfied that the default was accidental, or due to inadvertence, or because of some other sufficient cause, or that it was not of a nature to prejudice the position of creditors or shareholders.
  • Rule 12 permits the Central Government, on an application in Form CHG-8, to (a) direct rectification of the omission or misstatement of particulars in any filing previously recorded with the Registrar in respect of any charge or modification, or any memorandum of satisfaction or other entry under Section 82 or 83; and (b) direct extension of time for satisfaction of charge, if such filing is not made within a period of 300 days from the date of payment or satisfaction.
  • The order of rectification is made on such terms and conditions as the Central Government deems just and expedient.

Examples

  • Example 1 — Fixed charge (Pearl Electronics Limited): Pearl Electronics Limited raised a term loan of ₹10 lakh from Everest Commercial Bank Limited against the security of its office building. A charge is created on a specific asset — the office building — and is therefore a fixed charge. The company can sell that office building only by repaying the borrowed amount in full, or after seeking permission from the charge-holder, i.e. the lender bank.
  • Example 2 — Floating charge (Lajpat Nagar retail showroom): A retail showroom in Lajpat Nagar, New Delhi holds clothes, apparels, footwear, kitchen items, cosmetics, etc. kept for sale. The owner may have borrowed against the security of all these goods, but he may still sell or otherwise deal with them in the ordinary course of business. The buyer, i.e. the customer, gets the items purchased free of charge.
  • Example 3 — Floating charge on raw material (Smart Shoes Limited): Smart Shoes Limited manufactures leather goods. The raw material in the form of leather, which is the subject matter of a floating charge, may be used by the company to manufacture leather goods without seeking any permission from the lender.
  • Example 4 — Crystallisation (Prism Limited): Prism Limited had taken a loan from ABC Bank on the security of its stock. If Prism Limited fails to repay the security interest or enters liquidation, the floating charge changes to a fixed charge. Once converted, the stock can neither be sold nor used by the company in its business operations.
  • Example 5 — Deemed notice (Vishnu Marketing Limited / Neeraj): Vishnu Marketing Limited obtained a term loan of ₹50 lakh from Alpha Commercial Bank Limited by creating a charge on one of its office buildings and duly registered the charge. If the building is later sold to Neeraj, he is deemed to have notice of the charge — it is presumed he knew beforehand that the building was mortgaged to the bank. Neeraj therefore cannot plead against that presumption by contending that he did not know of the charge if he suffers loss later because of the mortgage.
  • Example 6 — Loss of priority (Vasudha Medicos Limited, Bank A vs Bank B): Bank A advanced ₹1 crore to Vasudha Medicos Limited against the security of the company's land and building at Mulund; the charge was created by deposit of title deeds on 1st June 2024. The company did not register within 30 days and registered only on 12th August 2024 after paying ad valorem fees and showing sufficient cause. Meanwhile Bank B advanced ₹2 crore against the same property on 18th June 2024 and duly registered its charge on 26th June 2024. The company then went into liquidation and the property realised only ₹2 crore. Conclusion: Bank B gets repayment of its loan in full and Bank A realises nothing, because the subsequent registration in favour of Bank A cannot prejudice the right Bank B acquired before Bank A's charge was actually registered — so Bank B gets priority over Bank A even though its charge was created later.
  • Illustrative instances of "modification of charge": (1) varying any terms and conditions of the existing charge through an agreement; (2) modification in pursuance of an agreement enhancing or decreasing the limits; (3) ceding a pari passu charge; (4) change in the rate of interest (other than bank rate); (5) change in the repayment schedule of the loan (not applicable to working loans repayable on demand); (6) partial release of the charge on a particular asset or property.

Test Your Knowledge — MCQs (with answers)

  • MCQ 1 — Date of deemed notice: Any person acquiring property on which a charge is registered under Section 77 is deemed to have notice of the charge from: (a) expiry of thirty days of such charge; (b) the date of application for registration of the charge; (c) the date of acquiring the property; (d) the date of such registration. Answer: (d) the date of such registration.
  • MCQ 2 — Cygnus Softwares Limited (last date to avoid ad valorem fees): A charge was created by Cygnus Softwares Limited on its office premises to secure a term loan of ₹1 crore from Next Gen Commercial Bank Limited through an instrument executed by both parties on 16th February 2023. The company inadvertently failed to register within the first statutory period and the lending banker warned it to act. Options: (a) 27th April 2023; (b) 17th April 2023; (c) 2nd May 2023; (d) 16th June 2023. Answer: (b) 17th April 2023 — the charge, created after 02-11-2018, may be registered in the further 30-day grace period, i.e. within 60 days from creation, on additional fees; going beyond that date attracts ad valorem fees.
  • MCQ 3 — Preservation of the instrument: The instrument creating a charge or modification thereon shall be preserved for ___ years from the date of satisfaction of charge by the company: (a) 5; (b) 7; (c) 8; (d) 15. Answer: (c) 8.
  • MCQ 4 — Nomenclature: An interest or lien created on the property or assets of a company or any of its undertakings or both as security is known as: (a) Debt; (b) Charge; (c) Liability; (d) Hypothecation. Answer: (b) Charge.
  • MCQ 5 — Free inspection: Who cannot inspect the register of charges and instrument of charges during business hours without paying any fees: (a) any member of the company; (b) the creditor of the company; (c) persons other than member and creditor of the company; (d) no person is allowed to inspect. Answer: (c) persons other than member and creditor of the company.

Test Your Knowledge — Descriptive Questions (with answers)

  • Q1 — Verification of the copy of the instrument: (a) Where the instrument or deed relates solely to property situated outside India, the copy shall be verified by a certificate issued either under the seal (if any) of the company, or under the hand of any director or company secretary of the company or an authorised officer of the charge-holder, or under the hand of some person other than the company who is interested in the mortgage or charge. (b) Where the instrument relates to property situated in India, whether wholly or partly, the copy shall be verified by a certificate issued under the hand of any director or company secretary of the company or an authorised officer of the charge-holder.
  • Q2 — Floating charge and crystallisation: A floating charge is created on assets or a class of assets of fluctuating or changing nature (raw material, stock-in-trade, debtors), upon a class of assets both present and future; the assets keep changing because the company is permitted to use them in the ordinary course of business, and buyers get them free of charge. It crystallises where: (i) the creditor enforces the security due to breach of the terms and conditions of the floating charge — such as non-payment of interest or default in repayment of instalments per the agreement; (ii) the company ceases to continue its business; (iii) the borrowing company goes into liquidation. Until then the floating charge remains dormant; on crystallisation the security becomes fixed and available for realisation so that the borrowed money is repaid.
  • Q3 — Definition and punishment: "Charge" is defined in Section 2(16) as an interest or lien created on the property or assets of a company or any of its undertakings or both as security, and includes a mortgage. Under Section 86, if a company is in default in complying with any provision of Chapter VI, the company is liable to a penalty of ₹5,00,000 and every officer in default to a penalty of ₹50,000. Further, a person wilfully furnishing false or incorrect information, or knowingly suppressing material information required to be registered under Section 77, is liable for action under Section 447 (punishment for fraud).
  • Q4 — Renuka Soaps and Detergents Limited (belated registration): Charge created 10th March 2024 in favour of Sankalp Commercial Bank Limited; non-registration discovered on 2nd May 2024. The charge was created after 02-11-2018. Particulars had to be filed within 30 days under Section 77(1) and were not. Under clause (b) of the First Proviso to Section 77(1) the Registrar may extend the original 30 days by another 30 days (i.e. 60 days from creation) on payment of prescribed additional fee, so the company should immediately file the particulars with the jurisdictional ROC after satisfying the Registrar by application that it had sufficient cause for not filing within 30 days. If the mistake is realised on 7th June 2024 instead: the sixty-day period has already expired (the first sixty days from creation expired on 9th May 2024). Clause (b) of the Second Proviso to Section 77(1) then grants a further period of sixty days from 9th May 2024, but the company must pay the prescribed ad valorem fees and apply to the Registrar giving sufficient cause for non-registration.
  • Q5 — Mr. Antriksh and NRT Limited (deemed notice): Mr. Antriksh purchased a commercial property in Delhi belonging to NRT Limited and, at registration, learnt that the title deed was not free; the company refused to get the title deed transferred, contending that he ought to have known of the charge. Under Section 80, any person acquiring such property, assets, undertakings or part thereof, or any share or interest therein, is deemed to have notice of the charge from the date of such registration. Antriksh ought to have been careful and verified beforehand that NRT Limited had already created a charge on the property. Conclusion: the contention of NRT Limited is correct.
  • Q6 — Register of Charges kept by a company: Section 85 with Rules 10 and 11 apply. Section 85(1): every company shall keep a Register of Charges in the prescribed form (Form CHG-7 per Rule 10(1)) and manner at its registered office, including all charges and floating charges affecting any property or assets or undertakings, with the prescribed particulars. Proviso to Section 85(1): a copy of the instrument creating the charge must also be kept at the registered office along with the Register. Rule 10(1) — entry of particulars of all charges registered with the Registrar, any property acquired subject to a charge, and any modification and satisfaction. Rule 10(2) — entries made forthwith after creation, modification or satisfaction. Rule 10(3) — entries authenticated by a director or the secretary or any other person authorised by the Board. Section 85(2) and Rule 11 — inspection during business hours by any member or creditor without fees and by any other person on payment of fee. Rule 10(4) — the Register is preserved permanently; the instrument creating a charge or modification thereon is preserved for eight years from the date of satisfaction of charge.
  • Q7 — ABC Limited and OK Bank (unregistered modification of ₹20 crore enhancement): ABC Limited created a charge in favour of OK Bank which was duly registered; the Bank later enhanced the facility by another ₹20 crore and, due to inadvertence, the modification of the original charge was not registered. ABC Limited is advised to immediately file an application for rectification of the Register of Charges in Form No. CHG-8 with the Central Government under Section 87. Section 87 with Rule 12 covers (i) omission in giving intimation to the Registrar regarding payment or satisfaction of charge within the specified time and (ii) omission or mis-statement of particulars in any previous filing relating to any charge, modification, memorandum of satisfaction or other entry under Section 82 or 83. The Central Government must first be satisfied that the default was accidental or due to inadvertence or some other sufficient cause, or was not of a nature to prejudice the position of creditors or shareholders. Since the application may be filed by the company or any interested person, OK Bank can also proceed under Section 87. The order is made on such terms and conditions as the Central Government deems just and expedient.
  • Q8 — Ranjit, PQR Limited and Pyramid Bank (no intimation of satisfaction): Ranjit acquired property from PQR Limited that was mortgaged to Pyramid Bank, settled the dues to the Bank in full, and the settlement was registered with the sub-registrar; but neither the company nor Pyramid Bank filed particulars of satisfaction with the jurisdictional ROC. Under Section 83, the Registrar may make entries of satisfaction and release even without intimation from the company: on evidence shown to his satisfaction that the debt secured has been paid or satisfied wholly or in part, or that part of the charged property or undertaking has been released or has ceased to form part of the company's property, he may enter a memorandum of satisfaction recording that the debt has been satisfied in whole or in part, or that the property has been released or has ceased to form part of the company's property. The Registrar shall inform the affected parties within 30 days of making the entry, and under Rule 8(2) shall issue a certificate of registration of satisfaction of charge in Form No. CHG-5 where satisfaction in full is entered. Conclusion: Ranjit can approach the Registrar, show evidence that the charge has been duly settled and satisfied, and request entry of a memorandum of satisfaction noting the release of charge.

Why It Matters / Application

The registration regime decides who actually gets paid out of a company's assets when it fails. A lender who took a perfect mortgage but skipped the ROC filing stands, in liquidation under the Companies Act, 2013 or the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, as an unsecured creditor — it keeps a suit for the debt but loses the asset. Conversely the record on the MCA21 portal is what a prospective lender or buyer must search before advancing money against, or purchasing, a company's land, plant, stock or receivables, because Section 80 fixes him with deemed knowledge whether or not he searched. Between two lenders, Example 6 shows that date of registration, not date of creation, sets priority. For the company's own officers, the compliance calendar is unforgiving: 30 days to file CHG-1/CHG-9, forthwith entry in the CHG-7 register at the registered office, 30 days to file CHG-4 on repayment, 30 days for CHG-6 on a receiver's appointment — with ₹5 lakh on the company and ₹50,000 per officer in default, and Section 447 fraud exposure for wilfully false or suppressed particulars.

Note

Exam traps and provisos to watch:

  • The 02-11-2018 dividing line is everything. Pre-02-11-2018 charges use the 300-day / six-months-from-02-11-2018 track; charges created on or after 02-11-2018 use the 30 + 30 (additional fees) + further 60 (ad valorem fees) track. Applying the 300-day rule to a 2023 or 2024 charge is the classic error.
  • 30 days for registration but 300 days for satisfaction. Section 82's extended window remained at 300 days (Rule 8(1) substituted w.e.f. 05-07-2018) even after Section 77's extended window was cut to 60 + 60 days — do not carry the 60-day figure across to satisfaction.
  • "Sufficient cause" plus a declaration. Extension under Rule 4 requires an application supported by a declaration signed by the company secretary or a director that the belated filing will not adversely affect the rights of intervening creditors — a fact-pattern hook whenever a second lender appears in the question.
  • Verification asymmetry. Only where the deed relates solely to property outside India may an outside person interested in the mortgage verify the copy; for property in India, wholly or partly, that mode is unavailable.
  • No show-cause notice where the charge-holder signs. Under Section 82(2) the Registrar need not send the 14-day notice at all if the intimation is in Form CHG-4 and signed by the holder of the charge.
  • Two different registers. Section 81 register is kept by the Registrar (MCA portal particulars are deemed to be it under Rule 7(1); inspection by any person on payment of fee). Section 85 register is kept by the company in Form CHG-7 at its registered office (members and creditors inspect free; others pay; subject to restrictions imposed by the articles).
  • Two different preservation periods. Register of Charges — permanently; instrument creating or modifying a charge — eight years from the date of satisfaction (Rule 10(4)).
  • Recent amendments: Fourth Proviso to Section 77(1) (RBI-consulted exempt charges) inserted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 w.e.f. 07-05-2018; Section 86(2) inserted and Section 87 substituted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2019, both w.r.e.f. 02-11-2018; Section 87 powers delegated to Regional Directors by Notification No. S.O. 4090(E) dated 19-12-2016.
  • Satisfaction is wider than repayment — it also covers substitution of an asset of equal value in place of the property being released from the charge.
  • Charge-holder's remedy is not free of cost to the company — under Section 78 the charge-holder who registers can recover from the company the fees and additional fees he paid to the Registrar.

Chapter 7 — Management and Administration

Source: 87776bos-aps2160-ch7.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Scope of Chapter VII: Sections 88 to 122 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014. It applies to all companies, public and private, with special carve-outs for One Person Company in Section 122. The sub-groups are: Registers — Sections 88–91 & 95; Annual Return — Sections 92 & 94; Meetings — Sections 96–102 & 121; Requisites of convening a meeting — Sections 103–120.
  • Separation of ownership and management: A company is an artificial legal entity distinct from its members. Day-to-day affairs are run by directors acting collectively as the Board; certain powers need the consent of members in general meeting. General meetings are where shareholders, as owners, ratify the Board's actions.
  • Three statutory registers under Section 88(1): register of members (equity and preference holdings of each member, residing in India or outside, shown separately), register of debenture-holders, and register of any other security holders. Failure attracts a penalty of ₹3,00,000 on the company and ₹50,000 on every officer in default — a compoundable offence under Section 441.
  • Annual Return is a post-AGM compliance: After the AGM concludes, the company prepares the annual return on the state of affairs as they stood at the close of the financial year and files it with the jurisdictional Registrar of Companies within 60 days. It is due even if no AGM was held — then within 60 days of the date on which the AGM ought to have been held, with reasons for not holding it.
  • Two kinds of general meeting: Annual General Meeting (Section 96) — a mandatory yearly gathering where members discuss the conduct of the company's affairs; and Extraordinary General Meeting (Section 100) — every general meeting that is not an AGM, held for urgent business that cannot wait until the next AGM.
  • Quorum is a continuing requirement: Quorum is the minimum number of members who must be personally present to constitute a valid meeting. Per Secretarial Standard-2 it must exist not only when the meeting commences but throughout the transaction of business; business transacted without quorum is a nullity.
  • Ordinary vs special resolution (Section 114): Ordinary resolution — votes cast in favour exceed votes cast against (simple majority, more than 50%). Special resolution — votes cast in favour are not less than 3 times the votes cast against (i.e. minimum 75% majority), the intention to propose it as a special resolution must be stated in the notice, and proper notice must have been given.
  • Minutes are statutory evidence: Minutes kept under Section 118 are evidence of the proceedings recorded; until the contrary is proved, the meeting is deemed to have been duly called and held, all proceedings duly taken place, postal-ballot resolutions duly passed, and all appointments of directors, KMP, auditors or company secretary in practice deemed valid.

Key Definitions / Terms

General Meeting
A meeting of the shareholders held as per the Act — either an AGM or an EGM. Its object is to give members an opportunity to discuss the functioning of the company and take steps to protect their interests.
Board Meeting
A meeting of the Board of Directors of a company.
Class Meeting
A meeting of a particular class of persons — creditors, preference shareholders, debenture-holders, etc.
Foreign Register [Section 88(4) read with Rule 7]
That part of the register of members / debenture-holders / other security holders / beneficial owners resident in a country outside India, kept in that country by a company having share capital or which has issued debentures or other securities, if so authorised by its articles.
Principal Register
The company's own register of members / debenture-holders / other security holders / beneficial owners, of which every foreign register (and every duplicate foreign register) is deemed to be a part.
Registered owner [Section 89(1)]
A person whose name is entered in the register of members as holder of shares but who does not hold the beneficial interest in them; he must file Form MGT-4 within 30 days of his name being entered.
Beneficial interest in a share [Section 89(10)]
Includes, directly or indirectly, through any contract, arrangement or otherwise, the right or entitlement of a person alone or with any other person to (i) exercise or cause to be exercised any or all rights attached to the share, or (ii) receive or participate in any dividend or other distribution in respect of the share.
Significant Beneficial Owner (SBO) [Section 90(1)]
Every individual who, acting alone or together, or through one or more persons or trust (including a trust and persons resident outside India), holds beneficial interests of not less than 25% (or such other prescribed percentage) in shares of a company, or the right to exercise / actual exercise of significant influence or control as defined in Section 2(27).
SBO under Rule 2(1)(h), SBO Rules 2018
An individual who, alone or together, or through one or more persons or trust, (i) holds indirectly (or with direct holdings) not less than 10% of shares; or (ii) not less than 10% of the voting rights in shares; or (iii) has the right to receive or participate in not less than 10% of the total distributable dividend or other distribution in a financial year through indirect holdings alone or with direct holdings; or (iv) has the right to exercise, or actually exercises, significant influence or control other than through direct holdings alone. If an individual holds no indirect right/entitlement under (i), (ii) or (iii), he is not an SBO.
Significant influence [Rule 2(1)(i), SBO Rules]
The power to participate, directly or indirectly, in the financial and operating policy decisions of the reporting company, but which is not control or joint control of those policies.
Majority Stake [Rule 2(1)(d), SBO Rules]
Holding more than one-half of the equity share capital of a body corporate; or more than one-half of its voting rights; or the right to receive or participate in more than one-half of its distributable dividend or other distribution.
Indirect shareholding (SBO Rules)
Arises where the shareholder is a (a) body corporate, (b) Hindu Undivided Family, (c) partnership entity, (d) trust, or (e) pooled investment vehicle.
21 clear days
Both the date on which the notice is served and the date of the meeting are excluded. A company cannot curtail the 21 clear days requirement through its Articles. A notice sent by post is deemed served at the expiration of 48 hours after posting [Rule 35(6), Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014].
Ordinary business [Section 102(2)]
Only four items, and only at an AGM: (i) consideration of financial statements and the reports of the Board and auditors; (ii) declaration of any dividend; (iii) appointment of directors in place of those retiring; (iv) appointment of, and fixing the remuneration of, the auditors. No explanatory statement is needed for ordinary business.
Special business
At an AGM, everything other than the four ordinary items. At an EGM, every business transacted is special business, and an explanatory statement under Section 102 must be annexed to the notice.
Quorum [Section 103]
The minimum number of members personally present to constitute a valid meeting; 'members personally present' means members entitled to vote on the items of business on the agenda.
Casting vote
The Chairman's right to cast a second vote in the event of equality of votes, available only if the articles specifically empower him. Without such an article, an ordinary resolution on which votes are equal is deemed dropped.
Proxy
An instrument in writing executed by a shareholder authorising another person to attend a meeting and vote thereat on his behalf in his absence; the term also applies to the person so appointed. A proxy need not be a member; he has no right to speak and cannot vote except on a poll (so he cannot vote on a show of hands). Form No. MGT-11.
Postal ballot [Section 2(65)]
Voting by post or through any electronic mode.
Remote e-voting [Explanation II(v) to Rule 20(2)]
The facility of casting votes by a member using an electronic voting system from a place other than the venue of the general meeting.
Cut-off date [Explanation II(ii) to Rule 20(2)]
A date not earlier than seven days before the date of the general meeting, for determining eligibility to vote by electronic means or at the meeting.
Electronic voting system [Explanation II(iv) to Rule 20(2)]
A secured, system-based process of display of electronic ballots and recording of members' votes and the number of votes polled for and against, such that the entire electronic voting gets registered and counted in an electronic registry on a centralised server with adequate cyber security.
Motion vs Resolution
A motion is a proposal; a resolution is the adoption of a motion duly made and seconded. Not every motion is followed by a resolution — e.g. a motion for adjournment of the meeting. A motion for closure of discussion or adjournment can be passed by ordinary resolution unless the articles provide otherwise.
National Holiday [Explanation to Section 96(2)]
A day declared as a National Holiday by the Central Government. An AGM cannot be held on such a day.
Records (Rule 27 Explanation, electronic form)
Any register, index, agreement, memorandum, minutes or any other document required by the Act or rules to be kept by a company.

Registers — Sections 88 to 91

  • Forms and rules: Register of members — Rule 3, Form MGT-1. Register of debenture-holders / any other security holder — Rule 4, Form MGT-2 (a separate register for each type of debenture or other security). Index of names — Rule 6. Foreign register — Rule 7, Form MGT-3.
  • Companies existing at the commencement of the 2013 Act must transfer the particulars available in the register maintained under the Companies Act, 1956 to the new register in Form MGT-1; additional information supplied by members may be added as and when provided [proviso to Rule 3(1) and Rule 3(2)].
  • Company without share capital [Rule 3(2)] — the register must contain, for each member: name; address (registered office address if the member is a body corporate); email address; PAN or CIN; nationality; if the member is a minor, the name of his guardian and the member's date of birth; name and address of nominee; date of becoming member; date of cessation; amount of guarantee, if any; any other interest; and instructions given by the member regarding sending of notices.
  • Entries within 7 days [Rule 5(1)]: entries are to be made in the register within 7 days of approval by the Board or its committee of the allotment or transfer of shares, debentures or other securities.
  • Rule 5(3) — seven-day rule extended to entries consequent on forfeiture, buy-back, reduction, sub-division, consolidation or cancellation of shares, issue of sweat equity shares, transmission of shares, shares issued under schemes of arrangement, mergers, reconstitution or ESOP, or issue of duplicate/new share, debenture or other security certificates.
  • Fifteen-day entries — the exception to the seven-day rule. Rule 5(7): for listed companies (in or outside India), particulars of any pledge, charge, lien or hypothecation created by promoters over the company's securities held by them, including names of the pledgee/pawnee and any revocation, must be entered within 15 days of the event. Rule 5(8): where promoters of a listed company that has formed a joint venture company have pledged, hypothecated or created charge or lien over any security of the listed company in connection with that joint venture, the particulars must be entered in the register of members of the listed company within 15 days of the event.
  • Place of maintaining registers [Rule 5(2)]: at the registered office, unless a special resolution in general meeting authorises keeping them at any other place within the city, town or village of the registered office, or at any other place in India where more than 1/10th of the total members entered in the register of members reside.
  • Rule 5(4) — change in status of a member/debenture-holder/other security holder due to death, insolvency, change of name, transfer to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF), or any other reason, must be entered with an explanation of the change. Rule 5(5): any rectification made pursuant to an order of a competent authority must carry a reference to that order in the register. Rule 5(6): an order of any judicial or revenue authority, or of SEBI, attaching securities and directing remittance of dividend or interest must be referenced in the register.
  • Index of names [Section 88(2), Rule 6]: every register must include an index — but not necessary where the number of members is less than 50. Entries in the index are to be made simultaneously with the entry for allotment or transfer.
  • Section 88(3): the register and index of beneficial owners maintained by a depository under Section 11 of the Depositories Act, 1996 is deemed to be the corresponding register and index for the purposes of this Act.
  • Authentication [Rule 8]: entries in registers and index under Section 88 are authenticated by the company secretary or any other person authorised by the Board, mentioning the date of the enabling board resolution. Entries in the foreign register are authenticated by the company secretary or a Board-authorised person by appending his signature to each entry.
  • Nominations: Forms MGT-1 and MGT-2 require details of nomination under Section 72 read with Rule 19 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 to be entered in the respective registers.

Foreign Register — the twelve requirements [Section 88(4) read with Rule 7]

  • (i) File notice of the situation of the office where the foreign register is kept with the Registrar in Form MGT-3 with fee, within 30 days of opening it.
  • (ii) On any change in the situation of that office or its discontinuance, file notice in Form MGT-3 within 30 days of the change or discontinuance.
  • (iii) A foreign register is deemed part of the company's principal register.
  • (iv) It must be maintained in the same format as the principal register.
  • (v) It is open to inspection, may be closed, and extracts and copies may be taken in the same manner as the principal register — but the advertisement before closing must be inserted in at least two newspapers circulating in the place where the foreign register is kept.
  • (vi) Where a foreign register is kept outside India, the decision of the appropriate competent authority in that country regarding rectification of the register is binding.
  • (vii) Entries in the foreign register are made after the Board or its duly constituted committee approves the allotment or transfer.
  • (viii) A copy of every entry must be transmitted to the registered office in India within 15 days after the entry is made.
  • (ix) A duplicate of every foreign register, duly updated, must be kept at the registered office; (x) every duplicate foreign register is deemed part of the principal register for all purposes of the Act.
  • (xi) No transaction in securities registered in a foreign register may, during the continuance of that registration, be registered in any other register.
  • (xii) On discontinuance, all entries are transferred to some other foreign register kept outside India or to the principal register.
  • Preservation [Rule 15]: the foreign register of members is preserved permanently unless discontinued and all entries transferred; the foreign register of debenture-holders/other security holders is preserved 8 years from redemption. Custody: the company secretary or a Board-authorised person.

Declaration of Beneficial Interest — Section 89

  • Registered owner: files Form MGT-4 with the company within 30 days from the date his name is entered in the register of members [Section 89(1), Rule 9(1)].
  • Beneficial owner: every person who holds or acquires beneficial interest files Form MGT-5 within 30 days after acquiring it, specifying the nature of his interest and the particulars of the registered holder [Section 89(2), Rule 9(2)].
  • Change in beneficial interest [Section 89(3)]: declaration to the company within 30 days of the change.
  • Company's return: note the declaration in the register concerned and file Form MGT-6 with the Registrar within 30 days of receipt of the declaration, with fee [Section 89(6), Rule 9(3)].
  • Designated person [Rule 9(4)–(8)]: every company designates a person responsible for furnishing information on beneficial interest to the Registrar. Designation order: (i) company secretary, if one is required to be appointed; (ii) a KMP other than the company secretary; (iii) every director if there is no CS or KMP. Until designation, the deemed designated persons are (i) the company secretary if required to be appointed; (ii) every Managing Director or Manager if no CS has been appointed; (iii) every director if there is no CS, MD or Manager. Details of the designated person go into the Annual Return; any change is intimated to the Registrar in e-Form GNL-2.
  • Consequence of non-declaration [Section 89(8)]: where the beneficial owner fails to make the declaration, no right in respect of such shares is enforceable by him or by anyone claiming through him.
  • Exemptions: Rule 9 does not apply to a trust created to set up a Mutual Fund or Venture Capital Fund or such other SEBI-approved fund. Section 89 does not apply to a Government company [GSR 463(E) dated 5-6-2015], provided it has not defaulted in filing financial statements under Section 137 or the annual return under Section 92 [GSR 582(E) dated 13-6-2017]. Under Section 89(11) the Central Government may by notification exempt any class of persons from any requirement of the section except sub-section (10), unconditionally or subject to conditions.
  • Dividend obligation unaffected: nothing in Section 89 prejudices the company's obligation to pay dividend to its members, and that obligation stands discharged on such payment.

Register of Significant Beneficial Owners — Section 90 and SBO Rules, 2018

  • Direct holding is excluded: an individual holds a right or entitlement directly if (a) the shares carrying that right are held in his own name, or (b) he holds/acquires beneficial interest under Section 89(2) and has declared it to the reporting company. A purely direct holder is not an SBO.
  • Onus on the company: the reporting company must identify its SBOs and cause them to declare. Under Section 90(5) read with Rule 7, notice in Form BEN-4 is given to any person (member or not) whom the company knows or reasonably believes (a) to be an SBO, (b) to have knowledge of the identity of an SBO or of another person likely to have such knowledge, or (c) to have been an SBO at any time during the three years immediately preceding the date of the notice, and who is not registered as an SBO.
  • Declaration and return: an individual who was an SBO as on the commencement of the Amendment Rules, 2019 (8-2-2019) files Form BEN-1 within 90 days of that commencement [Rule 3(1)]. Anyone who subsequently becomes an SBO, or whose significant beneficial ownership changes, files BEN-1 within 30 days of the acquisition or change [Rule 3(2)]. Explanation: if a person becomes an SBO or his SBO status changes within those 90 days, he is deemed to have become an SBO on the date of expiry of the 90 days and the 30-day period is reckoned accordingly. The reporting company files Form BEN-2 with the Registrar within 30 days of receipt of the declaration [Rule 4].
  • Register [Section 90(2)–(3), Rule 5]: a register of significant beneficial owners in Form BEN-3, open for inspection during business hours for not less than two hours on every working day as the Board may decide, by any member, on payment of a fee specified by the company not exceeding ₹50 for each inspection.
  • Tribunal route [Section 90(7)–(9)]: where the person fails to give the information required by the BEN-4 notice within the time specified (Rule 7: information to be given within 30 days of the date of notice), or where the information is unsatisfactory, the company applies to the Tribunal within 15 days of the expiry of the period specified in the notice. Restrictions sought may include restrictions on transfer of interest attached to the shares, suspension of the right to receive dividend or other distribution, suspension of voting rights, and any other restriction on the rights attached to the shares. The Tribunal, after giving an opportunity of being heard, makes the order within 60 days of receipt of the application or such other prescribed period. The company or the aggrieved person may apply for relaxation or lifting of restrictions within one year of the order; if no such application is made within one year, the shares are transferred without restrictions to the IEPF Authority constituted under Section 125(5).
  • Non-applicability [Rule 8]: the SBO Rules do not apply to the extent the shares of the reporting company are held by (a) the IEPF Authority under Section 125(5); (b) its holding reporting company, provided details of that holding reporting company are reported in Form BEN-2; (c) the Central Government, State Government or any local authority; (d) a reporting company, body corporate or entity controlled wholly or partly by the Central and/or State Government(s); (e) SEBI-registered and regulated investment vehicles such as mutual funds, AIFs, REITs and InvITs; (f) investment vehicles regulated by RBI, IRDAI or PFRDA.
  • False information: anyone wilfully furnishing false or incorrect information, or suppressing material information of which he is aware, in the declaration is liable for punishment for fraud under Section 447 [Section 90(12)]. Contraventions of Section 90 and the SBO Rules by the company and officers in default are compoundable. Section 90 does not apply to a Government company [GSR 463(E) dated 5-6-2015, subject to GSR 582(E) dated 13-6-2017].

Closure of Registers — Section 91

  • Closure period [Section 91(1)]: a company may close the register of members / debenture-holders / other security holders for an aggregate of 45 days in each year, but not exceeding 30 days at any one time.
  • Notice: minimum 7 days' notice, or such lesser period as SEBI may specify for listed companies or companies intending to list.
  • Manner [Rule 10(1)]: at least 7 days' previous notice by advertisement at least once in a vernacular newspaper in the principal vernacular language of the district having wide circulation in the place of the registered office, at least once in English in an English newspaper circulating in that district and having wide circulation in the place of the registered office, and by publishing the notice on the website notified by the Central Government and on the company's website, if any.
  • Private company exemption [Rule 10(2)]: exempt from public notice in newspapers, provided it gives minimum 7 days' notice to its members prior to closure.
  • Penalty [Section 91(2)]: where registers are closed without notice, on shorter notice, or beyond the continuous/aggregate limits — the company and every officer in default are liable to a penalty of ₹5,000 per day, subject to a maximum of ₹1,00,000, for the period the register is kept closed. Compoundable under Section 441.

Annual Return — Sections 92 and 94

  • Form [Rule 11]: every company files its annual return in Form MGT-7, except One Person Company and Small Company, which from the financial year 2020-2021 onwards file the abridged Form MGT-7A (second proviso to Section 92(1) empowers the Central Government to prescribe an abridged form).
  • Contents [Section 92(1)]: particulars as they stood at the close of the financial year regarding — (a) registered office, principal business activities, particulars of holding, subsidiary and associate companies; (b) shares, debentures and other securities and shareholding pattern; (c) omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 w.e.f. 5th March, 2021; (d) members and debenture-holders with changes since the close of the previous financial year; (e) promoters, directors, KMP with changes since the close of the previous financial year; (f) meetings of members or a class thereof, of the Board and its committees, with attendance details; (g) remuneration of directors and KMP; (h) penalty or punishment imposed on the company, its directors or officers, details of compounding of offences and appeals against such penalty or punishment; (i) matters relating to certification of compliances and prescribed disclosures; (j) prescribed details of shares held by or on behalf of Foreign Institutional Investors; (k) such other matters as may be prescribed. For a private company that is a small company, clause (g) reads as "aggregate amount of remuneration drawn by directors" [GSR 464(E) dated 5-6-2015 as amended by GSR 583(E) dated 13-6-2017].
  • Signing: by a director and the company secretary; where there is no company secretary, by a company secretary in practice. For OPC and small company: by the company secretary, or where there is none, by the director. For a private company that is a start-up, the same relaxed signing applies [substituted proviso, GSR 464(E) dated 5-6-2015 as amended by GSR 583(E) dated 13-6-2017], available only to a private company that has not defaulted in filing financial statements under Section 137 or the annual return under Section 92.
  • Certification [Section 92(2), Rule 11(2)]: the annual return of (i) a listed company, or (ii) a company having paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore or more or turnover of ₹50 crore or more, must be certified by a Company Secretary in practice in Form MGT-8, stating that the annual return discloses the facts correctly and adequately and that the company has complied with all the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Website [Section 92(3)]: every company places a copy of the annual return on its website, if any, and the web-link is disclosed in the Board's report. Section 92(3) does not apply to a Specified IFSC public company [GSR 8(E) dated 4-1-2017] or a Specified IFSC private company [GSR 9(E) dated 4-1-2017].
  • Filing [Section 92(4), Rule 12]: within 60 days from the date the AGM is held; where no AGM is held in any year, within 60 days from the date on which the AGM should have been held, together with the reasons for not holding it.
  • Penalty: Section 92(5) — company and every officer in default liable to a penalty of ₹10,000, and for continuing failure a further penalty of ₹100 per day, subject to a maximum of ₹2,00,000 for the company and ₹50,000 for an officer in default. Section 92(6) — a company secretary in practice who certifies the annual return otherwise than in accordance with Section 92 or the rules is liable to a penalty of ₹2,00,000.

Place of Keeping and Inspection of Registers — Sections 94 and 95

  • Section 94(1): registers under Section 88 and copies of annual returns filed under Section 92 are kept at the registered office; they may also be kept at any other place in India where more than one-tenth of the total number of members entered in the register of members reside, if approved by a special resolution passed at a general meeting. (Section 93 was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 w.e.f. 13-6-2018.)
  • Inspection [Section 94(2), Rule 14(1)]: registers, their indices (except when closed) and copies of all returns are open for inspection during business hours at such reasonable time on every working day as the Board may decide — free of charge for any member, debenture holder, other security holder or beneficial owner, and on payment of a fee specified in the Articles not exceeding ₹50 for each inspection for any other person. "Reasonable time" means not less than two hours on every working day.
  • Extracts and copies [Section 94(3), Rule 14(2)]: extracts without any fee; copies on payment of a fee not exceeding ₹10 for each page; the copies, entries or return must be supplied within 7 days of deposit of the fee.
  • Particulars shielded from inspection [Rule 14]: notwithstanding sub-rules (1) and (2), the following particulars of the register/index/return in respect of members are not available for inspection or for taking extracts or copies — (i) address or registered address (for a body corporate); (ii) e-mail ID; (iii) Unique Identification Number; (iv) PAN Number.
  • Preservation [Rule 15]: register of members with index — permanently, in the custody of the company secretary or a Board-authorised person. Register of debenture-holders / other security holders with index — 8 years from the date of redemption. Copies of all annual returns under Section 92 with all certificates and documents annexed — 8 years from the date of filing with the RoC.
  • Penalty [Section 94(4)]: refusal of inspection or of the making of any extract or copy — company and every officer in default liable, for each such default, to a penalty of ₹1,000 for every day subject to a maximum of ₹1,00,000 during which the refusal or default continues. Under Section 94(5) the Central Government (powers delegated to Regional Directors) may order immediate inspection or direct that the extract be forthwith allowed.
  • Section 95: the registers, indices and copies of annual return are prima facie evidence of any matter directed or authorised to be inserted therein by or under the Act.

Annual General Meeting — Sections 96 to 99 and 121

  • Section 96(1): every company, public or private, except One Person Company, shall hold an AGM every year; the gap between two AGMs shall not exceed 15 months. The notice must specify the meeting as an Annual General Meeting.
  • First AGM: within 9 months from the closing of the first financial year — hence no AGM is necessary in the year of incorporation. Subsequent AGMs: within 6 months from the closing of the financial year.
  • Extension: the Registrar may, for any special reason, extend the time for holding an AGM by a period not exceeding 3 months. No extension can be granted for the first AGM.
  • Time and place [Section 96(2)]: during business hours, i.e. between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m., on any day that is not a National Holiday, at the registered office or some other place within the city, town or village in which the registered office is situated. An unlisted company may hold its AGM at any place in India if consent is given in writing or by electronic mode by all the members in advance. The Central Government may exempt any company from Section 96(2) subject to conditions.
  • Section 8 company: a further proviso applies — the time, date and place of each AGM must be decided beforehand by the Board having regard to directions, if any, given by the company in general meeting [GSR 466(E) dated 5-6-2015], available to a Section 8 company that has not defaulted under Section 137 or Section 92 [GSR 584(E) dated 13-6-2017]. Government company: the AGM may also be held at such other place as the Central Government may approve [GSR 463(E) dated 5-6-2015 read with notification dated 13-6-2017, subject to GSR 582(E)].
  • Section 97 — Tribunal may call AGM: on default in holding an AGM under Section 96, the Tribunal may, on the application of any member, call or direct the calling of an AGM and give ancillary or consequential directions, including a direction that one member present in person or by proxy shall be deemed to constitute a meeting. Such a meeting is deemed to be an AGM under the Act.
  • Section 98 — Tribunal may call other meetings: where it is impracticable to call, hold or conduct a meeting other than an AGM in the manner prescribed by the Act or the articles, the Tribunal may act suo motu or on the application of any director or member entitled to vote, order the meeting to be called, held and conducted as it thinks fit, with ancillary directions modifying or supplementing the Act or the articles — again possibly deeming one member present in person or by proxy to constitute a meeting. Such a meeting is for all purposes deemed duly called, held and conducted.
  • Section 99 — punishment: default in holding a meeting under Section 96 or 97 or 98, or in complying with any directions of the Tribunal — the company and every officer in default are punishable with a fine which may extend to ₹1,00,000 and, for continuing default, a further fine which may extend to ₹5,000 for every day the default continues.
  • Section 121 — report on AGM: every listed public company prepares a report on each AGM including confirmation that the meeting was convened, held and conducted as per the Act and rules, and files a copy in Form MGT-15 with the Registrar within 30 days of the conclusion of the AGM with fee. Under Rule 31 the report is prepared in addition to the minutes; is signed and dated by the Chairman of the meeting or, if he is unable to sign, by any two directors, one of whom shall be the Managing Director (if there is one), and the company secretary; and contains (i) day, date, hour and venue of the AGM; (ii) confirmation of appointment of Chairman; (iii) number of members attending; (iv) confirmation of quorum; (v) confirmation of compliance with the Act, rules and secretarial standards on calling, convening and conducting the meeting; (vi) business transacted and result thereof; (vii) particulars of any adjournment, postponement or change in venue; (viii) any other relevant points; and (d) a fair and correct summary of proceedings.

Extraordinary General Meeting — Section 100 and Rule 17

  • Who can call: (1) the Board on its own, whenever it deems fit; (2) the Board on a valid requisition of members; (3) the requisitionists themselves if the Board does not act.
  • Place [proviso to Section 100(1)]: an EGM must be held at a place within India, except in the case of the wholly owned subsidiary of a company incorporated outside India. A Specified IFSC public or private company may, with the consent of all shareholders, convene its EGM at any place within or outside India [GSR 8(E) and GSR 9(E) dated 4-1-2017].
  • Requisition threshold [Section 100(2)]: members holding, on the date of receipt of the requisition, at least 1/10th of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights (company with share capital), or at least 1/10th of the total voting power (company without share capital). The requisition must set out the matters for consideration, be signed by the requisitionists and be sent to the registered office [Section 100(3)].
  • Board's timeline: within 21 days from receipt of a valid requisition the Board must proceed to call a meeting on a day not later than 45 days from the date of receipt of the requisition.
  • Requisitionists' meeting [Section 100(4)–(6)]: if the Board fails, the requisitionists may themselves call and hold the meeting within three months from the date of the requisition, in the same manner as the Board would; their reasonable expenses are reimbursed by the company and deducted from the fee or other remuneration under Section 197 payable to the directors who were in default in calling the meeting.
  • Rule 17 procedure: (1) requisition in writing or electronic mode at least clear 21 days prior to the proposed EGM date; (2) the notice specifies place, date, day and hour and the business to be transacted — the meeting must be convened at the registered office or in the same city or town where the registered office is situated, and on any day except a National Holiday; (3) if a special resolution is proposed, notice as required by Section 114(2); (4) the notice is signed by all requisitionists or by one duly authorised in writing by the others, or sent electronically attaching a scanned copy of the signed requisition; (5) no explanatory statement under Section 102 need be annexed to a requisitionists' EGM notice, though they may disclose the reasons for the resolutions; (6) notice is given to members on the register within three days of the requisitionists depositing a valid requisition; (7) if the meeting is not convened the requisitionists are entitled to the list of members with registered addresses and shareholdings, made as on the twenty-first day from receipt of the valid requisition, with changes, before the expiry of 45 days from receipt; (8) notice is given by speed post, registered post or electronic mode, and accidental omission or non-receipt does not invalidate the proceedings.

Notice, Explanatory Statement, Quorum, Chairman, Proxies

  • Section 101(1): a general meeting requires not less than 21 clear days' notice in writing or through electronic mode. Section 101 applies to a Specified IFSC public company unless its articles otherwise specify [GSR 8(E) dated 4-1-2017]. For a Section 8 company, "21 days" is substituted by "14 days" [GSR 466(E) dated 5-6-2015 as amended by GSR 584(E) dated 13-6-2017], available to a Section 8 company not in default under Section 137 or Section 92.
  • Contents [Section 101(2)]: place, date, day and hour of the meeting, and a statement of the business to be transacted.
  • Recipients [Section 101(3)]: every member; the legal representative of a deceased member; the assignee of an insolvent member; the auditor(s); and every director.
  • Shorter notice [proviso to Section 101(1)]: consent in writing or by electronic mode of (i) not less than 95% of the members entitled to vote for an AGM; (ii) for any other general meeting — where there is share capital, majority in number of members entitled to vote who represent not less than 95% of the paid-up share capital giving a right to vote; where there is no share capital, not less than 95% of the total voting power exercisable at the meeting. Second proviso: a member entitled to vote on only some resolutions is counted for those resolutions and not the others.
  • Electronic notice [Rule 18]: a notice may be sent by e-mail as text, as an attachment, or as a notification giving an electronic link or URL for accessing the notice. The e-mail is addressed to the person entitled as per the company's records provided by the depository; the company must give an advance opportunity at least once in a financial year for members to register or change their e-mail address (only for those not already registered or updating a fresh ID); the subject line must state the company's name, the type of meeting, place and scheduled date; a non-editable attachment must be in PDF or another non-editable format with a link or instructions for downloading the relevant software; the company's obligation is satisfied on transmission and it is not responsible for failure in transmission beyond its control; the company is not in default if the member fails to provide or update his e-mail address with the company or the depository participant; the e-mail may be sent in-house, through the registrar and transfer agent, or through an authorised third-party bulk e-mail agency; and the notice must simultaneously be placed on the company's website, if any, and on the website notified by the Central Government.
  • Section 101(4): accidental omission to give notice, or non-receipt of notice by any member or other entitled person, does not invalidate the proceedings; the onus is on the company to prove the omission was not deliberate.
  • Authority to call: a general meeting (AGM or EGM) must be called by the Board through a Board resolution. An individual director has no authority to call one; a notice issued without the Board's sanction is invalid, though it can be ratified by the Board.
  • Explanatory statement [Section 102]: where special business is to be transacted, a statement must be annexed to the notice specifying (a) the nature of concern or interest, financial or otherwise, in each item, of (i) every director and the manager, if any, (ii) every other KMP, and (iii) relatives of those persons; and (b) any other information and facts enabling members to understand the meaning, scope and implications of the item and to take a decision. Proviso to Section 102(2): if an item of special business relates to or affects any other company, the extent of shareholding in that other company of every promoter, director, manager and every other KMP must be disclosed if it is 2% or more of the paid-up share capital of that other company. Where an item refers to a document to be considered at the meeting, the time and place where it can be inspected must be stated.
  • Section 102(4): if, as a result of non-disclosure or insufficient disclosure, a benefit accrues to a promoter, director, manager, other KMP or their relatives, such person holds the benefit in trust for the company and is liable to compensate the company to the extent of the benefit received. Section 102(5) penalty: every promoter, director, manager or other KMP in default is liable to a penalty of ₹50,000 or five times the amount of benefit accruing to him or his relatives, whichever is higher.
  • Adjournment for want of quorum [Section 103(2)–(3)]: if quorum is not present within half-an-hour from the appointed time, (a) the meeting stands adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place, or to such other date, time and place as the Board may determine; or (b) if the meeting was called by requisitionists under Section 100, it stands cancelled. For an adjourned meeting or a change of day, time or place under clause (a), the company must give not less than three days' notice to members individually or by advertisement in newspapers (one English and one vernacular) circulating at the place of the registered office. If quorum is again absent at the adjourned meeting within half an hour, the members present shall form the quorum.
  • Secretarial Standard-2 points on quorum: (1) one person can be authorised representative of more than one body corporate and is then counted as more than one member present in person, but at least two individuals must be present in person to constitute a meeting — so in a public company with not more than 1,000 members (quorum 5), an authorised representative of five bodies corporate cannot form the quorum by himself but can if at least one more member is personally present; (2) quorum must be present at commencement and while transacting business; (3) members who voted by remote e-voting may attend and are counted for quorum; (4) a member not entitled to vote on a particular item because he is a related party is still counted for quorum if present; (5) the quorum stipulation does not apply to items transacted through postal ballot.
  • Chairman [Section 104]: unless the articles otherwise provide, the members personally present elect one of themselves as Chairman on a show of hands. If a poll is demanded on the election of the Chairman, the Chairman elected by show of hands continues until another person is elected as a result of the poll, and that person is Chairman for the rest of the meeting. The Chairman has prima facie authority to decide all questions arising at the meeting which require decision at that time, and must observe strict impartiality. He has a casting vote in Board and general meetings only if specifically empowered by the articles. For a private company Section 104 applies unless otherwise specified in the section or the articles provide otherwise [GSR 464(E) dated 5-6-2015, subject to GSR 583(E) dated 13-6-2017].
  • Proxies [Section 105, Rule 19]: any member entitled to attend and vote may appoint a proxy to attend and vote on his behalf; the proxy has no right to speak and cannot vote except on a poll. Unless the articles otherwise provide, Section 105(1) does not apply to a company not having share capital, and the Central Government may prescribe classes of companies whose members cannot appoint proxies. A member of a Section 8 company cannot appoint a proxy unless the proxy is also a member of that company [Rule 19]. A person can act as proxy for not more than fifty members and holding in aggregate not more than 10% of the total share capital carrying voting rights; a member holding more than 10% of such capital may appoint a single person as proxy, and that person shall not act as proxy for any other person or shareholder [Rule 19(2)].
  • Proxy formalities: every notice of a meeting of a company having share capital (or whose articles allow voting by proxy) must state with reasonable prominence that a member entitled to attend and vote may appoint a proxy (or, where allowed, more than one) and that a proxy need not be a member [Section 105(2)]. The appointment is in Form MGT-11 [Rule 19(3)]; if in the prescribed form it cannot be questioned for failing to comply with special requirements in the articles [Section 105(7)]; it must be in writing and signed by the appointer or his duly authorised attorney, and where the appointer is a body corporate, under its seal or signed by an officer or duly authorised attorney [Section 105(6)]. A proxy received 48 hours before the meeting is valid even if the articles prescribe a longer period [Section 105(4)] — any article requiring lodging more than 48 hours before takes effect as if 48 hours had been specified.
  • Inspection of proxies [Section 105(8)]: a member entitled to vote may inspect the proxies lodged, during the period beginning 24 hours before the time fixed for commencement of the meeting and ending with the conclusion of the meeting, at any time during business hours, on giving not less than three days' notice in writing of the intention to inspect.
  • Proxy penalties: default in complying with Section 105(2) — every officer in default liable to a penalty of ₹5,000 [Section 105(3)]. Issuing, at the company's expense, invitations to appoint a specified person (or one of a number of specified persons) as proxy — every officer who issues, authorises or permits the issue is liable to a penalty of ₹50,000; but not merely for issuing, at a member's written request, a form of appointment naming the proxy or a list of persons willing to act as proxies, if that form or list is available on written request to every member entitled to vote by proxy [Section 105(5)].

Voting — Sections 106 to 110

  • Modes: show of hands (Section 107), electronic means (Section 108), poll (Section 109), postal ballot (Section 110). An equity shareholder may vote on every motion; under Section 47 a preference shareholder can vote only on a resolution pertaining to his rights. The right to vote is a personal right and a member may split his vote for and against the resolution.
  • Restrictions [Section 106]: the articles may provide that a member shall not vote on shares on which calls or other sums presently payable have not been paid, or in regard to which the company has exercised a right of lien. Section 106(2) forbids the company from prohibiting voting on any other ground. Section 106(3): on a poll, a member entitled to more than one vote (or his proxy) need not use all his votes or cast them all the same way. Such a member also cannot sign a requisition for an EGM. Where the articles contain no restricting provision, a member cannot be prevented from voting even if calls are unpaid or a lien has been exercised; but where the articles do contain such a provision and forfeited shares have been re-allotted, the new allottee, being liable for the unpaid balance, cannot vote so long as calls presently payable remain unpaid.
  • Joint holders (Regulation 52 of Table F): the vote of the senior who tenders a vote, in person or by proxy, is accepted to the exclusion of the other joint holders; seniority is determined by the order in which the names stand in the register of members.
  • Show of hands [Section 107]: unless a poll or electronic voting is demanded, voting is by show of hands in the first instance. The Chairman's declaration of the passing (or otherwise) of a resolution on a show of hands, with an entry to that effect in the minutes book, is conclusive evidence that the resolution has been passed [Section 107(2)].
  • E-voting applicability [Rule 20(2)]: every company which (a) has listed its equity shares on a recognised stock exchange and (b) has not less than 1,000 members must provide the e-voting facility. Exempt: a Nidhi, or an enterprise or institutional investor referred to in Chapter XB or Chapter XC of the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2009.
  • E-voting procedure [Rule 20(4)]: notice to all members, directors and auditors by registered post or speed post, or through the recipient's registered e-mail ID, or by courier; the notice is placed on the company's website and the agency's website forthwith after dispatch; the notice must state that e-voting is provided, that facility for voting by electronic voting system, ballot or polling paper will also be available at the meeting for members who have not already voted by remote e-voting, and that members who voted by remote e-voting may attend but cannot vote again; it must indicate the process and manner of e-voting, the time schedule for casting votes, login ID details, and the process for generating/receiving the password and secure casting of the vote.
  • E-voting advertisement contents: statement that business may be transacted by e-voting; dates and times of commencement and end of remote e-voting; cut-off date; manner in which persons who become members after dispatch of notice may obtain login ID and password; statements that remote e-voting is not allowed beyond the stated date and time, how voting will be provided at the meeting, that a member may participate in the meeting after remote e-voting but cannot vote again, and that only a person whose name is on the register of members or the depositories' register of beneficial owners as on the cut-off date may avail remote e-voting and voting at the meeting; the website addresses of the company and the agency; and the name, designation, address, e-mail ID and phone number of the grievance officer. The public notice is also placed on the websites of the company and the agency.
  • E-voting mechanics: once a vote is cast it cannot be changed or cast again; at the end of the remote e-voting period the facility is forthwith blocked (unless the same system is used at the meeting, in which case it stays live until all resolutions are voted upon, for members present who have not voted remotely); the Board appoints one or more scrutinizers — a CA in practice, Cost Accountant in practice, Company Secretary in practice, an Advocate, or any other person of repute not in the company's employment — who may take assistance of a person not in the company's employment well-versed with the system; the scrutinizer counts the votes cast at the meeting first, then unblocks remote e-votes in the presence of at least two witnesses not in the company's employment, and gives a consolidated report to the Chairman not later than three days of the conclusion of the meeting; the Chairman or his authorised person countersigns and declares the result forthwith. The manner in which members cast their votes remains secret and unavailable to the Chairman, scrutinizer or anyone else till the votes are cast in the meeting. The scrutinizer keeps a register of assent/dissent (name, address, folio or client ID, number of shares, nominal value, whether shares carry differential voting rights) in safe custody until the Chairman approves and signs the minutes. Results with the scrutinizer's report go on the company's and the agency's websites immediately after declaration, and listed companies simultaneously forward them to the stock exchange(s), which place them on their websites. Subject to receipt of the requisite votes (ordinary or special resolution majority under Section 114), the resolution is deemed passed on the date of the relevant general meeting. A resolution proposed for e-voting cannot be withdrawn.
  • Poll [Section 109]: before or on the declaration of the result of voting on a show of hands, a poll may be ordered by the Chairman on his own motion, and shall be ordered on a demand by — (a) in a company having share capital, members present in person or by proxy having not less than 1/10th of the total voting power or holding shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than ₹5,00,000 (or such higher prescribed amount) has been paid up; (b) in any other company, members present in person or by proxy having not less than 1/10th of the total voting power. The demand may be withdrawn at any time by the persons who made it. A poll demanded for adjournment of the meeting or appointment of the Chairman is taken forthwith; on any other question, at such time not later than 48 hours from the demand as the Chairman directs. The result of the poll is deemed to be the decision of the meeting on the resolution [Section 109(7)].
  • Poll procedure [Rule 21(1)]: the Chairman ensures scrutinizers are given the Register of Members, specimen signatures, Attendance Register and Register of Proxies, and all documents received under Sections 105, 112 and 113. Scrutinizers arrange and distribute polling papers in Form MGT-12 to members and proxies present — for joint shareholders, to the first named holder or, in his absence, to the joint holder attending, in the chronological order in the folio; keep a record of polling papers received by initialling them; lock and seal an empty polling box in the presence of members and proxies; open the box after voting in the presence of two witnesses; decide the validity of an ambiguous proxy in consultation with the Chairman; disregard the proxy's vote if the appointing member has voted in person; count votes and prepare a report to the Chairman stating total votes cast, valid votes, votes in favour and against, including details of invalid polling papers and the votes comprised therein; and, where voting is electronic under Section 108, the company gives all necessary technical and other support. The scrutinizers submit the report in Form MGT-13, signed by all scrutinizers, to the Chairman within seven days from the date the poll is taken; the Chairman counter-signs and declares the result, personally or through a person authorised by him in writing.
  • Postal ballot [Section 110]: a company shall transact by postal ballot such items as the Central Government notifies, and may transact by postal ballot any item other than ordinary business and any business in respect of which directors or auditors have a right to be heard at any meeting. A resolution assented to by the requisite majority by postal ballot is deemed to have been duly passed at a general meeting convened in that behalf. Proviso: any item required to be transacted by postal ballot may be transacted at a general meeting by a company required to provide e-voting under Section 108.
  • Items transactable only by postal ballot [Rule 22]: (a) alteration of the objects clause of the memorandum (for pre-Act companies, alteration of the main objects); (b) alteration of the articles in relation to insertion or removal of provisions required under Section 2(68) to constitute a private company; (c) change of registered office outside the local limits of any city, town or village under Section 12(5); (d) change in objects for which money was raised from the public through a prospectus where any unutilised amount remains, under Section 13(8); (e) issue of shares with differential rights as to voting or dividend or otherwise under Section 43(a)(ii); (f) variation in the rights attached to a class of shares, debentures or other securities under Section 48; (g) buy-back of shares under Section 68(1); (h) election of a director under Section 151; (i) sale of the whole or substantially the whole of an undertaking under Section 180(1)(a); (j) giving loans, extending guarantee or providing security in excess of the limit specified under Section 186(3). One Person Companies and companies having members up to two hundred are not required to transact any business through postal ballot.
  • Postal ballot procedure [Rule 22]: notice to all shareholders with a draft resolution explaining the reasons, requesting assent or dissent in writing within thirty days from the date of dispatch; sent by registered post or speed post, through registered e-mail ID, or by courier; advertisement at least once in a vernacular newspaper in the principal vernacular language of the district of the registered office having wide circulation there and at least once in an English newspaper having wide circulation in that district, stating that business is to be transacted by postal ballot including e-voting, the date of completion of dispatch of notices, the dates of commencement and end of voting, that ballots received beyond that date are invalid and no voting is allowed beyond it, that members not receiving forms may obtain duplicates, and the contact details of the grievance officer; the notice is placed on the company's website forthwith after dispatch and stays till the last date for receipt of ballots; the Board appoints one scrutinizer not in the company's employment who is willing and available; ballots received are kept in the scrutinizer's safe custody and no person may deface or destroy a ballot paper or declare the identity of the shareholder; the scrutinizer reports as soon as possible after the last date but not later than seven days thereafter; he maintains a register of assent/dissent including details of defaced or mutilated ballots and invalid forms; papers stay with him until the Chairman approves and signs the minutes, after which they are returned to the company for safe preservation; assent or dissent received after thirty days from the date of issue of the notice is treated as no reply; results are declared by placing them with the scrutinizer's report on the company's website; and Rule 20 applies mutatis mutandis to e-voting under this rule.
  • Counting of postal ballots: a member voting by postal ballot has votes in proportion to his share in the paid-up share capital and need not use all his votes the same way. The ballots received are segregated into (i) assents; (ii) dissents; (iii) ballots where the member voted partially assenting, partially dissenting, or did not use all his shares in any particular way; and (iv) invalid ballots (absence or mismatch of signature, overwriting, etc.). The resolution is deemed passed if assents are greater in number.
