Members' Resolutions and Representation — Sections 111 to 113

  • Section 111 — circulation of members' resolutions: the number of members required to requisition is the same as for requisitioning a general meeting under Section 100(2). Prerequisites of a valid requisition [Section 111(2)]: (a) in writing and signed by members holding, on the date of receipt, not less than one-tenth of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights (or, for a company without share capital, one-tenth of the total voting power of members having a right to vote); (b) two or more copies of the requisition must together carry the signatures of all the requisitionists; (c) deposited at the registered office not less than six weeks before the meeting where notice of a resolution is required, and not less than two weeks before the meeting for other resolutions; (d) a sum reasonably sufficient to meet the company's expenses is deposited or tendered — on tender, no payment is made but an unconditional offer to pay is made. Proviso: if an AGM is called on a date within six weeks after the copy has been deposited, the copy is deemed properly deposited even though not deposited within the required time. The company is not bound to circulate the notice if the prerequisites are not complied with.
  • Refusal to circulate [Section 111(3)–(4)]: the company is not bound to circulate a statement if, on the application of the company or of any person claiming to be aggrieved, the Central Government (power delegated to the Regional Director, MCA Notification 4090(E) dated 19-12-2016) declares by order that the rights conferred are being abused to secure needless publicity for defamatory matter. The order may also direct that the company's costs be paid to it by the requisitionists, even though they are not parties to the application. Default: company and every officer in default liable to a penalty of ₹25,000.
  • Section 112: the President of India or the Governor of a State, if a member of a company, may appoint such person as he thinks fit to act as his representative at any meeting; that person may exercise the same rights and powers, including the right to vote by proxy and postal ballot, as the President or Governor could.
  • Section 113: where a body corporate is a member or a creditor (including a debenture-holder) and authorises a person as its representative at any meeting of the company, of any class of members, or of creditors, that representative may exercise the same rights and powers, including voting by proxy and by postal ballot, on behalf of the body corporate he represents.

Resolutions — Sections 114 to 117

  • Ordinary resolution [Section 114(1)]: the notice required under the Act has been duly given and the votes cast in favour — on a show of hands, electronically or on a poll, including the Chairman's casting vote if any, by members voting in person, by proxy where allowed, or by postal ballot — exceed the votes cast against by members so entitled and voting.
  • Special resolution [Section 114(2)]: (a) the intention to propose the resolution as a special resolution is duly specified in the notice calling the general meeting or in other intimation to members; (b) the notice required under the Act has been duly given; and (c) the votes cast in favour are not less than three times the votes cast against by members so entitled and voting. Characteristics: specified majority of three times the votes against; the resolution set out in the notice; proper 21 days' notice for the general meeting; and an explanatory statement annexed to the notice for special business.
  • Special notice [Section 115, Rule 23]: required where the Act or the articles so provide; given to the company by members holding not less than 1% of the total voting power, or holding shares on which an aggregate sum not exceeding ₹5,00,000, as prescribed, has been paid up — Rule 23(1) fixes the prescribed figure at shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than ₹5,00,000 has been paid up on the date of the notice. Cases: (a) resolution at an AGM appointing an auditor other than the retiring auditor [Section 140(4)]; (b) resolution at an AGM expressly providing that a retiring auditor shall not be re-appointed [Section 140(4)]; (c) resolution to remove a director before the expiry of his period of office [Section 169(2)]; (d) resolution to appoint another person as director in place of the removed director at the meeting at which he is removed [Section 169(2)]. The articles may add matters requiring special notice. Timing: members send the notice not earlier than 3 months but at least 14 days before the meeting, exclusive of the day of giving the notice and the day of the meeting; the company immediately on receipt gives its members notice of the resolution at least seven days before the meeting, exclusive of the day of dispatch and the day of the meeting, in the same manner as notice of a general meeting. Where that is not practicable, the notice is published in an English newspaper in English and in a vernacular newspaper in the vernacular language, both having wide circulation in the State of the registered office, and posted on the company's website, if any — at least seven days before the meeting, exclusive of the day of publication and the day of the meeting.
  • Section 116: a resolution passed at an adjourned meeting of a company, of the holders of any class of shares, or of the Board is treated as having been passed on the day on which it was actually passed and not on any earlier date.
  • Section 117 — filing: a copy of every resolution or agreement in respect of the matters in Section 117(3), together with the explanatory statement under Section 102, if any, annexed to the notice, must be filed with the Registrar in Form MGT-14 with fee within 30 days of the passing or making thereof [Rule 24] — read as 60 days for a Specified IFSC public company [GSR 8(E)] and a Specified IFSC private company [GSR 9(E)], both dated 4-1-2017. Proviso: every resolution that alters the articles, and every agreement referred to in Section 117(3), must be embodied in or annexed to every copy of the articles issued after the resolution is passed or the agreement made.
  • Resolutions and agreements to be filed [Section 117(3)]: special resolutions; resolutions agreed to by all the members which, if not so agreed, would have needed a special resolution to be effective; any Board resolution or agreement relating to the appointment, re-appointment, renewal of appointment, or variation of the terms of appointment of a managing director; resolutions or agreements agreed to by any class of members which, if not so agreed, would have needed a specified majority or a particular manner, and all resolutions or agreements binding a class of members though not agreed to by all of them; resolutions requiring a company to be wound up voluntarily passed under Section 59 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016; resolutions passed under Section 179(3) — clause (g) does not apply to a private company [GSR 464(E) dated 5-6-2015 as amended by GSR 583(E) dated 13-6-2017] nor to a Specified IFSC public company [GSR 8(E) dated 4-1-2017]; and any other prescribed resolution or agreement placed in the public domain. No person is entitled under Section 399 to inspect or obtain copies of Section 179(3) resolutions. Second proviso: the clause does not apply to a resolution passed to grant loans, give guarantee or provide security in respect of loans under Section 179(3)(f) in the ordinary course of business by (a) a banking company; (b) any prescribed class of NBFC registered under Chapter IIIB of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, prescribed in consultation with the RBI; (c) any prescribed class of housing finance company registered under the National Housing Bank Act, 1987, prescribed in consultation with the National Housing Bank.

Minutes, Inspection and Electronic Records — Sections 118 to 120

  • Section 118(1): every company must prepare, sign and keep minutes of every general meeting, every meeting of any class of shareholders or creditors (including a meeting called by requisitionists), every resolution passed by postal ballot, and every meeting of the Board or of any committee of the Board, within 30 days of the conclusion of the meeting or of the passing of the postal ballot resolution, in books kept for that purpose with pages consecutively numbered.
  • Contents: a fair and correct summary of the proceedings; all appointments made at the meeting; for a Board or committee meeting, also the names of directors present and, for each resolution, the names of directors dissenting from or not concurring with it.
  • Exclusions [Section 118(5)–(6)]: nothing may be included which, in the Chairman's opinion, is or could reasonably be regarded as defamatory of any person, or is irrelevant or immaterial to the proceedings, or is detrimental to the interests of the company. Inclusion or exclusion on these grounds is at the absolute discretion of the Chairman.
  • No document purporting to be a report of the proceedings of any general meeting may be circulated or advertised at the company's expense unless it includes the matters required by Section 118 to be contained in the minutes. Under Section 118(10) every company must observe the Secretarial Standards on general and Board meetings specified by the ICSI and approved by the Central Government — sub-section (10) does not apply to a Specified IFSC public company [GSR 8(E)] or a Specified IFSC private company [GSR 9(E)], both dated 4-1-2017. For Specified IFSC companies a proviso to Section 118(1) allows Board/committee minutes to be prepared and signed at or before the next Board or committee meeting.
  • Rule 25 — minute books: distinct minute books for each type of meeting — (i) general meetings of members; (ii) meetings of creditors; (iii) meetings of the Board; (iv) meetings of each committee of the Board. Resolutions passed by postal ballot are recorded in the minute book of general meetings as if deemed passed at a general meeting. Entries are made within 30 days of conclusion of the meeting, along with the date of entry. For each postal ballot resolution, a brief report on the postal ballot including the resolution proposed, the result of the voting and the summary of the scrutinizer's report is entered in the minute book of general meetings with the date of entry, within 30 days from the date of passing of the resolution.
  • Signing [Rule 25]: each page initialled or signed, and the last page of the record of each meeting dated and signed — (i) Board/committee minutes: by the Chairman of that meeting or the Chairman of the next succeeding meeting; (ii) general meeting minutes: by the Chairman of the same meeting within 30 days or, on his death or inability within that period, by a director duly authorised by the Board; (iii) postal ballot resolutions: by the Chairman of the Board within 30 days or, if there is no Chairman of the Board or on his death or inability within that period, by a director duly authorised by the Board.
  • Custody: minute books of general meetings are kept at the registered office, preserved permanently, in the custody of the company secretary or any director duly authorised by the Board. Minute books of Board and committee meetings are preserved permanently in the custody of the company secretary or an authorised director, kept at the registered office or such place as the Board may decide.
  • Section 8 companies: Section 118 does not apply as a whole, except that minutes may be recorded within 30 days of the conclusion of every meeting where the articles provide for confirmation of minutes by circulation [GSR 466(E) dated 5-6-2015 as amended by GSR 584(E) dated 13-6-2017, available to a Section 8 company not in default under Section 137 or Section 92].
  • Section 119 — inspection of minute-books of general meetings: kept at the registered office and open for inspection during business hours by any member without charge, subject to reasonable restrictions in the articles or imposed in general meeting, with at least 2 hours in each business day allowed. A member is entitled to a copy of any minutes within seven working days of a request, on payment of the prescribed fee. Rule 26: the fee is as specified in the articles but not exceeding ₹10 for each page or part of a page; a member requesting a soft copy of minutes of general meetings held during the three financial years immediately preceding is entitled to it free of cost. On refusal or default, the Tribunal may, without prejudice to the penalty under Section 119(3), order immediate inspection or direct that the copy be forthwith sent [Section 119(4)].
  • Section 120 and Rules 27–29 — electronic records: every listed company, or a company having at least 1,000 shareholders, debenture-holders and other security holders, may maintain its records in electronic form; for existing companies data may be converted from physical to electronic mode within six months from the date of notification of Section 120. Conditions: same formats and other requirements as under the Act/rules; information adequately recorded for future reference; records readable, retrievable and reproducible in printed form; capable of being dated and digitally signed where required; once dated and signed digitally, incapable of being edited or altered; and capable of being updated with the date of updating recorded on every updating.
  • Rule 28 — responsibility: the Managing Director, Company Secretary or any other director or officer as the Board may decide is responsible for maintenance and security of electronic records, and must provide adequate protection against unauthorised access, alteration or tampering; ensure against loss from damage to or failure of the media; ensure non-repudiation by the signatory; ensure computer systems, software and hardware are adequately secured and validated for accuracy, reliability and consistent intended performance; ensure the systems can discern invalid and altered records; ensure records are accurate, accessible and reproducible; ensure they are at all times retrievable to readable and printable form; keep records in a non-rewritable and non-erasable format like PDF; keep at least one backup taken at a periodicity not exceeding one day, each backup authenticated and dated and securely kept at places decided by the Board; limit access to the MD, company secretary or other director/officer or persons authorised by the Board; ensure any reproduction of non-electronic originals is complete, authentic, true and legible; arrange and index records for easy location, access and retrieval; and take necessary steps for security, integrity and confidentiality.
  • Rule 29: records in electronic form are made available for inspection in electronic form; copies containing a clear reproduction of the whole or part are provided on payment not exceeding ₹10 per page.

One Person Company — Section 122

  • Sections that do not apply to an OPC [Section 122(1)]: Section 98 (power of Tribunal to call meetings of members) and Sections 100 to 111 — namely 100 (calling of EGM), 101 (notice of meeting), 102 (statement to be annexed to notice), 103 (quorum), 104 (chairman), 105 (proxies), 106 (restrictions on voting rights), 107 (voting by show of hands), 108 (voting through electronic means), 109 (demand for poll), 110 (postal ballot) and 111 (circulation of members' resolution). An OPC is also outside Section 96 — it need not hold an AGM.
  • Section 122(2)–(3): the ordinary businesses under Section 102(2)(a) are transacted as provided in sub-section (3). For the purposes of Section 114, any business requiring an ordinary or special resolution at an AGM or other general meeting is sufficiently done if the resolution is communicated by the member to the company, entered in the minutes-book required under Section 118, and signed and dated by the member — that date is deemed to be the date of the meeting for all purposes under the Act.
  • Section 122(4): where there is only one director on the Board of an OPC, any business required to be transacted at a Board meeting is sufficiently done if the resolution by that director is entered in the minutes-book under Section 118 and signed and dated by him; that date is deemed to be the date of the Board meeting for all purposes.

Examples

  • Illustration 1 — minor in the register of members (Luxy Hairstyles Private Limited): the company allotted 500 shares to Mila, the 4-year-old daughter of Mr. Zoey. Mr. Joe, a director, asks how the register entry should be made since a minor is incompetent to contract. Answer: minors cannot contract, so their names cannot be entered in the register of members without the details of a guardian. While filling Form MGT-1, the name of a minor is entered only if the guardian's details are available — therefore Zoey's name must also appear in the register of members alongside Mila's.
  • Illustration 2 — joint holding (New Hospitality Services Private Limited): Tanya and Tarun, recently married, were jointly allotted 1,000 shares. Tarun asks that only his wife's name appear in the company's records. Answer: joint holders may request the company to enter their names in a particular order, or execute transfers to split the holding so that part is shown in one holder's name and part in the other's. But Tarun's condition that only Tanya's name appear as member cannot be acceded to — though the names can be entered so that his wife's name appears first. The articles of most companies provide for exclusion of the other joint holders with seniority determined by the order in which the names stand in the register of members.
  • Illustration 3 — annual return where the AGM did not happen (Big Fox Entertainment Limited): the AGM was called for 30th September, 2024 to lay the financial statements for the year ended 31st March 2024, but was cancelled for want of quorum, and no annual return was filed. The directors argue the 60-day period does not apply. Answer: the contention is incorrect. Under Section 92(4) the annual return must be filed within 60 days of the AGM, or where no AGM is held, within 60 days from the date the AGM should have been held, with the reasons for not holding it. The AGM should have been held by 30th September, 2024; the company was still required to file within the specified time with reasons. It has contravened Section 92 and is liable to the penalty in Section 92(5).
  • Illustration 4 — e-mail notice not received (Elixir Logistics Limited): Mr. Abhinav complains he was not served notice of the AGM; the company proves it e-mailed the notice; he says he never received it. Answer: under Rule 18(3)(v) the company's obligation is satisfied when it transmits the e-mail and it is not responsible for a failure in transmission beyond its control; under Rule 18(3)(vi) the company is not in default for not delivering notice by e-mail if the member failed to provide or update his e-mail address with the company or the depository participant. Elixir Logistics Limited is therefore not guilty if the transmission failure was beyond its control or if Mr. Abhinav did not update his e-mail address.
  • Illustration 5 — shorter notice for an EGM (Aakash Soaps Limited): paid-up share capital ₹50 lakh divided into 5 lakh shares of ₹10 each. Sixty percent of the members holding shares worth ₹40 lakh consented by electronic mode to shorter notice for an EGM. Answer: the consent obtained works out to 80% (40,00,000 / 50,00,000 × 100), whereas the requirement is a majority in number of members representing not less than 95% of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights — i.e. holders of shares worth ₹47,50,000. The EGM therefore cannot be validly called and held.
  • Illustration 6 — quorum in a private company (Nice Games Private Limited): 54 members; AGM called Friday, 1st July 2024 at 2:00 p.m. at the registered office; 28 members present till 2:30 p.m.; the Chairman initiated the meeting and passed the resolutions. Answer: under Section 103 the quorum for a private limited company is two members personally present within half an hour of the appointed time. The quorum was complied with and the company has not contravened the Act.
  • Illustration 7 — quorum lost mid-meeting (Abbey Lights and Sounds Limited): 2,300 members; AGM on Tuesday, 23rd August, 2024 at 10.30 a.m. at Connaught Place, New Delhi; only 18 members personally present by 11.00 a.m.; five special businesses on the agenda; Agenda 1 to 3 were discussed and resolutions passed by 2.30 p.m.; at about 3 p.m. 4 members left with the Chairman's permission and Agendas 4 and 5 were then passed. Answer: with 2,300 members the quorum is 15 members personally present, so 18 sufficed at commencement — but per Secretarial Standard-2 the quorum must be present not only at commencement but also while transacting business. After 4 members left only 14 remained, so quorum was not present when Agendas 4 and 5 were decided; that business cannot be transacted and is a nullity.
  • Illustration 8 — joint shareholders voting against each other (Sports Equipment Private Limited): Mr. Subramaniam and Mrs. Sneha jointly hold 500 equity shares; on a special business at an EGM he favours the resolution and she opposes it. Answer: voting by joint shareholders is done in order of seniority, determined by the order in which their names appear in the register of members; joint holders have a right to instruct the company as to that order. One must therefore see whose name appears first in the register of members and cast the vote accordingly.
  • Illustration 9 — director who is also a shareholder: Answer: directors who are also shareholders stand in a fiduciary relationship with the company in their capacity as directors; but when voting as a shareholder a director votes in the same manner as any common shareholder and, while casting his vote, is not supposed to be influenced by the fact that he is a director of the company.
  • Illustration 10 — insolvent shareholder voting on a show of hands: Answer: Yes. Notwithstanding that he no longer has any beneficial interest in the shares and dividends are payable only to his trustee in bankruptcy, an insolvent shareholder is entitled to exercise the votes attributed to his status as a member so long as he remains on the company's register as a member.
  • Illustration 11 — counting a special resolution (Super Star Bakers Limited): the AGM was attended by 60 members; 10 voted against; 5 abstained; Chairman Mr. Ravinder declared the special resolution passed. Answer: votes in favour must be three times the votes against, so a minimum of 30 members (3 × 10) had to vote in favour. Ignoring the 5 abstentions, 45 members (60 − 10 − 5) voted in favour, far exceeding the required 30. The Chairman's declaration that the special resolution was passed is valid.
  • Illustration 12 — moving several resolutions together (Steel Products Limited): the AGM notice contained the agenda for 8 special businesses and the Chairman decided to move all the resolutions at one time to save members' time. Answer: resolutions are moved separately to avoid confusion and mixing up, but there is nothing illegal if the Chairman decides that two or more resolutions be moved together, unless any member requires each resolution to be put to vote separately or a poll is demanded on any of them. The one case where a resolution must be moved separately is the appointment of directors at a general meeting of a public or private company — two or more directors may not be appointed by a single resolution. Where notice has been given of several resolutions, each must be put separately; however, if the meeting unanimously adopts all the resolutions, that would be immaterial.
  • Illustration 13 — due date of AGM (Abbeys Grocers Private Limited): financial year closed 31st March, 2024. Answer: under Section 96(1) the AGM for FY 2023-24 must be held latest by 30th September 2024 (6 months from close of the financial year), unless an extension is granted by the jurisdictional Registrar of Companies for any special reason.
  • Illustration 14 — first AGM (Abbyrush Mechanics Limited): incorporated 12th July, 2024. Answer: its financial year will close on 31st March, 2025; under Section 96(1) it must hold its first AGM latest by 31st December 2025, i.e. within 9 months of the close of its first financial year. If it does so, it need not hold any AGM in the year of its incorporation.
  • Illustration 15 — Board ignores a requisition (Blumove Peacocks Appliances Private Limited): members holding more than 1/10th voting power requisitioned a general meeting on 14th July, 2024; the directors ignored it. Answer: the requisition being by a sufficient number of requisitionists, the Board was required to initiate the process. Under Section 100(4), if the Board does not within 21 days of receipt of a valid requisition proceed to call a meeting for a day not later than 45 days from receipt, the requisitionists may themselves call and hold the meeting within three months from the date of the requisition; under Section 100(5) it is called and held in the same manner as by the Board. The requisitionists can therefore themselves call and hold the meeting within three months of the requisition.
  • Illustration 16 — requisitionists' meeting abroad on a National Holiday (Vishnu Orchards Limited): registered office in New Delhi; the Board did not call the meeting despite a valid requisition, and the requisitionists decided to hold it in Madrid, Spain on 2nd October, 2024. Answer: the meeting cannot be convened as proposed. Under Rule 17(2) the requisitionists must hold the meeting at the registered office or in the same city or town where the registered office is situated; and the day must be a working day and not a National Holiday — 2nd October, 2024 is a National Holiday.
  • Example — resolutions passed at an adjourned meeting (Purple Cosmetics Private Limited): the EGM was due on Thursday, 1st August, 2024 but was adjourned for want of quorum to Thursday, 8th August, 2024, when two resolutions were passed. Under Section 116 the two resolutions are deemed to have been passed on the adjourned date, 8th August, 2024, and not on the earlier date.
  • MCQ 1 — signing the AGM report (Green Limited): AGM held 31.8.2024; the Chairman went abroad two days later for 31 days; within the period for filing the report the report was signed by two directors, one of whom was an additional director. Answer: (d) — the signing is not in order, since where the Chairman is unable to sign, the report shall be signed by any two directors of the company, one of whom shall be the Managing Director, if there is one, and the company secretary of the company.
  • MCQ 2 — consent for shorter notice of an AGM: options 75%, 90%, 91%, 95% of members entitled. Answer: (d) 95% of members entitled.
  • MCQ 3 — which company need not provide e-voting: (a) B Limited whose equity shares are listed (having both equity and preference shares); (b) A Limited whose equity shares (its only class) are listed; (c) C Limited whose preference shares are listed (having both equity and preference shares); (d) D Limited whose equity as well as preference shares are listed. Answer: (c) C Limited — Rule 20(2) is triggered by listing of equity shares, so a company with only its preference shares listed is not required to provide the facility.
  • Descriptive Q1 — exclusion of matter from minutes (Alpha Software Limited): the Chairman directed exclusion of certain matters detrimental to the company's interest; shareholder Mukesh contended the minutes must contain a fair and correct summary. Answer: under Section 118(5) matters that are (or could reasonably be regarded as) defamatory, irrelevant or immaterial to the proceeding, or detrimental to the interests of the company shall not be included; under Section 118(6) the Chairman has absolute discretion on inclusion or non-inclusion on those grounds. Mukesh's contention is not valid.
  • Descriptive Q2 — competing proxies: general meeting scheduled Friday, 15th April, 2024 at 3.00 P.M.; proxy forms to reach the company at least 48 hours before. Member X appointed Y by a proxy form dated 09-04-2024 deposited at the registered office on 11-04-2024. Member W gave two separate proxies: to M (dated 12-04-2024, deposited the same day) and to N (deposited 14-04-2024). All three proxies attended. Answer: under Section 105 every member entitled to attend and vote has a statutory right to appoint a proxy, who need not be a member; any article requiring the instrument to be lodged more than 48 hours before the meeting takes effect as if 48 hours had been specified. A member may revoke the proxy's authority by voting himself before the proxy has voted, but once the proxy has voted the member cannot retract the authority. Where two proxy instruments by the same shareholder are lodged, one before and one after the expiry of the date fixed for lodging proxies, the former is counted. Therefore Y may vote for X (lodged within time), and for W it is M — not N — who may vote, because the proxy authorising N was deposited less than 48 hours before the meeting.
  • Descriptive Q3 — sweat equity not fully specified (M. H. Mechanics Company Limited): the notice said the issue of sweat equity shares would be considered; Mr. 'A' complains it was not specified fully. Answer: under Section 102(2)(b) all business at a meeting other than an AGM is deemed special business, and under Section 102(1) a statement of material facts must be annexed — (a) the nature of concern or interest, financial or otherwise, of every director and the manager, if any, every other KMP and their relatives, and (b) any other information and facts enabling members to understand the meaning, scope and implications and take a decision. The complete details of the sweat equity issue were required to be sent with the notice; the notice is therefore not valid under Section 102.
  • Descriptive Q4 — register kept at Kolkata (Tulip Gardens Ltd.): the register of members is at the registered office in Mumbai; members residing in Kolkata want it kept at Kolkata; and Mr. Rich, a director holding only 400 shares worth ₹4,000, wants to inspect it. Answer: (i) under Section 94(1) the registers under Section 88 and copies of the annual return under Section 92 are kept at the registered office, but may also be kept at any other place in India where more than one-tenth of the total number of members entered in the register of members reside, if approved by a special resolution at a general meeting. Tulip Gardens Ltd. can keep them at Kolkata only if more than one-tenth of the total members reside in Kolkata and a special resolution is passed. (ii) Under Section 94(2) the registers, their indices (except when closed) and copies of all returns are open for inspection by any member, debenture-holder, other security holder or beneficial owner during business hours without payment of any fees; Mr. Rich, being a shareholder, has the right to inspect the register of members free of charge irrespective of the small size of his holding.
  • Descriptive Q5 — requisitioned EGM adjourned for want of quorum (Shreya Transporters and Logistics Ltd.): the Board called an EGM on members' requisition but adjourned it because quorum was absent. Answer: under Section 100(2) the Board must convene a general meeting on requisition by the stipulated minimum number of members; and under Section 103(2)(b) if quorum is not present within half an hour, a meeting called on the requisition of members stands cancelled. The meeting therefore stands cancelled, and the Board's decision to adjourn it is not proper and valid.
  • Descriptive Q6 — amount of capital increase not specified (Zorab Garments Limited): the notice said a resolution to increase share capital would be considered; shareholder Roshni complained the amount of the proposed increase was not specified. Answer: under Section 102(2)(b) all business at a general meeting other than an AGM is special business, and Section 102(1) requires a statement of material facts to be annexed — the nature of concern or interest, financial or otherwise, of every director and the manager, every other KMP and their relatives, and any other information and facts enabling members to understand the meaning, scope and implications. The amount is a material fact with reference to a proposed increase of share capital; the objection is valid and the notice is not a valid notice under Section 102.
  • Descriptive Q7 — poll demanded and then withdrawn: (i) at an AGM of a company having share capital, 80 members present in person or by proxy holding more than 1/10th of the total voting power demanded a poll; the Chairman rejected it saying only members present in person can demand a poll. (ii) During the poll the members who demanded it wanted to withdraw; the Chairman rejected that too, saying once a poll starts it cannot be withdrawn. Answer: under Section 109(1) a poll shall be ordered on a demand by members present in person or by proxy, where allowed, having not less than one-tenth of the total voting power or holding shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than ₹5,00,000 (or higher prescribed amount) has been paid up; and under Section 109(2) the demand may be withdrawn at any time by the persons who made it. Hence (i) the Chairman cannot reject the demand for poll, subject to the provisions in the articles; and (ii) he cannot reject the request for withdrawal of the demand.
  • Descriptive Q8 — inspecting proxies (Surya): Surya gives notice for inspecting proxies five days before the meeting and approaches the company two days before the scheduled meeting to inspect. Answer: under Section 105(8) a member entitled to vote may inspect the proxies lodged during the period beginning 24 hours before the time fixed for commencement of the meeting and ending with its conclusion, at any time during business hours, provided not less than three days' notice in writing was given. Surya's notice (five days) is proper and its validity cannot be denied — but he can inspect only within the 24-hours-before-to-conclusion window, not two days prior to the meeting.
  • Descriptive Q9 — entities outside the SBO Rules: under Rule 8 of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018 (as amended w.e.f. 8-2-2019), the Rules do not apply to the extent the shares of the reporting company are held by (a) the IEPF Authority under Section 125(5); (b) its holding reporting company, provided details of that holding reporting company are reported in Form BEN-2; (c) the Central Government, State Government or any local authority; (d) a reporting company, a body corporate, or an entity controlled wholly or partly by the Central and/or State Government(s); (e) SEBI-registered investment vehicles such as mutual funds, AIFs, REITs and InvITs regulated by SEBI; (f) investment vehicles regulated by the RBI, IRDAI or PFRDA.
  • Descriptive Q10 — first AGM and ROC extension (Infotech Ltd.): incorporated 1.4.2022; no general meeting held till 30.4.2024. Answer: under Section 96 the first AGM must be held within 9 months from the closing of the first financial year. The first financial year runs 1st April 2022 to 31st March 2023, so the first AGM should have been held on or before 31st December, 2023. The Registrar may for special reason extend the time for holding an AGM other than the first AGM by a period not exceeding three months — hence for the first AGM the Registrar has no power to grant any extension.
  • Descriptive Q11 — composition of quorum (DJA Water Tanks Ltd.): the articles require the personal presence of 7 members; the company has 965 members on the date of the meeting; at the EGM to consider the appointment of a Managing Director those present were — (i) A, representative of the Governor of Uttar Pradesh; (ii) B and C, preference shareholders; (iii) D, representing Y Ltd. and Z Ltd.; (iv) E, F, G and H, proxies of shareholders. Answer: for a public company with not more than 1,000 members the statutory quorum is 5, but the articles may require a larger number — so the quorum here is 7 members personally present (higher of 5 and 7). Only members entitled to vote on the resolution proposed are counted, and only members present in person, not by proxy. A representative appointed by a body corporate that is a member is deemed a member present in person; where two or more member-companies appoint the same person, each such company is counted. The President/Governor's appointed representative is likewise deemed a member personally present. Applying this: A counts; B and C are excluded because they represent preference shares and the agenda is the appointment of a Managing Director, which does not directly affect their rights, so they have no voting rights; D counts as two (representing Y Ltd. and Z Ltd.); E, F, G and H are excluded as proxies. Only three members are personally present against a requirement of 7 — the quorum requirement is not met and the composition does not constitute a valid quorum.
  • Descriptive Q12 — meaning of proxy and provisions on appointment: a proxy is an instrument in writing executed by a shareholder authorising another person to attend a meeting and vote thereat on his behalf in his absence; the term also applies to the person so appointed. Under Section 105(1) any member entitled to attend and vote may appoint a proxy; a proxy has no right to speak and cannot vote except on a poll — meaning he cannot vote on a resolution by show of hands; the Central Government may prescribe classes of companies whose members cannot appoint proxies; under Section 105(6) the instrument must be in writing, signed by the appointer or his attorney duly authorised in writing, or, if the appointer is a body corporate, be under its seal or signed by an officer or duly authorised attorney; and under Section 105(7) an instrument in the prescribed form cannot be questioned for failing to comply with special requirements in the articles.
  • Descriptive Q13 — annual return not filed after a cancelled AGM (Super Mart Limited): the AGM called to lay the financial statements was cancelled for want of quorum and the directors did not file the annual return, believing the 60-day rule did not apply. Answer: under Section 92(4) the annual return is filed within 60 days of the AGM or, where no AGM is held in any year, within 60 days from the date on which it should have been held, together with a statement of the reasons for not holding it. The AGM should have been held within six months from the close of the financial year but did not take place. The directors' opinion is incorrect; the company has contravened Section 92. Penalty under Section 92(5): the company and every officer in default are liable to ₹10,000, and for continuing failure a further penalty of ₹100 for each day, subject to a maximum of ₹2,00,000 for the company and ₹50,000 for an officer in default.
  • Descriptive Q14 — short notice by post (Madurai Bakes Ltd.): AGM notice issued for 7th September, 2024, posted to members on 16th August, 2024. Answer: (i) Section 101(1) requires not less than 21 clear days' notice; both the date of service and the date of the meeting are excluded, and by Rule 35(6) of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014 service by post is deemed effected at the expiration of 48 hours after posting. After excluding those 48 hours, the day of sending and the date of meeting, only 19 clear days' notice was served, so the meeting was not validly called. (ii) The notice falls short by 2 days. (iii) The Companies Act, 2013 contains nothing specific on condonation of delay in giving notice, so the delay cannot be condoned.
  • Descriptive Q15 — quorum computation and adjournment (KMN Cables Ltd.): AGM scheduled 15th September, 2024 at 11:00 A.M.; the company has 900 members; present by 11:30 A.M. were P1, P2 and P3 (shareholders), P4 representing ABC Ltd., P5 representing DEF Ltd., and P6 and P7 as proxies. Answer: (i) with not more than 1,000 members the quorum is 5 members personally present. P1, P2 and P3 count as three. P4 and P5, being persons authorised by resolution by member companies ABC Ltd. and DEF Ltd., are deemed members present in person and count as two. P6 and P7, being proxies, are excluded. Total 5 members — the quorum requirement is fulfilled. (ii) If P4 reaches after 11:30 A.M., i.e. after half an hour from the starting time, he is essential to making up the quorum, so the meeting stands adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place, or such other time and place as the Board decides. (iii) On such adjournment or change of day, time or place, the company must give not less than 3 days' notice to the members individually or by publishing an advertisement in the newspaper. (iv) If quorum is again not present within half an hour at the adjourned meeting, the members present shall form the quorum.
  • Descriptive Q16 — entries permitted beyond seven days: the usual time for entries in the register of members / debenture-holders / other security holders is seven days after Board or committee approval. The events on which entries may be made later are those in Rule 5(7) — for companies whose securities are listed in or outside India, particulars of any pledge, charge, lien or hypothecation created by the promoters over the company's securities held by them, including names of pledgee/pawnee and any revocation — and Rule 5(8) — where promoters of a listed company that has formed a joint venture company have pledged, hypothecated or created charge or lien over any security of the listed company in connection with that joint venture. In both cases the entry may be made within fifteen days from the happening of the event.
  • Descriptive Q17 — shorter notice for a general meeting (Shilpkaar Constructions Limited): directors Ratna, Rimpi and Ratnesh wish to call a general meeting on shorter than 21 clear days' notice; the fourth director, Nilesh, says this attracts penalty for contravention. Paid-up share capital is ₹30 crore divided into 3 crore shares of ₹10 each. Answer: the first proviso to Section 101(1) permits a shorter notice with consent in writing or by electronic mode of (i) not less than 95% of the members entitled to vote, for an AGM; and (ii) for any other general meeting, where there is share capital, a majority in number of members entitled to vote who represent not less than 95% of the paid-up share capital giving a right to vote, or, where there is no share capital, not less than 95% of the total voting power exercisable at that meeting. The second proviso clarifies that a member entitled to vote only on some resolutions is counted for those and not the others. Shilpkaar Constructions Limited is permitted to call the meeting at shorter notice provided members holding at least 95% of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights consent. Nilesh's opinion that this is a contravention attracting penalty is not correct.
  • Descriptive Q18 — Chairman unavailable to sign minutes (Miraj Sugar Mills Limited): AGM held September 15, 2024, presided over by Mr. Venkat, Chairman of the Board; on September 17, 2024 he left India for London to look after his sick father without signing the minutes. Answer: Section 118 requires minutes of every general meeting (including one called by requisitionists), of meetings of any class of shareholders or creditors, of the Board or its committees, and of postal ballot resolutions to be prepared, signed and kept within thirty days of the conclusion of the meeting; minutes so kept are evidence of the proceedings. By Rule 25 of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014 read with Section 118, each page is initialled or signed and the last page of the record of each meeting is dated and signed, in the case of a general meeting, by the Chairman of the same meeting within thirty days, or, in the event of the death or inability of that Chairman within that period, by a director duly authorised by the Board. Hence the minutes may be signed, in Mr. Venkat's absence, by any other director authorised by the Board.
  • Descriptive Q19 — minutes of postal ballot resolutions (Shikhar Cement Limited): two resolutions were passed by postal ballot. Answer: Section 118 requires entries of postal ballot resolutions in the minutes book, and Rule 25(1)(b)(ii) requires that for every resolution passed by postal ballot a brief report on the postal ballot conducted — including the resolution proposed, the result of the voting thereon and the summary of the scrutinizer's report — be entered in the minutes book of general meetings along with the date of such entry, within thirty days from the date of passing of the resolution. The directors must therefore enter (i) the brief report including the resolution proposed, (ii) the result of the voting by shareholders, (iii) the summary of the scrutinizer's report, and (iv) the date of making the entry — all within thirty days of passing.
  • Descriptive Q20 — when must the annual return be certified (Disha Home Appliances Limited): paid-up share capital ₹8 crore divided into 80 lakh shares of ₹10 each. Answer: under Section 92(2) read with Rule 11(2) the annual return must be certified by a company secretary in practice where the company is (i) a listed company, or (ii) has paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore or more or turnover of ₹50 crore or more. Since its paid-up capital is only ₹8 crore, certification will be required only if Disha Home Appliances Limited gets listed, or its paid-up share capital rises to ₹10 crore or more, or its turnover becomes ₹50 crore or more. The certificate is given in Form MGT-8 and states, inter alia, that the annual return discloses the facts correctly and adequately and that the company has complied with all the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Descriptive Q21 — report on AGM and penalty (Prince Auto-parts Limited, a listed company): Answer: (i) under Section 121(2) the company must file a copy of the report on its AGM with the jurisdictional Registrar of Companies within a maximum of thirty days of the conclusion of the AGM. (ii) Under Section 121(3), on failure to file within the specified time — Company: ₹1,00,000 and, for continuing failure, a further penalty of ₹500 for each day after the first during which the failure continues, subject to a maximum of ₹5,00,000. Every officer in default: minimum ₹25,000 and, for continuing failure, a further penalty of ₹500 for each day after the first, subject to a maximum of ₹1,00,000.

Why It Matters / Application

Chapter VII supplies the procedural spine on which every corporate decision rests: an increase in authorised capital, a buy-back, a change of registered office or the removal of a director is legally effective only if the notice period, quorum, majority and filing steps of Sections 96 to 122 were observed. The recurring examination pattern is a numeric one — count the members personally present and test them against the Section 103 slab (5 / 15 / 30 for a public company; 2 for a private company), strip out proxies, add authorised representatives of bodies corporate (one representative of two member-companies counts twice), exclude preference shareholders whose rights the agenda does not touch; compute the 95% shorter-notice threshold on paid-up capital rather than on head-count (Aakash Soaps: 80% consent against a required ₹47,50,000 of ₹50,00,000); count 21 clear days after deducting the 48-hour postal deeming fiction (Madurai Bakes: 19 days, short by 2); and test a special resolution by the 3:1 ratio while ignoring abstentions (Super Star Bakers: 10 against, 45 for, valid). The register and return provisions supply the audit trail — MGT-1, MGT-2, MGT-3, MGT-4/5/6, BEN-1/2/3/4, MGT-7 or MGT-7A, MGT-8, MGT-11, MGT-12, MGT-13, MGT-14 and MGT-15 — and the timelines (7 days for register entries, 15 days for promoter pledges in listed companies, 30 days for beneficial-interest declarations and for filing resolutions, 60 days for the annual return) are the dates against which a Registrar measures default and levies the daily-accruing penalties.

Note

Traps and provisos worth memorising. (1) A cancelled AGM does not postpone the annual return — the 60 days run from the date the AGM ought to have been held (Big Fox, Super Mart). (2) The Registrar's 3-month extension is available for every AGM except the first (Infotech Ltd.). (3) Quorum failure at a requisitioned meeting means the meeting stands cancelled under Section 103(2)(b), not adjourned (Shreya Transporters); for a Board-called meeting it is adjourned to the same day next week, and at the adjourned meeting the members present are the quorum. (4) An index is unnecessary where members are fewer than 50; a proxy can act for a maximum of 50 members holding not more than 10% of the voting share capital, but a member holding more than 10% must appoint a sole proxy who can act for no one else. (5) A proxy cannot speak and cannot vote on a show of hands — only on a poll — and a proxy lodged 48 hours before the meeting is valid however long a period the articles demand; of two competing instruments, the one lodged in time prevails (Members X and W). (6) Explanatory statements are needed for special business but not for the four ordinary businesses, and not for an EGM called by requisitionists [Rule 17(5)]. (7) Rule 20(2) is triggered by listing of equity shares plus not less than 1,000 members — listing of preference shares alone does not attract e-voting (MCQ 3). (8) OPCs and companies with up to 200 members need not use postal ballot at all, and quorum rules do not apply to postal-ballot items. (9) Special notice under Section 115 is a members' notice to the company (not earlier than 3 months, at least 14 days before), distinct from the company's 7-day notice to members. (10) Section 116 fixes the date of a resolution at an adjourned meeting on the day it was actually passed (Purple Cosmetics: 8th August 2024). (11) Section 93 stands omitted w.e.f. 13-6-2018, and Section 92(1)(c) was omitted w.e.f. 5th March 2021. (12) Exemptions are conditional — the Government-company exemptions from Sections 89 and 90, the private-company and Section 8 relaxations, all lapse if the company has defaulted in filing financial statements under Section 137 or the annual return under Section 92. (13) Address, e-mail ID, UIN and PAN in the register of members are shielded from inspection and from extracts/copies under Rule 14. (14) Wilfully false or suppressed information in an SBO declaration attracts punishment for fraud under Section 447, not merely a penalty.

Chapter 8 — Declaration and Payment of Dividend

Source: 87777bos-aps2160-ch8.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Dividend is a distribution of profits, not a statutory entitlement: Section 2(35) defines "dividend" only inclusively — it "includes any interim dividend". In substance it is a distribution of sums to members out of profits, and wherever permitted, out of free reserves. It is the shareholder's return on capital invested and is part of distributable profits paid out to them.
  • Dividend is not a liability until declared: It becomes a debt only when declared by shareholders at a validly constituted general meeting by ordinary resolution, at the rate recommended by the Board or such lower rate as the members may decide.
  • Board recommends, members declare — but members cannot increase: Under Clause 80 of Table F, Schedule I, the company in general meeting may declare dividends, but no dividend shall exceed the amount recommended by the Board. Declaration at a rate higher than that recommended by the Board is not permitted, even unanimously.
  • Dividend is computed on face value, not market price: A "20% dividend" means 20% of the nominal/face value of the share, wholly irrespective of the market quotation or the price the shareholder paid.
  • Ordinary business at the AGM: Under Section 102(2), declaration of dividend at the AGM is ordinary business requiring an ordinary resolution. At any other general meeting it becomes special business. The Board's recommendation itself is disclosed in the Board's Report under Section 134(3)(k).
  • Dividend must never be paid out of capital: This is why Section 123(2) mandates providing depreciation as per Schedule II before declaration, and why capital profits and revaluation surpluses are excluded.
  • Transfer to reserves is entirely discretionary: The Companies Act, 2013 prescribes no mandatory percentage transfer to reserves before declaring dividend — the company is free to transfer any portion, or nothing at all.

Key Definitions / Terms

Dividend [Section 2(35)]
"Dividend" includes any interim dividend. In common parlance, a distribution of any sums to members out of profits and, wherever permitted, out of free reserves available for the purpose.
Free Reserves [Section 2(43)]
Such reserves which, as per the latest audited balance sheet of a company, are available for distribution as dividend. The following shall not be treated as free reserves: (a) any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets, whether shown as a reserve or otherwise; or (b) any change in carrying amount of an asset or of a liability recognised in equity, including surplus in the profit and loss account on measurement of the asset or the liability at fair value.
Interim Dividend [Sections 123(3) & 123(4)]
Dividend declared by the Board of Directors at any time during the period from closure of the financial year till the holding of the AGM — i.e. out of profits before the final adoption of the accounts by shareholders. It is said to be declared and paid between two AGMs.
Final Dividend
Dividend declared at the Annual General Meeting of the company, on the recommendation of the Board, after the close of the financial year and after preparation of the financial statements.
Cumulative Preference Shares
Shares in respect of which dividend gets accumulated; arrears arising due to insufficiency of profits in the current year are payable out of profits earned in later years. Until dividend on cumulative preference shares is paid in full including arrears, no dividend is payable on equity shares.
Non-cumulative Preference Shares
Dividend is payable only in a year of profit; there is no accumulation. If no dividend is declared in a year for any reason, the right to receive dividend for that year lapses and the holder is not entitled to arrears out of future years' profits.
Equity Shares
Shares which are not preference shares. They enjoy no preferential right as to payment of dividend or repayment of capital. The rate is recommended by the Board, may vary year to year, and depends on the dividend policy and availability of profits after satisfying preference shareholders' rights.
Unpaid Dividend Account (UDA) [Section 124]
A special account opened by the company in any scheduled bank to which the total amount of declared dividend that remains unpaid or unclaimed for 30 days from declaration must be transferred, within 7 days from expiry of that 30-day period.
Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) [Section 125]
A fund established by the Central Government, governed by Section 125 read with the Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority (Accounting, Audit, Transfer and Refund) Rules, 2016 (Notification No. GSR 854(E) dated 05.09.2016, w.e.f. 07.09.2016), credited with specified amounts and utilised for refund of unclaimed and unpaid amounts, promotion of investor awareness and protection of investors' interests.
Depreciation
A notional estimate of the reduction in the value of an asset due to (i) wear and tear, (ii) efflux of time, and (iii) improvements in technology, etc. To be provided in accordance with Schedule II before declaring dividend [Section 123(2)].
Record Date
The date announced by the company for determining entitlement to dividend — all persons whose names appear in the register of members on that date are entitled to the dividend.
Disgorgement
The legally enforced repayment of ill-gotten gains imposed on wrongdoers by the courts. Funds received through illegal or unethical business transactions are disgorged, or paid back, often with interest and/or penalties, to those affected by the action.

Types of Dividend

I. Classification based on time of declaration — Interim Dividend and Final Dividend.

Basis for ComparisonInterim DividendFinal Dividend
DefinitionDeclared and paid during an accounting year, i.e. before finalisation of accounts for the year.Recommended by the Board of Directors and approved by shareholders at the AGM, after the close of the financial year.
AnnouncementAnnounced by the Board of Directors.Recommended by the Board of Directors and approved by shareholders.
Time of DeclarationBefore preparation of financial statements.After preparation of financial statements.
RevocationCan be revoked with the consent of all shareholders.Cannot be revoked.

Sources permitted for declaring interim dividend [Section 123(3)]:

  • Surplus in the profit and loss account; or
  • Profits of the financial year in which such dividend is sought to be declared; or
  • Profits generated in the financial year till the quarter preceding the date of declaration of the interim dividend.

Loss-year cap on interim dividend: If the company has incurred a loss during the current financial year up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the date of declaration of interim dividend, such interim dividend shall not be declared at a rate higher than the average rate of dividend declared during the immediately preceding three financial years.

II. Classification based on nature of shares — this classification does not require any specific provision in the articles. Under Section 43, holders of preference shares are assured a preferential dividend at a fixed rate during the life of the company. Preference dividend, unless agreed to be cumulative, need not be paid every year — a company may decide not to declare any dividend where there is a deficiency of profits.

How It Works / Logic

  • Sources for declaration [Section 123(1)]: (a) profits of the current financial year arrived at after providing for depreciation in accordance with Schedule II; (b) profits of any previous financial year(s) arrived at after providing for depreciation as per Schedule II and remaining undistributed — i.e. credit balance in profit and loss account and free reserves; (c) both (a) and (b); (d) money provided by the Central Government or a State Government for payment of dividend in pursuance of a guarantee given by that Government.
  • Only free reserves may be used: Under the Third Proviso to Section 123(1), only free reserves and no other reserves are to be used for declaration or payment of dividend.
  • Set-off of carried-over losses [Fourth Proviso to Section 123(1)]: Before declaration of any dividend, carried-over previous losses and depreciation not provided in previous year(s) must be set off against the profit of the company for the current year.
  • Exclusion of notional gains [Proviso to Section 123(1)(a)]: In computing profits, any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets, and any change in carrying amount of an asset or liability on measurement at fair value, shall be excluded.
  • Capital profits: Capital profits are not the same as distributable profits because they are not earned in the normal course of business, and therefore are normally not available for distribution as dividend.
  • Why depreciation must be provided: Dividend is an apportionment from revenue profits and must never be declared out of capital (the same logic underlies the prohibition on issue of shares at a discount). If depreciation is not provided: (i) the value of the asset will be overstated in the Balance Sheet, and (ii) the profits of the current year will be overstated. If a company declared all such "profits" as dividend, on winding up the asset values appearing in the Balance Sheet would appear sufficient to repay shareholders' capital, but the actual realisable value would be a paltry sum which may not even meet the expenses of winding up — in effect the company would have declared dividend out of capital, which is prohibited.
  • Transfer to reserves: Left entirely to the discretion of the company. It may transfer any portion of profits it deems fit, or transfer nothing at all.
  • Depositing the dividend [Section 123(4)]: The amount of the dividend, including interim dividend, must be deposited in a separate account maintained with a scheduled bank within 5 days from the date of declaration.
  • Payment [Section 123(5)]: Dividend is payable only to the registered shareholder, or to his order, or to his banker. If a shareholder directs payment to a particular banker and the company pays accordingly, it is deemed to be payment to the shareholder himself. A purchaser of shares whose name is not entered in the Register of Members cannot claim payment of dividend even though he has paid the seller in full.
  • Mode of payment: Dividends are payable in cash and not in kind. Cash dividends may also be paid by cheque, dividend warrant, or through any electronic mode.
  • Partly paid shares [Section 51]: A company may, if authorised by its articles, pay dividend in proportion to the amount paid-up on each share.
  • Bonus shares [First Proviso to Section 123(5)]: The only exception to cash-only payment is capitalisation of profits or reserves for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares, or paying up any amount for the time being unpaid on shares held by members. Declaration of dividend does not affect the company's power to issue fully paid-up bonus shares, but such shares cannot be issued in lieu of dividend.
  • Abeyance pending transfer registration [Section 126]: Where an instrument of transfer has been delivered for registration but the transfer has not been registered, the company must (a) transfer the dividend on such shares to the Unpaid Dividend Account, unless authorised in writing by the registered holder to pay it to the transferee named in the instrument; and (b) keep in abeyance any offer of rights shares under Section 62(1)(a) and any issue of fully paid-up bonus shares under the first proviso to Section 123(5).

Declaration Out of Free Reserves in a Year of Inadequacy or Absence of Profits — Rule 3

Where in any year there are no adequate profits for declaring dividend, the company may declare dividend out of the accumulated profits earned in previous years and transferred to free reserves, only in accordance with the procedure in Rule 3 of the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014, read with the Second Proviso to Section 123. The conditions are cumulative — all of them have to be satisfied.

ConditionRequirementFormula
IThe rate of dividend declared shall not exceed the average of the rates at which dividend was declared by the company in the immediately preceding three years. This condition shall not apply if the company has not declared any dividend in each of the three preceding financial years.Rate of Dividend ≤ (RD1 + RD2 + RD3) / 3
IIThe total amount to be drawn from such accumulated profits shall not exceed 10% of its paid-up share capital and free reserves as appearing in the latest audited financial statement.Amount drawn ≤ 10% of (paid-up share capital + free reserves)
IIIThe amount so drawn shall first be utilised to set off the losses incurred in the financial year in which dividend is declared; only thereafter may any dividend in respect of equity shares be declared.Available = 10% figure − current year loss
IVThe balance of reserves after such withdrawal shall not fall below 15% of its paid-up share capital as appearing in the latest audited financial statement.Free Reserves − Amount of withdrawal ≥ 15% of paid-up share capital

Exemption: The conditions prescribed by Rule 3 are not applicable to a Government company in which the entire paid-up share capital is held by the Central Government, or by any State Government or Governments, or by the Central Government and one or more State Governments (vide Notification No. 463(E), dated 05-06-2015).

Prohibition on Declaration of Dividend

  • Defaulting company [Section 123(6)]: A company which fails to comply with Section 73 (prohibition on acceptance of deposits from public) and Section 74 (repayment of deposits, etc., accepted before the commencement of the Act of 2013) shall not, so long as such failure continues, declare any dividend on its equity shares.
  • Section 8 companies [Section 8(1)]: A company holding a licence under Section 8 (formation of companies with charitable objects, etc.) is prohibited from paying any dividend to its members; its profits are intended to be applied only in promoting the objects for which it is formed.

Unpaid Dividend Account — Section 124

  • (i) Transfer to UDA: Where a dividend has been declared but not paid or claimed within 30 days from the date of declaration, the company shall, within 7 days from the expiry of that 30-day period, transfer the total amount of unpaid or unclaimed dividend to a special account called the Unpaid Dividend Account, opened in any scheduled bank.
  • (ii) Statement of unpaid dividend: Within 90 days of transferring any amount to the UDA, the company shall prepare a statement containing the names, last known addresses and the amount of unpaid dividend payable to each person, and place it on its website (if any) and also on any other website approved by the Central Government for this purpose.
  • (iii) Interest on default: If default is made in transferring the total unpaid dividend amount or any part of it to the UDA, the company shall pay, from the date of such default, interest at 12% per annum on the amount not so transferred. The interest accruing shall enure to the benefit of the members in proportion to the amount remaining unpaid to them.
  • (iv) Claims: Any person claiming to be entitled to money transferred to the UDA may apply to the company concerned for payment of the money claimed.
  • (v) Transfer to IEPF: Any money in the UDA which remains unpaid or unclaimed for 7 years from the date of such transfer shall be transferred by the company, along with interest accrued thereon, to the IEPF. The company shall send a prescribed statement of details of such transfer to the IEPF Authority, which shall issue a receipt to the company as evidence of the transfer.
  • (vi) Transfer of shares to IEPF [Section 124(6)]: All shares in respect of which dividend has not been paid or claimed for 7 consecutive years or more shall be transferred by the company into the name of the IEPF along with a statement containing prescribed details. Explanation: if any dividend is paid or claimed for any year during that period of seven consecutive years, the share shall not be transferred to the IEPF.
  • (vii) Right to reclaim: Any claimant of shares so transferred is entitled to reclaim the 'transferred shares' from the IEPF in accordance with the prescribed procedure and on submission of prescribed documents.

Time Limits — Consolidated

EventTime limitProvision
Deposit dividend (incl. interim) in a separate scheduled bank accountWithin 5 days of declarationSection 123(4)
Pay dividend / post dividend warrant to entitled shareholdersWithin 30 days of declarationSection 127

Penalties

DefaultOn the companyOn every officer in default / director
Failure to comply with any requirement of Section 124 (UDA) — Section 124(7)Penalty of ₹1,00,000; continuing failure — further ₹500 for each day after the first, subject to a maximum of ₹10,00,000Penalty of ₹25,000; continuing failure — further ₹100 for each day after the first, subject to a maximum of ₹2,00,000

Note on the Section 127 summary: the chapter's Summary also restates the consequence for failure to pay declared dividend/post warrants within 30 days in penalty form — company liable to a penalty of ₹1,00,000 with a further ₹500 per day of continuing failure subject to a maximum of ₹10,00,000, and every officer in default ₹25,000 with a further ₹100 per day subject to a maximum of ₹2,00,000.

Punishment for Failure to Distribute Dividends within 30 Days — Section 127

  • A. Time limit: Where a company declares dividend, it must be paid, or the dividend warrant posted, within 30 days from the date of declaration to the shareholders entitled to it. Posting of dividend warrants within 30 days absolves the company from punishment, irrespective of whether the shareholder actually receives it within that time. The offence is committed only when the company fails to post dividend warrants to the registered addresses of members within 30 days of declaration; non-receipt by shareholders within the prescribed time does not attract punishment.
  • B. Punishment: (i) every director shall be punishable with imprisonment of up to two years if he is knowingly a party to the default, and shall also be liable to a minimum fine of ₹1,000 for every day during which the default continues; (ii) the company shall be liable to pay simple interest at 18% p.a. during the period for which the default continues.
  • C. Exemptions from punishment — no offence is deemed committed where:
    • (a) the dividend could not be paid by reason of the operation of any law;
    • (b) a shareholder has given directions to the company regarding payment of the dividend, those directions cannot be complied with, and the same has been communicated to him;
    • (c) there is a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend;
    • (d) the dividend has been lawfully adjusted by the company against any sum due to it from the shareholder;
    • (e) for any other reason, the failure to pay the dividend or to post the warrant within the prescribed 30 days was not due to any default on the part of the company.

Investor Education and Protection Fund — Section 125

1. Amounts credited to the Fund [Section 125(2)]:

  • (a) amount given by the Central Government by way of grants after due appropriation made by Parliament;
  • (b) donations given by the Central Government, State Governments, companies or any other institution for the purposes of the Fund;
  • (c) the amount lying in the Unpaid Dividend Account of companies transferred to the Fund under Section 124(5);
  • (d) the amount in the General Revenue Account of the Central Government transferred to that account under Section 205A(5) of the Companies Act, 1956 as it stood immediately before the commencement of the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1999, and remaining unpaid or unclaimed on the commencement of the Act of 2013;
  • (e) the amount lying in the Investor Education and Protection Fund under Section 205C of the Companies Act, 1956;
  • (f) the interest or other income received out of investments made from the Fund;
  • (g) the amount received under Section 38(4), i.e. through disgorgement or disposal of securities seized from a person convicted for personation for acquisition of securities as provided in Section 38(3);
  • (h) application money received by companies for allotment of any securities and due for refund — only if unclaimed and unpaid for 7 years from the date it became due for payment;
  • (i) matured deposits with companies other than banking companies — only if unclaimed and unpaid for 7 years from the date due for payment;
  • (j) matured debentures with companies — only if unclaimed and unpaid for 7 years from the date due for payment;
  • (k) interest accrued on the amounts referred to in clauses (h) to (j);
  • (l) amount received from sale proceeds of fractional shares arising out of issuance of bonus shares, merger and amalgamation for seven or more years;
  • (m) redemption amount of preference shares remaining unpaid or unclaimed for seven or more years;
  • (n) such other amounts as prescribed in Rule 3 of the IEPF Authority (Accounting, Audit, Transfer and Refund) Rules, 2016.

Rule 3 additions: (a) all amounts payable as mentioned in clauses (a) to (n) of Section 125(2); (b) all shares in accordance with Section 124(6), i.e. shares whose dividends have not been claimed or paid for seven consecutive years or more; (c) all resultant benefits arising out of shares held by the Authority under (b); (d) all grants, fees and charges received by the Authority under these rules; (e) all sums received by the Authority from such other sources as may be decided by the Central Government; (f) all income earned by the Authority in any year; (fa) all shares held by the Authority in accordance with the proviso to Section 90(9) and all resultant benefits arising out of such shares, without any restrictions; (g) all amounts payable under Section 10B(3) of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970, Section 10B of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1980, Section 38A(3) of the State Bank of India Act, 1955 and Section 40A of the State Bank of India (Subsidiary Bank) Act, 1959; and (h) all other sums of money collected by the Authority as envisaged in the Act. Under Rule 3(3), in the case of term deposits and debentures of companies, due unpaid or unclaimed interest shall be transferred to the Fund along with the transfer of the matured amount.

2. Utilisation of the Fund [Section 125(3)]:

  • (a) refund of unclaimed dividends, matured deposits, matured debentures, application money due for refund, and interest thereon;
  • (b) promotion of investors' education, awareness and protection;
  • (c) distribution of any disgorged amount among eligible and identifiable applicants for shares or debentures, shareholders, debenture-holders or depositors who have suffered losses due to wrong actions by any person, in accordance with the orders of the Court which ordered disgorgement;
  • (d) reimbursement of legal expenses incurred in pursuing class action suits under Sections 37 and 245 by members, debenture-holders or depositors, as sanctioned by the Tribunal;
  • (e) any other purpose incidental thereto in accordance with the IEPF Authority (Accounting, Audit, Transfer and Refund) Rules, 2016.

Refund of amount: A person whose amounts referred to in clauses (a) to (d) of sub-section (2) of Section 205C of the Companies Act, 1956 were transferred to the IEPF after the expiry of 7 years shall be entitled to a refund out of the Fund in respect of such claims, in accordance with the rules made under this section.

3. Application for payment [Section 125(4)]: Any person claiming to be entitled to the amounts referred to in Section 125(2) may apply to the Authority constituted under Section 125(5) for payment of the money claimed.

4. Other provisions governing the IEPF:

  • Constitution of the Authority: By Notification No. GSR 26(E), dated 13.01.2016, the MCA notified Section 125(5), 125(6) (except with respect to the manner of administration of the Fund) and 125(7) w.e.f. 13.01.2016, constituting an Authority for administration of the Fund and maintenance of its accounts and records. Under the IEPF Authority (Appointment of Chairperson and Members, holding of Meetings and provision for Offices and Officers) Rules, 2016, notified on 13.01.2016, the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs is the ex-officio Chairperson; there shall be six members (maximum limit seven) and a Chief Executive Officer who is the convenor of the Authority.
  • Resources: The Central Government may provide the Authority with offices, officers, employees and other resources in accordance with those 2016 Rules.
  • Consultation with CAG: The Authority shall administer the Fund and maintain separate accounts and records in such form as may be prescribed after consultation with the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.
  • Spending: The Authority is competent to spend money out of the Fund for carrying out the objects specified in Section 125(3).
  • Audit: The accounts of the Fund shall be audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India at such intervals as he may specify; the audited accounts with the audit report shall be forwarded annually by the Authority to the Central Government.
  • Annual report: For each financial year the Authority shall prepare, in the prescribed form and at the prescribed time, an annual report giving a full account of its activities and forward a copy to the Central Government, which shall cause the annual report and the CAG's audit report to be laid before each House of Parliament.

Examples

  • Example 1 — Dividend is on face value (AB Ltd. / Mr. Shekar): AB Ltd. has issued equity shares of face value ₹10 per share, currently quoting on the NSE at ₹250 per share. At its AGM held on 27.7.24 the company declared a dividend of 20%. Mr. Shekar owns 1,000 shares purchased at ₹300 per share. Answer: The dividend is calculated on face value, i.e. ₹10. Dividend per share = 20% of ₹10 = ₹2 per share. Mr. Shekar will receive ₹2 × 1,000 shares = ₹2,000.
  • Example 2 — Members cannot exceed the Board's recommended rate: Shareholders at an AGM unanimously passed a resolution for payment of dividend at a rate higher than that recommended by the directors. Answer: Articles usually contain provisions on the pattern of regulations 80 to 85 of Table F to Schedule I. Under regulation 80, although the power to declare a dividend vests with the shareholders, under no circumstances can they declare dividend exceeding the amount recommended by the Board. The resolution is therefore not valid.
  • Example 3 — Interim dividend cap in a loss year: A company declared dividend at 16% during the immediately preceding three financial years. If it incurs a loss in the current financial year, it is permitted to declare interim dividend at a rate not higher than 16%.
  • Example 4 — Revaluation profit is not a free reserve (Shreyas Mechanics Limited): The company owns a plot of land purchased long ago. As property rates rose, it decided to revalue the plot at fair value, moderately ten times the original price, resulting in a revaluation profit of ₹20,00,000. The Board wished to use this ₹20,00,000 along with free reserves of ₹24,00,000 for declaring dividend at the AGM to be held on 28th September, 2023. Answer: Under the Proviso to Section 123(1)(a), the ₹20,00,000 cannot be considered, as it does not form part of free reserves and hence cannot be utilised towards declaration of dividend.
  • Example 5 — Five-day deposit deadline (Avantika Ayurvedic Products Limited): Authorised and paid-up share capital is ₹50 lakh divided into 5,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. At its AGM held on 24th September, 2024, the company declared a dividend of ₹2 per share by ordinary resolution. Answer: The dividend amount must be deposited in a separate account with a scheduled bank latest by 29th September, 2024 (within 5 days of declaration).
  • Illustration 1 — Transfer of more than 10% to reserves (Alma Watches Limited): For the current year the company proposes to transfer more than 10% of its profits to reserves before declaring dividend at the rate of 12%. Can it? Answer: The amount to be transferred to reserves out of profits for any financial year before declaration of dividend has been left to the discretion of the company. Alma Watches Limited is therefore free to transfer any part of its profits to reserves as it may deem fit.
  • Illustration 2 — Nil transfer to reserves (Brix Shipyards Limited): The company earned a profit of ₹1,000 crore for FY 2023-24 and proposed a dividend @ 8.75%, but does not intend to transfer any amount to reserves.
