Answer: Transfer to reserves is at the discretion of the company; it may transfer any part of its profits, or even none, before declaring dividend. Brix Shipyards Limited is justified in not transferring any amount of profits to reserves.
  • Illustration 3 — Full Rule 3 computation (Capricorn Industries Limited): Paid-up capital ₹200 lakh; accumulated reserves ₹240 lakh; loss for the year ending 31st March 2024 is ₹30 lakh. Dividend declared in the three immediately preceding years: Year 1 — 9%, Year 2 — 10%, Year 3 — 12%. What is the maximum rate at which dividend can be declared for the current year?
    Answer: The company has not made adequate profits during the current year ending 31st March 2024 but still wants to declare dividend, so the Rule 3 conditions apply:
    Condition I: Average rate = (9 + 10 + 12) / 3 = 10.33%. Therefore the rate of dividend shall not exceed 10.33%, i.e. 10.3% of paid-up capital of ₹200 lakh = ₹20.6 lakh.
    Condition II: Paid-up capital + free reserves = ₹(200 + 240) lakh = ₹440 lakh (assuming all reserves are free). 10% thereof = ₹44 lakh.
    Condition III: Less: loss for the year = ₹30 lakh. Amount available = ₹14 lakh. Hence the quantum of dividend is further restricted to ₹14 lakh.
    Condition IV: Amount of reserves available after adjustment of current year loss = ₹210 lakh; proposed withdrawal for declaration of dividend ₹14 lakh; balance of reserves = ₹196 lakh. This is more than 15% of paid-up capital (15% of ₹200 lakh) i.e. ₹30 lakh.
    Conclusion: The company can declare a dividend of ₹14 lakh, i.e. at a rate of 7% on its paid-up capital of ₹200 lakh.
  • Illustration 4 — Maintaining a 20% rate out of free reserves (Shipra Sugar Mills Limited): The company has been regularly declaring dividend at 20% on its equity shares for the past 3 years. It has not made adequate profits during the current year ending 31st March 2024, but has adequate free reserves to maintain the 20% rate. Answer: The company can declare a dividend out of its accumulated free reserves subject to: (i) the rate declared shall not exceed the average of the rates at which dividend was declared in the immediately preceding three years — this condition not applying if the company has not declared any dividend in each of the three preceding financial years; (ii) the total amount drawn from free reserves shall not exceed 10% of paid-up share capital and free reserves as per the latest audited financial statement; (iii) the amount so drawn shall first be utilised to set off the losses incurred in the current financial year and only thereafter shall dividend at 20% be declared; (iv) after such withdrawal, the residual reserves shall not fall below 15% of paid-up share capital as per the latest audited financial statement. The company is advised to get the desired dividend recommended by the Board and propose it for members' approval at the ensuing AGM, as the authority to declare dividend lies with the members.
  • Illustration 5 — Record date decides entitlement (East West Limited; Mr. Binoy / Mr. Mohan): Directors proposed dividend at 15% on equity shares for FY 2023-2024. The record date announced was 7th September 2024; the dividend was approved at the AGM held on 3rd September 2024. Mr. Binoy held 2,000 equity shares since 31st March 2018 but transferred them to Mr. Mohan in 2024, whose name was entered in the register of members on 18th June 2024. Who is entitled? Answer: Under Section 123, dividend shall be paid only to the registered shareholder. The record date determines entitlement — all those whose names are in the register of members on that date are entitled. On the record date, Mr. Mohan's name is in the register of members (Mr. Binoy's is not). Therefore the dividend should be paid to Mr. Mohan.
  • Partly paid shares (note to Illustration 5) — proportionate dividend under Section 51: Suppose some shareholders have paid only ₹5 (face value ₹10) on each share held. On declaration of dividend at ₹5 per share, the company, if authorised by its articles, is justified in paying dividend of ₹2.50 per share on such partly paid shares.
  • Illustration 6 — Lawful adjustment against calls in arrear (Mr. Alok): Mr. Alok holds equity shares of face value ₹10 lakh and has not paid ₹80,000 towards call money due on shares. Can the dividend payable to him be adjusted against such dues? Answer: Yes. Under clause (d) of the Proviso to Section 127, where dividend is declared and there remain calls in arrears or any other sum due from a member, the dividend can be lawfully adjusted by the company against such dues. The company's action of adjusting the dividend payable to Mr. Alok towards call money of ₹80,000 is justified, and no punishment is attracted.
  • MCQ 1 — Dividend declared at the AGM is: (a) Final Dividend; (b) Interim Dividend; (c) Dividend on preference shares; (d) Scrip Dividend. Answer: (a) Final Dividend.
  • MCQ 2 — Amount to be transferred to reserves before declaration of dividend: (a) 5%; (b) 7.5%; (c) 10%; (d) at the discretion of the company. Answer: (d) at the discretion of the company.
  • MCQ 3 — Interim dividend cap (Vidyut Limited): The Board contemplates declaring interim dividend in the last week of July 2024, but the company incurred a loss during the current financial year up to the end of June 2024. During the previous five financial years — 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 — dividend was declared at 8%, 9%, 12%, 11% and 10% respectively. Maximum rate of interim dividend? Options: (a) 10%; (b) 11%; (c) 10.5%; (d) 11.5%. Answer: (b) Maximum at the rate of 11% — being the average of the immediately preceding three financial years, i.e. (12 + 11 + 10)/3 = 11%. The 8% and 9% of the earlier two years are irrelevant.
  • MCQ 4 — IEPF money shall NOT be used for: (a) refunds of unclaimed dividends, matured deposits, matured debentures, application money due for refund and interest thereon; (b) reimbursement of legal expenses in class action suits under sections 37 and 245; (c) grants or donation to the Central Government for the purpose of investor's education and training; (d) distribution of any disgorged amount among eligible and identifiable applicants who have suffered losses. Answer: (c) grants or donation to the Central Government for the purpose of investor's education and training.
  • MCQ 5 — Interest for failure to pay dividend/post warrants within 30 days: (a) 6% p.a.; (b) 12% p.a.; (c) 15% p.a.; (d) 18% p.a. Answer: (d) 18% p.a.
  • Descriptive Q1 — Claim of 20% interest (ABC Bakers Limited / Mr. Ranjan): The AGM held on 30th May 2024 declared a dividend at 30% on paid-up equity share capital as recommended by the Board. The company was unable to post the dividend warrant to Mr. Ranjan, an equity shareholder, up to 25th July 2024. Mr. Ranjan sued for payment of dividend together with interest at 20% per annum for the period of default. Answer: Section 127 lays down the penalty for non-payment within the prescribed 30 days: (a) every director knowingly a party to the default is punishable with imprisonment up to two years and with a minimum fine of ₹1,000 for every day during which the default continues; and (b) the company is liable to pay simple interest at 18% per annum during the period of default. Therefore, Mr. Ranjan will not succeed in claiming interest at 20%, as the limit under Section 127 is 18% per annum.
  • Descriptive Q2 — Diverting dividend to short-term investments (Future Fashions Limited): The Board recommended a dividend on paid-up equity share capital, later approved by shareholders at the AGM. Thereafter the directors passed a board resolution diverting the total dividend payable to shareholders towards purchase of certain short-term investments in the company's name. As a result, dividend was paid to shareholders after 45 days. Answer: (i) Under Section 124, since the declared dividend was not paid within 30 days of declaration, the company must, within 7 days from the expiry of that 30-day period, transfer the total unpaid or unclaimed dividend to a special account opened in a scheduled bank called the Unpaid Dividend Account. (ii) The Board has violated Section 127 by failing to pay dividend within 30 days on account of the diversion decision. Consequences: (a) every director knowingly a party to the default is punishable with maximum imprisonment of two years and a minimum fine of ₹1,000 for every day during which the default continues; (b) the company is liable to pay simple interest at 18% p.a. during the period of default.
  • Descriptive Q3 — Dividend despite deposit default (ABC Tractors Limited): The Board proposes to declare dividend at 20% to equity shareholders despite the company having defaulted in repayment of public deposits accepted before the commencement of the Act. Answer: Section 123(6) specifically provides that a company which fails to comply with Section 73 and Section 74 shall not, so long as such failure continues, declare any dividend on its equity shares. Hence the declaration of dividend by ABC Tractors Limited is not valid.
  • Descriptive Q4 — Two failures to pay (Star Computers Limited): The company declared and paid dividend in time to all equity holders for FY 2023-24, except: (i) Mrs. Sheela Bhatt, holding 250 shares, had mandated direct deposit of dividend into her bank account; the company remitted the dividend but the bank returned it because of a difference in the surname of the payee in the bank records, and the company did not inform Mrs. Sheela Bhatt of the discrepancy; (ii) dividend of ₹50,000 was not paid to the successor of Late Mr. Mohan in view of a court order restraining payment due to a family dispute about succession. Answer: (i) Section 127 exempts the case where a shareholder's directions could not be complied with only if the non-compliance was communicated to him. Here the company failed to communicate; hence the penal provisions under Section 127 will be applicable. (ii) Section 127 provides that no offence is deemed committed where dividend could not be paid by reason of operation of law. Here the dividend could not be paid because the court did not allow it until the succession matter was resolved; hence there is no liability on the company or its directors.
  • Descriptive Q5 — Section 8 company declaring dividend (Alpha Herbals / Mr. Chopra): Alpha Herbals, a Section 8 company, plans to declare dividend at the AGM for the financial year ended 31-03-2024. Mr. Chopra holds 800 equity shares as on date. Answer: Under Section 8(1), companies licensed under Section 8 are prohibited from paying any dividend to their members; their profits are to be applied only in promoting the objects for which they are formed. Hence the proposed act of Alpha Herbals is not according to the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Descriptive Q6 — No transfer to general reserves (YZ Medical Instruments Limited): A manufacturing company proposed a dividend @ 10% for the year 2023-2024 out of current year profits, having earned a profit of ₹910 crore during 2023-2024, and does not intend to transfer any amount to the general reserves. Answer: Under Section 123 a company may, before declaration of any dividend in any financial year, transfer such percentage of its profits for that financial year as it may consider appropriate to reserves. Such transfer is not mandatory and the percentage is at the discretion of the company acting through its Board. Therefore YZ Medical Instruments Limited is legally allowed not to transfer any profit to reserves before declaring dividend at 10%.
  • Descriptive Q7 — Bank rejection for wrong account number (PQ Ltd. / Mr. Kumar): PQ Ltd. declared and paid 10% dividend to all shareholders except Mr. Kumar, holding 500 equity shares, who had instructed the company to deposit the dividend directly into his bank account. The company remitted the dividend but the bank returned the payment on the ground that the account number given by Mr. Kumar did not tally with the bank's records. The company did not inform Mr. Kumar about the discrepancy. Answer: Section 127 exempts the situation where a shareholder has given directions regarding payment of dividend and those directions cannot be complied with only if the same has been communicated to the shareholder. PQ Ltd. failed to communicate the non-compliance to Mr. Kumar; hence the penal provisions under Section 127 will be attracted.
  • Descriptive Q8 — 12% interim dividend in a loss year (Alex Limited): Alex Limited is facing loss in business during FY 2023-2024. In the immediately preceding three financial years it declared dividend at 7%, 11% and 12% respectively. The Board decided to declare a 12% interim dividend for the current financial year, at least to be on par with the immediately preceding year. Answer: Under Section 123(3), the Board may declare interim dividend during any financial year out of the surplus in the profit and loss account and out of profits of the financial year in which such interim dividend is sought to be declared; provided that where the company has incurred a loss during the current financial year up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the date of declaration, the interim dividend shall not be declared at a rate higher than the average dividends declared during the immediately preceding three financial years. Here the rate shall not exceed 10%, being the average (7 + 11 + 12 = 30 ÷ 3 = 10). Therefore the Board's declaration of interim dividend at 12% for FY 2023-2024 is not valid.

Why It Matters / Application

The dividend provisions are the Act's main defence against a company distributing its own capital back to members and hollowing out the cushion available to creditors. Section 123(2) forces depreciation as per Schedule II through the profit and loss account first; the Fourth Proviso forces carried-over losses and unprovided depreciation of earlier years to be set off; and the Proviso to Section 123(1)(a) strips out revaluation surpluses, unrealised and notional gains so that a company like Shreyas Mechanics cannot convert a ₹20,00,000 land revaluation into distributable cash. Rule 3 then puts a hard ceiling on "borrowing from the past" in a bad year — a three-year average rate cap, a 10% of (paid-up capital + free reserves) cap, a mandatory set-off of the current year's loss, and a 15%-of-paid-up-capital reserve floor — which in the Capricorn Industries computation cuts an apparently permissible 10.33% down to an actual 7%. Sections 124 and 127 then police the cash: 5 days to ring-fence the money in a scheduled bank, 30 days to pay or post warrants (18% p.a. interest and director imprisonment up to 2 years if breached), 7 days more to move unpaid amounts into the Unpaid Dividend Account (12% p.a. interest if breached), 90 days to publish the list of unpaid claimants, and 7 years before the money — and the shares themselves — pass to the IEPF, from which claimants can still recover.

Note

  • Exam trap — three years, not five: In the Vidyut Limited MCQ five years of rates are given (8%, 9%, 12%, 11%, 10%) but only the immediately preceding three count: (12 + 11 + 10)/3 = 11%. The extra years are a deliberate distractor.
  • Exam trap — face value, not market price: In Example 1 both the NSE quote of ₹250 and the purchase price of ₹300 are irrelevant; only the ₹10 face value drives the ₹2,000 answer.
  • Exam trap — 18% vs 12%: 18% p.a. simple interest is the company's liability under Section 127 for failure to pay/post within 30 days; 12% p.a. is the interest under Section 124(3) for failure to transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account. Mr. Ranjan's claim for 20% fails because the statutory rate is capped at 18%.
  • Exam trap — the "communication" limb: The Section 127 exemption for a shareholder's unworkable payment directions applies only if the non-compliance was communicated to him. Both Mrs. Sheela Bhatt (Star Computers) and Mr. Kumar (PQ Ltd.) attract penalty precisely because the company stayed silent.
  • Posting, not receipt: Posting dividend warrants to the registered addresses within 30 days absolves the company; non-receipt by the shareholder within that time attracts no punishment.
  • Cumulative conditions: The source states that all the Rule 3 conditions have to be satisfied — the lowest of the caps governs.
  • Condition I carve-out: The three-year average rate cap does not apply if the company has not declared any dividend in each of the three preceding financial years.
  • Government company exemptions: Rule 3's conditions do not apply to a Government company wholly owned by the Central Government and/or State Governments (Notification No. 463(E), 05-06-2015). The same notification exempts such a Government company (including one where the capital is held by one or more Government companies) from the 5-day deposit requirement in Section 123(4).
  • Nidhi modifications (Notification No. GSR 465(E), dated 05-06-2015): (i) Section 123(5) applies to Nidhis subject to the modification that any dividend payable in cash may be paid by crediting it to the member's account if not claimed within 30 days of declaration; (ii) Section 127 applies subject to the modification that where the dividend payable to a member is ₹100 or less, it is sufficient compliance if the declaration is announced in the local language in one local newspaper of wide circulation and the announcement is also displayed on the Nidhi's notice board for at least 3 months.
  • Bonus shares are not a substitute: Declaration of dividend does not affect the company's power to issue fully paid-up bonus shares, but such shares cannot be issued in lieu of dividend.
  • Explanation to Section 124(6): If any dividend is paid or claimed for any year during the seven consecutive years, the shares shall not be transferred to the IEPF — a single claimed dividend resets the position.
  • Section 126 abeyance: Where a transfer instrument is pending registration, not only the dividend goes to the UDA — the rights offer under Section 62(1)(a) and the bonus issue under the first proviso to Section 123(5) are also held in abeyance, unless the registered holder authorises payment to the transferee in writing.

Chapter 9 — Accounts of Companies

Source: 87778bos-aps2160-ch9.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Scope of Chapter IX: Sections 128 to 138 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 — covering books of account, financial statements, periodical financial results, re-opening and voluntary revision of accounts, NFRA, accounting standards, Board's report, CSR, members' right to copies, filing with the Registrar and internal audit.
  • Why directors must report: Directors are agents of shareholders acting in a fiduciary capacity, so they are required to disclose financial performance and position through financial results, keeping shareholders aware of the working and affairs of the company.
  • Mandatory accrual + double entry [Sec 128(1)]: Books of account must give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company including its branch offices, explain the transactions effected both at the registered office and its branches, and must be kept on accrual basis and according to the double entry system. No exception has been granted to any class of companies from this requirement.
  • Eight-year preservation [Sec 128(5)]: Books of account together with the vouchers relevant to any entry must be preserved in good order for not less than eight years immediately preceding the relevant financial year. The eight-year window is also the outer limit for a re-opening order under Sec 130(3) — the two provisions are deliberately linked.
  • Sec 130 vs Sec 131 — compulsion vs volition: Section 130 is compulsory re-opening and recasting on the order of a court/Tribunal on an application by an outside authority; Section 131 is a voluntary revision undertaken because the directors themselves form the opinion that the financial statement or Board's report is non-compliant.
  • NFRA as an independent audit regulator [Sec 132]: Constituted with effect from 1st October 2018, head office at New Delhi; it recommends accounting and auditing standards, monitors and enforces compliance, oversees quality of service of auditors, and can investigate professional or other misconduct of CA members/firms with quasi-judicial powers.
  • Statutory CSR [Sec 135]: India became the torch-bearer for the rest of the world by giving a legal mandate to corporate social responsibility, requiring companies crossing prescribed financial thresholds to spend at least 2% of average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years on Schedule VII activities.
  • "Comply or explain plus transfer": Unlike a pure "comply or explain" regime, unspent CSR money cannot simply be retained — it must be transferred either to an Unspent CSR Account (ongoing projects) or to a Schedule VII Fund (all other cases), with penalties under Sec 135(7) if it is not.

Key Definitions / Terms

Books of account — Sec 2(13)
Records of all sums of money received and expended and the matters in relation to which receipts and expenditure take place; all sales and purchases of goods and services; the assets and liabilities of the company; and the items of cost prescribed under section 148 (cost audit) for companies of the specified class.
Book and paper / book or paper — Sec 2(12)
Includes books of account, deeds, vouchers, writings, documents, minutes and registers maintained on paper or in electronic form.
Financial statement — Sec 2(40)
Includes (i) a balance sheet as at the end of the financial year; (ii) a profit and loss account (or, for a not-for-profit activity, an income and expenditure account); (iii) a cash flow statement — except for a One Person Company, small company, dormant company and a private company that is a start-up and has not defaulted in filing financial statements under Sec 137 or the annual return under Sec 92 (exemption notification GSR 583(E) dated 13th June 2017); (iv) a statement of changes in equity, if applicable; and (v) any explanatory note annexed to or forming part of the above.
Start-up / start-up company
A private company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 or the Companies Act, 1956 and recognised as a start-up in accordance with the notification issued by the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
Financial year — Sec 2(41)
The period ending on the 31st day of March every year; and where the company is incorporated on or after the 1st day of January of a year, the period ending on the 31st day of March of the following year.
True and fair view
The financial statements are free from material misstatements and faithfully represent the financial performance and positioning of an entity.
Accrual basis
An accounting assumption/concept warranting recording of income and expenses as they accrue (earned or incurred), as opposed to the cash system where they are recorded when received or paid.
Double entry system
A method of recording each transaction in a set of accounts where every transaction has a dual aspect of debit and credit and must be posted in at least two accounts; the dual aspect enables effective control because all books must balance.
Electronic mode — Rule 3, Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014
Includes "electronic form" and "electronic record" as defined in clauses (r) and (t) respectively of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
CSR — Rule 2(d), CSR Rules
Activities undertaken by a company in pursuance of its statutory obligation under Sec 135 in accordance with the CSR Rules, but excluding: (i) activities in the normal course of business; (ii) activities outside India except training of Indian sports personnel representing any State/UT at national level or India at international level; (iii) contribution directly or indirectly to any political party under Sec 182; (iv) activities benefitting employees as defined in clause (k) of section 2 of the Code on Wages, 2019; (v) activities supported on sponsorship basis for deriving marketing benefits for products/services; (vi) activities carried out to fulfil any other statutory obligation under any law in force in India.
CSR Committee — Rule 2(e)
The Corporate Social Responsibility Committee of the Board constituted under sub-section (1) of section 135.
CSR Policy — Rule 2(f)
A statement containing the approach and direction given by the Board taking into account the recommendations of the CSR Committee, and including guiding principles for selection, implementation and monitoring of activities as well as formulation of the annual action plan.
Administrative overheads — Rule 2(b)
Expenses incurred by the company for general management and administration of CSR functions, but not expenses directly incurred for the designing, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of a particular CSR project or programme.
Net profit (for CSR) — Rule 2(h) read with Explanation to Sec 135
Net profit as per the financial statement prepared in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Act, calculated in accordance with section 198, but excluding (i) any profit arising from any overseas branch or branches, whether operated as a separate company or otherwise; and (ii) any dividend received from other companies in India which are covered under and complying with section 135. For a foreign company, net profit as per the profit and loss account prepared under clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 381 read with section 198.
Ongoing project — Rule 2(i)
(a) A multi-year project undertaken in fulfilment of the CSR obligation having timelines not exceeding three years excluding the financial year in which it was commenced; and (b) a project not initially approved as multi-year but whose duration has been extended beyond one year by the Board on reasonable justification.
International Organisation — Rule 2(g)
An organisation notified by the Central Government as an international organisation under section 3 of the United Nations (Privileges and Immunities) Act, 1947, to which the provisions of the Schedule to that Act apply.
Public Authority — Rule 2(j)
'Public Authority' as defined in clause (h) of section 2 of the Right to Information Act, 2005.
Internal financial controls — Explanation to Sec 134(5)(e)
The policies and procedures adopted by the company for ensuring the orderly and efficient conduct of its business, including adherence to the company's policies, safeguarding of its assets, prevention and detection of frauds and errors, accuracy and completeness of the accounting records, and timely preparation of reliable financial information.
Proficiency (of an independent director) — Rule 8, Companies (Accounts) Rules
Proficiency of the independent director as ascertained from the online proficiency self-assessment test conducted by the institute notified under sub-section (1) of section 150.

Books of Account [Section 128] — How It Works

  • Place of keeping: Books of account, other relevant books and papers and financial statements are to be kept at the registered office. First proviso to Sec 128(1): they may be kept at any other place in India as the Board of Directors may decide; where such a decision is taken, the company must, within seven days, file with the Registrar a written notice under rule 2A in Form AOC-5 giving the full address of that other place.
  • Electronic mode — Rule 3(1): Books maintained electronically must remain accessible in India at all times so as to be usable for subsequent reference.
  • Audit trail (proviso to Rule 3(1)): For the financial year commencing on or after 1st April 2023, every company using accounting software must use only software having a feature of recording an audit trail of each and every transaction, creating an edit log of each change made in the books along with the date of change, and ensuring that the audit trail cannot be disabled.
  • Rule 3(2) & 3(3): Records must be retained completely in the format in which they were originally generated, sent or received, or in a format that presents the information accurately; the information must remain complete and unaltered. Information received from branch offices shall not be altered and must be kept so as to depict what was originally received.
  • Rule 3(4) & 3(5): The electronic record must be capable of being displayed in a legible form; there must be a proper system for storage, retrieval, display or printout as the Audit Committee (if any) or the Board deems appropriate, and such records shall not be disposed of or rendered unusable unless permitted by law. Proviso: back-up of books maintained in electronic mode, including at a place outside India, must be kept in servers physically located in India on a daily basis.
  • Rule 3(6) — annual intimation to the Registrar at the time of filing the financial statement, giving: (a) name of the service provider; (b) the internet protocol (IP) address of the service provider; (c) the location of the service provider (wherever applicable); (d) where books are maintained on cloud, such address as provided by the service provider; and (e) where the service provider is located outside India, the name and address of the person in control of the books in India.
  • Branch offices [Sec 128(2)]: Deemed compliance where proper books relating to transactions effected at the branch are kept at that office and proper summarised returns are sent periodically to the registered office/other place. Rule 4(1): summarised returns of books kept and maintained outside India must be sent to the registered office at quarterly intervals, kept at the registered office and kept open to directors for inspection.
  • Inspection by directors [Sec 128(3) & (4)]: Any director may inspect the books of account and other books and papers maintained within India during business hours. For financial information maintained outside the country, the director must furnish a written request setting out full details of the information sought and the period (Rule 4(2)); the company must produce it within fifteen days of receipt of the written request (Rule 4(3)). The request must be made by the director himself, not through a power of attorney holder, agent or representative. Under Sec 128(4) the officers and employees must give the inspecting person all assistance which the company may reasonably be expected to give.
  • Subsidiary's books (proviso to Sec 128(3)): A person may inspect the books of account of a subsidiary only on authorisation by way of a Board resolution.
  • Preservation [Sec 128(5)]: Not less than eight years immediately preceding the relevant financial year. If the company was incorporated less than eight years before the financial year, books for the entire period preceding the financial year together with vouchers must be preserved. Proviso: where an investigation has been ordered under Chapter XIV (inspection, inquiry, investigation), the Central Government may direct that books be kept for a period longer than 8 years.

Financial Statement [Section 129] and Consolidation

  • Sec 129(1): The financial statement shall give a true and fair view of the state of affairs, comply with the accounting standards notified under section 133, and be in the form(s) provided for different classes of companies in Schedule III. Schedule III has two divisions — Division I for companies complying with the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 [GSR 432(E) dated 23rd June 2021]; Division II for companies complying with the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015 [GSR 111(E) dated 16th February 2015].
  • Carve-out: Sec 129(1) does not apply to an insurance company, a banking company, a company engaged in the generation or supply of electricity, or any other class of company for which a form of financial statement has been specified in or under its governing Act. Non-disclosure of matters not required to be disclosed by that governing Act (Insurance Act, 1938; IRDA Act, 1999; Banking Regulation Act, 1949; Electricity Act, 2003) shall not be treated as failure to present a true and fair view.
  • Any reference to the financial statement includes the notes annexed to or forming part of it.
  • Sec 129(2): At every annual general meeting the Board shall lay before the meeting the financial statements for the financial year.
  • Sec 129(3) — CFS: Where a company has one or more subsidiaries or associate companies, it shall, in addition to the standalone statements, prepare a consolidated financial statement of itself and of all subsidiaries, associate companies and joint ventures in the same form and manner as its own and in accordance with applicable accounting standards, and lay it before the AGM as well. The statement of salient features of the financial statement of subsidiaries/associates/JVs is in e-Form AOC-1 (Rule 5).
  • Manner of consolidation — Rule 6: in accordance with Schedule III and the applicable accounting standards. Exceptions: (1) a company covered by Sec 129(3) that is not required to prepare CFS under the Accounting Standards need only comply with the CFS provisions of Schedule III; (2) a company with no subsidiary but with associate companies and/or joint ventures was not required to consolidate in respect of them only for the financial year commencing 1st April 2014 and ending 31st March 2015; (3) the rule does not apply to consolidation by a company having subsidiary/subsidiaries incorporated outside India commencing on or after 1st April 2014.
  • Exemption from preparing CFS (all conditions to be met): (a) the company is a wholly owned subsidiary, or a partially owned subsidiary of another company and all its other members — including those not otherwise entitled to vote — having been intimated in writing (with proof of delivery available with the company) do not object; (b) its securities are not listed and are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange in or outside India; and (c) its ultimate or any intermediate holding company files CFS with the Registrar in compliance with applicable Accounting Standards.
  • Sec 129(4): Provisions applicable to the preparation, adoption and audit of the financial statements of a holding company apply mutatis mutandis to the consolidated financial statements.
  • Sec 129(5): Where financial statements do not comply with the accounting standards, the company must disclose the deviation, the reasons for the deviation and the financial effects, if any, arising out of the deviation.
  • Sec 129(6): The Central Government may, suo motu or on application by a class of companies, by notification exempt any class from any requirement of this section, unconditionally or subject to conditions, in the public interest. Section 129 does not apply to Government companies engaged in defence production to the extent of the relevant Accounting Standard on segment reporting [G.S.R. 463(E) dated 5th June 2015, substituted by G.S.R. 802(E) dated 23.02.2018], available only to Government companies that have not defaulted in filing under Sec 137 or Sec 92 [G.S.R. 582(E) dated 13th June 2017].
  • Listed companies: Regulations 33 and 52 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 apply in addition to section 129.

Periodical Financial Results [Section 129A]

  • The Central Government may require such class or classes of unlisted companies as may be prescribed to: (a) prepare financial results on such periodical basis and in such form as prescribed; (b) obtain Board approval and complete audit or limited review of such periodical results; and (c) file a copy with the Registrar within thirty days of completion of the relevant period with prescribed fees.
  • Rationale: approximately over 11 lakh unlisted companies operate actively in India, some large enough with widely-spread interests to make corporate governance a critical issue; the section was inserted by the Amendment Act of 2020.
  • Exam trap: No rule has been prescribed and no notification made under section 129A as on 30.04.2024 — the section is on the statute book but not yet operational.

Re-opening of Accounts [Section 130] and Voluntary Revision [Section 131]

Point of distinctionSection 130 — Re-opening & recastingSection 131 — Voluntary revision
TriggerApplication by Central Government, Income-tax authorities, SEBI, any other statutory regulatory body or authority, or any person concernedOpinion of the directors that the FS does not comply with Sec 129 or the Board's report does not comply with Sec 134
GroundsEarlier accounts prepared in a fraudulent manner; or affairs mismanaged during the relevant period casting doubt on the reliability of the financial statementsNon-compliance with Sec 129 / Sec 134
AuthorityCourt of competent jurisdiction or the TribunalTribunal (application in Form NCLT-1 within 14 days of the Board's decision)
Period coveredEight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year (longer if the Central Government has directed longer retention under the proviso to Sec 128(5))Any of the three preceding financial years
FrequencyNot limitedNot more than once in a financial year
Filing with ROC—Certified copy of the Tribunal's order within 30 days of receipt of the certified copy; revised FS with auditors' statement / revised Board's report within 30 days of approval by the general meeting
NoticeCourt/Tribunal shall give notice to the CG, Income-tax authorities, SEBI, other statutory body or person concerned and consider their representationsTribunal shall give notice to the Central Government and the Income-tax authorities and consider their representations (first proviso to Sec 131(1))
FinalitySec 130(2): accounts so revised or recast shall be finalRevisions confined to the corrections and consequential alterations only
  • Rule 77, NCLT Rules, 2016 — contents of the Sec 131 application: the financial year or period to which the accounts relate; the name and contact details of the Managing Director, CFO, directors, Company Secretary and the officer responsible for making and maintaining the books and financial statement; where audited, the name and contact details of the auditor or any former auditor who audited those accounts; a copy of the Board resolution; the grounds for seeking revision; and — where the majority of directors or the auditor has been changed immediately before the decision to apply under Sec 131 — disclosure of that fact in the application.
  • The company shall advertise the application at least fourteen days before the date of hearing; the Tribunal shall issue notice to the auditor of the original financial statement and hear him, and may pass such order as it deems fit.
  • On receipt of the Tribunal's approval a general meeting may be called, and notice of the meeting along with reasons for the change in financial statements may be published in a newspaper in English and in the vernacular language. At that meeting, the revised financial statements, the statement of directors and the statement of auditors may be put up for consideration before adoption is decided.
  • Third proviso to Sec 131(1): the detailed reasons for revision must also be disclosed in the Board's report of the relevant financial year in which the revision is made.
  • Sec 131(2) — scope of revision where copies of the previous FS/report were already sent to members, delivered to the Registrar or laid in general meeting: confined to (a) correction of non-compliance with Sec 129; (b) correction of non-compliance with Sec 134; and (c) making of any necessary consequential alteration.
  • Sec 131(3): the Central Government may make rules on the application of the Act to a revised financial statement or revised director's report, and in particular may make different provisions according as the previous statement/report is replaced or is supplemented by a document indicating the corrections, may provide for the functions of the company's auditor, and the steps to be taken by the directors. Rule 77 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 has been notified in this regard.

National Financial Reporting Authority [Section 132]

  • Constitution: Central Government notified 1st October 2018 as the date of constitution; head office at New Delhi (as required by sub-section 12).
  • Class of companies governed — Rule 3, NFRA Rules, 2018: (a) companies whose securities are listed on any stock exchange in India or outside India; (b) unlisted public companies having paid-up capital of not less than ₹500 crore, or annual turnover of not less than ₹1,000 crore, or aggregate outstanding loans, debentures and deposits of not less than ₹500 crore, as on the 31st March of the immediately preceding financial year; (c) insurance companies, banking companies, companies engaged in generation or supply of electricity, companies governed by any special Act, or bodies corporate incorporated by an Act per clauses (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f) of Sec 1(4); (d) any body corporate/company/person referred to the Authority by the Central Government in public interest; and (e) a body corporate incorporated or registered outside India which is a subsidiary or associate of a company/body corporate in India referred to in (a) to (d), if its income or net worth exceeds twenty percent of the consolidated income or consolidated net worth of that company/body corporate.
  • Functions [Sec 132(2) read with Rules 4, 6–9]: protect the public interest and the interests of investors, creditors and others by establishing high quality standards of accounting and auditing and exercising effective oversight; maintain details of particulars of auditors appointed in companies/bodies corporate governed by NFRA; recommend accounting and auditing standards for approval by the Central Government (Rule 6 — NFRA shall receive recommendations from the ICAI for new or amended standards and may seek additional information from ICAI); monitor and enforce compliance; oversee quality of service; promote awareness; co-operate with national and international organisations of independent audit regulators; and perform incidental functions. Sub-sections (2) and (4) have overriding effect over anything in any other law in force.
  • Rule 7 — enforcing accounting standards: NFRA may review the financial statements and direct the company/body corporate or its auditor by written notice to provide further information, explanation or documents within the specified reasonable time; may require the personal presence of officers and the auditor; shall publish its findings on non-compliance on its website and in such other manner as it considers fit unless it has public-interest reasons not to and records those reasons in writing; and where it finds or believes an accounting standard has been violated, may decide on further investigation or enforcement action through its concerned Division.
  • Rule 8 — enforcing auditing standards: NFRA may review working papers (including audit plan and other audit documents) and audit communications; evaluate the sufficiency of the auditor's quality control system and its documentation; perform other testing of audit, supervisory and quality control procedures; require an auditor to report on its governance practices and internal processes designed to promote audit quality, protect reputation and reduce risks including risk of failure of the auditor; seek additional information or require personal presence; shall perform monitoring through officers or experts with sufficient experience in audit of the relevant industry; shall publish findings on non-compliance; shall not publish proprietary or confidential information unless it has public-interest reasons recorded in writing; may send a separate report containing proprietary or confidential information to the Central Government.
  • Rule 9 — quality of service: NFRA may direct an auditor to take measures for improvement of audit quality, including changes in audit processes, quality control and audit reports, and specify a detailed plan with time-limits; it is the duty of the auditor to make the improvements and send a report explaining compliance; NFRA monitors the improvements; it may refer cases to the Quality Review Board constituted under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, or call for reports/information from that Board; and may take the assistance of experts.
  • Composition [Sec 132(3), (3A), (3B)]: a Chairperson — a person of eminence with expertise in accountancy, auditing, finance or law — and such other members not exceeding fifteen, consisting of part-time and full-time members. Each division is presided over by the Chairperson or a full-time member authorised by him; there is an executive body of the Chairperson and full-time members. Appointment is by the Central Government under the NFRA (Manner of Appointment and other Terms and Conditions of Service of Chairperson and Members) Rules, 2018; a declaration of no conflict of interest / independence must be made to the Central Government. Full-time Chairperson and members shall not be associated with any audit firm (including related consultancy firms) during their appointment and for two years after ceasing to hold it.
  • Part-time members (ex-officio unless stated): one member representing the MCA not below the rank of Joint Secretary; one representing the CAG not below the rank of Accountant General or Principal Director; one representing the RBI not below the rank of Executive Director; one representing SEBI not below the rank of Executive Director; President, ICAI; Chairperson, Accounting Standards Board, ICAI; Chairperson, Auditing and Assurance Standards Board, ICAI; and two experts from the field of accountancy, auditing, finance or law. Sec 132(11) empowers the Central Government to appoint a secretary and other employees.
  • Power to investigate [Sec 132(4)]: into matters of professional or other misconduct committed by any member or firm of chartered accountants registered under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, either suo motu or on a reference by the Central Government under Rule 10 of the NFRA Rules, 2018. Where NFRA has initiated an investigation, no other institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in such matters of misconduct. "Professional or other misconduct" carries the meaning assigned in section 22 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.
  • Quasi-judicial powers [Sec 132(4)(b)] — same powers as a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 while trying a suit, in respect of: discovery and production of books of account and other documents at such place and time as specified; summoning and enforcing attendance of persons and examining them on oath; inspection of any books, registers and other documents at any place; and issuing commissions for examination of witnesses or documents.
  • Appeal [Sec 132(5)]: any person aggrieved by an order under clause (c) of sub-section (4) may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal in the prescribed manner on payment of the prescribed fee.
  • Meetings [Sec 132(10)]: as prescribed under Rule 3 of the NFRA (Meeting for Transaction of Business) Rules, 2019; NFRA may meet at such other places in India as it deems fit.
  • Accounts and reporting [Sec 132(13), (14), (15)]: NFRA shall maintain books of account in the form and manner prescribed by the Central Government in consultation with the CAG; its accounts shall be audited by the CAG at such intervals as he specifies, and the certified accounts with the audit report shall be forwarded annually to the Central Government. NFRA shall prepare an annual report for each financial year giving a full account of its activities and forward it to the Central Government, which shall cause the annual report and the CAG's audit report to be laid before each House of Parliament.
  • Form NFRA-1: every existing body corporate other than a company governed by these rules shall inform NFRA within 30 days of commencement of the NFRA Rules of the particulars of its auditor as on the date of commencement.
  • Sticky jurisdiction: a company or body corporate governed by the NFRA Rules continues to be governed by NFRA for a period of 3 years after it ceases to be listed or its paid-up capital / turnover / aggregate loans, debentures and deposits fall below the stated limits.
  • Contravention of NFRA Rules: the company and every officer in default, or the auditor or such other person, shall be punishable as per section 450 of the Act.

NFRA — penalty and debarment on proved misconduct [Sec 132(4)(c)]

Liable (in case of)Minimum penaltyMaximum penalty
Individual₹1 lakhFive times of the fees received
Firms₹5 lakhTen times of the fees received
Debarment fromMinimum periodMaximum period
Being appointed as an auditor or internal auditor, or undertaking any audit in respect of financial statements or internal audit of the functions and activities of any company or body corporate; or performing any valuation as provided under section 247Six monthsTen years

Accounting Standards [Section 133]

  • Section 133 empowers the Central Government to prescribe the accounting standards or any addendum thereto, as recommended by the ICAI, in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations made by the NFRA.
  • Proviso (now spent): until NFRA was constituted, the Central Government could prescribe standards as recommended by ICAI in consultation with the National Advisory Committee on Accounting Standards (NACAS) constituted under the previous company law. Since NFRA was constituted in 2018, this proviso has lost its operating effect.
  • Notified so far under Sec 133: the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 [GSR 432(E) dated 23rd June 2021] and the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015 [GSR 111(E) dated 16th February 2015].
  • Regulation 48 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 supplements Sec 133 — the listed entity shall comply with all applicable and notified Accounting Standards from time to time.

Financial Statement, Board's Report etc. [Section 134]

  • Authentication [Sec 134(1)]: The financial statement (and the CFS, if any) shall be approved by the Board before being signed on behalf of the Board, for submission to the auditor for his report, at least by (a) the chairperson where authorised by the Board or two directors of whom one shall be the managing director, if any; (b) the Chief Executive Officer; (c) the Chief Financial Officer; and (d) the company secretary — wherever they are appointed. In a One Person Company, the financial statements shall be approved by only one director.
  • Sec 134(2): The auditors' report shall be attached to every financial statement.
  • Sec 134(7): A signed copy of every financial statement, including the CFS if any, shall be issued, circulated or published along with a copy of (a) any notes annexed to or forming part of the financial statement; (b) the auditor's report; and (c) the Board's report referred to in sub-section (3).
  • Sec 134(6) — signing of the Board's report and any annexures: by the chairperson if authorised by the Board; where not so authorised, by at least two directors, one of whom shall be a managing director, or by the director where there is one director.

Contents of the Board's Report [Sec 134(3) read with Rule 8]

  • (a) The web address, if any, where the annual return referred to in Sec 92(3) has been placed; (b) number of meetings of the Board; (c) the Directors' Responsibility Statement; (ca) details of frauds reported by auditors under Sec 143(12) other than those reportable to the Central Government; (d) a statement on declaration given by independent directors under Sec 149(6).
  • (e) For a company covered under Sec 178(1), the company's policy on directors' appointment and remuneration including criteria for determining qualifications, positive attributes, independence of a director and other matters under Sec 178(3). Clause (e) does not apply to Government companies [G.S.R. 463(E) dated 5th June 2015], and only to those that have not defaulted in filing under Sec 137 or Sec 92 [G.S.R. 582(E) dated 13th June 2017].
  • (f) Explanations or comments by the Board on every qualification, reservation, adverse remark or disclaimer made by the auditor in his report and by the company secretary in practice in his secretarial audit report; (g) particulars of loans, guarantees or investments under section 186; (h) particulars of contracts or arrangements with related parties under Sec 188(1) in e-Form AOC-2; (i) the state of the company's affairs; (j) amounts, if any, proposed to be carried to reserves; (k) the amount, if any, recommended to be paid by way of dividend; (l) material changes and commitments affecting the financial position occurring between the end of the financial year and the date of the report.
  • (m) Conservation of energy, technology absorption, foreign exchange earnings and outgo — Government companies producing defence equipment are exempted from disclosure under clause (m) [Companies (Accounts) Second Amendment Rules, 2015 dated 4th September 2015]; (n) a statement on development and implementation of a risk management policy including identification of elements of risk which in the Board's opinion may threaten the existence of the company; (o) details about the policy developed and implemented on CSR initiatives taken during the year.
  • (p) For a listed company and every other public company having paid-up share capital of ₹25 crore or more calculated at the end of the preceding financial year, a statement indicating the manner of formal annual evaluation of the performance of the Board, its Committees and individual directors. Clause (p) does not apply to Government companies [G.S.R. 463(E) dated 5th June 2015; subject to G.S.R. 582(E) dated 13th June 2017].
  • (q) Other matters prescribed by Rule 8: (i) financial summary or highlights; (ii) change in the nature of business; (iii) details of directors or KMP appointed or resigned during the year; (iiia) a statement of the Board's opinion on the integrity, expertise and experience (including proficiency) of independent directors appointed during the year; (iv) names of companies which became or ceased to be subsidiaries, joint ventures or associates during the year; (v) details relating to deposits accepted during the year, unpaid or unclaimed at year-end, and any default in repayment of deposits or interest with the number of cases and total amount involved at the beginning, the maximum during, and at the end of the year; (vi) details of deposits not in compliance with Chapter V; (vii) details of significant and material orders passed by regulators, courts or tribunals impacting the going concern status and future operations; (viii) details of adequacy of internal financial controls with reference to the financial statements; (ix) a disclosure whether maintenance of cost records under Sec 148(1) is required and accordingly made and maintained; (x) a statement of compliance with the constitution of the Internal Complaints Committee under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013, with (a) number of complaints of sexual harassment received in the year, (b) number disposed off during the year, and (c) number of cases pending for more than ninety days; (xi) details of application made or proceeding pending under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 during the year with status at year-end; (xii) details of the difference between the valuation done at the time of one-time settlement and the valuation done while taking the loan from banks or financial institutions with reasons; (xiii) a statement on compliance with the provisions of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961.
  • Anti-duplication: Where disclosures under Sec 134(3) have been included in the financial statements, such disclosures shall be referred to instead of being repeated in the Board's report (a benefit earlier available only to specified IFSC public companies [GSR 08(E) dated 4th January 2017] and specified IFSC private companies [GSR 09(E) dated 4th January 2017], extended to all w.e.f. 31.7.2018). Where the policy under clause (e) or (o) is on the company's website, it is sufficient compliance to state the salient features and any change in brief in the Board's report and indicate the web-address.
  • The Board's Report is prepared on the standalone financial statement and shall report on the highlights of performance of subsidiaries, associates and joint venture companies and their contribution to the overall performance of the company during the period under report.

Abridged Board's Report for OPC and Small Company [Sec 134(3A) read with Rule 8A]

  • Rule 8 does not apply to a One Person Company or a Small Company; Rule 8A applies instead. The abridged report, prepared on the stand-alone financial statement, contains: (a) the web address where the annual return under Sec 92(3) has been placed; (b) number of Board meetings; (c) the Directors' Responsibility Statement under Sec 134(5); (d) details of frauds reported by auditors under Sec 143(12) other than those reportable to the Central Government; (e) explanations or comments by the Board on every qualification, reservation, adverse remark or disclaimer by the auditor; (f) the state of the company's affairs; (g) financial summary or highlights; (h) material changes from the date of closure of the financial year in the nature of business and their effect on the financial position; (i) details of directors appointed or resigned during the year; (j) details of significant and material orders passed by regulators, courts or tribunals impacting going concern status and future operations; (k) particulars of contracts or arrangements with related parties under Sec 188(1) in Form AOC-2.
  • Sec 134(4) — OPC: the Board's report attached to the financial statement means a report containing explanations or comments by the Board on every qualification, reservation, adverse remark or disclaimer made by the auditor. After the insertion of sub-section 3A and Rule 8A, the importance of sub-section 4 has reduced substantially.

Directors' Responsibility Statement [Sec 134(5)]

  • (a) In preparing the annual accounts, the applicable accounting standards had been followed along with proper explanation relating to material departures; (b) the directors had selected accounting policies and applied them consistently and made judgments and estimates that are reasonable and prudent so as to give a true and fair view of the state of affairs at the end of the financial year and of the profit and loss for that period; (c) the directors had taken proper and sufficient care for the maintenance of adequate accounting records in accordance with the Act for safeguarding the assets and for preventing and detecting fraud and other irregularities; (d) the annual accounts had been prepared on a going concern basis; (e) in the case of a listed company, the directors had laid down internal financial controls to be followed and such controls are adequate and were operating effectively; and (f) the directors had devised proper systems to ensure compliance with the provisions of all applicable laws and such systems were adequate and operating effectively.

Penalty [Sec 134(8)]

Person liablePenalty
Company₹3,00,000
Every officer of the company who is in default₹50,000

Corporate Social Responsibility [Section 135]

Applicability thresholds — CSR Committee [Sec 135(1)]

Criterion (during the immediately preceding financial year)Threshold
Net worth₹500 crore or more
Turnover₹1,000 crore or more
Net profit₹5 crore or more
  • Any one of the three criteria being satisfied attracts section 135 — they are alternatives, not cumulative.
  • Rule 3(1), CSR Rules: every company including its holding or subsidiary, and a foreign company defined under Sec 2(42) having its branch office or project office in India, which fulfils the Sec 135(1) criteria, shall comply with section 135 and the CSR Rules. Proviso: a company having any amount/balance in its Unspent CSR Account under Sec 135(6) shall constitute a CSR Committee and comply with sub-sections (2) to (6).
  • Net worth and turnover are defined in Sec 2(57) and Sec 2(91); net profit is defined in Rule 2(h) read with the Explanation to Sec 135. For a foreign company, net worth/turnover/net profit are computed from the balance sheet and profit and loss account prepared under clause (a) of Sec 381(1) read with section 198.
  • Exception [Sec 135(9)]: where the amount to be spent under sub-section (5) does not exceed ₹50 lakh, the requirement to constitute a CSR Committee shall not apply, and the Committee's functions shall be discharged by the Board of Directors.
  • Sec 135(2): the Board's report under Sec 134(3) shall disclose the composition of the CSR Committee.
  • Specified IFSC companies: section 135 shall not apply for a period of 5 years from the commencement of business of a specified IFSC public company [GSR 08(E) dated 4th January 2017] and a specified IFSC private company [GSR 09(E) dated 4th January 2017].

Composition of the CSR Committee [Proviso to Sec 135(1) read with Rule 5(1)]

CategoryConstitution
Company covered under Sec 135(1) but not required to appoint an independent director under Sec 149(4)Two or more directors, without an independent director
Private company having only two directors on its BoardTwo such directors
Foreign company covered under the CSR RulesAt least two persons, of which one shall be as specified under clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 380 and the other nominated by the foreign company
Not covered in any of the sub-categories aboveThree or more directors, out of which at least one shall be an independent director (defined in Sec 2(47))

Duties of the CSR Committee [Sec 135(3) read with Rule 5(2)]

  • (a) Formulate and recommend to the Board a CSR Policy indicating the activities to be undertaken in areas or subjects specified in Schedule VII; (b) recommend the amount of expenditure to be incurred on those activities; and (c) monitor the CSR Policy from time to time.
  • Annual action plan (Rule 5(2)) to be formulated and recommended to the Board, including: (a) the list of CSR projects or programmes approved to be undertaken in Schedule VII areas; (b) the manner of execution as specified in Rule 4(1) (itself or through a section 8 company etc.); (c) the modalities of utilisation of funds and implementation schedules; (d) monitoring and reporting mechanism; and (e) details of need and impact assessment, if any. The Board may alter the plan at any time during the financial year on the recommendation of the CSR Committee, based on reasonable justification.

Duties of the Board [Sec 135(4) read with Rule 9]

  • After taking into account the CSR Committee's recommendations, approve the CSR Policy; disclose the contents of the Policy in its report; place the CSR Policy along with the composition of the CSR Committee and projects approved by the Board on the company's website; and ensure that the activities included in the CSR Policy are undertaken.

Amount and form of CSR expenditure [Sec 135(5) & (6) read with Rules 4, 7, 10]

  • Minimum spend: at least two percent of the average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years, in every financial year.
  • Local area preference: the company shall give preference to the local area and areas around it where it operates for spending the CSR amount.
  • Administrative overheads cap: shall not exceed five percent of total CSR expenditure of the company for the financial year.
  • Companies not yet three years old: where the company has not completed the period of three financial years since incorporation, it shall spend at least two percent of the average net profits made during such immediately preceding financial years (i.e., the shorter available period).
  • Surplus from CSR activities [Rule 7(2)]: shall not form part of the business profit of the company and shall be (i) ploughed back into the same project, or (ii) transferred to the Unspent CSR Account and spent per the CSR policy and annual action plan, or (iii) transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months of the expiry of the financial year.
  • Excess spending set-off [Second proviso to Sec 135(5) read with Rule 7(1)]: where a company spends in excess of the requirement, it may set off the excess against the requirement for up to the immediately succeeding three financial years, subject to (a) the excess available for set off not including the surplus arising out of CSR activities under Rule 7(2), and (b) a Board resolution being passed to that effect.
  • Failure to spend [Sec 135(5) & (6)]: the Board shall specify the reasons for not spending in the Board's report prepared under Sec 134(3)(o); and — where the unspent amount relates to projects other than ongoing projects — transfer it to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months of the expiry of the financial year; where it relates to an ongoing project, transfer it to the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account within thirty days from the end of the financial year.
  • The Unspent CSR Account shall be operated with a Scheduled bank. Sums transferred to it must be spent in pursuance of the CSR obligation within three financial years from the date of such transfer; on failure, the company shall transfer the same to a Schedule VII Fund within thirty days from the date of completion of the third financial year. Rule 10: until a fund is specified in Schedule VII for the purposes of Sec 135(5) and (6), the unspent amount shall be transferred to any fund included in Schedule VII.
  • Capital asset [Rule 7(4)]: CSR amount may be spent for creation or acquisition of a capital asset, which shall be held by (a) a section 8 company, or a Registered Public Trust or Registered Society having charitable objects and a CSR Registration Number under Rule 4(2); or (b) beneficiaries of the CSR project in the form of self-help groups, collectives or entities; or (c) a public authority. Any capital asset created before the commencement of the Companies (CSR Policy) Amendment Rules, 2021 shall comply within 180 days, extendable by a further period of not more than 90 days with Board approval on reasonable justification.

Unspent CSR amount — routing at a glance

Nature of unspent amountTransfer toTime limit
Relating to an ongoing projectUnspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account (with a Scheduled bank)Within thirty days from the end of the financial year
Relating to projects other than ongoing projectsA Fund specified in Schedule VIIWithin six months of the expiry of the financial year
Amount in the Unspent CSR Account not spent within three financial years from the date of transferA Fund specified in Schedule VIIWithin thirty days from the date of completion of the third financial year
Surplus arising out of CSR activities (if not ploughed back or transferred to Unspent CSR Account)A Fund specified in Schedule VIIWithin six months of the expiry of the financial year

CSR implementation [Rule 4 of the CSR Rules]

  • Sub-rule 1 — who may execute: the company itself, or through (a) a connected charitable entity — a section 8 company, registered public trust or registered society exempted under sub-clauses (iv), (v), (vi) or (via) of clause (23C) of section 10 or registered under section 12A and approved under 80G of the Income Tax Act, 1961, established by the company singly or with any other company; (b) an entity established by Government — a section 8 company or registered trust/society established by the Central or State Government; (c) a statutory entity — any statutory body established under an Act of Parliament or a State legislature to undertake Schedule VII activities; or (d) any charitable entity with a track record of at least three years in undertaking similar activities, with the same income-tax registration/approval credentials. The onus (ultimate responsibility) lies on the Board.
  • Sub-rule 2 — registration: every entity covered under sub-rule (1) intending to undertake CSR activity shall register with the Central Government by filing Form CSR-1 electronically with the Registrar with effect from 1st April 2021; this does not affect CSR projects or programmes approved prior to 1st April 2021. Form CSR-1 must be signed and submitted electronically by the entity and verified digitally by a Chartered Accountant in practice or a Company Secretary in practice or a Cost Accountant in practice. On submission, a unique CSR Registration Number is generated automatically by the system.
  • Sub-rule 3: a company may engage international organisations for designing, monitoring and evaluation of CSR projects or programmes as per its CSR policy, and for capacity building of its own personnel for CSR.
  • Sub-rule 4: a company may collaborate with other companies for undertaking projects/programmes in such a manner that the CSR committees of the respective companies are in a position to report separately on such projects.
  • Sub-rule 5: the Board shall satisfy itself that the funds disbursed have been utilised for the purposes and in the manner approved by it, and the Chief Financial Officer or the person responsible for financial management shall certify to that effect.
  • Sub-rule 6: for an ongoing project the Board shall monitor implementation with reference to approved timelines and year-wise allocation, and is competent to make modifications for smooth implementation within the overall permissible time period.
  • MCA General Circular No. 21/2014 dated 18th June 2014: CSR activities should be undertaken in project/programme mode; one-off events such as marathons, awards, charitable contributions, advertisements or sponsorship of TV programmes do not qualify as CSR expenditure. Expenses incurred for fulfilment of any Act/Statute of regulations (such as labour laws, the Land Acquisition Act) do not count as CSR. Registered Trusts include Trusts registered under the Income Tax Act, 1961 for States where registration of a Trust is not mandatory. Contribution to the corpus of a trust/society/section 8 company qualifies as CSR so long as (a) the entity is created exclusively for undertaking CSR activities, or (b) the corpus is created exclusively for a purpose directly relatable to a Schedule VII subject.
  • Foreign holding company: expenditure incurred by a foreign holding company for CSR activities in India qualifies as CSR spending of the Indian subsidiary if the CSR expenditures are routed through the Indian subsidiary and the Indian subsidiary is required to spend under section 135.

CSR reporting and impact assessment [Rule 8 of the CSR Rules]

  • Sub-rule 1: the Board's Report of a covered company for any financial year shall include an annual report on CSR. Sub-rule 2: for a foreign company, the balance sheet filed under clause (b) of Sec 381(1) shall contain the annual report on CSR. Annexure I is the format for financial years commencing before 1st April 2020; Annexure II for financial years commencing on or after 1st April 2020.
  • Sub-rule 3 — impact assessment: every company having average CSR obligation of ₹10 crore or more under Sec 135(5) in the three immediately preceding financial years shall undertake impact assessment through an independent agency of its CSR projects having outlays of ₹1 crore or more which have been completed not less than one year before undertaking the impact study. The impact assessment reports shall be placed before the Board and annexed to the annual report on CSR. The expenditure on impact assessment may be booked as CSR for that financial year, not exceeding two percent of the total CSR expenditure for that financial year or ₹50 lakh, whichever is higher.
  • Sec 135(8): the Central Government may give general or special directions to a company or class of companies to ensure compliance with this section, and such companies shall comply.

Penalty for default under Sec 135(5) or (6) [Sec 135(7)]

LiablePenalty
CompanyTwice the amount required to be transferred to the Fund specified in Schedule VII or to the Unspent CSR Account, as the case may be, or ₹1 crore, whichever is less
Every officer who is in defaultOne-tenth of the amount required to be transferred to the Fund specified in Schedule VII or to the Unspent CSR Account, as the case may be, or ₹2 lakh, whichever is less

Schedule VII activities

  • (i) Eradicating hunger, poverty and malnutrition; promoting health care including preventive health care and sanitation, including contribution to the Swach Bharat Kosh; making available safe drinking water. (ii) Promoting education, including special education and employment enhancing vocation skills especially among children, women, the elderly and the differently abled, and livelihood enhancement projects. (iii) Promoting gender equality, empowering women, setting up homes and hostels for women and orphans, old age homes, day care centres and other facilities for senior citizens, and measures for reducing inequalities faced by socially and economically backward groups. (iv) Ensuring environmental sustainability, ecological balance, protection of flora and fauna, animal welfare, agroforestry, conservation of natural resources and maintaining quality of soil, air and water, including contribution to the Clean Ganga Fund.
  • (v) Protection of national heritage, art and culture, including restoration of buildings and sites of historical importance and works of art; setting up public libraries; promotion and development of traditional arts and handicrafts. (vi) Measures for the benefit of armed forces veterans, war widows and their dependents, CAPF and CPMF veterans and their dependents including widows. (vii) Training to promote rural sports, nationally recognised sports, paralympic sports and Olympic sports. (viii) Contribution to the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund or PM CARES Fund or any other fund set up by the Central Government for socio-economic development and relief and welfare of Scheduled Castes, Tribes, other backward classes, minorities and women.
  • (ix)(a) Contribution to incubators or research and development projects in science, technology, engineering and medicine funded by the Central or State Government or any agency or PSU thereof; (ix)(b) contributions to public funded Universities, IITs, National Laboratories and Autonomous Bodies established under DAE, DBT, DST, Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of AYUSH, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, and DRDO, ICAR, ICMR, CSIR engaged in research in science, technology, engineering and medicine aimed at promoting Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). (x) Rural development projects. (xi) Slum area development (a 'slum area' being any area so declared by the Central Government, a State Government or any other competent authority under any law in force). (xii) Disaster management, including relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction activities.
  • The entries in Schedule VII must be interpreted liberally so as to capture the essence of the subjects enumerated; the items are broad-based and intended to cover a wide range of activities (General Circular No. 21/2014 dated 18th June 2014).

MCA clarifications on CSR — COVID-19 and Har Ghar Tiranga

Circular / MemorandumDateClarification
General Circular No. 10/202023rd March 2020Spending of CSR funds for COVID-19 is an eligible CSR activity under items (i) and (xii) of Schedule VII — promotion of health care including preventive health care and sanitation, and disaster management
General Circular No. 01/202113th January 2021Awareness campaigns/programmes and public outreach on the COVID-19 Vaccination programme are eligible under items (i), (ii) and (xii)
General Circular No. 05/202122nd April 2021Setting up makeshift hospitals and temporary COVID Care facilities is eligible under items (i) and (xii)
General Circular No. 09/20215th May 2021'Creating health infrastructure for COVID care', 'establishment of medical oxygen generation and storage plants', 'manufacturing and supply of oxygen concentrators, ventilators, cylinders and other medical equipment for countering COVID-19' or similar activities are eligible under items (i) and (xii); reference also drawn to item (ix)
General Circular No. 13/202130th July 2021COVID-19 vaccination for persons other than employees and their families is an eligible CSR activity under items (i) and (xii)
MCA Office Memorandum28th March 2021Any contribution made to the PM CARES Fund qualifies as CSR expenditure for the purpose of section 135
General Circular No. 08/202226th July 2022'Har Ghar Tiranga' campaign under Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav — mass scale production and supply of the National Flag, outreach and amplification efforts and related activities are eligible CSR under item (ii) of Schedule VII pertaining to promotion of education relating to culture

Also clarified for R&D: any company engaged in research and development of new vaccines, drugs and medical devices in its normal course of business may treat R&D of new vaccines, drugs and medical devices related to COVID-19 as CSR for the financial years 2020-21, 2021-22 and 2022-23, provided (a) the activity is carried out in collaboration with any of the institutes or organisations mentioned in item (ix) of Schedule VII, and (b) details of such activity are disclosed separately in the annual report on CSR included in the Board's Report.

Why the CSR rules were re-written in 2020-21 — the numbers
