COVID management highlighted the pitfalls in public infrastructure facilities which CSR could help improve provided accountability was tagged with a full-proof mechanism; that, plus CSR figures which did not show convincing and steady growth, drove the consolidation of the CSR provisions.

Right of Members to Copies of Audited Financial Statement [Section 136]

  • What is circulated: a copy of the financial statements including (a) consolidated financial statement, if any; (b) the auditor's report; and (c) every other document required by law to be annexed or attached to the financial statements which are to be laid before the general meeting. Proviso to Sec 136(2): every company having a subsidiary shall provide a copy of the separate audited or unaudited financial statements of each subsidiary to any member who asks for it.
  • To whom: every member; every trustee for the debenture-holder of any debentures issued by the company; and all persons other than such member or trustee being the persons so entitled.
  • When: at least twenty-one days before the date of the meeting. First proviso: even if sent less than 21 days before, they are deemed duly sent if so agreed by members — (a) where the company has share capital, members holding majority in number entitled to vote and representing not less than ninety-five percent of such part of the paid-up share capital as gives a right to vote at the meeting; or (b) where the company has no share capital, members having not less than ninety-five percent of the total voting power exercisable at the meeting. For a section 8 company, "twenty-one days" is substituted by "fourteen days" [GSR 466(E) dated 5th June 2015].
  • Mode of circulation [Rule 11]: for all listed companies and public companies having net worth of more than ₹1 crore and turnover of more than ₹10 crore, the financial statements may be sent (a) by electronic mode to members whose shareholding is in dematerialised format and whose e-mails are registered with the Depository for communication purposes, and to members holding otherwise than in dematerialised format who have positively consented in writing to electronic mode; and (b) by dispatch of physical copies through any recognised mode of delivery specified under section 20 in all other cases.
  • Listed company — salient features route (second proviso to Sec 136(1)): deemed compliance if (a) copies of the documents are made available for inspection at the registered office during working hours for twenty-one days before the meeting; and (b) a statement of salient features in Form AOC-3 (Form AOC-3A for companies required to comply with the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015), or copies of the documents as the company deems fit, is sent to every member and every debenture trustee not less than twenty-one days before the meeting; (c) unless the shareholders ask for full financial statements.
  • Website hosting (fourth and fifth provisos): a listed company shall place on its website (maintained by or on behalf of the company) its financial statements including consolidated financial statements, separate audited accounts of each subsidiary, and all other documents required to be attached.
  • Foreign subsidiary (sixth proviso): where the foreign subsidiary is statutorily required to prepare consolidated financial statements under the law of its country, the proviso is met if that CFS is placed on the listed company's website; where the foreign subsidiary is not required to get its financial statement audited under the law of its country and does not get it audited, the holding Indian listed company may place such unaudited financial statement on its website, and where it is in a language other than English, a translated copy in English must also be placed.
  • Nidhi company [GSR 465(E) dated 5th June 2015]: for members who do not individually or jointly hold shares of more than ₹1,000 in face value or more than one percent of the total paid-up share capital, whichever is less, it is sufficient compliance if an intimation is sent by public notice in a newspaper circulated in the district of the registered office stating the date, time and venue of the AGM, that the financial statement with enclosures can be inspected at the registered office, that the financial statement with enclosures is affixed on the notice board, and that a member is entitled to vote in person or through proxy.
  • Inspection [Sec 136(2)]: the company shall allow every member or debenture trustee to inspect the documents at its registered office during business hours.
  • General Circular No. 11/2015 dated 21 July 2015: a company holding a general meeting after shorter notice under section 101 may also circulate the financial statements at such shorter notice; and the format of accounts of foreign subsidiaries should be as far as possible in accordance with the Companies Act, 2013 — if not possible, a statement indicating the reasons for deviation may be placed/filed along with such accounts.
Default under Sec 136 [Sub-section 3]Penalty
Company₹25,000
Every officer of the company who is in default₹5,000

Filing of Financial Statement with the Registrar [Section 137]

SituationWhat is filedTime limit
Financial statements adopted at the AGM [Sec 137(1)]Copy of FS including CFS, if any, with all attached documentsWithin 30 days of the date of the AGM
One Person Company (no AGM required)FS duly adopted by its member with all attached documentsWithin 180 days from the closure of the financial year
Financial statements not adopted at the AGM or adjourned AGM [first proviso]Un-adopted FS with required documents — Registrar takes them on record as provisionalWithin 30 days of the date of the AGM
Financial statements later adopted at the adjourned AGM [second proviso]Adopted FSWithin 30 days of the date of the adjourned AGM
AGM not held [Sec 137(2)]FS with attached documents, duly signed, along with a statement of facts and reasons for not holding the AGMWithin 30 days of the last date before which the AGM should have been held
  • Forms [Rule 12]: Rule 12(1) — every company files the financial statement with Form AOC-4 and the consolidated financial statement, if any, with Form AOC-4 CFS. Rule 12(1A) — every NBFC required to comply with Ind AS files with Form AOC-4 NBFC (Ind AS) and the CFS with Form AOC-4 CFS NBFC (Ind AS). Rule 12(1B) — every company covered under Sec 135(1) shall furnish a report on CSR in Form CSR-2 to the Registrar for the preceding financial year (2020-2021) and onwards, as an addendum to Form AOC-4 or AOC-4 XBRL or AOC-4 NBFC (Ind AS). Rule 12(1C) — every company shall also file, along with the relevant e-Form AOC-4 / AOC-4 CFS / AOC-4 XBRL / AOC-4 NBFC (Ind AS) / AOC-4 CFS NBFC (Ind AS), the e-Forms Extract of Board Report, Extract of Auditor's Report (Standalone) and Extract of Auditor's Report (Consolidated); a copy of the signed financial statements duly authenticated under section 134 (including Board's report, auditors' report and other documents) in PDF shall also be attached with the XBRL forms. Fees/additional fees are as prescribed by the Companies (Registration Offices and Fees) Rules, 2014.
  • XBRL filing — Rule 3(1), Companies (Filing of Documents and Forms in Extensible Business Reporting Language) Rules, 2015 — filing in e-Form AOC-4 XBRL as per Annexure-I is mandatory for: (i) companies listed with stock exchanges in India and their Indian subsidiaries; (ii) companies having paid up capital of ₹5 crore or above; (iii) companies having turnover of ₹100 crore or above; and (iv) all companies required to prepare financial statements in accordance with the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015. Rule 3(1A) — such companies shall also attach a copy of the signed financial statements duly authenticated under section 134 (including Board's report, auditors' report and other documents) in PDF format in e-Form AOC-4 XBRL.
  • Taxonomy: Annexure-II taxonomy if preparing financial statements as per the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021; Annexure-II A taxonomy if preparing as per the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015.
  • XBRL exemption: non-banking financial companies, housing finance companies and companies engaged in the business of banking and insurance sector are exempted from filing financial statements in XBRL format under these Rules.
  • "Once in XBRL, always in XBRL": companies that have filed under Rule 3(1) of the 2015 Rules (and the erstwhile 2011 Rules) shall continue to file in XBRL in succeeding years even if they no longer fall within the specified class.
  • Subsidiaries incorporated outside India (fourth and fifth provisos to Sec 137(1)): a company shall attach to its filed financial statements the accounts of its subsidiaries incorporated outside India which have not established their place of business in India. Where such a foreign subsidiary is not required to get its financial statement audited under the law of its country and does not get it audited, the fourth proviso is met if the holding Indian company files such unaudited financial statement along with a declaration to this effect, and where it is in a language other than English, along with a translated copy in English.
Person liable under Sec 137(3)Penalty
Company₹10,000 and, in case of continuing failure, a further penalty of ₹100 for each day during which the failure continues, subject to a maximum of ₹2 lakh
The Managing Director and the Chief Financial Officer, if any; in their absence any other director charged by the Board with the responsibility; in the absence of any such director, all the directors of the company₹10,000 and, in case of continuing failure, a further penalty of ₹100 for each day after the first during which the failure continues, subject to a maximum of ₹50,000

Internal Audit [Section 138 read with Rule 13]

Class of companyCriterion (during the preceding financial year)Threshold
Every listed company—Applicable in all cases
Every unlisted public company (any one criterion)Paid up share capital₹50 crore or more during the preceding financial year
Turnover₹200 crore or more during the preceding financial year
Outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutionsExceeding ₹100 crore or more at any point of time during the preceding financial year
Outstanding deposits₹25 crore or more at any point of time during the preceding financial year
Every private company (any one criterion)Turnover₹200 crore or more during the preceding financial year
Outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutionsExceeding ₹100 crore or more at any point of time during the preceding financial year
  • Note: a private company is not tested on paid-up capital or on outstanding deposits — only turnover and borrowings.
  • An existing company covered under any of the above criteria shall comply with section 138 and Rule 13 within 6 months of commencement of such section.
  • Who may be appointed [Sec 138(1)]: a chartered accountant, or a cost accountant, or such other professional as may be decided by the Board to conduct internal audit of the functions and activities of the company. "Chartered Accountant" or "Cost Accountant" means such a person whether engaged in practice or not. The internal auditor may or may not be an employee of the company.
  • Manner and interval [Sec 138(2) read with Rule 13(2)]: the Audit Committee or the Board shall, in consultation with the Internal Auditor, formulate the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology for conducting the internal audit.
  • IFSC: in the case of a specified IFSC public company [GSR 08(E) dated 4th January 2017] and a specified IFSC private company [GSR 09(E) dated 4th January 2017], section 138 applies only if the articles of the company provide for the same.

Examples

  • Example 1 — first financial year (Mahindra Limited): Mahindra Limited was incorporated on 22nd February 2023. Since it was incorporated on or after 1st January of a year, under Sec 2(41) its first financial year comprises the period ending on the 31st day of March of the following year, i.e. 31st March 2024.
  • Illustration 1 — True/False on vouchers: Statement — "Vouchers need not be preserved as part of the requirement of preserving books for a period of 8 years." Answer: False. Under Sec 128(5), the books of account together with vouchers relevant to any entry in such books must be preserved in good order for not less than eight years immediately preceding the relevant financial year.
  • Illustration 2 — cash basis (XYZ Limited): Can XYZ Limited maintain its books of account on cash basis? Answer: No. Sec 128(1) requires every company to prepare books of account, other relevant books and papers and financial statement for every financial year on accrual basis and according to the double entry system. No exception has been given to any class or classes of companies, so XYZ Limited cannot maintain its books on cash basis.
  • Illustration 3 — deviation from accounting standards (Modern Furniture Limited) [MCQ]: MFL must prepare financial statements complying with accounting standards in the Schedule III form, but the statements prepared are not in compliance with applicable accounting standards. It must disclose which of — (i) deviation, (ii) reason of deviation, (iii) financial effects arising out of such deviation? Options: (a) only i; (b) only i and ii; (c) only i and iii; (d) all of i, ii and iii. Answer: (d) — all three, under Sec 129(5).
  • Illustration 4 — circulating unaudited accounts (ABC Ltd.): The Board of ABC Ltd. wants to circulate unaudited accounts before the AGM. Answer: not tenable. Sec 129(2) requires the Board to lay financial statements before every AGM, and Sec 134(7) requires a signed copy of every financial statement (including CFS) to be issued, circulated or published along with the notes, the auditor's report and the Board's report. It follows that unaudited accounts can neither be sent to members nor filed with the Registrar of Companies.
  • Illustration 5 — internal financial controls (Modern Furniture Limited, listed): MFL has internal financial controls in place; during the financial year a failure in the control system was reported and controls were reinstated soon after. Can the directors state in the Directors' Responsibility Statement that controls are adequate and operating efficiently? Answer: No. "Adequacy" refers to the design of the control/system — whether it is fit for purpose; "operating effectively" refers to whether the control has the desired effect of mitigating the risk. Read together, they mean adequate, operating effectively and applicable throughout the year — which was not the case here.
  • Illustration 6 — authentication in an OPC (ABC Company): ABC Company is a one-person company with only one director. Who authenticates the balance sheet, statement of profit & loss and the Board's report? Answer: in the case of a One Person Company the financial statements shall be signed by only one director for submission to the auditor for his report; financial statements signed by that one director are in order.
  • Example 2 — re-categorising as an ongoing project (Modern Furniture Limited): MFL undertook a CSR project of placing and installing benches in public parks and gardens under the supervision of the district administration, initially estimated to be completed in 8-10 months. Because half a dozen parks were being renovated, installation there was postponed until construction was complete (expected to take a further couple of quarters). The Board declared the project an ongoing project, extended its duration beyond one year and gave reasonable justification. Answer: valid. Rule 2(i) provides that projects initially of less than a year's duration (hence not registered as multi-year projects) whose duration is extended beyond one year by the Board on reasonable causes or justification shall be re-categorised as ongoing projects.
  • Illustration 7 — CSR applicability despite a loss (ABC Ltd): ABC Ltd has a turnover of more than ₹1,000 crore in each of the preceding three financial years and incurred a loss in one of those years. Must it constitute a CSR committee? Answer: Yes. Under Sec 135(1), if any one of the three criteria (net worth, turnover, or net profit) is satisfied, the company must constitute a CSR committee and comply with the CSR provisions. The mere fact that it incurred a loss in one of the preceding three financial years is not considered in determining applicability — here turnover triggers it.
  • Illustration 8 — CSR computation for a company under three years old (Modern Furniture Limited) [MCQ]: Compute the minimum amount MFL must spend on CSR for the year 2022-2023. MFL was incorporated in August 2020. Net profits for FY 2020-2021 and FY 2021-2022 are ₹20 crore and ₹38 crore respectively. Options: (a) ₹76 lakh; (b) ₹1.16 crore; (c) ₹58 lakh; (d) no CSR spending required as three financial years are not complete. Answer: (c) ₹58 lakh — under Sec 135(5), where the company has not completed three financial years since incorporation, it spends 2% of the average net profits of such immediately preceding financial years: average = (₹20 crore + ₹38 crore) ÷ 2 = ₹29 crore; 2% of ₹29 crore = ₹58 lakh. Option (d) is wrong because the shortfall of three years does not suspend the obligation.
  • Illustration 9 — engaging an international organisation: Can an international organisation be engaged for implementation of a CSR project? Answer: Yes, but restricted. Under Rule 4(3), engagement is limited to the designing, monitoring and evaluation of the CSR projects or programmes as per the CSR policy, and to capacity building of the company's own personnel for CSR.
  • Illustration 10 — website hosting of a foreign subsidiary's accounts (RELM Industries Limited): RELM Industries Limited, listed on a recognised stock exchange in India, placed its audited financial statement including CFS on its website, and also the separate audited accounts of all Indian subsidiaries — but omitted one foreign subsidiary on the ground that it is not required to get its financial statement audited under the company law of its country of incorporation. Answer: RELM has not complied with section 136. The holding Indian listed company is required to place the unaudited financial statement of the foreign subsidiary on its website even where audit is not required there; and where that statement is in a language other than English, a translated copy in English must also be placed on the website.
  • Example 3 — continuing XBRL filing (Amazon Company Limited): Turnover of ₹150 crore for the financial year ended 31st March 2023 and ₹90 crore for the year ended 31st March 2024. Amazon Company Limited must continue to file its financial statements and other documents under section 137 in e-Form AOC-4 XBRL for the financial year ended 31st March 2024 even though it no longer falls within the class of companies specified under Rule 3 of the Companies (Filing of Documents and Forms in XBRL) Rules, 2015.
  • Illustration 11 — unaudited foreign subsidiary accounts (Vandana Ltd. / Italian subsidiary): Vandana Ltd., based in India, has many subsidiaries in India and outside India plus associates and joint ventures. For consolidation for the year ended 31st March 2024, its Italian subsidiary supplied standalone financial statements in the local language and unaudited, since audit is not required for that subsidiary. Answer: Vandana Ltd. must get the Italian subsidiary's standalone financial statements translated into English and aligned to its own accounting policies for consolidation. Under Sec 137(1), it must file the unaudited financial statement of the Italian subsidiary along with a declaration to this effect and a translated English copy. Further, the format of the Italian subsidiary's accounts should as far as possible follow the Companies Act, 2013; if not possible, a statement indicating the reasons for deviation may be placed/filed along with such accounts.
  • Illustration 12 — AGM not held (R Ltd.): The AGM of R Ltd. for laying the annual accounts for the year ended 31 March 2024 was not held. Answer: Under section 96 the AGM ought to have been held by 30 September 2024. Therefore under Sec 137(2), the financial statements with the documents required to be attached, duly signed, along with the statement of facts and reasons for not holding the AGM, must be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the last date before which the AGM should have been held, i.e. by 30 October 2024, with such fees or additional fees as may be prescribed.
  • Illustration 13 — AGM held but accounts not adopted (continuation of Illustration 12): The annual accounts were duly laid before the AGM held on 27 September 2024 but were not adopted by the shareholders. Answer: Since the AGM was held in time on 27 September 2024, the un-adopted financial statements with the required documents shall be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the date of the AGM under Sec 137(1), and the Registrar shall take them in his records as provisional until the financial statements are filed after adoption in the adjourned AGM.
  • Illustration 14 — replacing the internal auditor (Perfect Ltd.): Perfect Ltd. is a listed steel manufacturing company with head office in Karnataka and operations across India. It appointed a firm of Chartered Accountants, N & Co. LLP, as internal auditors for the year ended 31st March 2024. For FY 2024-25 it plans an in-house internal audit system commensurate with its size and operations and, if so, not to continue with N & Co. LLP. Answer: if the internal audit function of the company is fine as per its size and operations, it may decide not to continue with N & Co. LLP — section 138 does not compel appointment of an external firm.
  • MCQ 1 — outer limit for re-opening (ABC Limited / SEBI): ABC Limited is listed in India; during the current financial year ending 31st March 2024 SEBI found irregularities in the company's filings and proposes to apply to the Tribunal for re-opening of the books. Up to which financial year may the Tribunal grant re-opening? Options: (a) 2019-2020; (b) 2017-2018; (c) 2014-2015; (d) 2015-2016. Answer: (d) 2015-2016 — Sec 130(3) permits re-opening only for the eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year.
  • MCQ 2 — surplus from CSR activities: Which statement is correct about the surplus arising out of CSR activities? Options: (a) the surplus cannot exceed five percent of total CSR expenditure for the financial year; (b) the surplus shall not form part of the business profit of a company; (c) the surplus cannot exceed 10 percent of total CSR expenditure for the financial year; (d) the surplus shall form part of the business profit of a company. Answer: (b).
  • MCQ 3 — CSR spent on employees (Shri Limited): Shri Limited, which has a CSR Committee under section 135, decides to spend and utilise the CSR amount on activities for the benefit of all the employees of Shri Limited. Options: (a) this is the total amount spent on CSR for that financial year; (b) no amount spent on CSR by Shri Limited for that financial year; (c) only half of the total amount spent shall be considered CSR; (d) only the amount spent on employees having salary of ₹20,000 per month or less shall be considered CSR. Answer: (b) — Rule 2(d)(iv) excludes activities benefitting employees of the company (as defined in clause (k) of section 2 of the Code on Wages, 2019) from the definition of CSR.
  • Descriptive Q1 — books at a place other than the registered office (Bharat Ltd.): Bharat Ltd.'s registered office is in a classified backward area of Maharashtra; the Board wants to keep its books of account at its conveniently located corporate office in Mumbai. Answer: Sec 128(1) requires books, other relevant books and papers and the financial statement to be kept for every financial year giving a true and fair view, on accrual basis and double entry system; but the proviso allows all or any of the books to be kept at such other place in India as the Board may decide, provided that where such a decision is taken the company files with the Registrar, within seven days, a written notice giving the full address of that other place. It may also keep such books in electronic mode under Rule 3. Therefore the Board of Bharat Ltd. can keep its books at its Mumbai corporate office by following this procedure.
  • Descriptive Q2 — authentication (Vishwakarma Electronics Limited): The Board consists of Mr. Ghanshyam (Director), Mr. Hyder (Director) and Mr. Indersen (Managing Director); the company has also employed a Company Secretary. The financial statements were signed by Mr. Ghanshyam and Mr. Hyder only. Answer: not in accordance with Sec 134(1). Where two directors sign, one of them must be the managing director — so Mr. Indersen should have been one of the two signing directors; and since the company has employed a Company Secretary, he should also sign the financial statements.
  • Descriptive Q3 — XBRL for a housing finance company (A Housing Finance Ltd.): Paid-up share capital of ₹11 crore and turnover of ₹145 crore during FY 2023-24 — must it file in XBRL? Answer: No. Although it crosses the ₹5 crore paid-up capital and ₹100 crore turnover thresholds in Rule 3(1), the proviso exempts non-banking financial companies, housing finance companies and companies engaged in the business of banking and insurance from filing financial statements under those Rules. Being a housing finance company, A Housing Finance Ltd. is exempted from filing in XBRL mode.
  • Descriptive Q4 — different financial year for consolidation (Herry Limited / SKP Limited): Herry Limited is registered in Thailand; SKP Limited (registered in India) is its wholly owned subsidiary and wishes to follow a different financial year for consolidation of accounts outside India. Answer/procedure: where a company or body corporate which is a holding, subsidiary or associate company of a company incorporated outside India is required to follow a different financial year for consolidation of its accounts outside India, the Central Government may, on an application made in the prescribed form and manner, allow any period as its financial year, whether or not that period is a year. Any application pending before the Tribunal as on the date of commencement of the Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 2018 shall be disposed of by the Tribunal under the provisions applicable before such commencement. A company existing on the commencement of the Act had to align its financial year within two years of such commencement. SKP Limited is advised to follow this procedure.
  • Descriptive Q5(i) — single entry system (Ravi Limited): Ravi Limited maintained its books under the Single Entry System. Answer: not permitted — Sec 128(1) requires books to give a true and fair view including of branch offices and to be kept on accrual basis and according to the double entry system.
  • Descriptive Q5(ii) — persons responsible: Under Sec 128(6) the persons responsible to take all reasonable steps to secure compliance with the requirement of maintenance of books of account are: (a) the Managing Director; (b) the Whole-Time Director in charge of finance; (c) the Chief Financial Officer; and (d) any other person of the company charged by the Board with the duty of complying with section 128.
  • Descriptive Q5(iii) — electronic books accessible only outside India: Answer: No. Under Rule 3, books maintained in electronic mode must remain accessible in India so as to be usable for subsequent reference; there must be a proper system for storage, retrieval, display or printout as the Audit Committee or Board deems appropriate, and such records shall not be disposed of or rendered unusable unless permitted by law; and the back-up of books maintained in electronic mode, including at a place outside India, must be kept in servers physically located in India. (The answer text also reproduces the audit-trail proviso for the financial year commencing on or after the 1st day of April, 2022 requiring accounting software with audit trail, an edit log of each change with the date, and an audit trail that cannot be disabled.) Hence a company cannot keep books of account in electronic mode accessible only outside India.
  • Descriptive Q6 — filing after an adjourned AGM (Sun Ltd.): The Government of India holds 51% of the paid-up equity share capital of Sun Ltd. The audited financial statements for FY 2022-23 were placed at the AGM held on 31st August 2023, but pending the CAG's comments the meeting was adjourned without adoption. On receipt of the CAG comments the adjourned AGM was held on 15th October 2023 where the accounts were adopted, and Sun Ltd. filed its financial statements with the Registrar on 12th November 2023. Answer: the filing of the adopted accounts on 12th November 2023 is within 30 days of the adjourned AGM of 15th October 2023, so the second proviso to Sec 137(1) is satisfied. However, Sun Ltd. did not file its un-adopted financial statements within 30 days of the AGM held on 31st August 2023 as required by the first proviso. Hence Sun Ltd. has not complied regarding filing of un-adopted accounts, though it has complied by filing the adopted accounts within the due date.
  • Descriptive Q7 — re-opening beyond eight years (Chetan Ltd.): In the current financial year 2023-24 the Income Tax Authorities, during assessment proceedings, saw a need to re-open the accounts of Chetan Ltd. for the financial year 2012-13 and filed an application before the NCLT for re-opening and recasting. Answer: Section 130 permits an application by the Central Government, Income-tax authorities, SEBI, any other statutory body or authority or any person concerned, and an order by a court of competent jurisdiction or the Tribunal on the grounds of fraudulent preparation or mismanagement casting doubt on reliability. But no order can be made for re-opening books relating to a period earlier than eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year. The application by the Income Tax Authorities to the NCLT is itself valid, but its recommendation for re-opening and recasting the financial statements for a period earlier than the eight financial years immediately preceding FY 2023-2024 is invalid.

Penalties at a glance

129(7) — financial statementMD, WTD in charge of finance, CFO or any other person charged by the Board with the duty; in the absence of any of them, all the directorsImprisonment up to one year, or fine not less than ₹50,000 extending to ₹5 lakh, or both

Why It Matters / Application

Chapter IX is where the accounting record itself becomes a statutory object: Sec 128 fixes what must be recorded, where it must sit (registered office, or another Indian place notified in Form AOC-5 within 7 days), how it must be recorded (accrual, double entry, tamper-proof audit trail from FY commencing on or after 1st April 2023) and for how long it must survive (8 years with vouchers) — and each of these becomes the factual foundation for later enforcement. The 8-year preservation period is not decorative: it is exactly the window inside which a court or Tribunal can order re-opening under Sec 130(3), which is why the Chetan Ltd. application for FY 2012-13 filed in FY 2023-24 fails and why the SEBI question in the MCQ answers 2015-2016. Sec 137 converts the adopted financial statement into a public document, and the AOC-4 / AOC-4 CFS / AOC-4 XBRL / AOC-4 NBFC (Ind AS) / CSR-2 form matrix decides the mode; the "once in XBRL always in XBRL" rule and the NBFC/HFC/banking/insurance exemption together explain both the Amazon Company Limited and A Housing Finance Ltd. answers. Section 135 is the one place in the Act that turns a percentage of profit into a compulsory application of funds, and the machinery around it — the 2% of three-year average net profits computed under section 198, the ₹50 lakh de-minimis that dispenses with the CSR Committee, the 5% cap on administrative overheads, the 30-day/6-month transfer routes, the three-year set-off for excess spending, and the ₹10 crore / ₹1 crore impact-assessment trigger — is where the marks in a practical question actually sit. Section 138's thresholds matter for identifying which unlisted public and private companies must carry an internal auditor at all, and Sec 132 explains why a defaulting auditor now faces an NFRA order with penalties up to ten times the fees received and debarment up to ten years, appealable only to the Appellate Tribunal.

Note

Exam traps and provisos worth memorising. (1) Section 129A is not operational — no rule prescribed or notification made as on 30.04.2024, so a question asking what the "prescribed class of unlisted companies" is has no answer beyond the section's text. (2) A private company under Sec 138 is tested only on turnover (₹200 crore) and borrowings (exceeding ₹100 crore) — not on paid-up capital or deposits, unlike an unlisted public company. (3) The CSR trigger under Sec 135(1) is tested on the immediately preceding financial year and any one of the three limits suffices; a loss in one of the preceding years is irrelevant (Illustration 7). (4) The ₹50 lakh exception in Sec 135(9) removes only the Committee, not the spending obligation — the Board discharges the Committee's functions. (5) An ongoing project may run up to three years excluding the year of commencement — an easy place to lose a mark by counting the commencement year. (6) The excess CSR set-off cannot include the surplus arising out of CSR activities, and needs a Board resolution. (7) Under Sec 134(1), if two directors sign, one must be the managing director where there is one, and the CEO, CFO and company secretary sign wherever they are appointed — the Vishwakarma Electronics answer turns on precisely this. (8) The OPC exceptions run through the chapter: one director signs the FS, an abridged Rule 8A Board's report applies (also to small companies), and filing with the ROC is within 180 days from closure of the financial year, not 30 days from an AGM. (9) Under Sec 130, only a court of competent jurisdiction or Tribunal can order re-opening; an applicant's own view is not enough, and the court/Tribunal must first give notice to the CG, income-tax authorities, SEBI or other body and consider their representations. (10) A Sec 131 revision cannot be made more than once in a financial year, and the detailed reasons must be disclosed in the Board's report for the year of revision. (11) The audit trail proviso is dated 1st April 2023 in the main text of the chapter but appears as 1st April 2022 in the answer to Descriptive Question 5(iii) — reproduce the date as given in the question paper's source provision. (12) Government company reliefs (Sec 129 segment reporting; Sec 134(3) clauses (e), (m) and (p)) are available only to Government companies that have not defaulted in filing under Sec 137 or Sec 92. (13) For specified IFSC companies: Sec 135 does not apply for 5 years from commencement of business, and Sec 138 applies only if the articles so provide. (14) In a section 8 company the 21-day circulation period becomes 14 days; in a Nidhi company, newspaper public notice suffices for small holders (₹1,000 face value or 1% of paid-up capital, whichever is less). (15) Where NFRA has initiated an investigation, no other institute or body may initiate or continue proceedings on the same misconduct.

Chapter 10 — Audit and Auditors

Source: 87779bos-aps2160-ch10.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Scope of the chapter: Chapter X of the Companies Act, 2013 — sections 139 to 148 — supplemented by the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014. The Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014 and the NFRA Rules, 2018 also feed into this chapter.
  • Why an independent auditor exists: directors act as fiduciaries to the members (the real owners) and are the ones who prepare the financial statements and lay them before the general meeting. Without a check, directors may mismanage the finances. The members therefore appoint an auditor to give an independent professional opinion on whether the statements show a true and fair view of financial position and performance.
  • "Appointment" includes re-appointment throughout section 139, and "firm" includes a limited liability partnership incorporated under the LLP Act, 2008.
  • Standard tenure: an auditor appointed at an AGM holds office from the conclusion of that AGM till the conclusion of the 6th AGM (i.e. a block of five years), and thereafter till the conclusion of every sixth meeting.
  • Rotation is class-specific: the 5-year individual / 10-year firm ceiling in section 139(2) applies only to listed companies and to the prescribed classes of other companies — not to every company.
  • Independence is enforced two ways: ex-ante through the disqualification list in section 141(3) and the prohibited-services list in section 144; ex-post through mandatory rotation and cooling-off, deemed vacation under section 141(4), and NCLT power to force a change of auditor under section 140(5).
  • Auditor as whistle-blower: section 143(12) converts the auditor into a statutory fraud reporter — frauds of ₹1 crore or above go to the Central Government in Form ADT-4; smaller frauds go to the Audit Committee/Board and get disclosed in the Board's report.

Key Definitions / Terms

Auditor (eligibility) — Sec 141(1)
A person is eligible only if he is a chartered accountant as defined in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 who holds a valid certificate of practice under section 6(1) of that Act. Where a firm is appointed, the proviso requires that a majority of its partners practising in India are qualified for appointment.
Who signs for a firm — Sec 141(2)
Where a firm (including an LLP) is appointed auditor, only the partners who are Chartered Accountants are authorised to act and sign on behalf of the firm.
First auditor — Sec 139(6)
For a non-Government company: appointed by the Board of Directors within 30 days of the date of registration; holds office until the conclusion of the first AGM.
Subsequent auditor — Sec 139(1)
Appointed by the members at the first AGM; holds office from the conclusion of that meeting till the conclusion of the sixth AGM.
Casual vacancy — Sec 139(8)
A vacancy in the office of auditor arising otherwise than by normal expiry of term (e.g. death, resignation, disqualification). A deemed casual vacancy also arises under section 141(4) when a sitting auditor incurs a disqualification.
Cooling period
The five-year break after completion of the maximum term, during which the outgoing individual/firm cannot be re-appointed in the same company — designed to re-instate independence. For rotation purposes, a break of a continuous period of five years is treated as fulfilling the rotation requirement.
Same network — Rule 6(3)
Firms operating or functioning, hitherto or in future, under the same brand name, trade name or common control. An incoming auditor in the same network as the outgoing auditor is ineligible.
Consecutive years (for rotation)
All the preceding financial years for which the individual/firm has been the auditor until there has been a break by five years or more. "Individual auditor" includes other individuals or firms whose name, trademark or brand is used by such individual; "audit firm" includes other firms whose name, trademark or brand is used by the firm or any of its partners.
Business relationship — Sec 141(3)(e)
Any transaction entered into for a commercial purpose, except (i) commercial transactions in the nature of professional services permitted to be rendered by an auditor/audit firm under the Act and the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, and (ii) commercial transactions in the ordinary course of business at arm's length price, such as sale of products or services to the auditor as a customer by companies engaged in telecommunications, airlines, hospitals, hotels and such other similar businesses.
Audi Alteram Partem
Latin maxim / principle of natural justice — every person gets a chance of being heard to respond to the charge, evidence or action against them. Applied by the proviso to section 140(1): the auditor must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before removal.
Cost Accountant — Sec 2(28)
Defined by clause (b) of section 2(1) of the Cost and Works Accountants Act, 1959; must hold a valid certificate of practice under section 6(1) of that Act and be in whole-time practice. Includes a firm of cost accountants and an LLP of cost accountants.
Cost auditing standards — Sec 148(3), 2nd proviso
Standards issued by the Institute of Cost Accountants of India (erstwhile ICWAI), constituted under the Cost and Works Accountants Act, 1959, with the approval of the Central Government.
NFRA
National Financial Reporting Authority — monitors and enforces compliance with auditing standards under Rule 8 of the NFRA Rules, 2018 and oversees audit quality under Rule 9.

Appointment of Auditors — Section 139

  • Manner of selection — Rule 3: where the company must constitute an Audit Committee under section 177, that committee is the competent authority; otherwise the Board of Directors is. The competent authority must consider (a) whether the qualifications and experience of the individual/firm are commensurate with the size and requirements of the company; (b) any order or pending proceeding relating to professional matters of conduct against the proposed auditor before the ICAI, any competent authority or any Court; and it may call for such other information from the proposed auditor as it deems fit.
  • Audit Committee route: the committee recommends a name to the Board. If the Board agrees, it recommends the appointment to the members at the AGM. If the Board disagrees, it refers the recommendation back to the committee for reconsideration citing reasons. If the committee, after considering the Board's reasons, decides not to reconsider its original recommendation, the Board shall record reasons for its disagreement and send its own recommendation for consideration of the members at the AGM.
  • Who must constitute an Audit Committee (Sec 177 + Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014): every listed public company; and public companies having paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more, or turnover of ₹100 crore or more, or aggregate outstanding loans/borrowings/debentures/deposits exceeding ₹50 crore or more. Figures as existing on the date of the last audited financial statements are taken. If a company ceases to fulfil any of the three conditions for three consecutive years, it need not comply until it again meets any such condition.
  • Written consent of the proposed auditor must be obtained before the appointment is made (Rule 4).
  • Certificate from the auditor must state: (a) the individual/firm is eligible and not disqualified under the Act, the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and the rules/regulations thereunder; (b) the proposed appointment is as per the term provided under the Act; (c) it is within the limits laid down by or under the authority of the Act; (d) the list of proceedings against the auditor/audit firm/any partner pending on professional matters of conduct, as disclosed, is true and correct. The certificate shall also indicate whether the auditor satisfies the section 141 criteria.
  • Notice to Registrar: the company informs the auditor of his appointment and files Form ADT-1 with the Registrar within 15 days of the meeting in which the auditor is appointed.
  • NFRA intimation: under Rule 3(2) of the NFRA Rules, 2018, every existing body corporate (other than a company) governed by NFRA rules informs NFRA within 30 days of commencement of the NFRA rules in Form NFRA-1. Under Rule 3(3), such a body corporate formed in India informs NFRA in Form NFRA-1 within 15 days of appointment of an auditor under section 139(1).
  • Re-appointment of retiring auditor — Sec 139(9): a retiring auditor may be re-appointed at an AGM if (a) he is not disqualified for re-appointment; (b) he has not given written notice of unwillingness to be re-appointed; and (c) a special resolution has not been passed at that meeting appointing some other auditor or expressly providing that he shall not be re-appointed.
  • Deemed continuation — Sec 139(10): where at any AGM no auditor is appointed or re-appointed, the existing auditor shall continue. Even then, the section 139(9) conditions must be checked.
  • Sec 139(11): where an Audit Committee is required under section 177, all appointments — including the filling of a casual vacancy — shall be made after taking into account the recommendations of that committee.

Rotation of Auditors — Section 139(2), (3), (4) and Rule 5 & 6

Section 139(2) applies to listed companies and to all companies (excluding one person companies and small companies) falling in the classes below:

Class of companyThreshold
Listed companiesAll — no threshold
Unlisted public companiesPaid-up share capital of ₹10 crore or more
Private limited companiesPaid-up share capital of ₹50 crore or more
Any company having public borrowings from financial institutions, banks or public deposits₹50 crore or more
ExcludedOne person companies and small companies

Such companies shall not appoint or re-appoint: an individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years; an audit firm as auditor for more than two terms of five consecutive years. Nothing in sub-section (2) prejudices the right of the company to remove an auditor, or of the auditor to resign.

AuditorAppointed/re-appointed forNot eligible for re-appointment
IndividualOne term of five consecutive years (1st AGM to 6th AGM)For five years from completion of his term (till 11th AGM)
FirmTwo terms of five consecutive years (1st AGM to 11th AGM)For five years from completion of its second term (till 16th AGM)
  • Common-partner bar: on the date of appointment, an audit firm shall not have any partner(s) who is/was also a partner of another audit firm whose tenure expired in that company in the immediately preceding financial year. In effect, an audit firm with a common partner cannot be appointed as the succeeding auditor of the same company after two terms of five consecutive years.
  • Same network bar — Rule 6(3): the incoming auditor or audit firm is ineligible if associated with the outgoing auditor/audit firm under the same network. Also, if a common partner who is in charge of an audit firm and certifies the financial statements of the company retires from that firm and joins another firm of chartered accountants, that other firm is also ineligible for five years.
  • Members' powers — Sec 139(3): members may resolve that (a) in the audit firm appointed by them, the auditing partner and his team shall be rotated at such intervals as the members resolve; or (b) the audit shall be conducted by more than one auditor.
  • Manner of rotation — Rule 6(1)&(2): where an Audit Committee is required, it recommends to the Board the name of the individual/firm who may replace the incumbent on expiry of his term; the Board considers it and makes its recommendation to the members at the AGM. In other cases the Board itself considers rotation and recommends the next auditor to the members at the AGM.
  • Voluntary audit committee: where an audit committee is not required under section 177 but is constituted voluntarily, it shall still recommend the replacement name to the Board — but in such cases the Board may or may not consider the recommendation.
  • Pre-Act service counts — Rule 6(3): for computing five/ten consecutive years, the period for which the individual or firm held office as auditor prior to the commencement of the Act is taken into account.
  • Joint auditors — Rule 6(4): where two or more individuals or firms (or a combination) are appointed joint auditors, the company may follow rotation so that all the joint auditors do not complete their term in the same year.
  • Transitional period — Sec 139(2) proviso: every company existing on or before commencement of the Act required to comply shall do so not later than the date of the first AGM held, within the period specified under section 96(1), after three years from the date of commencement of the Act.

Government Companies and Casual Vacancy — Sec 139(5), (7), (8)

Applies to a Government company, or any other company owned or controlled, directly or indirectly, by the Central Government, or by any State Government(s), or partly by the Central Government and partly by one or more State Governments.

SituationWho appointsTime limitTenure

Removal, Resignation and Special Notice — Section 140

  • Removal before expiry of term — Sec 140(1) + Rule 7: only by (a) a special resolution of the company and (b) after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government (powers delegated to the Regional Director vide notification S.O. 4090(E) dated 19th December 2016, in supersession of S.O. 1352(E) dated 21st May 2014), by application in Form ADT-2 with fees under the Companies (Registration Offices and Fees) Rules, 2014.
  • Sequence and clock: the application to the Central Government shall be made within 30 days of the resolution passed by the Board; the company shall hold the general meeting to pass the special resolution within 60 days of receipt of the Central Government's approval. Central Government approval comes first, the special resolution afterwards. In Basant Ram & Sons v Union of India, (2002) 110 Comp Cas 38 (Del), it was held that after approval of the Central Government, general body approval is necessary to make the removal effective.
  • Opportunity of being heard: before any action for removal before expiry of term, the auditor concerned shall be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard (Audi Alteram Partem).
  • Full removal sequence: special notice received for removal of auditor → Board meeting held (to decide and authorise filing of the application to CG by Board Resolution) → application to CG in Form ADT-2 within 30 days of the Board Resolution → approval of CG received → special notice sent for the AGM (meeting within 60 days of receipt of approval) → auditor given a reasonable opportunity of being heard → special resolution passed on removal → auditor removed.
  • IFSC deeming provision: for a Specified IFSC public company (inserted vide GSR 08(E) dated 04.01.2017) and a Specified IFSC private company (GSR 09(E) dated 04.01.2017), if no decision is communicated by the Central Government within 60 days of submission of the application, the CG is deemed to have approved it, and the company shall appoint a new auditor at a general meeting convened within three months from the date of expiry of that 60-day period.
  • Resignation — Sec 140(2) + Rule 8: a resigning auditor shall file a statement in Form ADT-3 with the company and the Registrar within 30 days from the date of resignation, indicating the reasons and other relevant facts. For a Government company (or a government-owned/controlled company), the statement must additionally be filed with the CAG.
  • Penalty for not filing ADT-3 — Sec 140(3): penalty of ₹50,000 or an amount equal to the remuneration of the auditor, whichever is less; and for continuing failure, a further penalty of ₹500 for each day after the first during which the failure continues, subject to a maximum of ₹2 lakh.
  • Special notice — Sec 140(4): if the retiring auditor has not completed a consecutive tenure of 5 years (or 10 years in case of a firm), a special notice is required for a resolution at an AGM appointing a person other than the retiring auditor, or expressly providing that the retiring auditor shall not be re-appointed. On receipt, the company shall forthwith send a copy to the retiring auditor.
  • Representation: if the retiring auditor makes a written representation of reasonable length and requests its notification, the company shall — unless received too late — (a) state the fact of the representation in any notice of the resolution given to members, and (b) send a copy of the representation to every member to whom notice of the meeting is sent, whether before or after receipt of the representation.
  • If a copy is not sent: whether because it was received too late or through the company's default, the auditor may require that the representation be read out at the meeting (without prejudice to his right to be heard orally), and a copy shall be filed with the Registrar.
  • Abuse of the right — second proviso to Sec 140(4) + Rule 78 of the NCLT Rules, 2016: on an application in Form No. NCLT-1 by the director on behalf of the company or by the aggrieved auditor, if the Tribunal is satisfied that the rights conferred by section 140 are being abused by the auditor, the copy of the representation need not be sent and it need not be read out at the meeting.
  • Fraudulent auditor — Sec 140(5): the Tribunal (NCLT) may act suo motu, or on an application in Form No. NCLT-9 by the Central Government, or on an application in Form No. NCLT-9 by any person concerned. If satisfied that the auditor has, directly or indirectly, acted in a fraudulent manner or abetted or colluded in any fraud by or in relation to the company or its directors or officers, it may by order direct the company to change its auditors.
  • 15-day order (first proviso to Sec 140(5) / Rule 78(3) NCLT Rules, 2016): where the application is made by the Central Government and the Tribunal is satisfied that a change of auditor is required, it shall within 15 days of receipt of such application order that the auditor shall not function as an auditor, and the Central Government may appoint another auditor in his place.
  • Consequences of a final order under Sec 140: the auditor (individual or firm) shall (a) not be eligible to be appointed as auditor of any company for 5 years from the date of passing of the order, and (b) also be liable for action under section 447. In case of a firm, the liability is of the firm and of every partner who acted fraudulently or abetted/colluded. The word "auditor" includes a firm of auditors.

Disqualifications — Section 141(3) read with Rule 10

The following persons shall not be qualified for appointment as auditor of a company:

  • (a) A body corporate, other than a limited liability partnership registered under the LLP Act, 2008.
  • (b) An officer or employee of the company.
  • (c) A person who is a partner of, or who is in the employment of, an officer or employee of the company.
  • (d) A person who himself or his partner is holding any security of or interest in the company, or its subsidiary, or its holding or associate company, or a subsidiary of such holding company (fellow subsidiary), or his relative or partner. Under the Companies Act, 2013 not a single rupee of such holding by the auditor is allowed.
  • (e) A person whose relative (defined under section 2(77)) holds any security of or interest in the company, or its subsidiary, or its holding or associate company or a fellow subsidiary, of face value exceeding ₹1,00,000.
  • (f) A person who himself, or whose partner or relative, is indebted to the company, or its subsidiary, or its holding or associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company, in excess of ₹5 lakh.
  • (g) A person who, or whose relative or partner, has given a guarantee or provided any security in connection with the indebtedness of any third person to the company, or its subsidiary, or its holding or associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company, in excess of one lakh rupees.
  • (h) A person or firm who, directly or indirectly, has a business relationship with the company, or its subsidiary, or its holding or associate company, or a subsidiary of such holding company or associate company (subject to the two carve-outs defined above).
  • (i) A person whose relative is a director or is in the employment of the company as a director (section 2(34)) or key managerial personnel (section 2(51)).
  • (j) A person who is in full time employment elsewhere.
  • (k) A person, or a partner of a firm holding appointment as its auditor, who at the date of such appointment or reappointment is holding appointment as auditor of more than 20 companies.
  • (l) A person who has been convicted by a court of an offence involving fraud and a period of 10 years has not elapsed from the date of such conviction.
  • (m) A person who, directly or indirectly, renders any service referred to in section 144 to the company or its holding company or its subsidiary company.
  • Relative-holding mechanics (Rule 10(1)): although the rule speaks of "a relative", a reasonable rather than literal construction applies — the holding of all the relatives together is checked against the ₹1,00,000 threshold. Further, if the relative of even one partner of a firm holds securities/interest exceeding the threshold, not only that partner but the whole firm is ineligible. The threshold also applies, wherever relevant, to a company not having share capital or other securities.
  • Corrective window: if the relative acquires any security or interest above ₹1,00,000, corrective action to restore the limit must be taken by the auditor within 60 days of such acquisition or interest.
  • Ceiling of 20 audits — exclusions: while computing the ceiling of 20, one person companies, small companies and private companies having paid-up share capital of less than ₹100 crore are excluded (Notification G.S.R. 464(E) dated 5th June 2015). These exceptions apply only to those private companies which have not defaulted in filing financial statements under section 137 or the annual return under section 92 with the Registrar (Notification G.S.R. 583(E) dated 13th June 2017). Before appointment, the company must obtain a certificate from the auditor that the appointment will not result in an excess over the section 141(3)(g) limit.
  • Vacation of office — Sec 141(4): if a person appointed as auditor incurs any disqualification in section 141(3) after his appointment, he shall vacate his office; such vacation is deemed to be a casual vacancy.

Remuneration — Section 142

  • Subsequent auditors: remuneration fixed by the company in general meeting, or in such manner as the general meeting may determine.
  • First auditor: remuneration fixed by the Board which appointed him.
  • Includes: in addition to the fee payable to the auditor — (a) the expenses incurred by him in connection with the audit (out-of-pocket expenses) and (b) any facility extended to him.
  • Excludes: any remuneration paid to him for any other service rendered at the request of the company.

Powers and Duties of Auditors — Section 143

  • Powers [143(1)]: right of access at all times to the books of account and vouchers, whether kept at the registered office or at any other place; entitlement to require from the officers such information and explanations as he considers necessary. The auditor of a holding company also has right of access to the records of all its subsidiaries and associate companies so far as it relates to consolidation of financial statements.
  • Matters of inquiry [143(1)]: (a) whether loans and advances made on the basis of security have been properly secured and whether their terms are prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members; (b) whether transactions represented merely by book entries are prejudicial to the interests of the company; (c) where the company is not an investment company or a banking company, whether assets consisting of shares, debentures and other securities have been sold at a price less than that at which they were purchased; (d) whether loans and advances have been shown as deposits; (e) whether personal expenses have been charged to revenue account; (f) where shares are stated to have been allotted for cash, whether cash has actually been received, and if not, whether the position stated in the account books and balance sheet is correct, regular and not misleading.
  • Report to members [143(2)]: on the accounts examined by him and on every financial statement required to be laid before the company in general meeting, taking into account the Act, the accounting and auditing standards, and matters required under any rules or any order under section 143(11). He must express an opinion whether the accounts/financial statements give a true and fair view of the state of the company's affairs at the end of the financial year, of the profit or loss and cash flow for the year, and such other prescribed matters.

The auditor's report shall also state [Sec 143(3)]:

  • (a) Whether he has sought and obtained all information and explanations necessary to the best of his knowledge and belief; if not, the details and the effect of such information on the financial statements.
  • (b) Whether proper books of account as required by law have been kept, and whether proper returns adequate for audit have been received from branches not visited by him.
  • (c) Whether the report on any branch office audited under section 143(8) by a person other than the company's auditor has been sent to him, and the manner in which he has dealt with it.
  • (d) Whether the balance sheet and profit and loss account dealt with in the report are in agreement with the books of account and returns.
  • (e) Whether the financial statements comply with the accounting standards.
  • (f) The observations or comments of the auditors on financial transactions or matters which have any adverse effect on the functioning of the company.
  • (g) Whether any director is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2).
  • (h) Any qualification, reservation or adverse remark relating to the maintenance of accounts and other matters connected therewith.
  • (i) Whether the company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements in place and the operating effectiveness of such controls.
  • (j) Such other matters as may be prescribed — see Rule 11 below.

Rule 11 of the Companies (Audit & Auditors) Rules, 2014 — other matters to be included:

  • (i) Whether the company has disclosed the impact, if any, of pending litigations on its financial position in its financial statement.
  • (ii) Whether provision has been made, as required under any law or accounting standards, for material foreseeable losses on long-term contracts including derivative contracts.
  • (iii) Whether there has been any delay in transferring amounts required to be transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund.
  • (iv) Whether management has represented that, to the best of its knowledge and belief and other than as disclosed in the notes: (1) no funds have been advanced/loaned/invested (from borrowed funds, share premium or any other source) by the company to any other person(s) or entity(ies) including foreign entities ("Intermediaries"), with the understanding, whether recorded in writing or otherwise, that the Intermediary shall directly or indirectly lend or invest in other persons/entities identified by or on behalf of the company ("Ultimate Beneficiaries") or provide any guarantee, security or the like on their behalf; (2) no funds have been received by the company from any person(s)/entity(ies) including foreign entities ("Funding Parties") with a like understanding that the company shall lend or invest in Ultimate Beneficiaries or provide guarantee/security on their behalf; and (3) based on audit procedures considered reasonable and appropriate, nothing has come to the auditor's notice causing him to believe that representations (1) and (2) contain any material misstatement.
  • (v) Whether the dividend declared or paid during the year is in compliance with section 123.
  • (vi) Whether the company, for financial years commencing on or after 1st April 2022, has used accounting software having an audit trail (edit log) feature, whether it was operated throughout the year for all transactions recorded, whether the audit trail feature has not been tampered with, and whether the audit trail has been preserved as per statutory record-retention requirements.
  • Sec 143(4): where any of these matters is answered in the negative or with a qualification, the auditor's report shall state the reason for the same.
  • Exemption from clause (i) of Sec 143(3) (internal financial controls reporting) — vide Exemption Notification G.S.R. 583(E) dated 13th June 2017 — does not apply to a private company which: (i) is a one person company or a small company; or (ii) has turnover less than ₹50 crore as per the latest audited financial statement and aggregate borrowings from banks or financial institutions or any body corporate at any point of time during the financial year less than ₹25 crore. The exemption applies only to a private company which has not defaulted in filing financial statements under section 137 or the annual return under section 92.
  • Auditing standards [143(9), (10)]: every auditor shall comply with the auditing standards. The Central Government may prescribe standards of auditing or any addendum thereto, as recommended by the ICAI, in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations of the NFRA. Until standards are notified, the standards specified by the ICAI are deemed to be the auditing standards.
  • Sec 143(11): for such class or description of companies as the Central Government may specify by general or special order, in consultation with the NFRA, the auditor's report shall also include a statement on such specified matters — CARO 2020 issued by MCA is to be complied with by the statutory auditor of every company to which it applies.
  • Sec 143(14): the provisions of section 143 apply mutatis mutandis to the cost accountant conducting cost audit under section 148 and to the company secretary in practice conducting secretarial audit under section 204 (confirmed by sub-rule 5 to Rule 13).

Filed electronically in Form ADT-4.

  • Good faith protection [143(13)]: no duty to which the auditor is subject shall be regarded as contravened by reason of his reporting a matter under sub-section (12), if it is done in good faith.
