Audit of Government Companies and Branch Offices — Sec 143(5)–(8)

  • Sec 143(5): for a Government company (or company owned/controlled by Central/State Government), the CAG appoints the auditor under section 139(5) or 139(7) and directs the manner in which the accounts are to be audited; the auditor so appointed shall submit a copy of the audit report to the CAG. The audit report shall include (a) the directions, if any, issued by the CAG; (b) the action taken thereon; and (c) its impact on the accounts and financial statement of the company.
  • Sec 143(6) — supplementary audit: the CAG has, within 60 days from the date of receipt of the audit report, the right to (a) conduct a supplementary audit of the financial statement by persons authorised by him, requiring information or additional information in such form as the CAG may direct, and (b) comment upon or supplement the audit report. Any comments or supplement by the CAG shall be sent by the company to every person entitled to copies of audited financial statements under section 136(1) and shall be placed before the AGM at the same time and in the same manner as the audit report.
  • Sec 143(7) — test audit: the CAG may, if he considers it necessary, by order cause a test audit of the accounts of such company; the provisions of section 19A of the Comptroller and Auditor-General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 apply to the report of such test audit.
  • Sec 143(8) — branch audit: a branch office in India shall be audited either by the company's auditor appointed under section 139 or by any other person qualified for appointment as an auditor of the company under section 139. A branch office outside India shall be audited either by the company's auditor, or by an accountant, or by any other person duly qualified to act as auditor of the branch accounts in accordance with the laws of that country.
  • Rule 12: the duties and powers of the company's auditor with reference to the branch audit and the branch auditor are as contained in sub-sections (1) to (4) of section 143. The branch auditor submits his report to the company's auditor. The fraud-reporting provisions extend to the branch auditor to the extent they relate to the concerned branch.

Prohibited Services — Section 144

An auditor may provide to the company only such other services as are approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee, as the case may be. Such services shall not include the following — whether rendered directly or indirectly to the company, its holding company or its subsidiary company:

  • (a) Accounting and book keeping services;
  • (b) Internal audit;
  • (c) Design and implementation of any financial information system;
  • (d) Actuarial services;
  • (e) Investment advisory services;
  • (f) Investment banking services;
  • (g) Rendering of outsourced financial services;
  • (h) Management services; and
  • (i) Any other kind of services as may be prescribed — no other kind of service has been prescribed till date under this clause.

Meaning of "directly or indirectly":

Auditor is an INDIVIDUAL — coversAuditor is a FIRM — covers
Self; relatives; any other person connected or associated with such individual; any entity in which such individual has significant influence or control; any entity whose name, trademark or brand is used by such individualThe firm; partners of the firm; parent of the firm; subsidiary of the firm; associate entity of the firm; any entity in which the firm has significant influence; any entity in which any partner of the firm has significant influence or control; any entity whose name, trademark or brand is used by the firm or any of its partners

Also note: by the proviso to section 148(3), no person (or firm, including an LLP) appointed under section 139 as auditor of the company shall be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records, or vice-versa.

Signing and Attendance — Sections 145 and 146

  • Sec 145: the person appointed as auditor shall sign the auditor's report, or sign or certify any other document of the company, in accordance with section 141(2) (i.e. where a firm/LLP is appointed, only partners who are Chartered Accountants may act and sign on behalf of the firm).
  • Sec 145 — reading at the general meeting: the qualifications, observations or comments on financial transactions or matters which have any adverse effect on the functioning of the company mentioned in the auditor's report shall be read before the company in general meeting and shall be open to inspection by any member. Not the whole report — only those items.
  • Sec 146: all notices of, and other communications relating to, any general meeting shall be forwarded to the auditor. The auditor shall, unless otherwise exempted by the company, attend either by himself or through his authorised representative, who shall also be qualified to be an auditor, any general meeting; and he has the right to be heard at such meeting on any part of the business which concerns him as the auditor.

Punishment for Contravention — Section 147

Who / whatProvisionMinimumMaximum
Company contravening any of sections 139 to 146 (both inclusive)Sec 147(1)₹25,000₹5,00,000
Every officer of the company who is in defaultSec 147(1)₹10,000₹1,00,000
Auditor contravening section 139, 144 or 145Sec 147(2)₹25,000Lower of (i) ₹5,00,000 or (ii) 4 times the remuneration of the auditor
Auditor contravening section 139, 144 or 145 knowingly or wilfully with intention to deceive the company, its shareholders, creditors or tax authoritiesProviso to Sec 147(2)Fine of ₹50,000Fine — lower of ₹25,00,000 or 8 times the remuneration; and imprisonment for a term which may extend to 1 year
  • Sec 147(3): an auditor convicted under sub-section (2) shall (a) refund the remuneration received by him to the company, and (b) pay damages to the company, statutory bodies or authorities, or to members or creditors, for loss arising out of incorrect or misleading statements of particulars made in his audit report.
  • Sec 147(4): the Central Government may, by notification, specify any statutory body, authority or officer to ensure prompt payment of damages; such body/authority/officer shall, after payment, file a report with the Central Government in the manner specified in the notification.
  • Sec 147(5) — audit firm: where it is proved that the partner(s) of the audit firm acted in a fraudulent manner or abetted or colluded in any fraud by, in relation to or by the company or its directors or officers, the liability — civil or criminal, under the Companies Act, 2013 or any other law in force — shall be that of the concerned partner(s) and of the firm, jointly and severally. In case of criminal liability of an audit firm, in respect of liability other than fine, only the concerned partner(s) who acted fraudulently or abetted/colluded shall be liable. Since the act constitutes fraud, liability under section 447 also arises.

Cost Records and Cost Audit — Section 148

  • Sec 148(1) + Rule 3 of the Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014: the Central Government may by order direct that particulars relating to the utilisation of material or labour or other items of cost be included in the books of account kept under section 128 by a prescribed class of companies engaged in the production of prescribed goods or provision of prescribed services. Before issuing such an order for a class of companies regulated under a special Act, the Central Government shall consult the regulatory body constituted or established under that special Act.
  • Applicability of cost records: companies (including foreign companies defined in section 2(42)) engaged in the production of goods or providing services specified in Table A (6 Regulated Sectors) and/or Table B (33 Non-Regulated Sectors), having an overall turnover from all its products and services of ₹35 crore or more during the immediately preceding financial year, shall include cost records in their books of account.
  • Rule 3 exclusion: Rule 3 does not apply to a company classified as a micro enterprise or a small enterprise, including as per the turnover criteria under section 7(9) of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006.
  • Sec 148(2) — cost audit: if the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary, it may by order direct that the audit of cost records of the class of companies covered under sub-section (1), and which have a prescribed net worth or prescribed turnover, be conducted in the manner specified in the order. Per Sec 148(4), a cost audit is in addition to the audit conducted under section 143.
  • Board approval: cost statements, including other statements annexed to the cost audit report, shall be approved by the Board of Directors before being signed on behalf of the Board by a director authorised by the Board, for submission to the cost auditor to report thereon.
  • Sec 148(3) — who may be cost auditor: only a Cost Accountant as defined under section 2(28), holding a valid certificate of practice under section 6(1) of the Cost and Works Accountants Act, 1959 and in whole-time practice; includes a firm and an LLP of cost accountants. First proviso: a person appointed under section 139 as auditor of the company shall not be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records. Second proviso: the cost auditor shall comply with the cost auditing standards.
  • Sec 148(5): the qualifications, disqualifications, rights, duties and obligations applicable to the company auditor apply, so far as may be applicable, to the cost auditor; it is the duty of the company to give all assistance and facilities to the cost auditor. The report on the audit of cost records shall be submitted by the cost accountant to the Board of Directors. Section 143(12) and the rules thereunder apply mutatis mutandis to a cost auditor.
  • Sec 148(6): the company shall, within thirty days from the date of receipt of a copy of the cost audit report, furnish the Central Government with such report along with full information and explanation on every reservation or qualification contained therein.
  • Sec 148(7): if, after considering the cost audit report and the information/explanation furnished under sub-section (6), the Central Government is of the opinion that further information or explanation is necessary, it may call for it and the company shall furnish the same within such time as may be specified.
  • Sec 148(8) — default: (a) the company and every officer in default shall be punishable in the manner provided in section 147(1); (b) the cost auditor in default shall be punishable in the manner provided in sub-sections (2) to (4) of section 147.

NFRA and the Auditor — NFRA Rules, 2018

  • Rule 8 — monitoring and enforcing compliance with auditing standards for companies/bodies corporate governed under Rule 3. NFRA may: (a) review working papers (including audit plan and other audit documents) and communications related to the audit; (b) evaluate the sufficiency of the quality control system of the auditor and the manner of its documentation; (c) perform such other testing of the audit, supervisory and quality control procedures as considered necessary or appropriate.
  • NFRA may require: (1) an auditor to report on its governance practices and internal processes designed to promote audit quality, protect its reputation and reduce risks including the risk of failure of the auditor, and may act on that report; (2) additional information, or the personal presence of the auditor, for explanation in connection with the conduct of an audit; (3) send a separate report containing proprietary or confidential information to the Central Government for its information; (4) where NFRA finds or has reason to believe that any law or professional or other standard has or may have been violated, it may decide on further investigation or enforcement action through its concerned Division.
  • NFRA shall: perform monitoring and enforcement through officers or experts with sufficient experience in audit of the relevant industry; and publish its findings relating to non-compliances on its website and in such other manner as it considers fit, unless it has reasons not to do so in the public interest and records those reasons in writing.
  • NFRA shall not publish proprietary or confidential information, unless it has reasons to do so in the public interest and records the reasons in writing.
  • Rule 9 — overseeing quality of services: NFRA may direct an auditor to take measures for improvement of audit quality, including changes in audit processes, quality control and audit reports, and specify a detailed plan with time-limits. It is the auditor's duty to make the improvements and send a report to NFRA explaining compliance. NFRA shall monitor the improvements and take such action as it deems fit. NFRA may refer cases to the Quality Review Board constituted under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, or call for reports/information from that Board, and may take the assistance of experts.
  • Rule 5 — annual return: every auditor of the classes of companies and bodies corporate governed by NFRA shall file a return with NFRA on or before 30th November every year in Form NFRA-2.

Examples

  • Example 1 — Rashail Tech Labs Private Limited (tenure): incorporated during FY 2023-24; first AGM held on 30.09.2024; the company appointed M/s. Rams & Associates, Chartered Accountant firm, for a period of 5 years as subsequent statutory auditor — illustrating that the auditor appointed at the first AGM holds office from the conclusion of that AGM till the conclusion of the 6th AGM.
  • Example 2 — Surya Solar Limited (Board disagrees with Audit Committee): the Audit Committee recommended KPM & Associates, Chartered Accountants, for appointment as statutory auditor to the Board. The Board disagreed. Conclusion: the Board shall refer the recommendation back to the committee for reconsideration, citing reasons for such disagreement.
  • Example 3 — XYZ Ltd. (listed), individual auditor, AGM 29th September 2022: Mr. Raghav holds office from the conclusion of that meeting up to the conclusion of the sixth AGM, i.e. the AGM to be held in 2027. Conclusion: per section 139(2), Mr. Raghav shall not be re-appointed at the 6th AGM (2027).
  • Example 4 — XYZ Ltd. (listed), audit firm, AGM 29th September 2016: M/s Raghav & Associates hold office from the conclusion of that meeting up to the conclusion of the sixth AGM, held in 2021. Conclusion: the firm can be re-appointed for one more term of five years, i.e. up to 2026; it shall not be re-appointed at the 11th AGM (2026).
  • Example 5 — XYZ Ltd., individual, cooling period: Mr. Raghav appointed at the AGM dated 29th September 2016 holds office up to the conclusion of the sixth AGM in 2021. Conclusion: he cannot be re-appointed as auditor in XYZ Ltd. for a further term of five years, i.e. not up to the year 2026.
  • Example 6 — XYZ Ltd., firm, cooling period: M/s Raghav & Associates appointed at the AGM dated 29th September 2016 hold office up to the sixth AGM in 2021 and may be re-appointed for one more term up to 2026. Conclusion: they shall not be re-appointed for a further term of five years after 2026, i.e. from 2026 to 2031.
  • Example 7 — M/s Krishna & Associates / M/s Kukreja & Associates (common partner): M/s Krishna & Associates has 2 partners, Mr. Krishna and Mr. Shyam; Mr. Shyam is also a partner of M/s Kukreja & Associates. M/s Krishna & Associates was appointed auditor of Golden Smith Ltd. for two consecutive periods of 5 years, i.e. from 2016 to 2026. Conclusion: Golden Smith Ltd. cannot appoint M/s Kukreja & Associates, because Mr. Shyam is a common partner between both audit firms. This prohibition lasts 5 years, i.e. up to 2031; after the cooling period of 5 years, Golden Smith Ltd. may appoint either M/s Kukreja & Associates or M/s Krishna & Associates.
  • Example 8 — Dass & Dass Co / Modern Furniture (pre-Act service counts): Dass & Dass Co, a Chartered Accountants firm, was appointed auditor of Modern Furniture since 28th September 2012. Conclusion: the firm can continue to hold office as auditor till the AGM conducted for the financial year 2021-22 — because the period held prior to commencement of the Act is counted towards the ten consecutive years.
  • Example 9 — Prakash Carriers Limited (casual vacancy by resignation): Mr. Raman was appointed auditor at the AGM held on 30th September 2023 and accepted, but resigned on 31st October 2023 for personal reasons. The Board seeks advice on appointing Mr. Albert. Conclusion: as the vacancy arose by resignation, the Board may fill it by appointing Mr. Albert, but that appointment must be approved by the company by an ordinary resolution at a general meeting convened by the Board within 3 months of the Board's recommendation. Mr. Albert holds office till the conclusion of the next AGM.
  • Example 10 — AB Limited (removal of first auditor without CG approval): Mr. Suresh, a Chartered Accountant, was appointed by the Board of AB Limited as First Auditor. The company in general meeting removed him without seeking the approval of the Central Government and appointed Mr. Gupta in his place. Conclusion: the first auditor appointed by the Board can be removed only in accordance with section 140(1); hence the removal is invalid and the company has contravened the Act.
  • Example 11 — SHRD Private Ltd (fee not fixed in engagement letter): the company (software and consultancy) has an annual turnover of ₹2,000 crore but poor profit margins. For FY ended 31st March 2024, appointment of statutory auditors was proposed at the Board meeting but the remuneration was not finalised; the engagement letter was signed without a fee, with a clause that the fee would be mutually decided. Conclusion: in this situation, an engagement letter with such an arrangement is valid — section 142 permits remuneration to be fixed in general meeting or in such manner as the general meeting may determine.
  • Example 12 — MNP Ltd (GST auditor): MNP Ltd., a medium-sized pharmaceuticals company, for the year ended 31st March 2024 is looking to appoint a GST (Goods and Services Tax) auditor, and wants someone already familiar with its business so that lesser effort is required; it has the option of appointing the statutory auditors for this work. Point: GST audit is not among the nine services prohibited by section 144, but any such other service must be approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee before the statutory auditor takes it up.
  • Example 13 — Modern Furniture Limited (notice not served on auditor): MFL convened its general meeting on 21st March 2024 but the notice was not served on the auditor. Conclusion: since the company is obligated under section 146 to forward notice of a general meeting to the auditor, non-service of the notice is a contravention of section 146 and MFL is liable for penalty under section 147.
  • Illustration 1 — Modern Furniture Limited (voluntary audit committee): MFL, though not mandated by section 177 read with the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014, voluntarily constituted an audit committee. That committee recommended to the Board the name of an individual/firm to replace the incumbent auditor on expiry of his term, but the Board did not consider the recommendation. Answer: Rule 6(1) read with Rule 6(2) provides that where an audit committee is not required under section 177 but is constituted by the company, the committee shall still recommend the replacement to the Board, but in such cases the Board may or may not consider the recommendation. Hence the act of the audit committee and the Board at MFL is legally valid.
  • Illustration 2 — Unicorn Steel Private Limited (MCQ, first auditor for 5 years): incorporated on 02.06.2024; the Board held a board meeting on 15.06.2024 to appoint Jain Ajmera & Associates as first auditor for a term of 5 years. Options: (a) Valid; (b) Invalid; (c) Valid after approval of shareholders in general meeting; (d) Valid only after approval of Central Government. Answer — (b) Invalid. Reason: under section 139(6) the first auditor appointed by the Board holds office only until the conclusion of the first AGM, so a 5-year term cannot be given (the Board did meet the 30-day requirement).
  • Illustration 3 — PQR Limited (Managing Director appoints first auditor): the Managing Director of PQR Limited, without consulting the Board, himself appointed Mr. Ganpati, a practising Chartered Accountant, as first auditor. Answer: section 139(6) requires the first auditor to be appointed by the Board of Directors within 30 days from the date of registration; hence the appointment of Mr. Ganpati by the Managing Director himself is invalid for violation of section 139(6).
  • Illustration 4 — MCQ on timing of special resolution for removal: "Special resolution to remove an auditor at general meeting shall be passed within ______ from the approval from Central Government." Options: (a) 30 days; (b) 1 month; (c) 60 days; (d) 3 months. Answer — (c) 60 days. Reason: Rule 7(3) of the Companies (Audit & Auditors) Rules, 2014 states the company shall hold the general meeting within sixty days of receipt of approval of the Central Government for passing the special resolution.
  • Illustration 5 — FLP Ltd (auditors involved in fraud): FLP Ltd., in real estate and energy, defaulted on borrowings amounting to thousands of crore. During the year ended 31st March 2024 a fraud was uncovered in various transactions and the Central Government observed that the auditors were involved. Answer: the Central Government may apply to the Tribunal highlighting that the auditors failed to fulfil their duties. If the Tribunal is satisfied that the auditors were involved in the fraud, it may direct the company to change its auditors; those auditors shall not be eligible to be appointed as auditor of any company for 5 years and are also liable for action under section 447.
  • Illustration 6 — Mr. Anil / Laxman Ltd. (employee joining the audit firm): Mr. Anil, a Chartered Accountant and partner of a firm, was appointed auditor of Laxman Ltd. at the AGM held in September 2023 and accepted. In January 2024 he offered Bharat, another Chartered Accountant who is the Manager Finance of Laxman Ltd., to join Anil's firm as a partner. Answer: section 141(3)(c) disqualifies any person who is a partner or in the employment of an officer or employee of the company; section 141(4) deems an auditor who becomes subject to a section 141(3) disqualification after appointment to have vacated his office. Hence no employee of Laxman Ltd. can become a partner of Anil's firm; if that happens, he/the firm shall be deemed to have vacated the office of auditor of Laxman Limited.
  • Illustration 7 — Mr. Ashish / XYZ Ltd. (auditor holding ₹900 securities): Mr. Ashish, a practising Chartered Accountant, holds securities of XYZ Ltd. of face value ₹900. Answer: under section 141(3)(d)(i) an auditor is disqualified if he or his partner holds any security or interest in the company or its subsidiary, holding or associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company. Mr. Ashish holds ₹900 in XYZ Ltd., therefore he is not eligible for appointment as auditor of XYZ Ltd. (Note: under the Companies Act, 1956 holding securities of par value up to ₹1,000 was not a disqualification; under the Companies Act, 2013 not a single rupee of holding by the auditor is allowed.)
  • Illustration 8 — Mr. P / Mr. Q / ABC Ltd. (relative holding ₹90,000): Mr. Q, the relative of Mr. P (a practising Chartered Accountant), holds securities of ABC Ltd. of face value ₹90,000. Answer: the proviso to section 141(3)(d)(i) permits a relative to hold securities/interest of face value not exceeding ₹1,00,000. ₹90,000 is within the limit, therefore Mr. P will not be disqualified from being appointed as auditor of ABC Ltd.
  • Illustration 9 — BC & Co. / MWF Ltd. (relative of a partner holding ₹1,10,000): BC & Co. is an audit firm with partners Mr. B and Mr. C; Mr. A, a relative of Mr. C, holds securities of MWF Ltd. of face value ₹1,10,000. Answer: the holding exceeds the ₹1,00,000 limit in the proviso to section 141(3)(d)(i), so BC & Co. is disqualified for appointment as auditor of MWF Ltd. — the disqualification of one partner's relative taints the entire firm.
  • Illustration 10 — ABC & Co. (ceiling of 20 audits): ABC & Co. has three partners, Mr. A, Mr. B and Mr. C, holding appointments as auditors in 4, 6 and 10 companies respectively — 20 audits in aggregate. Answer: the limit of 20 company audits under section 141(3)(g) is per person; for a firm of 3 partners the overall ceiling is 3 × 20 = 60 company audits. Audits already taken by all partners in their individual capacity = 4 + 6 + 10 = 20. Remaining audits available to the firm = 60 − 20 = 40. Individually: (i) Mr. A can hold 20 − 4 = 16 more audits; (ii) Mr. B can hold 20 − 6 = 14 more; (iii) Mr. C can hold 20 − 10 = 10 more. Where a Chartered Accountant is a partner in several auditing firms, all the firms in which he is a partner or proprietor are together entitled to only 20 company audits on his account. It is assumed the companies are not one person companies, dormant companies, small companies or private companies having paid-up share capital less than ₹100 crore.
  • Illustration 11 — MNO Ltd. (auditor demanding Directors' Report and MD&A): MNO Ltd., a listed trading company planning to start manufacturing, was audited; the auditors completed all procedures but withheld conclusion pending review of the Directors' report and Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A), which management was not ready with. Answer: the requirement is not valid — the auditor is required to audit the financial statements and express an opinion on them; he does not audit this additional information. The auditor should conclude the work without delaying on account of it.
  • Illustration 12 — NSH Ltd. (fraud first identified by management): NSH Ltd., a retail company listed on the National Stock Exchange, acquired a business undertaking. During the year, transactions amounting to thousands of rupees carried out by employees/directors were found suspicious by management, which appointed a forensic consultant; suspicious transactions were identified and management reported them to the appropriate authorities. These were then made known to the statutory auditors during the audit. Answer: under section 143(12) the auditor must report fraud by officers or employees to the Audit Committee/Board and, where applicable, to the Central Government only if he is the first person to identify/note such instance in the course of his duties. Here management identified the transactions first and informed the auditor. The auditor should therefore report the matter to the Audit Committee/Board of Directors but is not required to report it to the Central Government. The auditors need to report the matter appropriately in their CARO report.
  • Illustration 13 — reading the audit report at the general meeting: Question: must the entire audit report be read before the company in general meeting? Answer: No. Under section 145, only the qualifications, observations or comments on financial transactions or matters which have any adverse effect on the functioning of the company mentioned in the auditor's report shall be read before the company in general meeting and be open to inspection by any member.
  • Illustration 14 — attendance at a general meeting: (i) Is the auditor mandatorily required to attend the general meeting for which notice is served on him? (ii) If yes, must he attend personally? Answer: yes to the first, no to the second — under section 146 the auditor shall, unless otherwise exempted by the company, attend either by himself or through his authorised representative, who shall also be qualified to be an auditor.
  • Illustration 15 — professional LLP as both cost auditor and statutory auditor: Can a professional LLP having CAs and CMAs as partners be appointed as Cost Auditor under section 148 as well as Statutory Independent Auditor under section 139? Answer: No — per the proviso to section 148(3), no person (or firm including an LLP) appointed under section 139 as auditor of the company shall be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records, or vice-versa.

Test Your Knowledge — MCQs

  • MCQ 1 — Birthday Card Limited: a listed company can appoint or re-appoint Mishra & Associates (a firm of Chartered Accountants) as statutory auditors for: (a) one year only; (b) one term of 3 consecutive years only; (c) one term of 4 consecutive years only; (d) two terms of 5 consecutive years. Answer — (d) Two terms of 5 consecutive years.
  • MCQ 2 — tenure from the first AGM: an auditor appointed at the first AGM holds office from the conclusion of that meeting till the conclusion of its: (a) second AGM; (b) fourth AGM; (c) sixth AGM; (d) eighth AGM. Answer — (c) Sixth annual general meeting.
  • MCQ 3 — appointing an auditor other than the retiring auditor: (a) special notice is required; (b) ordinary notice is required; (c) neither ordinary nor special notice is required; (d) approval of Central Government is required. Answer — (a) Special notice is required.

Test Your Knowledge — Descriptive Questions

  • Q1(i) — Board fails to appoint the first auditor within one month of registration: Answer: section 139(6) requires the Board to appoint the first auditor within 30 days of registration; on failure, it shall inform the members, who shall within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting appoint such auditor, and that auditor holds office till the conclusion of the first AGM. Steps: (a) inform the members of the company; (b) immediately take steps to convene an EGM not later than 90 days; (c) members appoint the first auditors at that EGM; (d) the first auditors so appointed hold office up to the conclusion of the first AGM.
  • Q1(ii) — Removal of a statutory auditor (appointed at the last AGM) before expiry of his term: Answer: under section 140(1) removal before expiry of term is only by a special resolution after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government — CG approval is taken first and the special resolution passed thereafter; before any action, the auditor must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Read with Rule 7: the application to the CG shall be in Form ADT-2 with fees under the Companies (Registration Offices and Fees) Rules, 2014; the application shall be made within thirty days of the resolution passed by the Board; and the company shall hold the general meeting within sixty days of receipt of the CG's approval for passing the special resolution.
  • Q2 — AMC Limited (Government of Rajasthan holds one-fourth of subscribed capital): Mr. Neeraj, a Chartered Accountant, was appointed auditor at the AGM held on 30 April 2024 by an ordinary resolution; Mr. Sanjay, a shareholder, objects. Answer: under section 2(45) the holding of 25% of shares by the Government of Rajasthan does not make AMC Ltd. a government company — it is a non-government company. Under section 139 the appointment of an auditor vests generally with the members, except for first auditors and for filling a casual vacancy not caused by resignation (where the Board appoints). Appointment by members is by ordinary resolution only; no exception in the Act requires a special resolution. Hence Mr. Sanjay's contention is not tenable and the appointment is valid.
  • Q3 — EF Limited / Naresh & Company (wife acquires ₹1 lakh face value shares): Naresh & Company, Chartered Accountants, were appointed auditors at the AGM held on 30 September 2023. Mrs. Kamala, wife of Mr. Naresh, invested in equity shares of EF Limited of face value ₹1 lakh on 15 October 2023; the firm continued as statutory auditors. Answer: under section 141(3)(d)(i) a person whose relative or partner holds any security carrying voting rights of the company (or its subsidiary/holding/associate/fellow subsidiary) cannot be appointed auditor, provided a relative may hold security or interest of face value not exceeding ₹1 lakh. Mr. Naresh holds no such security, and Mrs. Kamala's holding of ₹1 lakh face value is within the specified limit. Section 141(4) (deemed vacation on subsequently incurring a disqualification) is therefore not triggered — Naresh & Company can continue to function as auditors even after 15 October 2023.
  • Q4(i) — Government company within the meaning of section 394: Answer: the first auditor is appointed by the CAG within 60 days from the date of incorporation; on failure, the Board appoints within the next 30 days; on the Board's failure, it informs the members, who appoint within 60 days at an EGM; such auditor holds office till the conclusion of the first AGM. For a subsequent auditor of an existing government company, the CAG appoints within 180 days from the commencement of the financial year, and the auditor so appointed holds office till the conclusion of the AGM.
  • Q4(ii) — public company in which XYZ Bank (a nationalised bank) holds 18% of subscribed capital: Answer: since the bank's shareholding is only 18%, it is not a government company, so the non-government company provisions apply: (1) the company shall at the first AGM appoint an individual or firm as auditor to hold office from the conclusion of that meeting till the conclusion of its sixth AGM, and thereafter till the conclusion of every sixth meeting; (2) before appointment, the written consent of the auditor and the prescribed certificate shall be obtained; and the company shall inform the auditor of his appointment and file notice with the Registrar within 15 days of the meeting in which the auditor is appointed.
  • Q5 — Mr. Abhi / Abhiman Ltd. (₹1,000 face value): Mr. Abhi, a practising Chartered Accountant, holds securities of Abhiman Ltd. of face value ₹1,000. Answer: section 141(3)(d)(i) disqualifies an auditor holding any security or interest in the company or its subsidiary/holding/associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company; therefore Mr. Abhi is not eligible for appointment as auditor of Abhiman Ltd.
  • Q6(i) — Mr. Prakash / Mr. Aakash / ABC Ltd.: Mr. Aakash, a relative of Mr. Prakash, holds securities of ABC Ltd. of face value ₹70,000 (market value ₹1,10,000). Answer: the proviso to section 141(3)(d)(i) sets the limit by face value — not exceeding ₹1,00,000. ₹70,000 face value is within the limit, so Mr. Prakash will not be disqualified from being appointed as auditor of ABC Ltd.
  • Q6(ii) — Mr. Ramesh / MNP Ltd. (indebtedness of ₹6 lakh): Answer: under section 141(3)(d)(ii) an auditor is disqualified if he, his relative or his partner is indebted to the company (or its subsidiary/holding/associate/fellow subsidiary) in excess of ₹5 lakh. Mr. Ramesh is indebted to MNP Ltd. for ₹6 lakh, so he will be disqualified from appointment as auditor of MNP Ltd.
  • Q6(iii) — Mr. Kumar / PRC Ltd. (spouse is a store keeper): Mrs. KVJ, spouse of Mr. Kumar, a Chartered Accountant, is the store keeper of PRC Ltd. Answer: section 141(3)(f) disqualifies a person whose relative is a director or is in the employment of the company as a director or key managerial personnel. A store keeper is neither a director nor a KMP; hence Mr. Kumar will not be disqualified from being appointed auditor of PRC Ltd.
  • Q7 — A Limited (statutory auditor asked to design and implement a financial information system): the Board of A Limited requested its statutory auditor to accept the assignment of designing and implementing a suitable financial information system to strengthen the internal control mechanism. Answer: under section 144 an auditor may provide only such other services as are approved by the Board or audit committee, but such services shall not include design and implementation of any financial information system — the service is strictly prohibited. If the statutory auditor accepts the assignment, he will attract the penal provisions of section 147. The auditor should therefore be advised not to take up the assignment.

Why It Matters / Application

These sections decide whether a specific appointment, removal or engagement stands up. The tenure clock (conclusion of AGM to conclusion of the 6th AGM), the 5-year/10-year rotation ceilings with a 5-year cooling-off, and the transitional tables in Rule 6 determine, on given AGM dates and years of past service, exactly which year an auditor must retire and which year he may return — as computed in Examples 3 to 8. The disqualification list in section 141(3) is a live test to apply on facts: a single rupee of the auditor's own shareholding disqualifies (Illustrations 7 and Q5), a relative's holding is measured by face value against ₹1,00,000 with a 60-day correction window (Illustrations 8, 9 and Q3, Q6(i)), indebtedness bites above ₹5 lakh (Q6(ii)), guarantees above ₹1 lakh bite, and "relative" for the director/KMP bar does not extend to a store keeper (Q6(iii)). The 20-audit ceiling multiplies by partner and is netted against existing appointments (Illustration 10). Section 144 tells a firm which engagements it must decline (Q7 — designing a financial information system), and the proviso to section 148(3) keeps the statutory audit and the cost audit in different hands (Illustration 15). Section 143(12) settles the practical question of whether a suspicious transaction must go to the Central Government in Form ADT-4 or only to the Audit Committee (Illustration 12), and section 147 attaches specific rupee consequences — including refund of remuneration and joint and several firm liability — to getting any of it wrong.

Note

  • Order of steps in removal is an exam trap: Central Government approval comes first, then the special resolution (Basant Ram & Sons v Union of India). Application to CG in Form ADT-2 within 30 days of the Board resolution; general meeting within 60 days of receipt of CG approval.
  • Two different 30-day/60-day clocks: Board appoints the first auditor of a non-Government company within 30 days of registration (members within 90 days at an EGM on the Board's failure); the CAG appoints the first auditor of a Government company within 60 days (Board within the next 30 days, then members within 60 days at an EGM). Do not swap them.
  • A first auditor cannot be given a five-year term — he holds office only till the conclusion of the first AGM (Illustration 2), and only the Board (not the Managing Director) may appoint him (Illustration 3).
  • Casual vacancy caused by resignation requires the Board's appointment to be additionally approved by the members at a general meeting within 3 months of the Board's recommendation — a plain casual vacancy does not.
  • Rotation does not apply to every company — one person companies and small companies are excluded, and the private-company trigger is paid-up capital of ₹50 crore or more (unlisted public: ₹10 crore; borrowings/deposits: ₹50 crore).
  • Relative's securities limit is on FACE VALUE, not market value — ₹70,000 face value with ₹1,10,000 market value is within the limit (Q6(i)). Contrast: the auditor's or his partner's own holding has a nil tolerance (Illustration 7 — ₹900; Q5 — ₹1,000). Under the Companies Act, 1956 par value up to ₹1,000 was permitted; that concession is gone.
  • Aggregate the relatives: Rule 10(1) is read reasonably — the holdings of all relatives together are tested against ₹1,00,000, and a breach by the relative of even one partner disqualifies the whole firm.
  • The 20-audit ceiling excludes one person companies, small companies and private companies with paid-up share capital less than ₹100 crore — but only where the private company has not defaulted in filing under section 137 or section 92.
  • Sec 143(3)(i) internal financial controls reporting is switched off for a private company that is an OPC or small company, or whose turnover is less than ₹50 crore and aggregate borrowings from banks/FIs/any body corporate at any point during the year are less than ₹25 crore — subject to no default under section 137 or section 92.
  • Fraud reporting turns on who found it first: section 143(12) is triggered only if the auditor is the first person to identify the fraud in the course of his duties; if management identified and reported it, the auditor reports to the Audit Committee/Board only, plus appropriate CARO reporting (Illustration 12).
  • Amendment: clauses (e) and (f) of Rule 13(2) were omitted with effect from 14th July 2025 vide the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Amendment Rules, 2025 [G.S.R. 359(E)].
  • Deemed CG approval for IFSC companies only: the 60-day deemed-approval rule on removal applies only to Specified IFSC public companies (GSR 08(E) dated 04.01.2017) and Specified IFSC private companies (GSR 09(E) dated 04.01.2017).
  • Only the qualifications/adverse observations are read out at the general meeting under section 145 — not the entire audit report (Illustration 13). And attendance under section 146 may be by an authorised representative who is himself qualified to be an auditor (Illustration 14).
  • Penalty caps under section 147(2) are "whichever is less" — ₹5,00,000 or 4 times remuneration for ordinary contravention; ₹25,00,000 or 8 times remuneration plus imprisonment up to 1 year where the contravention is knowing or wilful with intent to deceive.
  • Cost records apply from ₹35 crore overall turnover of all products and services in the immediately preceding financial year (Table A — 6 regulated sectors; Table B — 33 non-regulated sectors), and Rule 3 does not apply to a micro or small enterprise under section 7(9) of the MSMED Act, 2006.
  • NFRA annual return in Form NFRA-2 is due on or before 30th November every year; particulars of auditor appointment go in Form NFRA-1 within 15 days of appointment.

Chapter 11 — Companies Incorporated Outside India

Source: 87780bos-aps2160-ch11.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Scope of the chapter: Chapter XXII of the Companies Act, 2013 comprises sections 379 to 393A, read with the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014. It does not incorporate a foreign company in India — it regulates the Indian business operations of a body corporate already incorporated abroad.
  • Two-limb test for a foreign company [Sec 2(42)]: The entity must (a) be incorporated outside India, (b) have a place of business in India — by itself, through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, and (c) conduct any business activity in India in any other manner. Incorporation abroad alone is not enough, and a place of business alone is not enough; business activity in India must also exist.
  • Electronic mode makes physical presence unnecessary: Because "place of business" extends to electronic mode, a company with no branch, office or employee in India can still be a foreign company if it sells or services Indian customers online. The Rules expressly say this applies whether the main server is installed in India or not.
  • The 50% control test [Sec 379(2)]: Sections 380–386, 392 and 393 apply to every foreign company. But where not less than 50% of the paid-up share capital (equity, preference, or partly both) of the foreign company is held by Indians/Indian bodies corporate, the company must additionally comply with Chapter XXII and such other provisions of the Act as may be prescribed, in respect of its Indian business, as if it were a company incorporated in India — an "Indian-owned foreign company" is treated far more like a domestic company.
  • Registrar-centric compliance: All filings under this chapter go to the Registrar having jurisdiction over New Delhi (Form FC-1 to the Registrar, Central Registration Centre), irrespective of where in India the place of business actually is.
  • Default does not void contracts, but disarms the company [Sec 393]: Non-compliance leaves contracts valid and the company suable, yet strips the company of the right to sue, set off or counter-claim until it complies. Compliance is the price of access to Indian courts.

Key Definitions / Terms

Foreign company [Section 2(42)]
Any company or body corporate incorporated outside India which (a) has a place of business in India whether by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode; and (b) conducts any business activity in India in any other manner.
Electronic mode [Rule 2(1)(h), Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, 2014]
Carrying out electronically based transactions, whether the main server is installed in India or not, including but not limited to: (a) business-to-business and business-to-consumer transactions, data interchange and other digital supply transactions; (b) offering to accept deposits, inviting or accepting deposits or subscriptions in securities, in India or from citizens of India; (c) financial settlements, web based marketing, advisory and transactional services, database services and products, supply chain management; (d) online services such as telemarketing, telecommuting, telemedicine, education and information research; and (e) all related data communication services — whether conducted by e-mail, mobile devices, social media, cloud computing, document management, voice or data transmission or otherwise.
Explanation to "electronic mode" — IFSC carve-out
Electronic based offering of securities, subscription thereof, or listing of securities in the International Financial Services Centres set up under section 18 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 shall not be construed as "electronic mode" for the purposes of clause (42) of section 2.
Certified [Section 386(a)]
Certified in the prescribed manner to be a true copy or a correct translation.
Director, in relation to a foreign company [Section 386(b)]
Includes any person in accordance with whose directions or instructions the Board of Directors of the company is accustomed to act.
Place of business [Section 386(c)]
Includes a share transfer or registration office.
Indian Depository Receipt (IDR) [Rule 13, Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014]
Any instrument in the form of a depository receipt created by a Domestic Depository in India and authorised by a company incorporated outside India making an issue of such depository receipts.
Financial year (proviso relevant to foreign groups)
The period ending on the 31st day of March every year; where incorporated on or after the 1st day of January of a year, the period ending on 31st March of the following year. Proviso: where a company is a holding/subsidiary/associate of a company incorporated outside India and must follow a different financial year for consolidation abroad, the Central Government may, on application, allow any period as its financial year, whether or not that period is a year. Further proviso: applications pending before the Tribunal as on commencement of the Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 2018 shall be disposed of by the Tribunal under the pre-amendment provisions.
Foreign company for merger purposes [Explanation to Section 234(2)]
Any company or body corporate incorporated outside India whether having a place of business in India or not — a wider meaning than section 2(42).

How It Works / Logic

  • Sec 379(1) — baseline applicability: Sections 380 to 386 (both inclusive) and sections 392 and 393 apply to all foreign companies falling within section 2(42).
  • Sec 379(2) — the 50% test: Holding of not less than 50% of paid-up capital by (i) one or more citizens of India; or (ii) one or more companies/bodies corporate incorporated in India; or (iii) a combination of both — whether singly or in the aggregate — triggers full Chapter XXII compliance plus other prescribed provisions for the Indian business.
  • Sec 380(1) — first filing: Within 30 days of establishment of its place of business in India, deliver to the Registrar for registration: (a) certified copy of the charter, statutes or memorandum and articles or other constituting instrument (with certified English translation if not in English); (b) full address of the registered or principal office; (c) list of directors and secretary with prescribed particulars; (d) name(s) and address(es) of one or more persons resident in India authorised to accept service of process, notices and documents; (e) full address of the office in India deemed to be its principal place of business in India; (f) particulars of opening and closing of a place of business in India on earlier occasion(s); (g) a declaration that none of the directors or the authorised representative in India has ever been convicted or debarred from formation of companies and management in India or abroad; and (h) any other prescribed information.
  • Rule 3 particulars for each director/secretary (14 items): (1) personal name and surname in full; (2) any former name(s) and surname(s) in full; (3) father's name or mother's name or spouse's name; (4) date of birth; (5) residential address; (6) nationality; (7) nationality of origin, if different from present nationality; (8) passport number, date of issue and country of issue (details of all passports if more than one is held); (9) income-tax PAN, if applicable; (10) occupation, if any; (11) whether directorship in any other Indian company — DIN, Name and CIN of that company; (12) other directorship(s) held; (13) Membership Number (for Secretary only); and (14) e-mail ID.
  • Form and support documents: The information is filed in Form FC-1 with the Registrar, Central Registration Centre within 30 days, with prescribed fees, plus an attested copy of RBI approval under FEMA/Regulations and from any other regulator — or a declaration from the authorised representative that no such approval is required.
  • Rule 8 — where documents go: Any document a foreign company must deliver to the Registrar shall be delivered to the Registrar having jurisdiction over New Delhi; documents for registration under sub-rule (3) of rule 3 go in Form FC-1 to the Registrar, Central Registration Centre. Fees under Rule 12 of the Companies (Registration Offices and Fees) Rules, 2014.
  • Ceasing business: If a foreign company ceases to have a place of business in India, it shall forthwith notify the Registrar; from the date of that notice the obligation to deliver documents ceases — provided it has no other place of business in India.
  • Sec 380(2) — transitional: A foreign company existing at the commencement of the 2013 Act which had not delivered the documents and particulars specified in section 592(1) of the Companies Act, 1956 continues to be under the obligation to deliver them in accordance with the Companies Act, 1956.
  • Sec 380(3) — alterations: Any alteration made or occurring in the documents delivered under section 380 must be reported by a return of particulars of the alteration within 30 days, filed in Form FC-2 with prescribed fees.
  • Sec 381(1) — accounts: In every calendar year, make out a balance sheet and profit and loss account in the prescribed form with prescribed annexures, and deliver a copy to the Registrar. Rule 4 requires financial statements of the Indian business operations prepared as per Schedule III or as near thereto as possible, with (1) annexures per Chapter IX (Accounts of Companies), and (2) copies of the latest consolidated financial statements of the parent foreign company as submitted to the prescribed authority in its country of incorporation.
  • Sec 381(1) power to exempt: The Central Government may direct by notification that clause (a) shall not apply, or shall apply with specified exceptions and modifications, to any foreign company or class of foreign companies.
  • Sec 381(2): Any of the specified documents not in English must have a certified English translation annexed.
  • Sec 381(3) / Rule 6: Along with the financial statement, file Form FC-3 with fee — a list of all places of business established by the foreign company in India as on the date of the balance sheet.
  • Rule 4 attachments and the 6-month deadline: Attach to the financial statement (1) Statement of related party transaction, (2) Statement of repatriation of profits, (3) Statement of transfer of funds (including dividends, if any). All these documents must reach the Registrar within 6 months of the close of the financial year of the foreign company; the Registrar may, for any special reason and on written application by the foreign company, extend that period by not exceeding three months.
  • Rule 5 — audit: Accounts pertaining to Indian business operations prepared under section 381(1) must be audited by a practising Chartered Accountant in India, or a firm or LLP of practising chartered accountants. Chapter X (Audit and Auditors) and its rules apply mutatis mutandis.
  • Sec 382 — display of name: (a) Conspicuously exhibit outside every office/place of business in India the company's name and country of incorporation in easily legible English characters and also in the characters of a language in general use in that locality; (b) state the name and country of incorporation in legible English characters on all business letters, bill-heads, letter paper, notices and other official publications; (c) if members' liability is limited, state that fact in every prospectus and all business letters, bill-heads, letter paper, notices, advertisements and other official publications in legible English characters, and exhibit it conspicuously outside every office/place in India in English and in the local language characters.
  • Sec 383 — service: Any process, notice or document is deemed sufficiently served if addressed to a person whose name and address were delivered to the Registrar under section 380, and left at or sent by post to that delivered address, or by electronic mode.
  • Sec 384 — cross-applied provisions: Section 71 (issue of debentures) applies mutatis mutandis; section 92 (annual return) applies subject to prescribed exceptions, modifications and adaptations; section 128 applies to the extent of requiring books of account with respect to monies received and spent, sales and purchases made, and assets and liabilities in the course of or in relation to its business in India, to be kept at its principal place of business in India; Chapter VI (Registration of Charges) applies mutatis mutandis to charges on properties created or acquired by a foreign company; Chapter XIV (Inspection, inquiry and investigation) applies mutatis mutandis to the Indian business. Also, under Rule 3 of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014, a foreign company meeting the section 135(1) criteria must comply with section 135.
  • Rule 7 — annual return: Every foreign company shall prepare and file an annual return in Form FC-4 with prescribed fees within 60 days from the last day of its financial year, containing particulars as they stood at the close of the financial year.
  • Sec 385 / Rule 8 — fee: Fee for registering any document required to be registered under this Chapter is as prescribed in the Companies (Registration Offices and Fees) Rules, 2014.
  • Sec 387 — dating and contents of prospectus: No person shall issue, circulate or distribute in India any prospectus offering to subscribe for securities of a company incorporated or to be incorporated outside India — whether or not it has or will establish a place of business in India — unless the prospectus is dated and signed and contains particulars of: (1) the instrument constituting/defining the constitution of the company; (2) the enactments or provisions under which incorporation was effected; (3) an address in India where that instrument/enactments (or certified English translation) can be inspected; (4) the date on which and the country in which the company was or would be incorporated; (5) whether it has established a place of business in India and, if so, the address of its principal office in India; and states the matters specified under section 26. Proviso: items (1), (2) and (3) do not apply to a prospectus issued more than 2 years after the date the company became entitled to commence business.
  • Sec 387(2) — no waiver: Any condition requiring or binding an applicant for securities to waive compliance with section 387(1), or purporting to impute to him notice of any contract, document or matter not specifically referred to in the prospectus, is void. Section 387(2) grants no exception to a person responsible for issuing or circulating the prospectus for non-compliance with section 387(1).
  • Sec 387(3) — application forms: No application form for securities of such a company may be issued in India unless issued with a prospectus complying with Chapter XXII and not contravening section 388. Exception: where the form was issued in connection with a bona fide invitation to enter into an underwriting agreement in respect of the securities.
  • Sec 387(4) — carve-outs: Section 387 does not apply to (a) the issue, to existing members or debenture holders, of a prospectus or application form relating to the company's securities, whether or not the applicant has a right of renunciation in favour of others; and (b) except so far as it requires a prospectus to be dated, to a prospectus relating to securities uniform in all respects with securities previously issued and for the time being dealt in or quoted on a recognised stock exchange. Subject to that, section 387 applies whether the prospectus/form is issued on or with reference to the formation of the company or subsequently. Section 387 does not limit or diminish any liability incurred under any other law in force in India or under the Act apart from section 387.
  • Sec 388 — expert's consent and allotment: No prospectus offering securities of a company incorporated or to be incorporated outside India may be issued, circulated or distributed in India if (a) it includes a statement purporting to be made by an expert who has not given, or has withdrawn before delivery of the prospectus for registration, his written consent to the issue of the prospectus with the statement in the form and context in which it appears, or the prospectus does not state that he has given and has not withdrawn such consent; or (b) the prospectus does not have the effect, where an application is made under it, of rendering all persons concerned bound by section 33 (issue of application forms for securities) and section 40 (securities to be dealt with in stock exchanges) so far as applicable. A statement is deemed included in a prospectus if contained in any report or memorandum appearing on its face, or incorporated therein by reference, or issued therewith.
  • Sec 389 — registration of prospectus: Before issue, circulation or distribution in India: (i) a copy certified by the chairperson and two other directors as approved by resolution of the managing body must be delivered to the Registrar for registration; (ii) the prospectus must state on its face that a copy has been so delivered; and (iii) any consent required by section 388 and the prescribed documents must be endorsed on or attached to the copy.
  • Rule 11 — documents annexed to the prospectus: (a) any consent to the issue of the prospectus required from any person as an expert; (b) a copy of contracts for appointment of managing director or manager, and where the contract is not in writing, a memorandum giving full particulars; (c) a copy of any other material contracts not entered into in the ordinary course of business but entered into within the preceding 2 years; (d) a copy of the underwriting agreement; and (e) a copy of the power of attorney, if the prospectus is signed through a duly authorised agent of directors.
  • Sec 390 — IDRs: Notwithstanding anything in any other law, the Central Government may make rules for (i) the offer of IDRs; (ii) disclosure requirements in the prospectus or letter of offer issued in connection with IDRs; (iii) the manner of dealing with IDRs in depository mode and by custodian and underwriters; and (iv) the manner of sale, transfer or transmission of IDRs. Under Rule 13, no such company may issue IDRs unless it complies with that rule in addition to the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2009 and any RBI directions.
  • Sec 391 — mis-statement and winding up: Sections 34 (criminal liability for mis-statements in prospectus), 35 (civil liability for mis-statement) and 36 (punishment for fraudulently inducing persons to invest money) apply to (i) the issue of a prospectus by a company incorporated outside India under section 389 as they apply to an Indian company's prospectus, and (ii) the issue of IDRs by a foreign company. Under section 391(2), subject to section 376 (power to wind up foreign companies although dissolved), Chapter XX (Winding up) applies mutatis mutandis to closure of the foreign company's place of business in India as if it were an Indian company, where it has raised monies through offer or issue of securities under this Chapter which have not been repaid or redeemed.
  • Sec 234 — cross-border mergers: Section 234(1) applies Chapter XV (Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations) mutatis mutandis to schemes of merger and amalgamation between companies registered under the Act and companies incorporated in jurisdictions notified from time to time by the Central Government; the Central Government may make rules in consultation with the RBI. Section 234(2) permits a foreign company, with prior approval of the RBI, to merge into a company registered under the Act or vice versa, with consideration to shareholders of the merging company payable in cash, or in Depository Receipts, or partly in cash and partly in Depository Receipts.
  • Rule 12 — improper use of the description: Any person(s) trading or carrying on business under any name, title or description as a foreign company registered under the Act or rules, without being duly registered as a foreign company, shall be liable for investigation under section 210 and consequent action.
  • Exemption power (IFSC): The Central Government may, by notification, exempt any class of (a) foreign companies, and (b) companies incorporated or to be incorporated outside India, whether or not they have or will establish a place of business in India, in so far as the provisions relate to offering for subscription in securities, prospectus requirements and all incidental matters in International Financial Services Centres set up under section 18 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005.
