Punishment [Section 392]

Without prejudice to section 391, if a foreign company contravenes the provisions of Chapter XXII:

Person in defaultFine — minimumFine — maximumContinuing offence
Foreign company₹1,00,000₹3,00,000Additional fine which may extend to ₹50,000 for every day after the first during which the contravention continues
Every officer of the foreign company who is in default₹25,000₹5,00,000—

Examples

  • Example 1 — foreign subsidiary of an Indian company: ABC Entertainment Limited (an Indian company) has a foreign subsidiary, UVW Limited, which renders satellite services to the group. UVW Limited will be covered under the definition of Foreign Company under the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Example 2 — airlines with booking agents: Airline companies which operate through their booking agents in India will be covered under the definition of Foreign Company under the Companies Act, 2013 (the agent constitutes the place of business).
  • Example 3 — Zakpak Ltd. branch office: Zakpak Ltd. is a shipping company incorporated in Japan which has set up a branch office in India after obtaining necessary approvals from the RBI. Branch offices are generally treated as a reflection of the parent company's office. Therefore, the branch office of a company incorporated outside India is a place of business for conducting business activity in India, and Zakpak Ltd. must follow the provisions of this chapter and such other provisions as may be specified elsewhere under the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Example 4 — Emaar Company LLC (the Section 379(2) control test): Emaar Company LLC is incorporated in Dubai and has a place of business in India. Its shareholding is: (1) Hinduja Company Limited (Indian company) — 26%; (2) Vaishali Company Limited (Indian company) — 25%; (3) Citizens of Dubai — remaining holding. Conclusion: 26% + 25% = 51%, i.e. not less than 50% is held in the aggregate by bodies corporate incorporated in India. Under section 379(2), Emaar Company LLC must therefore also comply with Chapter XXII and such other provisions of the Act as may be prescribed with regard to the business carried on by its place of business in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India.
  • Example 5 — ROK Limited's financial year: ROK Limited is a company incorporated outside India with a place of business in India, and is a subsidiary of HOK Limited (holding company) registered in Australia, with which it must consolidate its accounts. If HOK Limited follows a financial year other than one ending on the 31st day of March, ROK Limited can apply to the Central Government to follow the same financial year as HOK Limited.
  • Example 6 — Mukesh & Jordan LLC filings: Mukesh & Jordan LLC is a foreign company and must file its financial statements with the Registrar within six months of the close of the financial year on an annual basis, along with (1) Statement of related party transaction, (2) Statement of repatriation of profits, and (3) Statement of transfer of funds (including dividends, if any). However, where the Central Government has exempted or specified different documents for any foreign company or class of foreign companies, the documents so specified shall be submitted.
  • Example 7 — Mir Company LLC and the 2-year proviso: Mir Company LLC was incorporated in Dubai on 28th April 2019 and established a place of business in Mumbai in 2022. The place of business in India now proposes to offer subscription to securities of Mir Company LLC. Before proceeding, it must file a prospectus that is dated and signed; but the prospectus need not contain the particulars in points (1), (2) and (3) of section 387(1)(a) — the constituting instrument, the enactments of incorporation, and the Indian inspection address — because the prospectus is being issued more than 2 years after Mir Company LLC became entitled to commence business.
  • Illustration 1 — Search & Find Pte. Ltd. (e-commerce, no office in India): Search & Find Pte. Ltd. is incorporated in Singapore and sells its goods through electronic mode on e-commerce platforms in India, but has no branch or office in India. Is it required to submit documents under section 380? Answer: Yes. Under section 2(42), a body corporate incorporated outside India which has a place of business in India by itself, through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, and conducts any business activity in India, is a foreign company. Since Search & Find Pte. Ltd. conducts business through electronic mode, it is a foreign company and must submit the documents mentioned under section 380 of the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Illustration 2(i) — share registration office at Mumbai: A company incorporated outside India having a share registration office at Mumbai. Answer: Under section 386(c), "place of business" includes a share transfer or registration office. Hence such a company will be treated as a foreign company, provided it conducts any business activity in India.
  • Illustration 2(ii) — Indian citizens incorporating in Singapore: Indian citizens incorporated a company in Singapore for the purpose of carrying on business there. Answer: It does not fall within the definition of a foreign company. Its incorporation outside India by Indian citizens is immaterial; to be a foreign company it must have a place of business in India and must also conduct a business activity in India. (The four features required are: incorporated outside India; a place of business in India; that place of business being in its own name, through an agent or through electronic mode; and conducting a business activity of any nature in India.)
  • Statistical fact: Union Minister of State for Corporate Affairs Shri Rao Inderjit Singh, in a written reply in the Rajya Sabha, stated that 320 foreign companies were registered in India between 2018 and 2021 (Press release dated July 27, 2021, Press Information Bureau, Delhi).
  • IDR fact: Standard Chartered PLC was the first global company to file for an issue of IDRs in India, in 2010.

Test Your Knowledge — MCQs

  • MCQ 1 — Jackson Communications LLC: Incorporated in Arizona, USA, it has established a principal place of business at Kolkata, West Bengal and must deliver the requisite documents. Options offered: 10 days / 15 days / 30 days / 45 days. Answer: (c) — within 30 days of the establishment of a principal place of business in India, it shall deliver the requisite documents to the specified authority.
  • MCQ 2 — Morgen Stern Digi Cables GmbH: Incorporated in Berlin, Germany, it established a place of business at Mumbai for data interchange and other digital supply transactions online, and failed to deliver certain documents to the jurisdictional Registrar within the prescribed time. Answer: (d) — punishable with fine not less than ₹1,00,000 but which may extend to ₹3,00,000, and in the case of a continuing offence, an additional fine up to ₹50,000 for every day after the first during which the contravention continues. (Options (a) ₹50,000–₹5,00,000 with ₹25,000/day, (b) ₹1,00,000–₹5,00,000 with ₹20,000/day, and (c) ₹2,00,000–₹5,00,000 with ₹50,000/day are wrong.)
  • MCQ 3 — Radix Healthcare Ltd.: Registered in Thailand, with no place of business established in India, but engaged in online business through remote delivery of healthcare services in India. Identify the incorrect statement. Answer: (a) — "Radix Healthcare Ltd. is not a foreign company as it has no place of business established in India" is the incorrect statement. It is a foreign company: telemedicine is expressly within "electronic mode", so it has a place of business in India through electronic mode and conducts business activity in India.
  • MCQ 4 — 5K Cosmetic Shop plc.: Incorporated in Switzerland, involved in digital supply services through electronic mode with its server located outside India, and following the calendar year as its financial year; it must annually prepare a balance sheet and profit and loss account. Timeline for filing with the Registrar? Options: 30 days / 3 months / 60 days / 6 months. Answer: (d) — within a period of 6 months from the close of the financial year of 5K Cosmetic Shop plc.

Test Your Knowledge — Descriptive Questions

  • Q1(i) — ABC Ltd., Kolkata (where to file): ABC Ltd. is a foreign company with its Indian principal place of business at Kolkata, West Bengal. Answer: Section 380 requires delivery of the specified documents to the Registrar for registration within 30 days of establishment of the office in India, and under the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules, 2014, any document which any foreign company must deliver to the Registrar shall be delivered to the Registrar having jurisdiction over New Delhi — not the Kolkata Registrar.
  • Q1(ii) — penalty for non-delivery: Chapter XXII comprises sections 379 to 393. Penalties for non-filing or contravention, including non-filing of documents required by section 380, are in section 392: the foreign company is punishable with a fine not less than ₹1,00,000 but which may extend to ₹3,00,000, with an additional fine which may extend to ₹50,000 for every day after the first during which a continuing offence continues, and every officer of the foreign company in default is punishable with a fine not less than ₹25,000 but which may extend to ₹5,00,000.
  • Q2 — DEJY Company Limited (Singapore) branch office at Mumbai: A practising Chartered Accountant is appointed liaison officer. (i) Yes — a branch office is generally a reflection of the parent company's office, so the branch office of a company incorporated outside India is a place of business for conducting business activity in India, and the company falls under section 2(42). (ii) Under section 380(1), within 30 days of establishment of the place of business, deliver to the Registrar: certified copy of the charter/statutes/MOA and AOA or other constituting instrument (with certified English translation if not in English); full address of the registered or principal office; a list of directors and secretary with the 14 prescribed particulars (name and surname in full; former names; father's/mother's/spouse's name; date of birth; residential address; nationality; nationality of origin if different; passport number, date and country of issue for all passports held; PAN if applicable; occupation if any; whether directorship in any other Indian company with DIN, name and CIN; other directorships; Membership Number for Secretary only; and e-mail ID); name(s) and address(es) of person(s) resident in India authorised to accept service of process and notices; full address of the office in India deemed the principal place of business; particulars of earlier opening and closing of a place of business in India; a declaration that no director or the authorised representative in India has been convicted or debarred from formation of companies and management in India or abroad; and any other prescribed information. These are delivered to the Registrar having jurisdiction over New Delhi.
  • Q3 — Galilio Ltd. (Germany) with a place of business in Mumbai: Under section 381, in every calendar year it must make out a balance sheet and profit and loss account in the prescribed form and deliver a copy to the Registrar; under the Rules, prepare financial statements of its Indian business operations as per Schedule III or as near thereto as possible, annexing documents in accordance with Chapter IX and copies of the latest consolidated financial statements of the parent foreign company as submitted in its country of incorporation. The Central Government may exempt or modify the section 381(1)(a) requirement for any foreign company or class of companies. Documents not in English need a certified English translation annexed [Sec 381(2)]. It must also send a list of all places of business established in India as at the balance sheet date, filed in Form FC-3 with fee. If it ceases to have a place of business in India it must forthwith notify the Registrar, whereupon the delivery obligation ceases if it has no other place of business in India. Attachments to the financial statement: statement of related party transaction, statement of repatriation of profits, and statement of transfer of funds (including dividends, if any) — all to be delivered within 6 months of the close of the financial year.
  • Q4(i) — Red Stone Limited (Singapore), board meetings in India: Red Stone Limited is registered in Singapore and its Board meets and executes business decisions in India. Answer: It has no place of business in India by itself, through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, and conducts no business activity in India in any other manner. Mere holding of board meetings and executing business decisions in India cannot be termed as conducting business activity in India. Hence Red Stone Limited is not a foreign company.
  • Q4(ii) — Xen Limited Liability Company (Dubai), cloud computing: Xen LLC is registered in Dubai and has installed its main server in Dubai for maintaining office automation software by cloud computing for its clients in India. Answer: Since "electronic mode" applies whether or not the main server is installed in India, and cloud computing is expressly covered, Xen LLC has a place of business in India through electronic mode and conducts business activity in India. Hence Xen Limited Liability Company is a foreign company under the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Q5 — Abroad Ltd. (no place of business in India) issuing a prospectus: Under section 389, no person shall issue, circulate or distribute in India any prospectus offering for subscription in securities of a company incorporated or to be incorporated outside India — whether or not it has established or will establish a place of business in India — unless, before the issue, circulation or distribution: a copy certified by the chairperson and two other directors as having been approved by resolution of the managing body is delivered to the Registrar for registration; the prospectus states on its face that a copy has been so delivered; and any consent to the issue required by section 388, together with the documents prescribed under Rule 11, is endorsed on or attached to the copy. Abroad Ltd. must proceed with its issue in compliance with these provisions.
  • Q6 — Jackson & Jackson LLC (Germany), documents in German: The company proposes to establish a business in Mumbai and its official documents are in German. Answer: Under section 380 it must deliver the documents to the Registrar within 30 days of establishing its place of business in India; where the original instruments/documents are not in the English language, a certified translation in the English language is required and must be submitted to the Registrar. It cannot file in German alone.
  • Q7 — Swift Pharmaceuticals (Singapore), shift of principal office: The company registered in Singapore started business in India in the financial year 2016 and had submitted all required documents within the due date. On March 1, 2024 it shifted its principal office in Singapore. Answer: Section 380(3) requires that where any alteration is made or occurs in the documents delivered under section 380, the foreign company shall, within 30 days of such alteration, deliver a return of the particulars of the alteration to the Registrar in Form FC-2 with prescribed fees. Accordingly, Swift Pharmaceuticals must submit the full address of its new registered or principal office by March 30, 2024.

Why It Matters / Application

Chapter XXII is what converts an offshore incorporation into an Indian-regulated presence. For a CA advising an inbound client, the practical chain is: first decide whether the client is even a foreign company under section 2(42) — and the modern trap is that a purely digital seller with servers abroad and no Indian office (Search & Find Pte. Ltd., Radix Healthcare Ltd., Xen LLC) still qualifies, while a Singapore company whose only Indian nexus is board meetings (Red Stone Limited) does not. Next, apply the section 379(2) 50% test, because Indian shareholding of 51% (as with Emaar Company LLC) pulls the entity into compliance "as if it were a company incorporated in India". Then run the calendar: Form FC-1 within 30 days of setting up, Form FC-2 within 30 days of any alteration (Swift Pharmaceuticals' office shift), Form FC-4 within 60 days of the financial year end, and financial statements plus FC-3 and the three statements (related party transactions, repatriation of profits, transfer of funds) within 6 months of the year end, extendable by up to 3 months. Note that all of it goes to the Registrar having jurisdiction over New Delhi, whatever the client's Indian address. On the capital-raising side, sections 387–389 govern any prospectus offering foreign securities in India, section 391 attaches sections 34, 35 and 36 liability for mis-statements including in IDR issues, and section 234 with prior RBI approval governs cross-border mergers with consideration in cash or Depository Receipts.

Note

  • The 2-year proviso to section 387(1): Only points (1), (2) and (3) of clause (a) — constituting instrument, incorporating enactments, Indian inspection address — drop away where the prospectus is issued more than 2 years after entitlement to commence business. The date and signature requirement, points (4) and (5), and the section 26 matters continue to apply.
  • Section 387(4)(b) never removes the dating requirement: Even for securities uniform in all respects with previously issued securities dealt in or quoted on a recognised stock exchange, the prospectus must still be dated.
  • Underwriting exception: Section 387(3) does not bite where the application form was issued in connection with a bona fide invitation to enter into an underwriting agreement.
  • Exam trap on financial year: A foreign company with a place of business in India need not follow a 31st March year end — but only if it has obtained the requisite Central Government approval under the proviso to the definition (as in ROK Limited / HOK Limited). Note that section 381(1) speaks of "every calendar year" while the Rules speak of the financial year, and the 6-month filing deadline runs from the close of the financial year.
  • Two deadlines that are commonly swapped: annual return in Form FC-4 within 60 days of the last day of the financial year, versus financial statements within 6 months of its close (MCQ 4 tests exactly this).
  • Extension is discretionary and capped: the Registrar may extend the 6-month accounts deadline only for a special reason, only on a written application by the foreign company, and only by a period not exceeding three months.
  • Section 393 in full: Failure to comply with Chapter XXII does not affect the validity of any contract, dealing or transaction, or the company's liability to be sued on it. But the company cannot bring any suit, claim any set-off, make any counter-claim or institute any legal proceeding in respect of such contract, dealing or transaction until it has complied with the applicable provisions of the Act.
  • IFSC carve-outs are two-fold: electronic based offering, subscription or listing of securities in an IFSC under section 18 of the SEZ Act, 2005 is not "electronic mode" for section 2(42); and the Central Government may separately exempt classes of foreign companies from securities-offering and prospectus requirements in IFSCs.
  • Rule 12 sting: holding out as a registered foreign company without being duly registered exposes the person to investigation under section 210 and consequent action — a liability that attaches to persons, not just companies.
  • CSR applies: under Rule 3 of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014, a foreign company satisfying the section 135(1) criteria must comply with section 135 — often overlooked because CSR is thought of as a domestic obligation.
  • Section 386(b) is a deeming provision: "Director" of a foreign company includes any person on whose directions or instructions the Board is accustomed to act — so shadow directors must be disclosed in the section 380 list.
  • Section 391(2) winding-up trigger: Chapter XX applies to closure of the Indian place of business only where the foreign company has raised monies through offer or issue of securities under this Chapter which have not been repaid or redeemed.
  • Wider definition under section 234: for merger/amalgamation purposes, "foreign company" means any company or body corporate incorporated outside India whether having a place of business in India or not — do not import the section 2(42) test there.

Chapter 12 — The Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008

Source: 87782bos-aps2160-ch12.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • What an LLP is: A hybrid vehicle carrying elements of both a corporate structure and a partnership firm structure. It gives the limited liability of a company at low compliance cost, while letting partners organise their internal structure by mutual agreement like a traditional partnership.
  • Two-tier liability: The LLP itself is liable to the full extent of its assets; the liability of each partner is limited to his agreed contribution. Creditors of the LLP are creditors of the LLP alone and cannot reach the partners' personal assets (except in fraud under Section 30).
  • Legislative history: The Ministry of Law and Justice notified the LLP Act on 9th January 2007; Parliament passed the LLP Bill on 12th December 2008; the President assented on 7th January 2009. The Act applies to the whole of India and was made applicable from 31st March 2009. It was amended by the Limited Liability Partnership (Amendment) Act, 2021 dated 13th August 2021.
  • Structure of the Act: 81 sections (of which Section 81 is now omitted with effect from 1st April 2022) and 4 Schedules. First Schedule — mutual rights and duties of partners and of the LLP and its partners where there is no formal agreement. Second Schedule — conversion of a firm into LLP. Third Schedule — conversion of a private company into LLP. Fourth Schedule — conversion of an unlisted public company into LLP.
  • Administration: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs and the Registrar of Companies (ROC) administer the Act. The Central Government frames and amends the Rules by notification in the Official Gazette.
  • Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does not apply: Section 4 expressly excludes the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 from application to an LLP, save as otherwise provided. Section 2(2) imports definitions from the Companies Act, 2013 for words used but not defined in the LLP Act.
  • Why the form was created: Lawmakers wanted an alternative to traditional partnership (with unlimited personal liability) on the one hand and the statute-based governance structure of a limited liability company on the other — so that professional expertise and entrepreneurial initiative could combine and operate in a flexible, innovative and efficient manner. The LLP suits small enterprises and investment by venture capital.

Key Definitions / Terms

Address [Section 2(1)(a)]
In relation to a partner: if an individual, his usual residential address; if a body corporate, the address of its registered office.
Body corporate [Section 2(1)(d)]
A company as defined in clause (20) of section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013 and includes an LLP registered under this Act, an LLP incorporated outside India, and a company incorporated outside India; but does not include a corporation sole, a co-operative society registered under any law in force, and any other body corporate notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette.
Business [Section 2(1)(e)]
Includes every trade, profession, service and occupation, except any activity the Central Government may exclude by notification.
Chartered Accountant [Section 2(1)(f)]
A CA as defined in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 who has obtained a certificate of practice under sub-section (1) of section 6 of that Act.
Designated partner [Section 2(1)(j)]
Any partner designated as such pursuant to Section 7.
Entity [Section 2(1)(k)]
Any body corporate; and for the purposes of Sections 18, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 52 and 53 it also includes a firm set up under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
Financial year [Section 2(1)(l)]
The period from 1st April of a year to 31st March of the following year. Proviso: where an LLP is incorporated after 30th September of a year, the financial year may end on 31st March of the year next following that year.
Foreign LLP [Section 2(1)(m)]
An LLP formed, incorporated or registered outside India which establishes a place of business within India.
Limited liability partnership [Section 2(1)(n)]
A partnership formed and registered under this Act.
LLP agreement [Section 2(1)(o)]
Any written agreement between the partners of the LLP, or between the LLP and its partners, determining the mutual rights and duties of the partners and their rights and duties in relation to the LLP. The First Schedule applies to all matters not covered by the agreement.
Name [Section 2(1)(p)]
In relation to a partner: if an individual, his forename, middle name and surname; if a body corporate, its registered name.
Partner [Section 2(1)(q)]
Any person who becomes a partner in the LLP in accordance with the LLP agreement.
Regional Director [Section 2(1)(ra)]
A person appointed as such by the Central Government for the purpose of this Act or the Companies Act, 2013.
Registrar [Section 2(1)(s)]
A person appointed by the Central Government as Registrar, Additional Registrar, Joint Registrar, Deputy Registrar or Assistant Registrar for the purpose of this Act or the Companies Act, 2013.
Small limited liability partnership [Section 2(1)(ta)]
An LLP (i) whose contribution does not exceed ₹25 lakh, or such higher amount as may be prescribed not exceeding ₹5 crore; and (ii) whose turnover as per the Statement of Account and Solvency for the immediately preceding financial year does not exceed ₹40 lakh, or such higher amount as may be prescribed not exceeding ₹50 crore; or (iii) which meets such other requirements as may be prescribed and fulfils such prescribed terms and conditions.
Tribunal [Section 2(1)(u)]
The National Company Law Tribunal constituted under Section 408 of the Companies Act, 2013.
Resident in India [Explanation to Section 7]
A person who has stayed in India for a period of not less than 120 days during the financial year.

Characteristics of an LLP

  • Body corporate [Section 2(1)(d)] and separate legal entity [Section 3]: An LLP is a body corporate formed and incorporated under the Act and a legal entity separate from its partners; any change in partners does not affect the existence, rights or liabilities of the LLP.
  • Perpetual succession: Death, insanity, retirement or insolvency of partners has no impact on the LLP's existence. It can enter into contracts and hold property in its own name.
  • Mutual agency: All partners are agents of the LLP alone. No partner is liable for the independent or unauthorised acts of other partners; no one partner can bind another partner by his acts.
  • LLP agreement: Mutual rights and duties are governed by the agreement between partners; in its absence, by Schedule I of the LLP Act, 2008.
  • Artificial legal person: Created by a legal process and clothed with the rights of an individual. It can do everything a natural person can do except be sent to jail, take an oath, marry or divorce, or practise a learned profession such as CA or Medicine. It is invisible, intangible and immortal (dissolvable by law alone) but not fictitious, because it really exists.
  • Common seal [Section 14(c)]: Optional, not mandatory. If adopted, it stays in the custody of a responsible official and must be affixed in the presence of at least 2 designated partners.
  • Limited liability [Section 26]: Every partner is the agent of the LLP but not of other partners; liability is limited to agreed contribution, which may be tangible or intangible or both.
  • Management: All partners are entitled to manage the business, but only designated partners are responsible for legal compliances.
  • Numbers: Minimum 2 partners and at least 2 individuals as designated partners, of whom at least one is resident in India. No maximum limit on the number of partners.
  • Business for profit only: An LLP must carry on a lawful business with a view to earn profit; it cannot be formed for charitable or non-economic purposes.
  • Investigation, compromise, conversion, e-filing, foreign LLPs: The Central Government may investigate LLP affairs through a competent authority; compromises/mergers/amalgamations follow the LLP Act; a firm, private company or unlisted public company may convert into an LLP; every form or document must be filed in computer-readable electronic form on www.mca.gov.in authenticated by electronic or digital signature of a partner or designated partner; a foreign LLP can become a partner in an Indian LLP.

Advantages of the LLP form

  • Organised and operated on the basis of an agreement.
  • Provides flexibility without imposing detailed legal and procedural requirements.
  • Easy to form.
  • All partners enjoy limited liability.
  • Easy to dissolve.

Partners and Designated Partners

  • Who may be a partner [Section 5]: Any individual or body corporate. An individual is not capable of becoming a partner if (a) he has been found to be of unsound mind by a Court of competent jurisdiction and the finding is in force; (b) he is an undischarged insolvent; or (c) he has applied to be adjudicated an insolvent and his application is pending.
  • Eligible persons: Individuals (resident Indians, NRIs, OCIs and foreign nationals), LLPs, companies (including foreign companies), foreign LLPs, LLPs incorporated outside India, and foreign companies. A co-operative society and a corporation sole cannot become a partner in an LLP. Where capital is introduced or existing stake acquired by persons resident outside India (other than NRIs and OCIs investing on a non-repatriation basis), the LLP must undertake FDI compliances.
  • Minimum partners [Section 6]: Every LLP shall have at least two partners. If the number falls below two and the LLP carries on business for more than six months while so reduced, the sole partner during that time — knowing the business is carried on with him alone — is personally liable for the obligations of the LLP incurred during that period.
  • Designated partners [Section 7(1)]: At least two designated partners who are individuals, at least one resident in India. Proviso: if all partners are bodies corporate, or some are individuals and some bodies corporate, at least two individuals who are partners or nominees of such bodies corporate shall act as designated partners.
  • Appointment mechanics [Section 7(2)]: If the incorporation document specifies who are to be designated partners, those persons are designated partners on incorporation; if it states that each partner from time to time is to be a designated partner, every partner is one. Any partner may become — or cease to be — a designated partner in accordance with the LLP agreement.
  • Consent and filing [Section 7(3) & 7(4)]: Prior consent in the prescribed form is required; the LLP must file the particulars of every individual who has consented with the Registrar within 30 days of his appointment.
  • DPIN [Section 7(6)]: Every designated partner must obtain a Designated Partner Identification Number (DPIN) from the Central Government; Sections 153 to 159 of the Companies Act, 2013 apply mutatis mutandis.
  • Liabilities of designated partners [Section 8]: Responsible for doing all acts required of the LLP for compliance with the Act — including filing of any document, return, statement and the like — and as specified in the LLP agreement; and liable to all penalties imposed on the LLP for contravention of those provisions.
  • Changes in designated partners [Section 9]: A vacancy may be filled within 30 days. If no designated partner is appointed, or if at any time there is only one designated partner, each partner shall be deemed to be a designated partner.
  • Cessation [Section 24]: A partner may cease by agreement or, absent agreement, by giving not less than 30 days' written notice to the other partners. A person also ceases on death or dissolution of the LLP, on being declared of unsound mind by a competent court, or on applying to be adjudged / being declared insolvent. Cessation does not by itself discharge obligations incurred while a partner. Unless the LLP agreement provides otherwise, the former partner (or the person entitled to his share on death or insolvency) is entitled to receive an amount equal to his capital contribution actually made plus his share in accumulated profits after deducting accumulated losses, determined as at the date of cessation — but has no right to interfere in the management of the LLP.
  • Deemed continuation [Section 24(3)]: A former partner is still regarded as a partner towards anyone dealing with the LLP unless that person has notice of the cessation, or notice of cessation has been delivered to the Registrar.
  • Registration of changes [Section 25]: A partner must inform the LLP of any change in his name or address within 15 days. The LLP must file notice with the Registrar within 30 days of a person becoming or ceasing to be a partner, and within 30 days of any change in a partner's name or address. A person who ceases may himself file the notice if he reasonably believes the LLP will not; the Registrar then seeks confirmation from the LLP, and if no confirmation is given within 15 days, the Registrar shall register the notice filed by the outgoing partner.
  • Transferable interest [Section 42]: A partner's right to a share of profits and losses and to receive distributions is transferable wholly or in part. Such transfer does not by itself cause disassociation of the partner or dissolution and winding up of the LLP, and does not by itself entitle the transferee/assignee to participate in management or to access information about the LLP's transactions.
  • Business transactions of partner with LLP [Section 66]: A partner may lend money to and transact other business with the LLP, with the same rights and obligations as a person who is not a partner.

Incorporation — Procedure and Sections

  • Incorporation document [Section 11(1)]: Two or more persons associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to earn profit subscribe their names to the incorporation document, which is filed with prescribed fees with the Registrar of the State in which the registered office is to be situated. (Incorporation documents are processed electronically by the Registrar, Central Registration Centre, since 2nd October 2018.)
  • Statement to be filed [Section 11(1)(c)]: A statement in the prescribed form made by an advocate, or a Company Secretary, or a Chartered Accountant, or a Cost Accountant engaged in the formation of the LLP, and by any one subscriber to the incorporation document, that all requirements of the Act and rules in respect of incorporation and matters precedent and incidental thereto have been complied with.
  • Contents of the incorporation document [Section 11(2)]: the prescribed form; the name of the LLP; the proposed business; the address of the registered office; the name and address of each person to be a partner on incorporation; the name and address of the persons to be designated partners on incorporation; and such other prescribed information.
  • Registration [Section 12]: On compliance with clauses (b) and (c) of Section 11(1), the Registrar retains the incorporation document and within 14 days registers it and issues a certificate that the LLP is incorporated by the name specified. The Registrar may accept the Section 11(1)(c) statement as sufficient evidence of compliance with clause (a). The certificate is signed by the Registrar, authenticated by his official seal, and is conclusive evidence that the LLP is incorporated by that name.
  • Registered office [Section 13]: Every LLP shall have a registered office for receiving all communications and notices. Documents may be served on the LLP, a partner or a designated partner by post under a certificate of posting, by registered post, or in any other prescribed manner, at the registered office or any other address specifically declared by the LLP. A change of registered office takes effect only upon filing of notice with the Registrar.
  • Effect of registration [Section 14]: The LLP by its name is capable of (i) suing and being sued; (ii) acquiring, owning, holding and developing or disposing of property — movable or immovable, tangible or intangible; (iii) having a common seal, if it decides to have one; and (iv) doing and suffering other acts and things as bodies corporate may lawfully do and suffer.
  • Name [Section 15]: Every LLP must have the words "limited liability partnership" or the acronym "LLP" as the last words of its name. No LLP shall be registered by a name which in the Central Government's opinion is (a) undesirable; or (b) identical or too nearly resembling that of any other LLP or a company or a registered trademark of any other person under the Trade Marks Act, 1999.
  • Reservation of name [Section 16]: On application in the prescribed form with fee, if the Registrar is satisfied the name is not rejectable under Section 15(2), he reserves it for a period of 3 months from the date of intimation.
  • Rectification of name [Section 17]: If through inadvertence or otherwise an LLP is registered (on first registration or on registration by a new name) with a name identical with or too nearly resembling that of any other LLP or a company, or a registered trade mark under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, so as to be likely to be mistaken, then on application of such LLP, proprietor or company, the Central Government may direct the LLP to change its name within 3 months of the direction. Proviso: an application by the proprietor of a registered trade mark is maintainable only within 3 years from the date of incorporation, registration or change of name of the LLP. On change, the LLP must notify the Registrar within 15 days with the Central Government's order, and must change its name in the LLP agreement within 30 days of the change in the certificate of incorporation. On default, the Central Government allots a new name, the Registrar enters it in the register and issues a fresh certificate of incorporation — without preventing the LLP from subsequently changing its name.

Steps to Incorporate an LLP (Forms)

StepActionForm

Relationship of Partners and the LLP Agreement

  • Eligibility to be partners [Section 22]: On incorporation, the subscribers to the incorporation document become partners; any other person may become a partner in accordance with the LLP agreement.
  • Section 23(1) & (2): Mutual rights and duties of partners, and between the LLP and its partners, are governed by the LLP agreement; the agreement and any changes must be filed with the Registrar in the prescribed form and manner with prescribed fees.
  • Section 23(3): A written agreement made before incorporation between the subscribers to the incorporation document may impose obligations on the LLP, provided it is ratified by all the partners after incorporation.
  • Section 23(4) — the default rule: In the absence of agreement on any matter, the mutual rights and duties of the partners, and of the LLP and the partners, are determined by the provisions on that matter set out in the First Schedule.
  • Form of contribution [Section 32]: A partner's contribution may consist of tangible, movable or immovable or intangible property or other benefit to the LLP, including money, promissory notes, other agreements to contribute cash or property, and contracts for services performed or to be performed. The monetary value of each partner's contribution must be accounted for and disclosed in the LLP's accounts in the prescribed manner.
  • Obligation to contribute [Section 33]: The obligation to contribute money, property, other benefit or services is as per the LLP agreement. A creditor who extends credit or otherwise acts in reliance on an obligation described in that agreement, without notice of any compromise between partners, may enforce the original obligation against such partner.

Extent and Limitation of Liability

  • Partner as agent [Section 26]: Every partner is, for the purpose of the business of the LLP, the agent of the LLP, but not of the other partners.
  • Extent of liability of LLP [Section 27]: The LLP is not bound by anything done by a partner in dealing with a person if (a) the partner in fact has no authority to act for the LLP in doing that act, and (b) the person knows he has no authority or does not know or believe him to be a partner of the LLP. The LLP is liable where a partner is liable to any person as a result of a wrongful act or omission on his part in the course of the LLP's business or with its authority. An obligation of the LLP, whether arising in contract or otherwise, is solely the obligation of the LLP, and the liabilities of the LLP are met out of the property of the LLP.
  • Extent of liability of partner [Section 28]: A partner is not personally liable, directly or indirectly, for an obligation referred to in Section 27(3) solely by reason of being a partner. But this does not affect the personal liability of a partner for his own wrongful act or omission; a partner is not personally liable for the wrongful act or omission of any other partner.
  • Holding out [Section 29]: Any person who by words spoken or written or by conduct represents himself, or knowingly permits himself to be represented, to be a partner in an LLP is liable to any person who on the faith of such representation has given credit to the LLP — whether or not the person representing himself knows the representation reached the person giving credit. Where credit is received by the LLP as a result of such representation, the LLP is liable to the extent of the credit received or any financial benefit derived thereon, without prejudice to the liability of the person holding out. Where after a partner's death the business is continued in the same LLP name, continued use of that name (or the deceased partner's name as part of it) does not by itself make his legal representative or estate liable for any act of the LLP done after his death.
  • Unlimited liability in case of fraud [Section 30(1)]: Where an act is carried out by an LLP or any of its partners with intent to defraud creditors of the LLP or any other person, or for any fraudulent purpose, the liability of the LLP and of the partners who so acted shall be unlimited for all or any of the debts or other liabilities of the LLP. Where such an act is carried out by a partner, the LLP is liable to the same extent as the partner unless the LLP establishes that the act was without its knowledge or authority.
  • Section 30(2) punishment: Every person knowingly a party to carrying on the business in that manner is punishable with imprisonment up to 5 years and with fine not less than ₹50,000 extending to ₹5 lakh.
  • Section 30(3) compensation: Where an LLP, or any partner, designated partner or employee, has conducted the affairs of the LLP in a fraudulent manner, then without prejudice to any criminal proceedings, the LLP and such person is liable to pay compensation to any person who has suffered loss or damage by reason of such conduct. The LLP is not liable if such partner, designated partner or employee acted fraudulently without knowledge of the LLP.
  • Whistle blowing [Section 31]: The Court or Tribunal may reduce or waive any penalty leviable against a partner or employee if satisfied that he provided useful information during the investigation of the LLP, or that information given by him (whether or not during an investigation) led to the LLP or any partner or employee being convicted under this Act or any other Act. No partner or employee may be discharged, demoted, suspended, threatened, harassed or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of his LLP or employment merely for providing, or causing to be provided, such information.

Financial Disclosures, Returns and Registrar's Powers

  • Books of account [Section 34(1)]: The LLP shall maintain prescribed proper books of account relating to its affairs for each year of its existence, on cash basis or accrual basis, according to the double entry system, at its registered office, for such period as may be prescribed.
  • Statement of Account and Solvency [Section 34(2) & (3)]: Prepared within 6 months from the end of each financial year, as at the last day of that financial year, in the prescribed form, signed by the designated partners, and filed with the Registrar every year within the prescribed time with prescribed fees.
  • Audit [Section 34(4)]: Accounts shall be audited in accordance with prescribed rules; the Central Government may by notification in the Official Gazette exempt any class or classes of LLP from this requirement.
  • Accounting and auditing standards [Section 34A]: The Central Government may, in consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority constituted under Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013, prescribe standards of accounting and standards of auditing as recommended by ICAI.
  • Annual return [Section 35(1)]: Every LLP shall file a duly authenticated annual return with the Registrar within 60 days of closure of its financial year in the prescribed form and manner with prescribed fee.
  • Inspection of documents [Section 36]: The incorporation document, name of partners and changes therein, Statement of Account and Solvency, and annual return filed by each LLP with the Registrar shall be available for inspection by any person in the prescribed manner and on payment of the prescribed fee.
  • Penalty for false statement [Section 37]: If in any return, statement or other document required under the Act any person makes a statement which is false in any material particular knowing it to be false, or which omits any material fact knowing it to be material, he is punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years and fine not less than ₹1 lakh extending to ₹5 lakh.
  • Power of Registrar to obtain information [Section 38]: The Registrar may require any person — including any present or former partner, designated partner or employee — to answer questions, make declarations or supply details in writing within a reasonable period. If the person fails to do so within the time given, or the Registrar is not satisfied with the reply, the Registrar may summon that person to appear before him, an inspector or a designated public officer. Failure without lawful excuse to comply with any summons or requisition is punishable with fine not less than ₹2,000 extending to ₹25,000.
  • Compounding of offences [Section 39]: Notwithstanding the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the Regional Director (or an officer not below that rank authorised by the Central Government) may compound any offence punishable with fine only, collecting a sum which may extend to the maximum fine for the offence but not lower than the minimum. Compounding is not available for an offence committed by the LLP, its partner or designated partner within 3 years from the date on which a similar offence by it or him was compounded; a second or subsequent offence after that 3-year period is deemed a first offence. Every application is made to the Registrar, who forwards it with his comments to the Regional Director. Intimation of compounding must be given to the Registrar within 7 days. If compounded before prosecution is instituted, no prosecution shall be instituted; if after, the Registrar brings it in writing to the notice of the court and the offender is discharged. The Regional Director may direct any partner, designated partner or employee to file or register documents (with fee or additional fee) within the time specified; failure to comply with such an order makes the maximum fine for the offence under consideration twice the amount provided in the corresponding section.
  • Payment of additional fee [Section 69]: Any document or return not registered or filed in time may be filed later on payment of prescribed additional fee in addition to the normal fee. Proviso: such late filing is without prejudice to any other action or liability under the Act. Further proviso: different fee or additional fee may be prescribed for different classes of LLPs or for different documents or returns.
  • Enhanced punishment [Section 70]: For a second or subsequent offence, the LLP, partner or designated partner is punishable with imprisonment as provided, but where fine is prescribed (along with or exclusive of imprisonment) with fine which shall be twice the amount of fine for such offence.

Conversion into LLP

  • Section 55: A firm may convert into an LLP in accordance with this Chapter and the Second Schedule.
  • Section 56: A private company may convert into an LLP in accordance with this Chapter and the Third Schedule.
  • Section 57: An unlisted public company may convert into an LLP in accordance with this Chapter and the Fourth Schedule. (A listed company cannot convert into an LLP.)
  • Registration of conversion [Section 58]: On being satisfied that the firm, private company or unlisted public company has complied with the respective Schedule, the Act and the rules, the Registrar registers the documents and issues a certificate of registration stating that the LLP is registered under this Act on and from the date specified in the certificate.
  • Intimation: The LLP must, within 15 days of the date of registration, inform the concerned Registrar of Firms or Registrar of Companies with which it was registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 or the Companies Act, 1956 (now the Companies Act, 2013) about the conversion and the particulars of the LLP in the prescribed form and manner.
  • Effect of registration: Notwithstanding any other law in force, on and from the date of registration specified in the certificate — (a) there shall be an LLP by the name specified in the certificate; (b) all tangible (movable or immovable) and intangible property, assets, interests, rights, privileges, liabilities and obligations of the firm or company and the whole of its undertaking are transferred to and vest in the LLP without further assurance, act or deed; and (c) the firm or company is deemed to be dissolved and removed from the records of the Registrar of Firms or Registrar of Companies. Partners of the firm / shareholders of the company and the partners of the LLP are bound by the respective Schedules.
  • Foreign LLPs [Section 59]: The Central Government may make rules for the establishment of a place of business in India by a foreign LLP and for carrying on business here, by applying or incorporating, with appropriate modifications, the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 or such regulatory mechanism with such composition as may be prescribed.

Compromise, Arrangement, Reconstruction and Amalgamation

  • Section 60(1): Where a compromise or arrangement is proposed between an LLP and its creditors, or between an LLP and its partners, the Tribunal may — on the application of the LLP, any creditor or partner, or (if the LLP is being wound up) the liquidator — order a meeting of the creditors or partners to be called, held and conducted as prescribed or as the Tribunal directs.
  • Section 60(2): If a majority representing three-fourths in value of the creditors or partners at the meeting agree, the compromise or arrangement, if sanctioned by the Tribunal, binds all creditors or all partners and also the LLP (or, if being wound up, the liquidator and contributories). Proviso: no sanction order shall be made unless the Tribunal is satisfied that the applicant has disclosed, by affidavit or otherwise, all material facts including the LLP's latest financial position and the pendency of any investigation proceedings.
  • Section 60(3) & (5): The Tribunal's order must be filed with the Registrar within 30 days of making it and has effect only after it is so filed. The Tribunal may at any time after an application is made stay the commencement or continuation of any suit or proceeding against the LLP until the application is finally disposed of.
  • Section 61 — enforcement: Where the Tribunal sanctions a compromise or arrangement it shall have power to supervise its carrying out and may, then or later, give directions or make modifications necessary for its proper working. If satisfied the compromise or arrangement cannot be worked satisfactorily with or without modifications, the Tribunal may, on its own motion or on the application of any interested person, order winding up of the LLP — and such an order is deemed to be an order made under Section 64.
  • Section 62 — reconstruction / amalgamation: Where a compromise or arrangement is proposed for a scheme of reconstruction of one or more LLPs or amalgamation of two or more LLPs, and the whole or part of the undertaking, property or liabilities of a transferor LLP is to be transferred to a transferee LLP, the Tribunal may provide for (i) the transfer of the undertaking, property or liabilities; (ii) the continuation by or against the transferee LLP of legal proceedings pending by or against the transferor LLP; (iii) the dissolution without winding up of any transferor LLP; (iv) provision for dissenting persons within such time and manner as the Tribunal directs; and (v) incidental, consequential and supplemental matters.
  • Provisos to Section 62(1): No amalgamation of an LLP which is being wound up shall be sanctioned unless the Tribunal has received a report from the Registrar that the LLP's affairs have not been conducted in a manner prejudicial to the interests of its partners or to public interest. No order for dissolution of a transferor LLP under clause (iii) shall be made unless the Official Liquidator, on scrutiny of the books and papers, has reported likewise to the Tribunal.
  • Section 62(2) & (3): Where the order provides for transfer of property or liabilities, the property vests in and the liabilities become those of the transferee LLP — and in the case of property, if the order so directs, freed from any charge which is to cease to have effect by virtue of the compromise or arrangement. A certified copy of the order must be filed with the Registrar for registration within 30 days.
  • Explanation to Section 62: "Property" includes property, rights and powers of every description; "liabilities" includes duties of every description. An LLP shall not be amalgamated with a company.

Winding Up and Dissolution

  • Section 63: Winding up of an LLP may be either voluntary or by the Tribunal, and an LLP so wound up may be dissolved.
  • Section 64 — grounds for winding up by the Tribunal: (a) if the LLP decides that it be wound up by the Tribunal; (b) if, for a period of more than six months, the number of partners is reduced below two; (c) if the LLP has acted against the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State or public order — this clause was omitted by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 with effect from 15.11.2016; (d) if the LLP has defaulted in filing with the Registrar the Statement of Account and Solvency or annual return for any five consecutive financial years; or (e) if the Tribunal is of the opinion that it is just and equitable that the LLP be wound up.
  • Section 65: The Central Government may make rules for provisions relating to winding up and dissolution of LLPs.
  • Application of the Companies Act, 2013 [Section 67]: The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that any provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 specified in the notification shall apply to any LLP, either as such or with specified exceptions, modifications and adaptations. A draft of every such notification must be laid before each House of Parliament while in session for a total period of 30 days (in one session or two or more successive sessions); if before the expiry of the session immediately following, both Houses agree in disapproving the notification it shall not be issued, and if both agree in modifying it, it shall be issued only in the modified form.

LLP vs Partnership Firm vs Limited Liability Company
