Examples

  • Example 1 — Financial year of a late-incorporated LLP: An LLP incorporated on 15th October 2022 (i.e. after 30th September) may have its financial year running from 15th October 2022 to 31st March 2024. It may instead always maintain its first accounts from 15th October 2022 to 31st March 2023, i.e. for a period of less than 12 months. The period for which the first accounts of an LLP are prepared shall not exceed 18 months. Since the Income Tax department has prescribed a uniform financial year of 1st April to 31st March, the financial year for an LLP should always be 1st April to 31st March each year.
  • Example 2 — Why professionals choose the LLP: Professionals such as engineering consultants, legal advisors and accounting professionals are afraid of entering into business because of unlimited liability. The LLP Act provides an avenue for these professionals to form LLP firms restricting their liability to the agreed amount, which has encouraged professionals to form LLPs.
  • Example 3 — Mixed individual and body corporate partners: An LLP has three partners: one individual, Mr. X, and two bodies corporate, M/s XYZ Ltd and M/s ABC Ltd. Conclusion: Mr. X and one nominee of any of the bodies corporate shall be the designated partners.
  • Example 4 — SMY LLP, all body corporate partners: SMY LLP has three partners: 1. SI Limited, 2. MIS Limited, 3. YI Private Limited. As there is no individual as a partner in the LLP, nominees of any two of the said bodies corporate shall act as designated partners.
  • Example 5 — Indian Helicopters LLP, residency test: The LLP has 5 partners — Mr. A (Non Resident), Mr. B (Non Resident), Ms. C (resident), Ms. D (resident) and Ms. E (resident). At least 2 must be named as designated partners, of whom 1 should be resident. If only Mr. A and Mr. B are designated, it will not serve the purpose; one of the designated partners must be from among Ms. C, Ms. D and Ms. E.
  • Example 6 — Annual return deadline: If the financial year of an LLP closes on 31st March 2022, the LLP has to file its annual return with the Registrar latest by 30th May 2022 (60 days).

MCQs (with answers)

  • MCQ 1: Which of the following cannot be converted into LLP? (a) Partnership firm (b) Private company (c) Listed company (d) Unlisted company. Answer: (c) Listed company.
  • MCQ 2: The approved name of an LLP shall be valid for a period of ___ from the date of approval: (a) 1 Month (b) 2 Months (c) 3 months (d) 6 months. Answer: (c) 3 months.
  • MCQ 3: The name of the Limited Liability Partnership shall be ended by: (a) Limited (b) Limited Liability partnership or LLP (c) Private Limited (d) OPC. Answer: (b) Limited Liability partnership or LLP.
  • MCQ 4: Which one of the following statements about LLPs is incorrect? (a) An LLP has a legal personality separate from that of its members (b) The liability of each partner in an LLP is limited (c) Members of an LLP are taxed as partners (d) A listed company can convert to an LLP. Answer: (d) A listed company can convert to an LLP.
  • MCQ 5: For the purpose of LLP, "Resident in India" means: (a) stayed in India for not less than 182 days during the current year (b) not less than 180 days during the immediately preceding one year (c) not less than 181 days during the immediately preceding one year (d) not less than 120 days during the financial year. Answer: (d) Person who has stayed in India for a period of not less than 120 days during the financial year.

Descriptive Questions (with answers)

  • Q1 — "LLP is an alternative corporate business form that gives the benefits of limited liability of a company and the flexibility of a partnership." Explain. Answer: Limited liability — every partner of an LLP is, for the purpose of the business of the LLP, the agent of the LLP but not of other partners (Section 26); the liability of partners is limited to their agreed contribution while the LLP itself is liable for the full extent of its assets. Flexibility of a partnership — the LLP allows its members to organise their internal structure as a partnership based on a mutually arrived agreement; the form enables entrepreneurs, professionals and enterprises providing services of any kind or engaged in scientific and technical disciplines to form commercially efficient vehicles suited to their requirements, and owing to flexibility in structure and operation it is a suitable vehicle for small enterprises and for investment by venture capital.
  • Q2 — Mr. Ankit Sharma wants to form an LLP with himself, his wife Mrs. Archika Sharma and one HUF as partners. Can this LLP be incorporated? Answer: Section 5 provides that any individual or body corporate may be a partner, except an individual found to be of unsound mind by a Court of competent jurisdiction (finding in force), an undischarged insolvent, or one who has applied to be adjudicated insolvent with the application pending. Section 2(1)(d) defines "body corporate" as a company under clause (20) of section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013 and includes an LLP registered under the Act, an LLP incorporated outside India and a company incorporated outside India, but excludes a corporation sole, a co-operative society and any other body corporate notified by the Central Government. Therefore an HUF is not covered in the definition of body corporate and cannot be a partner in an LLP.
  • Q3 — Ram Infra Development LLP has 4 partners: Mr. Rahul, Mr. Raheem, Mr. Kartar and Mr. Albert. Mr. Rahul and Mr. Albert are non-resident; the other two are resident. The LLP wants Mr. Rahul and Mr. Raheem as designated partners. Can it do so? Answer: Under Section 7, every LLP shall have at least two designated partners who are individuals, at least one of whom is resident in India; "resident in India" means a person who has stayed in India for not less than 120 days during the financial year. Since Mr. Raheem is a resident, Mr. Rahul and Mr. Raheem can be appointed as designated partners.
  • Q4 — Mr. Mudit is a creditor of Devi Ram Food Circle LLP with a claim of ₹10,00,000; the assets of the LLP are worth only ₹7,00,000. Can he make the partners personally liable for the deficiency of ₹3,00,000? Answer: An LLP is a body corporate and a legal entity separate from its partners. The LLP is liable to the full extent of its assets, but the liability of partners is limited to their agreed contribution. Creditors of the LLP are creditors of the LLP alone and cannot claim from the partners. Mr. Mudit cannot claim the deficiency of ₹3,00,000 from the partners of Devi Ram Food Circle LLP.
  • Q5 — M/s Vardhman Steels LLP was incorporated on 01.09.2022. On 01.01.2023 a partner of M/s Vardhimaan Steels, a partnership firm registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 since 01.01.2000, asked the ROC that the LLP change its name as it nearly resembles the firm's name. Is the LLP liable to change its name? Answer: Section 15 bars registration of an LLP by a name which the Central Government considers undesirable, or identical with or too nearly resembling that of any other LLP or a company or a registered trade mark under the Trade Marks Act, 1999. Section 17 permits the Central Government, on application, to direct a change of name within 3 months on the same grounds. These provisions apply only where the name resembles that of an LLP, a company or a registered trade mark — not a partnership firm. Hence M/s Vardhman Steels LLP need not change its name.
  • Q6 — Kanik, Priyansh, Abhinav and Bhawna were partners in Singh Jain & Associates LLP. Abhinav resigned with effect from 01.11.2022 but neither the LLP nor Abhinav informed the ROC. Is Abhinav still liable for losses on transactions entered after 01.11.2022? Answer: Under Section 24(3), a former partner is still regarded (in relation to any person dealing with the LLP) as being a partner unless the person has notice of the cessation, or notice of the cessation has been delivered to the Registrar. As no notice of resignation was given to the ROC, Abhinav will still be liable for the loss of the firm on transactions entered after 01.11.2022.

Why It Matters / Application

The LLP is the vehicle of choice for CA, CS, legal and consulting practices precisely because Section 27(3) makes an obligation of the LLP solely the obligation of the LLP and Section 28 shields a partner from another partner's wrongful act — while Section 28(2) still leaves each professional answerable for his own negligence. In practice the decisions that follow from this chapter are concrete: whether the entity converting is a firm (Second Schedule), a private company (Third Schedule) or an unlisted public company (Fourth Schedule) — a listed company can never convert; whether the LLP has at least two individual designated partners with one satisfying the 120-day residency test, failing which every partner is deemed a designated partner under Section 9 and carries Section 8 penalty exposure; and whether the compliance calendar is met — Statement of Account and Solvency within 6 months of financial year end and annual return within 60 days of closure, each carrying ₹100-per-day penalties on both the LLP and every designated partner, and five consecutive years of default being an independent ground for winding up by the Tribunal under Section 64(d).

Note

  • Exam trap — "resident in India" is 120 days, not 182 days. The Income-tax residency test does not apply here; Section 7 uses 120 days during the financial year.
  • Exam trap — name resemblance. Sections 15 and 17 protect only another LLP, a company, or a registered trade mark. Resemblance to a partnership firm's name gives no right to demand a change (Descriptive Q5). Note that the chapter Summary states the ground more loosely ("any other partnership firm or LLP or company or a registered trade mark") than the operative sections — the answer key follows the sections.
  • Exam trap — HUF and co-operative societies. An HUF is not a "body corporate" and cannot be a partner; a co-operative society and a corporation sole are expressly excluded by Section 2(1)(d). A minor cannot be admitted to the benefits of an LLP, unlike a partnership firm.
  • Proviso to Section 30(1): Where the fraudulent act is by a partner, the LLP escapes liability only if the LLP establishes that the act was without its knowledge or authority — the burden is on the LLP. Similarly under Section 30(3), the LLP is not liable if the partner, designated partner or employee acted fraudulently without the LLP's knowledge.
  • Proviso to Section 17(1): A registered trade mark proprietor's application is maintainable only within 3 years from incorporation, registration or change of name of the LLP.
  • Section 64(c) is omitted by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 with effect from 15.11.2016, and Section 81 is omitted with effect from 1st April 2022 — do not quote them as live grounds.
  • Section 39(2) three-year bar: compounding is unavailable for a similar offence within 3 years of an earlier compounding; a second or subsequent offence after those 3 years is deemed a first offence. Read together with Section 70, a repeat offence attracts twice the fine.
  • Small LLP [Section 2(1)(ta)] was introduced by the LLP (Amendment) Act, 2021 — note the conjunction: contribution up to ₹25 lakh and turnover up to ₹40 lakh, with prescribed ceilings of ₹5 crore and ₹50 crore respectively.
  • Forms to remember: RUN-LLP (name reservation), FiLLiP (incorporation), e-Form 3 (LLP agreement, within 30 days of incorporation), Form 8 (Statement of Account and Solvency, within 30 days from the end of six months of the financial year) and Form 11 (annual return, within 60 days of closure of the financial year).
  • New feature versus the 1932 Act: the LLP Act, in contra-distinction to the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, prescribes the filing of an annual return in line with the Companies Act, 2013 — a partnership firm files no annual document with the Registrar of Firms.
  • An LLP shall not be amalgamated with a company (Explanation (ii) to Section 62), although an LLP may amalgamate with another LLP.

Other Laws · Chapter 1 — The General Clauses Act, 1897

Source: 87784bos-aps2160-p2-ch1.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • What the Act is: The General Clauses Act, 1897 was enacted on 11th March, 1897 to consolidate and extend the General Clauses Acts of 1868 and 1887. It is not a substantive law — it is a statutory dictionary plus a set of standing rules of construction that are read into every Central Act.
  • Gap-filling function: The general definitions in it apply to all Central Acts and Regulations in the absence of a definition of that word in the particular Central Act or Regulation, and only "unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context". A special definition inside a particular enactment always prevails over the General Clauses Act definition.
  • Four objects of the Act: (1) to shorten the language of Central Acts; (2) to provide, as far as possible, for uniformity of expression in Central Acts by giving definitions of a series of terms in common use; (3) to state explicitly certain convenient rules for the construction and interpretation of Central Acts; (4) to guard against slips and oversights by importing into every Act certain common-form clauses which otherwise ought to be inserted in every Central Act.
  • Purpose as stated by the Supreme Court: in The Chief Inspector of Mines v. Karam Chand Thapar the Court said the purpose is "to place in one single Statute different provisions as regards interpretation of words and legal principles which would otherwise have to be specified separately in many different Acts and regulations" — i.e. to avoid superfluity of language in statutes wherever possible. In Chief Inspector of Mines v. K. C. Thapar it further observed: "Whatever the General Clauses Act says, whether as regards the meanings of words or as regards legal principles, has to be read into every Act to which it applies."
  • Conflict resolution: the Act comes to the rescue where there is no clear definition in a specific enactment and where there is a conflict between pre-constitutional and post-constitutional laws, differentiating legislation according to commencement and enforcement so as to avoid uncertainty.
  • No territorial extent clause: the Act does not contain a "territorial extent" clause. It is in a sense part of every Central Act or Regulation — if a Central Act is extended to any territory, the General Clauses Act is deemed applicable in that territory too for construing that Central Act.
  • Interpretation of the Constitution: Article 367 of the Constitution says — "Unless the context otherwise requires, the General Clauses Act, 1897, shall, subject to any adaptations and modifications that may be made therein under Article 372, apply for the interpretation of this Constitution as it applies for the interpretation of an Act of the Legislature of the Dominion of India."
  • "General Clauses Act" vs "Interpretation Act": in many countries legislation of this kind is called an Interpretation Act; because these provisions are common to every Central Act so far as necessary, the title "General Clauses Act" is not less appropriate.
  • Model for the States: the Act also serves as a model for State General Clauses Acts, which should conform to it — otherwise divergent rules of construction and interpretation would apply and great confusion might ensue.
  • Section-by-section scope: the scope and effect of each section depends on the text of that particular section; the language of each section has to be referred to in order to ascertain which class of instruments or enactments it applies to. Even where no section applies to a particular case, courts sometimes apply the general principles of the Act.

Chapter Overview — Structure of the Act

PartSections
PreliminarySection 1
General DefinitionsSections 3 to 4A
General Rules of ConstructionSections 5 to 13
Powers & FunctionariesSections 14 to 19
Provisions as to orders, rules etc. made under enactmentsSections 20 to 24
MiscellaneousSections 25 to 30

Which Central Acts the Act Applies To

  • (a) Acts of the Indian Parliament (Central Acts) along with the rules and regulations made under the Central Act;
  • (b) Acts of the Dominion Legislature passed between 15th August, 1947 and 26th January, 1950;
  • (c) Acts passed before the commencement of the Constitution by the Governor-General in Council or the Governor-General acting in a legislative capacity.

Basic Understanding of Legislation (foundation concepts)

  • Preamble: every Act has a preamble expressing the scope, object and purpose of the Act; it is the main source for understanding the intention of the lawmaker. It is part of the enactment and can legitimately be used for construing it, but it does not override the plain provisions of the Act. It may be brought in as an aid to construction only where the language of the statute is not clear — e.g. where a word or phrase has more than one meaning and doubt arises as to which is intended.
  • Act vs Bill: an Act is a bill passed by both Houses of Parliament and assented to by the President. A Bill is a draft of a legislative proposal put in proper form which, on being passed by both Houses and assented to by the President, becomes an Act. On receiving the President's assent an Act is notified in the Official Gazette of India.
  • Definitions clause: usually placed in Section 2 of an Act, but in some Acts in Section 3 or other initial sections. Its object is to avoid the necessity of frequent repetition in describing the subject matter to which the defined word applies. If a word is not defined in the Act, its meaning may be taken from the General Clauses Act, 1897.
  • "Means" (exhaustive) vs "includes" (extensive): a definition using "means" is exhaustive and exactly defines the term; a definition using "include" does not define the word but is inclusive and prima facie extensive — the word is not restricted to the meaning assigned but carries an extended meaning that also covers what is listed. "Means and includes" is again exhaustive; "to apply to and include" is understood as extensive.
  • "Shall" vs "may": "shall" raises a presumption of something mandatory or imperative; "may" connotes something not mandatory but only directory or enabling. Sometimes the two are interpreted interchangeably depending on the legislator's intention.
  • Borrowed definitions: Section 2(95) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that words and expressions used and not defined in that Act but defined in the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, the SEBI Act, 1992 or the Depositories Act, 1996 shall have the meanings respectively assigned to them in those Acts.

Key Definitions / Terms — Section 3 (statutory wording)

Section 3 opens: "In this Act, and in all Central Acts and Regulations made after the commencement of this Act, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context,—". Section 3 is the principal definitions section; it applies to the General Clauses Act itself and to post-1897 Central Acts and Regulations unless those laws contain separate definitions of their own or there is something repugnant in the subject or context. It seeks to define 67 phrases and terms commonly used in enactments and is intended to serve as a dictionary for those phrases. Bartley, in his commentary on the Act, has pointed out that a definition may be explanatory, restrictive or extensive.

"Act" [Section 3(2)]
'Act', used with reference to an offence or a civil wrong, shall include a series of acts, and words which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions. An act required to be done cannot necessarily mean a positive act only and may also include acts which one is precluded from doing by decree. The definition is based on sections 32 and 33 of the Indian Penal Code and applies to civil wrongs as well as crimes. 'Act' includes illegal omissions but not an omission which is not illegal.
"Affidavit" [Section 3(3)]
'Affidavit' shall include affirmation and declaration in the case of persons by law allowed to affirm or declare instead of swearing. Two points derive from it: (1) affirmation and declaration; (2) in the case of persons allowed to affirm or declare instead of swearing. The definition is inclusive — it does not define "affidavit" itself; in general parlance an affidavit is a written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation for use as evidence in court or before any authority.
"Central Act" [Section 3(7)]
'Central Act' shall mean an Act of Parliament, and shall include — (a) an Act of the Dominion Legislature or of the Indian Legislature passed before the commencement of the Constitution, and (b) an Act made before such commencement by the Governor General in Council or the Governor General acting in a legislative capacity. The date of commencement of the Constitution is 26th January, 1950.
"Central Government" [Section 3(8)]
(a) In relation to anything done before the commencement of the Constitution — the Governor General in Council, as the case may be, and shall include (i) in relation to functions entrusted under sub-section (1) of section 124 of the Government of India Act, 1935 to the Government of a Province, the Principal Government acting within the scope of the authority given under that sub-section; and (ii) in relation to the administration of a Chief Commissioner's Province, the Chief Commissioner acting within the scope of the authority given under sub-section (3) of section 94 of that Act. (b) In relation to anything done or to be done after the commencement of the Constitution — the President, and shall include (i) in relation to functions entrusted under clause (1) of the article of the Constitution to the Government of a State, the State Government acting within the scope of the authority given under that clause; (ii) in relation to the administration of a Part C State before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, the Chief Commissioner or the Lieutenant Governor or the Government of a neighbouring State or other authority acting within the scope of the authority given under article 239 or article 243; and (iii) in relation to the administration of a Union territory, the administrator thereof acting within the scope of the authority given under article 239. The date of commencement of the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956 is stated in the text as 01st January, 1956.
"Commencement" [Section 3(13)]
'Commencement', used with reference to an Act or Regulation, shall mean the day on which the Act or Regulation comes into force. Coming into force (entry into force / commencement) is the process by which legislation, regulations, treaties and other legal instruments come to have legal force and effect. A law cannot be said to be in force unless brought into operation by legislative enactment or by exercise of authority by a delegate empowered to bring it into operation — the theory of a statute being "in operation in a constitutional sense" though not in fact in operation has no validity [State of Orissa v. Chandrasekhar Singh Bhoi, AIR 1970 SC 398].
"Document" [Section 3(18)]
'Document' shall include any matter written, expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures or marks or by more than one of those means, which is intended to be used or which may be used, for the purpose of recording that matter. Examples of documents: a book, file, painting, inscription and even computer files. It does not include Indian currency notes.
"Enactment" [Section 3(19)] (printed in the source as Section 2(19))
'Enactment' shall include a Regulation (as defined in the Act) and any Regulation of the Bengal, Madras or Bombay Code, and shall also include any provision contained in any Act or in any such Regulation. It has been held that "enactment" would include any Act (or a provision contained therein) made by the Union Parliament or a State Legislature. Because "enactment" includes any provision of an Act, Section 6 (Effect of repeal) applies not only where the entire Act is repealed but also where any provision of an Act is repealed [State of Punjab v. Sukh Deo Sarup Gupta, A.I.R. 1970 SC 1661, 1942, para 3, affirming A.I.R. 1965 Punj. 399, and Godhra Electricity Co. v. Somalal, A.I.R. 1967 Guj. 772, 776, para 6]. Rules and regulations are a species of legislation — whatever is enacted by the delegate of the legislature is also an enactment.
"Financial Year" [Section 3(21)]
'Financial year' shall mean the year commencing on the first day of April. Read with Section 3(66) ("year" = a year reckoned according to the British calendar), the financial year runs from 1st April to the end of March, whereas the calendar year starts on the first day of January.
"Good Faith" [Section 3(22)]
A thing shall be deemed to be done in 'good faith' where it is in fact done honestly, whether it is done negligently or not. Good faith under this Act is a question of fact, determined with reference to the facts and circumstances of each case; anything done with due care and attention which is not mala fide is presumed to have been done in good faith. An authority is not acting honestly where it had a suspicion that something was wrong and did not make further enquiries. This definition does not apply to an enactment containing its own special definition of "good faith", and applies only if there is nothing repugnant in the subject or context.
"Government" [Section 3(23)]
'Government' or 'the Government' shall include both the Central Government and State Government. The object is to make it clear that the word, frequently used as a convenient abbreviation, may be construed according to context in either sense. "Government" generally connotes three wings — the Legislature, the Executive and the Judiciary — but in a narrow sense it connotes the Executive only; the meaning depends on the context.
"Government Securities" [Section 3(24)]
'Government securities' shall mean securities of the Central Government or of any State Government, but in any Act or Regulation made before the commencement of the Constitution shall not include securities of the Government of any Part B State. By virtue of Section 4A this definition applies to all Indian laws.
"Immovable Property" [Section 3(26)]
'Immovable property' shall include: (i) land, (ii) benefits to arise out of land, and (iii) things attached to the earth, or (iv) permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth. It is an inclusive definition with four elements. Where, in any enactment, the definition of immovable property is in the negative and not exhaustive, the General Clauses Act definition will apply to the expression in that enactment.
"Imprisonment" [Section 3(27)]
'Imprisonment' shall mean imprisonment of either description as defined in the Indian Penal Code. By section 53 IPC imprisonment is of two descriptions — rigorous (with hard labour) and simple. So where an Act provides that an offence is punishable with imprisonment, the Court may in its discretion make the imprisonment rigorous or simple.
"Indian law" [Section 3(29)]
'Indian law' shall mean any Act, Ordinance, Regulation, rule, order, bye-law or other instrument which before the commencement of the Constitution had the force of law in any Province of India or part thereof, or thereafter has the force of law in any Part A or Part C State or part thereof, but does not include any Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom or any Order in Council, rule or other instrument made under such Act.
"Month" [Section 3(35)]
'Month' shall mean a month reckoned according to the British calendar.
"Movable Property" [Section 3(36)]
'Movable property' shall mean property of every description, except immovable property. Thus any property which is not immovable property is movable property. Debts, shares and electricity are movable property.
"Oath" [Section 3(37)]
'Oath' shall include affirmation and declaration in the case of persons by law allowed to affirm or declare instead of swearing.
"Offence" [Section 3(38)]
'Offence' shall mean any act or omission made punishable by any law for the time being in force.
"Official Gazette" [Section 3(39)]
'Official Gazette' or 'Gazette' shall mean (i) the Gazette of India, or (ii) the Official Gazette of a State. The Gazette of India is a public journal and an authorised legal document of the Government of India, published weekly by the Department of Publication, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, and printed by the Government of India Press.
"Person" [Section 3(42)]
'Person' shall include (i) any company, or (ii) association, or (iii) body of individuals, whether incorporated or not.
"Registered" [Section 3(49)]
'Registered', used with reference to a document, shall mean registered in India under the law for the time being in force for the registration of documents.
"Rule" [Section 3(51)]
'Rule' shall mean a rule made in exercise of a power conferred by any enactment, and shall include a Regulation made as a rule under any enactment.
"Schedule" [Section 3(52)]
'Schedule' shall mean a schedule to the Act or Regulation in which the word occurs.
"Section" [Section 3(54)]
'Section' shall mean a section of the Act or Regulation in which the word occurs.
"Sub-section" [Section 3(61)]
'Sub-section' shall mean a sub-section of the section in which the word occurs.
"Swear" [Section 3(62)]
'Swear', with its grammatical variations and cognate expressions, shall include affirming and declaring in the case of persons by law allowed to affirm or declare instead of swearing.
"Writing" [Section 3(65)]
Expressions referring to 'writing' shall be construed as including references to printing, lithography, photography and other modes of representing or reproducing words in a visible form.
"Year" [Section 3(66)]
'Year' shall mean a year reckoned according to the British calendar — i.e. the calendar year from January to December.

Note: the terms "Affidavit" [3(3)], "Oath" [3(37)] and "Swear" [3(62)] carry the same definition in the Act — affirmation/declaration by persons allowed by law to affirm or declare instead of swearing.

Which Definitions Reach Back to Earlier Laws — Sections 4 and 4A

ProvisionWords coveredApplies to
Section 4(1)'affidavit', 'immovable property', 'imprisonment', 'month', 'movable property', 'oath', 'person', 'section', 'year'All Central Acts made after 3rd January, 1868 and all Regulations made on or after 14th January, 1887 (unless repugnant in subject or context)
Section 4(2)'commencement', 'financial year', 'offence', 'registered', 'schedule', 'sub-section', 'writing'All Central Acts and Regulations made on or after 14th January, 1887 (unless repugnant in subject or context)
Section 4A(1)'Central Act', 'Central Government', 'Gazette', 'Government', 'Government Securities', 'Indian Law', 'Official Gazette'All Indian laws (unless repugnant in subject or context)
Section 4A(2)References to revenues of the Central Government or of any State GovernmentOn and from 1st April, 1950, construed as references to the Consolidated Fund of India or the Consolidated Fund of the State, as the case may be

How It Works / Logic — General Rules of Construction [Sections 5 to 13]

  • Section 1 — Short title: "This Act may be called the General Clauses Act, 1897." The Preliminary part of an Act generally contains short title, extent, commencement and application; this Act contains only the short title in its Preliminary part. The title, though part of the Act, is not itself an enacting provision. Section 2 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 has been repealed.
  • Section 5 — Coming into operation of enactment: where a Central Act has not specifically mentioned a particular date to come into force, it is implemented on the day it receives the assent of the Governor General (for Central Acts made before the commencement of the Constitution) and/or of the President (in the case of an Act of Parliament). Where a specific date of enforcement is prescribed in the Official Gazette, the Act comes into force from such date.
  • No mandamus to bring an Act into force: in A.K. Roy v. UOI, AIR 1982 SC 710 the Supreme Court observed that where an Act empowers the Government to bring any of its provisions into operation on any day it deems fit, no Court can issue a mandamus to compel the Government to bring it into operation on a particular day. However, in Altemeis Rein v. UOI, AIR 1988 SC 1768 it was held that if sufficient time has elapsed since an Act or any of its provisions was passed and it has not been brought into force, the Court may through a writ direct the Government to consider the question as to when it should begin to operate.
  • Rules take effect on Gazette publication: in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Mahesh Narain, AIR 2013 SC 1778 the Supreme Court held that the effective date of Rules is when the Rules are published vide Gazette notification, and not the date when the Rules were under preparation.
  • No fraction of a day: law takes no cognizance of a fraction of a day — where an Act provides that it is to come into force on the first day of January, it comes into force as soon as the clock strikes 12 on the night of 31st December.
  • Presumption against retrospectivity: all laws affecting substantive vested rights generally operate prospectively; there is a presumption against retrospectivity unless there are express words giving retrospective effect or the language used necessarily implies that retrospective operation is intended. Whether a provision has retrospective effect depends primarily on the language in which it is couched.
  • Section 6 — Effect of repeal: where any Central legislation or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act repeals any Act made or yet to be made, then unless another purpose exists, the repeal shall not: (i) revive anything not enforced or prevailing during the period at which the repeal is effected; (ii) affect the previous operation of any enactment so repealed or anything duly done or suffered thereunder; (iii) affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under any enactment so repealed; (iv) affect any penalty, forfeiture or punishment incurred in respect of any offence committed against any enactment so repealed; (v) affect any inquiry, litigation or remedy in respect of such claim, privilege, debt or responsibility — and any such inquiry, litigation or remedy may be initiated, continued or insisted upon.
  • Repeal obliterates the Act: in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Hirendra Pal Singh, (2011) 5 SCC 305 the Supreme Court held that whenever an Act is repealed it must be considered as if it had never existed; the object of repeal is to obliterate the Act from statutory books, except for the purposes saved by Section 6.
  • Limits of Section 6: in Kolhapur Canesugar Works Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 2000 SC 811 the Supreme Court held that Section 6 applies only to a repeal and not to omissions, and applies when the repeal is of a Central Act or Regulation and not of a Rule.
  • Section 6A — Repeal of an Act making textual amendment: where a Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act repeals an enactment by which the text of any Central Act or Regulation was amended by express omission, insertion or substitution of any matter, then unless a different intention appears, the repeal shall not affect the continuance of that amendment made by the enactment so repealed and in operation at the time of such repeal.
  • Section 7 — Revival of repealed enactments: (1) in any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act, it shall be necessary, for the purpose of reviving wholly or partially any enactment wholly or partially repealed, expressly to state that purpose. (2) This section applies also to all Central Acts made after the third day of January, 1968 and to all Regulations made on or after the fourteenth day of January, 1887. In short — to revive a repealed statute, an intention to do so must be stated.
  • Section 8 — Construction of references to repealed enactments: (1) where this Act or a Central Act or Regulation made after its commencement repeals and re-enacts (with or without modification) any provision of a former enactment, references in any other enactment or instrument to the repealed provision shall, unless a different intention appears, be construed as references to the re-enacted provision. (2) Where, before the fifteenth day of August, 1947, any Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom repealed and re-enacted (with or without modification) any provision of a former enactment, references in any Central Act, Regulation or instrument to the repealed provision shall likewise be construed as references to the re-enacted provision unless a different intention appears.
  • Reference vs incorporation: in Gauri Shankar Gaur v. State of U.P., AIR 1994 SC 169 it was held that every Act has its own distinction; if a later Act merely makes a reference to a former Act or existing law, it is only by reference, and all amendments, repeals and new law subsequently made will have effect unless its operation is saved by the relevant provision of the section of the Act.
  • Section 9 — Commencement and termination of time: in any legislation or regulation it shall be sufficient, for the purpose of excluding the first in a series of days or any other period of time, to use the word "from", and for the purpose of including the last in a series of days or any other period of time, to use the word "to".
  • Section 10 — Computation of time (court/office closed): where by any legislation or regulation any act or proceeding is directed or allowed to be done or taken in any court or office on a certain day or within a prescribed period, then if the Court or office is closed on that day or on the last day of the prescribed period, the act or proceeding shall be considered as done or taken in due time if it is done or taken on the next day afterwards on which the Court or office is open.
  • Section 11 — Measurement of distances: in the measurement of any distance for the purposes of any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act, that distance shall, unless a different intention appears, be measured in a straight line on a horizontal plane.
  • Section 12 — Duty to be taken pro rata: where by any enactment now or hereafter in force, any duty of customs or excise (or in the nature thereof) is leviable on any given quantity by weight, measure or value of any goods or merchandise, then a like duty is leviable according to the same rate on any greater or less quantity. "Pro rata" is a Latin term describing a proportionate allocation.
  • Section 13 — Gender and number: in all legislation and regulations, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context — (1) words importing the masculine gender shall be taken to include females, and (2) words in the singular shall include the plural and vice versa. Accordingly, "men" may properly be held to include women, and the pronoun 'he' and its derivatives may be construed to refer to any person whether male or female. The words "his father and mother" in Section 125(1)(d) of the CrPC, 1973 have been construed to include "her father and mother", so a daughter has been held liable to maintain her father unable to maintain himself.
  • Limits of Section 13(1): the rule must be applied with circumspection when interpreting laws dealing with succession — the words "male descendants" in Sections 7 and 8 of the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908 were not interpreted to include female descendants. Further, where a word connoting a common gender is available but the word used conveys a specific gender, there is a presumption that the General Clauses Act does not apply — thus the word 'bullocks' could not be interpreted to include 'cows'.

Powers and Functionaries [Sections 14 to 19]

  • Section 14 — Power conferred to be exercisable from time to time: (1) where by any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act any power is conferred, then unless a different intention appears, that power may be exercised from time to time as occasion requires. (2) This section applies to all Central Acts and Regulations made on or after the fourteenth day of January, 1887. Relying on Section 14, the Supreme Court held that the power under Section 51(3) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 can be exercised by the Chief Justice as and when the occasion arose for its exercise.
  • Section 15 — Power to appoint includes power to appoint ex-officio: where by any legislation or regulation a power to appoint any person to fill any office or execute any function is conferred, then unless expressly otherwise provided, any such appointment may be made either by name or by virtue of office. "Ex-officio" is Latin for "by virtue of one's position or office".
  • Section 16 — Power to appoint includes power to suspend or dismiss: the authority having for the time being the power to make the appointment shall also have the power to suspend or dismiss any person appointed, whether by itself or by any other authority in exercise of that power. Order 40, Rule 1(a) of the CPC, 1908, which authorises a court to appoint a receiver, has been construed to embrace the power of removing a receiver. Article 229(1) of the Constitution, empowering the Chief Justice to appoint officers and servants of a High Court, has been interpreted to include a power to suspend or dismiss.
  • Section 17 — Substitution of functionaries: (1) it shall be sufficient, for the purpose of indicating the application of a law to every person or number of persons for the time being executing the functions of an office, to mention the official title of the officer at present executing the functions, or that of the officer by whom the functions are commonly executed. (2) Applies also to all Central Acts made after the third day of January, 1868 and to all Regulations made on or after the fourteenth day of January, 1887.
  • Section 18 — Successors: (1) it shall be sufficient, for the purpose of indicating the relation of a law to the successors of any functionaries or of corporations having perpetual succession, to express its relation to the functionaries or corporations. (2) Applies also to all Central Acts made after the third day of January, 1868 and to all Regulations made on or after the fourteenth day of January, 1887.
  • Section 19 — Official Chiefs and subordinates: a law relative to the chief or superior of an office shall apply to the deputies or subordinates lawfully performing the duties of that office in the place of their superior, to prescribe the duty of the superior. Applies to all Central Acts made after the third day of January, 1868 and to all Regulations made on or after the fourteenth day of January, 1887.
  • Successor authority may continue: in K.G. Krishnayya v. State, AIR 1959 it was held that it is not essential that the same statutory authority which initiated a scheme under the Road Transport Corporation Act, 1950 should also implement it — it is open to the successor authority to implement or continue it. Similarly, in a case under the Preventive Detention Act, where there is a change in the Advisory Board after service of the detention order, the new Advisory Board can consider the case pending before the earlier board.

Provisions as to Orders, Rules etc. Made Under Enactments [Sections 20 to 24]

  • Section 20 — Construction of orders etc. issued under enactments: where by any legislation or regulation a power to issue any notification, order, scheme, rule, form or bye-law is conferred, then expressions used in that notification/order/scheme/rule/form/bye-law shall, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context, have the same respective meanings as in the Act or Regulation conferring the power.
  • Meaning of "notification": in Subhash Ram Kumar v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 2003 SC 269 it was held that 'notification' in common English acceptation means a formal announcement of a legally relevant fact, and "notification published in Official Gazette" means a notification published by the authority of law. It is a formal declaration and should be in accordance with declared policies or statute; a notification cannot be substituted by administrative instructions.
  • Section 21 — Power to issue includes power to add to, amend, vary or rescind: where by any legislation or regulation a power to issue notifications, orders, rules or bye-laws is conferred, that power includes the power — exercisable in the like manner and subject to the like sanction and conditions (if any) — to add to, amend, vary or rescind any notifications, orders, rules or bye-laws so issued.
  • Section 21 case law: in Rasid Javed v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 2010 SC 2275 the Supreme Court held that an authority which has the power to issue a notification has the undoubted power to rescind or modify it in the like manner. In Shreesidhbali Steels Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 2011 SC 1175 it was held that the power under Section 21 is not limited to being exercised only once — it can be exercised from time to time having regard to the exigency of time.
  • Section 22 — Rules/bye-laws/orders made between passing and commencement: where, by a Central Act or Regulation which is not to come into force immediately on its passing, a power is conferred to make rules or bye-laws, or to issue orders with respect to the application of the Act/Regulation, or the establishment of any Court, or the appointment of any Judge or officer thereunder, or with respect to the person by whom, the time when, the place where, the manner in which, or the fees for which anything is to be done under the Act or Regulation, then that power may be exercised at any time after the passing of the Act or Regulation; but the rules, bye-laws or orders so made shall not take effect till the commencement of the Act or Regulation. It is an enabling provision that validates rules, bye-laws and orders made before the enactment comes into force, provided they are made after its passing and as preparatory to its coming into force.
  • Section 23 — Rules or bye-laws made after previous publication: where a power to make rules or bye-laws is expressed to be given subject to the condition of previous publication, the following apply — (1) the authority shall, before making them, publish a draft of the proposed rules or bye-laws for the information of persons likely to be affected; (2) the publication shall be made in such manner as that authority deems sufficient, or, if the condition so requires, in such manner as the Government concerned prescribes; (3) there shall be published with the draft a notice specifying a date on or after which the draft will be taken into consideration; (4) the authority having power to make the rules (and, where the rules are to be made with the sanction, approval or concurrence of another authority, that authority also) shall consider any objection or suggestion received from any person with respect to the draft before the date so specified; (5) publication in the Official Gazette of a rule or bye-law purporting to have been made in exercise of a power to make rules after previous publication shall be conclusive proof that the rule or bye-law has been duly made.
  • Effect of Section 23(5): it raises a conclusive presumption that after publication of the rules in the Official Gazette the rule-making procedure was followed; any irregularities in publication of the draft cannot therefore be questioned. It is also open to the authority to make suitable changes in the draft before finally publishing; re-publication is not necessary so long as the changes made are ancillary to the earlier draft and cannot be regarded as foreign to its subject matter.
  • Section 24 — Continuation of orders etc. issued under enactments repealed and re-enacted: where any Central Act or Regulation is, after the commencement of this Act, repealed and re-enacted with or without modification, then unless expressly otherwise provided, any appointment, notification, order, scheme, rule, form or bye-law made or issued under the repealed Act continues in force and is deemed to have been made or issued under the provisions so re-enacted. Also, where a Central Act or Regulation which, by a notification under section 5 or 5A of the Scheduled District Act, 1874 (or any like law), has been extended to any local area, has by a subsequent notification been withdrawn from or re-extended to such area or part thereof, the provisions shall be deemed to have been repealed and re-enacted in such area or part within the meaning of this section.
  • Principle behind Section 24: if a statute is repealed and re-enacted in the same or substantially the same terms, the re-enactment neutralises the previous repeal and the re-enacted provisions continue in force without interruption. If, however, the statute is repealed and re-enacted in somewhat different terms, the amendments and modifications operate as a repeal of those provisions of the repealed Act which are changed by, and are repugnant to, the repealing Act.
  • Section 24 case law and illustrations: in State of Punjab v. Harnek Singh, AIR 2002 SC 1074 it was held that an investigation conducted by Inspectors of Police under the authorisation of a notification issued under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 will be proper and will not be quashed under a new notification taking away that power, until the earlier notification is specifically superseded, withdrawn or modified under the new notification. Likewise, the Mines Act of 1923 was repealed and replaced by the Mines Act of 1952; rules made under the repealed Act must be deemed to continue in force by virtue of this section until superseded. Further, where an Act is repealed and re-enacted, the fact that the repealed Act stated that rules made under it shall have effect as if enacted in the Act does not mean the rules automatically disappear with the repeal — there is still room for the application of this section.

Miscellaneous [Sections 25 to 30]

  • Section 25 — Recovery of fines: Sections 63 to 70 of the Indian Penal Code and the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the time being in force relating to the issue and execution of warrants for the levy of fines shall apply to all fines imposed under any Act, Regulation, rule or bye-law, unless that Act, Regulation, rule or bye-law contains an express provision to the contrary.
  • Section 26 — Offence punishable under two or more enactments: where an act or omission constitutes an offence under two or more enactments, the offender shall be liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of those enactments, but shall not be punished twice for the same offence. Article 20(2) of the Constitution states that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. According to the Supreme Court, a plain reading of Section 26 shows that there is no bar to trial or conviction under two enactments — there is only a bar to punishing the offender twice for the same offence.
  • When Section 26 / Article 20(2) apply: only when the two offences forming the subject of prosecution are the same, i.e. the ingredients constituting the two offences are the same. If the offences under the two enactments are distinct and not identical, neither provision applies.
  • Section 27 — Meaning of service by post: where any legislation or regulation requires any document to be served by post, then unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by — (i) properly addressing, (ii) pre-paying, and (iii) posting by registered post — a letter containing the document, and to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post.
  • Section 28 — Citation of enactments (printed in the source as Section 3(28)): (1) in any Central Act or Regulation, and in any rule, bye-law, instrument or document made under or with reference to any such Act or Regulation, any enactment may be cited by reference to the title or short title (if any) conferred thereon, or by reference to the number and year thereof; and any provision in an enactment may be cited by reference to the section or sub-section in which the provision is contained. (2) In this Act and in any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act, a description or citation of a portion of another enactment shall, unless a different intention appears, be construed as including the word, section or other part mentioned as forming the beginning and as forming the end of the portion comprised in the description or citation.
  • Section 29 — Saving for previous enactments, rules and bye-laws: the provisions of this Act respecting the construction of Acts, Regulations, rules or bye-laws made after the commencement of this Act shall not affect the construction of any Act, Regulation, rule or bye-law which is continued or amended by an Act, Regulation, rule or bye-law made after the commencement of this Act.
  • Section 30 — Application of the Act to Ordinances: the expression "Central Act" wherever it occurs — except in Section 5, and the word "Act" in clauses (9), (13), (25), (40), (43), (53) and (54) of section 3 and in section 25 — shall be deemed to include an Ordinance made and promulgated by the Governor General under section 23 of the Indian Councils Act, 1861, or section 72 of the Government of India Act, 1915, or section 42 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and an Ordinance promulgated by the President under Article 123 of the Constitution.

Examples

  • Example 1 — Power to appoint a receiver (Rayarappan v. Madhavi Amma, A.I.R. 1950 F.C. 140): wherever the law provides that a court will have the power to appoint, suspend or remove a receiver, the legislature simply enacted that wherever convenient the court may appoint a receiver, and it was implied within that language that it may also remove or suspend him.
  • Example 2 — Right to catch fish (Ananda Behera v. State of Orissa): a claim of the right to catch fish came before the court, which had to decide whether the right to catch or carry fish is movable or immovable property. Section 3(26) of the General Clauses Act defines "immovable property" to include land, benefits to arise out of land, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth. Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act does not define the term except to say that immovable property does not include standing timber, growing crops or grass. As fish do not come under that category, the General Clauses Act definition applies, and as a profit a prendre (French for "right of taking" — the right of persons to share in land owned by another, enabling a person to take part of the soil or produce of land someone else owns) is regarded as a benefit arising out of land, it follows that it is immovable property within the meaning of the Transfer of Property Act. Conclusion: the court construed the "right to catch or carry fish" as immovable property.
  • Example 3 — Different sections have different reach: Section 3 (definitional clause) applies to the General Clauses Act itself and to all Central Acts and Regulations made after the commencement of the General Clauses Act in 1897. Section 4 (application of foregoing definitions to previous enactments) applies to Central Acts after January 3, 1868 and to Regulations made after January 14, 1887. So there is a difference in the applicability of each section as regards the statutes to which it applies.
  • Example 4 — Preamble of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881: "An Act to define and amend the law relating to Promissory Notes, Bills of Exchange and Cheque."
  • Example 5 — Preamble of the Companies Act, 2013: "An Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to companies."
  • Example 6 — Word defined in the same Act: the word 'Company' used in the Companies Act, 2013 is defined in section 2(20) of that very Act.
  • Example 7 — Word borrowed from another statute: the word 'Security' used in the Companies Act, 2013 is not defined in that Act; it is defined under section 2(h) of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and that meaning applies equivalently to the Companies Act, 2013. Similarly, 'Digital signature' used in the Companies Act shall be construed as per section 2(1)(p) of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
  • Example 8 — Word taken from the General Clauses Act: the word 'Affidavit' used in section 7 of the Companies Act, 2013 (incorporation of a company) derives its meaning from 'Affidavit' as defined in the General Clauses Act, 1897.
  • Example 9 — "Means" (exhaustive): section 2(20) of the Companies Act, 2013 — "Company" means a company incorporated under this Act or under any previous company law.
  • Example 10 — "Means" (exhaustive): section 2(34) of the Companies Act, 2013 — "director" means a director appointed to the Board of a company.
  • Example 11 — "Includes" (inclusive): 'debenture' in section 2(30) of the Companies Act, 2013 — "debenture" includes debenture stock, bonds or any other instrument of a company evidencing a debt, whether constituting a charge on the assets of the company or not. This is a definition of inclusive nature.
  • Example 12 — "Includes" (inclusive): "Body Corporate" or "Corporation" includes a company incorporated outside India [section 2(11) of the Companies Act, 2013]. This does not define "Body Corporate" — it merely states that companies incorporated outside India will also be covered, apart from other entities called body corporate.
  • Example 13 — "Means and includes" (exhaustive): 'Share' under section 2(84) of the Companies Act, 2013 — "Share" means a share in the share capital of a company and includes stock.
  • Example 14 — "May" read as "shall": Section 3 of the Companies Act, 2013 states "A company may be formed for any lawful purpose by…". Here the word "may" shall be read as "shall" — the usage makes compliance with section 3 mandatory for the formation of a company.
  • Example 15 — "May" read as "may": Section 21 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that documents/proceedings requiring authentication, or contracts made by or on behalf of the company, may be signed by any Key Managerial Personnel or an officer of the company duly authorised by the Board in this behalf. Here "may" shall be read as "may" (discretionary).
  • "Shall" and "may" in the same section (Labour Commr., M.P.V. v. Burhanpur Tapti Mill, AIR 1964 SC 1687): the use of "shall" with respect to one matter and "may" with respect to another matter in the same section of a statute will normally lead to the conclusion that "shall" imposes an obligation whereas "may" confers a discretionary power. In Sainik Motors v. State of Rajasthan, J. Hidayatullah observed: "the word Shall is ordinarily mandatory but it is sometimes not so interpreted if the context or the intention otherwise demands."
  • Example 16 — Trees are immovable property (Shantabai v. State of Bombay): the Supreme Court pointed out that trees must be regarded as immovable property because they are attached to or rooted in the earth. An agreement to convey forest produce like tendu leaves, timber, bamboos etc., the soil for making bricks, the right to build on and occupy the land for business purposes, and the right to grow new trees and to get leaves from trees that grow in future are all included in the term immovable property.
  • Example 17 — Right of way vs right to drain water: a right of way to access from one place to another may come within the definition of immovable property, whereas the right to drain water is not immovable property. Any machinery fixed to the soil and standing crops can be held to be immovable property according to the General Clauses Act, 1897.
  • Example 18 — Commencement of the Companies Act, 2013: the Act received the assent of the President of India on 29th August, 2013 and was notified in the Official Gazette on 30th August, 2013 with the enforcement of section 1 of the Act. Accordingly, the Companies Act, 2013 came into enforcement on the date of its publication in the Official Gazette.
  • Example 19 — Date specified in the notification prevails: the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) (Fifth Amendment) Regulations, 2015 were issued by SEBI vide Notification dated 14th August, 2015 with effect from 1 January, 2016. The regulation comes into force on 1st January, 2016 and not on the date of its notification in the Gazette.
  • Example 20 — Section 8 in action (Income Tax / Companies Act): section 115JB of the Income Tax Act, 1961 requires reference to the Companies Act, 1956 for the calculation of book profits. With the advent of the Companies Act, 2013 the corresponding change was not made in section 115JB. Applying section 8 of the General Clauses Act, book profits under section 115JB will be calculated as per the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Example 21 — Section 9 computation, dividend (AGM on 30/09/2022): a company declares dividend for its shareholders in its AGM held on 30/09/2022. Under the Companies Act, 2013 the company must pay the declared dividend within 30 days from the date of declaration, i.e. from 01/10/2022 to 30/10/2022. In this series of 30 days, 30/09/2022 is excluded and the last 30th day, 30/10/2022, is included.
  • Case on Section 10 (K. Soosalrathnam v. Div. Engineer, N.H.C. Tirunelveli): the Madras High Court held that since the last date of the prescribed period fell after the date of the notification declaring that day a holiday, then on the principles laid down in this section the last date of the prescribed period for obtaining the tender schedules was extended to the next working day.
  • Example 22 — Pro rata debtors: where several debtors are liable for the whole debt and each is liable for his own share or proportion only, they are said to be bound pro rata.
  • Example 23 — Pro rata dividend computation: a company has 100 shares outstanding and issues a dividend of ₹2 per share, so the total dividend paid is ₹200. No matter how many shareholders there are, the total dividend payments cannot exceed this limit — ₹200 is the whole, and the pro rata calculation determines each shareholder's portion. Assume four shareholders holding 50, 25, 15 and 10 shares. The amount due to each is their pro rata share, calculated by dividing each person's ownership by the total number of shares and multiplying the resulting fraction by the total dividend. The majority shareholder's portion is (50/100) × ₹200 = ₹100 — sensible, since he owns half the shares and receives half the dividend. The remaining shareholders get ₹50, ₹30 and ₹20 respectively.
  • Example 24 — Section 20 in action: the term 'collector' used in Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 will have the same meaning as in Section 3(c) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
  • Case on Section 27 — registered post AD (United Commercial Bank v. Bhim Sain Makhija, AIR 1994 Del 181): where a notice required under statutory rules to be sent by 'registered post acknowledgement due' is instead sent by 'registered post' only, the protection of the presumption regarding service of notice under 'registered post' under this section is neither tenable nor based upon sound exposition of law.
  • Case on Section 27 — refusal (Jagdish Singh v. Natthu Singh, AIR 1992 SC 1604): where a notice is sent to the landlord by registered post and the same is returned by the tenant with an endorsement of refusal, it will be presumed that the notice has been served.
  • Case on Section 27 — "not claimed / not met" (Smt. Vandana Gulati v. Gurmeet Singh alias Mangal Singh, AIR 2013 All 69): a notice sent by registered post to the person concerned at the proper address is deemed to be served in due course unless the contrary is proved; the endorsement 'not claimed / not met' is sufficient to prove deemed service of notice.
  • Case on Section 26 — alternative charges (State of M.P. v. V.R. Agnihotri, AIR 1957 SC 592): when there are two alternative charges in the same trial — e.g. section 409 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act — the fact that the accused is acquitted of one of the charges will not bar his conviction on the other.

Test Your Knowledge — MCQs (with answers)

  • MCQ 1: Which of the following is not an Immovable Property? (a) Land (b) Building (c) Timber (d) Machinery permanently attached to the land. Answer: (c) Timber.
  • MCQ 2: Where an Act of Parliament does not expressly specify any particular day as the day of coming into operation of such Act, then it shall come into operation on the day on which — (a) it receives the assent of the President (b) it receives the assent of the Governor General (c) it receives assent of both the Houses of Parliament (d) it receives assent of the Prime Minister. Answer: (a) It receives the assent of the President.
  • MCQ 3: An act or omission constitutes an offence under two enactments — which is correct? (a) prosecuted and punished only under the enactment enacted last (b) only under the enactment enacted first (c) under both the enactments (d) under either or any of those enactments, but shall not be punished twice for the same offence. Answer: (d).
  • MCQ 4: Every Act has a ………. which expresses the scope, object and purpose of the Act and is the main source for understanding the intention of the lawmaker. (a) Definition (b) Preamble (c) Affidavit (d) Document. Answer: (b) Preamble.

Test Your Knowledge — Descriptive Questions (with answers)

  • Q1 — What is "Financial Year"? Under Section 3(21), 'Financial Year' means the year commencing on the first day of April. Under Section 3(66), 'Year' means a year reckoned according to the British calendar, i.e. the calendar year from January to December. Conclusion: reading both, the financial year is a year which starts from the first day of April to the end of March.
  • Q2 — What is "Immovable Property"? Under Section 3(26) it shall include (i) land, (ii) benefits to arise out of land, and (iii) things attached to the earth, or (iv) permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth. Trees are immovable property because they are benefits arising out of the land and are attached to the earth; timber is not immovable property as it is not permanently attached to the earth. Buildings are immovable property.
  • Q3 — Whole-time KMP in more than one subsidiary: Section 203(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that a whole-time key managerial personnel shall not hold office in more than one company except in its subsidiary company at the same time. The issue is whether a whole-time KMP of a holding company may be appointed in more than one subsidiary or only in one. Section 13 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 provides that the singular shall include the plural, unless there is anything repugnant to the subject or context. Conclusion: a whole-time KMP may hold office in more than one subsidiary company as per the present law.
  • Q4 — Notice sent by 'registered post' where rules require 'registered post AD': Under Section 27, where any legislation or regulation requires a document to be served by post, then unless a different intention appears, service is deemed effected by (i) properly addressing, (ii) pre-paying, and (iii) posting by registered post — a letter containing the document, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post. Conclusion: since the statutory rules themselves provide that the notice must be sent by 'registered post acknowledgement due', sending it by 'registered post' only will not be compliance with those rules. However, if the statutory rules had not so provided, service by registered post only would be deemed effected. This follows United Commercial Bank v. Bhim Sain Makhija, AIR 1994 Del 181, where the presumption of service under 'registered post' was held neither tenable nor based upon sound exposition of law.
  • Q5 — X's land and fifty tamarind trees: X owned land with fifty tamarind trees. He sold his land and the timber (obtained after cutting the fifty trees) to Y, and asks whether the sale of timber amounts to a sale of immovable property. Applying the inclusive four-element definition in Section 3(26): Land is immovable property; however, timber cannot be immovable property since it is not attached to the earth. Where in any enactment the definition of immovable property is in the negative and not exhaustive, the General Clauses Act definition applies to that enactment.
  • Q6 — Meaning of service by post: Under Section 27, service is deemed effected by (i) properly addressing, (ii) pre-paying, and (iii) posting by registered post a letter containing the document — and to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post.
  • Q7 — Komal Ltd., AGM on 27th September, 2022: Applying Section 9 ("from" excludes the first day, "to" includes the last day):
    (i) Payment of dividend — under Section 127 of the Companies Act, 2013 the company must pay the declared dividend within 30 days from the date of declaration, i.e. from 28/09/2022 to 27/10/2022. 27/09/2022 is excluded and the 30th day, 27/10/2022, is included. Komal Ltd. must pay the dividend between 28/09/2022 and 27/10/2022 (both days inclusive).
    (ii) Transfer of unpaid/unclaimed dividend — under Section 124 of the Companies Act, 2013, where a dividend has been declared but not paid or claimed within 30 days from the date of declaration to any shareholder entitled to it, the company shall, within 7 days from the date of expiry of the said period of 30 days, transfer the total unpaid or unclaimed amount to a special account opened in any scheduled bank called the "Unpaid Dividend Account" (UDA). Therefore Komal Ltd. shall transfer the amount to the UDA within the period 28th October, 2022 to 3rd November, 2022 (both days inclusive).
  • Q8 — 'Repeal' vs 'deletion': In Navrangpura Gam Dharmada Milkat Trust v. Ramtuji Ramaji, AIR 1994 Guj 75 it was decided that 'Repeal' brings about complete obliteration (abolition) of the provision as if it never existed, thereby affecting all incoherent rights and all causes of action related to the repealed provision, while 'deletion' ordinarily takes effect from the date of the legislature effecting the said deletion, and never effects a total wiping out of the provision as if it never existed. This distinction is essential for the purposes of Section 6.
  • Q9 — Transfer of unpaid dividend where the 30 days expire on 30.10.2022: The Companies Act, 2013 requires the unpaid/unclaimed dividend to be transferred to the unpaid dividend account within 7 days from the date of expiry of the 30-day period. Applying Section 9, 30th October, 2022 is excluded and 6th November, 2022 is included, i.e. the transfer must be made between 31st October, 2022 and 6th November, 2022 (both days inclusive).
  • Q10 — Date of coming into force: (1) An Act of Parliament which has not specifically mentioned a particular date — under Section 5 it is implemented on the day on which it receives the assent of the President in the case of an Act of Parliament. (2) The SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) (Fifth Amendment) Regulations, 2015, issued vide Notification dated 14th August, 2015 with effect from 1st January, 2016 — since a specific date of enforcement is prescribed, the Regulations come into enforcement on 1st January, 2016 and not on the date of notification in the Gazette.
