Why It Matters / Application

The General Clauses Act is the reason a Companies Act, 2013 deadline expressed as "within thirty days from the date of declaration" can be converted into an exact pair of calendar dates: Section 9 supplies the exclusion of the first day and the inclusion of the last, and Section 10 rescues a filing whose last day falls on a day the Registry is closed. It is also the source of meaning for words the Companies Act, 2013 itself leaves undefined — "affidavit" in section 7 on incorporation, "document", "person", "immovable property", "financial year" — and for the singular/plural reading in Section 13 that decides whether a whole-time KMP may sit in one subsidiary or several under section 203(3). Sections 6, 6A, 7, 8 and 24 govern what survives when a company or securities law is repealed and re-enacted: accrued rights, incurred penalties, pending prosecutions and subordinate rules (as with the Mines Act 1923 → 1952, or the Companies Act 1956 reference in section 115JB of the Income Tax Act, 1961). Sections 14, 15, 16 and 21 explain why a power to appoint carries the power to suspend or dismiss, why an appointment may be made ex-officio, and why an authority that issued a notification may vary or rescind it more than once. Section 27 decides when a statutory notice is deemed served, which drives the validity of meeting notices, demand notices and tenancy notices.

Note

Exceptions, provisos and exam traps:

  • Every Section 3 definition is subject to the standing proviso "unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context", and yields to a special definition in the particular enactment. The "good faith" definition in Section 3(22) (honest, whether negligent or not) is a classic trap: it does not displace an enactment with its own definition. In Maung Aung Pu v. Maung Si Maung it was pointed out that "good faith" is not defined in the Indian Contract Act, 1872 and the General Clauses Act definition does not expressly apply to it — the civil-law understanding is that nothing is done in good faith which is done without due care and attention as expected of a man of ordinary prudence, and an honest purchase made carelessly without proper enquiries cannot be said to have been made in good faith so as to convey good title.
  • Timber trap: trees are immovable property (attached to the earth) but timber cut from them is not — the same fact pattern is examined both in the MCQ (answer "Timber") and in the descriptive question on X's fifty tamarind trees.
  • Section 6 does not cover everything: it applies to a repeal, not an omission, and to a Central Act or Regulation, not a Rule (Kolhapur Canesugar Works Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 2000 SC 811). Also, because "enactment" [Section 3(19)] includes any provision of an Act, Section 6 applies to the repeal of a single provision, not only of an entire Act.
  • Revival is never implied: under Section 7 a repealed enactment can be revived only by expressly stating that purpose.
  • Section 13(1) is not absolute: it is applied with circumspection in succession law ("male descendants" in Sections 7 and 8 of the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908 do not include female descendants), and it does not apply where a common-gender word was available but a specific-gender word was used ('bullocks' does not include 'cows').
  • Section 26 vs Article 20(2): double prosecution under two enactments is permitted; only double punishment for the same offence is barred — and both provisions apply only where the ingredients of the two offences are identical.
  • Section 22 rules are premature but valid: rules made between the passing and the commencement of an Act are validly made but do not take effect until commencement.
  • Section 23(5) is conclusive: once rules made after previous publication appear in the Official Gazette, irregularities in the publication of the draft cannot be questioned; and re-publication is unnecessary if the changes from the draft are merely ancillary.
  • Section 30 carve-outs: "Central Act" includes an Ordinance except in Section 5, and the word "Act" is so extended only in clauses (9), (13), (25), (40), (43), (53) and (54) of section 3 and in section 25.
  • Numbering quirks in the study material: the definition of "Enactment" is printed as "[Section 2(19)]" and "Citation of enactments" as "[Section 3(28)]" — these are Sections 3(19) and 28 respectively. Also note that Section 2 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 stands repealed, and Section 7(2) is printed as applying to Central Acts made after the third day of January, 1968 (elsewhere the Act uses 3rd January, 1868).

Other Laws · Chapter 2 — Interpretation of Statutes

Source: 87785bos-aps2160-p2-ch2.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Why a CA needs this: enactments are frequently capable of more than one interpretation; the chapter supplies the rules of interpretation, the internal and external aids, and the rules for construing deeds and documents.
  • Statute = will of the legislature: Maxwell defines "statute" as the will of the legislature. In India a statute is an enacted law — law made by Parliament or a State legislature. The Constitution provides for passing a Bill in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha and, after the assent of the President of India, it becomes an Act of Parliament or Statute. The Constitution itself does not use the term "statute"; it uses "law", defined as including any ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification and the like. In short, statute signifies written law as against unwritten law.
  • Interpretation vs Construction: where the Court adheres to the plain meaning of the language used by the legislature, it is interpretation; where the meaning is not plain and the court has to decide whether the wording was meant to cover the situation before it, the court resorts to construction. Conclusions drawn by construction are within the spirit though not necessarily within the letter of the law. In practice construction includes interpretation and the terms are frequently used synonymously. [Bhagwati Prasad Kedia v. C.I.T., (2001) — interpretation is the drawing of conclusions from a statute that lie beyond the direct expression of the words used therein.]
  • Words of legal import: words of legal import occurring in a statute which have acquired a definite and precise sense must be understood in that sense. (State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerly & Co., AIR 1958)
  • Grammatical vs Logical interpretation: grammatical (literal) interpretation concerns itself with the words and expressions used in a statute and only that — the emphasis is on "what the law says". Logical interpretation seeks to ascertain "what the law means". Normally grammatical interpretation is the only approach; the court cannot add to or modify a single word or phrase used in an enactment — absoluta sententia expositore non indiget ("clear words need no explanation").
  • When logic may displace grammar: where grammatical interpretation leads to a manifest absurdity or is logically flawed, the courts can adopt the logical interpretation that advances the true purpose of the legislation rather than reduce it to futility. Where two constructions are reasonably applicable — one mechanical and grammar-based, the other vibrant and more in tune with the basic intention of the Act — the latter shall be preferred. (Arora v. State of UP) But where the law is clear and unambiguous the court shall construe it on the strict grammatical meaning, however harsh or burdensome it may be.
  • Penalty with no named recipient: if a statute levies a penalty without expressly mentioning the recipient of the penalty, then by implication it goes to the coffers of the State.
  • Rules are guides only: the recognised rules of interpretation/construction are considered guides only and are not inflexible.

Key Definitions / Terms

Document — Section 3, Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Any matter expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures or marks, or by more than one of those means, intended to be used, or which may be used, for the purpose of recording that matter.
Document — Section 3(18), General Clauses Act, 1897
Shall include any matter written, expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures or marks, or by more than one of those means, which is intended to be used, or which may be used, for the purpose of recording this matter.
Four elements of a document
(i) Matter — used with the word "any", showing the definition is comprehensive; (ii) Record — some mutual or mechanical device employed on the substance, by writing, expression or description; (iii) Substance — that on which the mental or intellectual element takes permanent form; (iv) Means — that by which the permanent form is acquired: letters, figures, marks, symbols usable to communicate between two persons.
Instrument — Section 2(14), Indian Stamp Act, 1899
Includes every document by which any right or liability is, or purports to be, created, transferred, extended, extinguished or recorded. In common parlance, a formal legal document which creates or confirms a right or records a fact — an agreement, deed, charter or record drawn up and executed in technical form.
Deed (Legal Glossary)
An instrument in writing (or other legible representation or words on parchment or paper) purporting to effect some legal disposition. Deeds are instruments, though all instruments may not be deeds; however, in India no distinction seems to be made between instruments and deeds.
Interpretation
The process by which the Courts seek to ascertain the meaning of the legislature through the medium of the words in which it is expressed; the art of finding out the true sense of words, i.e. the sense in which their author intended to convey the subject matter. Resorted to in order to resolve ambiguity.
Construction
As applied to a written statute or document, to determine from its known elements its true meaning or the intention of its framers; it involves drawing conclusions beyond the actual expressions used, by referring to other parts of the enactment and the context in which the law was made.
Legal interpretation (Jolowicz, Lectures on Jurisprudence, 1963 ed., p. 280)
Where an actual rule of law binds the Judge to place a certain interpretation on the statute. Sub-divided into authentic (rule derived from the legislator himself) and usual (from some other source such as custom or case law). Justinian ordering that all difficulties out of his legislation be referred to him, and the Prussian Code, 1794 requiring Judges to report doubts to a Statute Commission and abide by its ruling, are examples of authentic interpretation.
Doctrinal interpretation
Interpretation whose purpose is to discover the "real" and "true" meaning of the statute. Divided into grammatical (court applies only the ordinary rules of speech) and logical (court goes beyond the words to discover the intention of the statute in some other way).
Literal and Functional interpretation (Fitzerald; Salmond: Jurisprudence, 12th ed., pp. 131–132)
Literal regards conclusively the verbal expression of the law and does not look beyond the literaligis. Functional departs from the letter of the law and seeks elsewhere for other and more satisfactory evidence of the true intention of the legislature.
Mandatory provision
Where the enactment prescribes that the contemplated action be taken without any option or discretion. It must be strictly observed.
Directory provision
Where the acting authority is vested with discretion, choice or judgment. It is sufficient that it is substantially complied with.
Non-obstante clause
A clause beginning "notwithstanding anything contained"; unlike a "subject to" clause it makes the provision prevail over the others mentioned in it. (K. Parasurammaiah v. Pakari Lakshman, AIR 1965 AP 220)

Classification of Interpretation

ClassSub-classMeaning
Legal (an actual rule of law binds the Judge)AuthenticRule of interpretation derived from the legislator himself
UsualRule derived from some other source such as custom or case law
Doctrinal (purpose is to find the real and true meaning)GrammaticalCourt applies only the ordinary rules of speech to find the meaning of the words used
LogicalCourt goes beyond the words and tries to discover the intention of the statute in some other way

Why Interpretation Is Needed

  • Laws are drafted with care, but such a degree of precision as to be free from all ambiguity is perhaps unattainable; legislators cannot foresee all contingencies at the time of passing the law.
  • Words of a statute may be vague, ambiguous or reasonably capable of more than one meaning — it is then that a need for interpretation/construction arises. Rules of interpretation are required to ensure just and uniform decisions.
  • Denning L.J. on the need: "It is not within human powers to foresee the manifold sets of facts which may arise; and that, even if it were, it is not possible to provide for them in terms free from all ambiguity. The English language is not an instrument of mathematical precision. Our literature would be much the poorer if it were… when a defect appears, a judge cannot simply fold his hands and blame the draftsman. He must set to work on the constructive task of finding the intention of Parliament, and he must do this, not only from the language of the statute, but also from a consideration of the social conditions which gave rise to it, and of the mischief which it was passed to remedy, and then he must supplement the written word so as to give 'force and life' to the intention of the legislature."
  • Where the intention is express, the task is one of verbal construction alone; where no intention is expressed but some intention must of necessity be imputed, the interpreter determines it by inference based on legal principles, and the interpretation adopted must be commensurate with the public benefit.

How It Works / Logic — Primary Rules

  • (1) Rule of Literal Construction: the intention of the legislature must be found in the words used by the legislature itself. If the words are capable of one construction only, the court may not adopt a hypothetical construction on the ground that it is more consistent with the alleged object and policy of the Act. Maxim: absoluta sententia expositore non indiget — "an absolute sentence or preposition needs not an expositor", i.e. plain words require no explanation.
  • Narrower vs wider choice: where a choice must be made between a narrower and a wider/bolder interpretation, if the narrower interpretation would fail to achieve the manifest purpose of the legislation, the wider one should be adopted. Applied to disclosure of "the nature of concern or interest, financial or otherwise" of a director or manager under section 102 of the Companies Act, 2013: it must be read broadly to cover any information and facts enabling members to understand the meaning, scope and implications of the items of business — a full and frank disclosure without reservation or suppression. For instance, where a son, daughter, father, mother, brother or sister is concerned in any contract or matter, the shareholders ought fairly to be informed and the material facts disclosed. A restricted narrow interpretation would defeat the very purpose of disclosure.
  • Courts cannot legislate: a matter which should have been, but has not been, provided for in a statute cannot be supplied by courts — to do so would amount to legislation and not construction.
  • Natural and grammatical meaning: statutes are first understood in their natural, ordinary or popular sense. If there is inconsistency with any express intention or declared purpose, or it involves absurdity, repugnancy or inconsistency, the grammatical sense must then be modified, extended or abridged only to avoid such an inconvenience, but no further. [State of HP v. Pawan Kumar (2005)]
  • Technical words in technical sense: technical words are understood in the technical sense only.
  • (2) Rule of Reasonable Construction (Golden Rule): words must be construed ut res magis valeat quam pereat — so as to lead to a sensible meaning. Only when the words of an enactment are capable of two constructions is there scope for interpretation; then the interpretation which furthers the object is preferred to one likely to defeat or impair the policy or object. Where grammatical interpretation leads to a manifest absurdity, the court interprets so as to resolve the inconsistency and make the enactment a consistent whole — maxim Interpretatio fienda est ut res magis valeat quam pereat. The departure from grammatical construction is permissible only to the extent it avoids the absurdity and no further. This is also called the Golden Rule of Interpretation. The court departs from the dictionary meaning to adopt a construction which advances the remedy and suppresses the mischief, provided the Court does not have to resort to conjecture or surmise.
  • (3) Rule of Harmonious Construction: applied when there is a conflict between two provisions of a statute, or between the provisions and the object the legislature had in view. The statute must be read as a whole and every provision construed with reference to the context and other clauses so as to make it a consistent enactment and not reduce it to futility. Where an expression is susceptible of a narrow/technical meaning as well as a popular meaning, the court is justified in assuming the legislature used it in the sense which carries out its objects, and in rejecting that which renders it invalid. (New India Sugar Mills Ltd. v. Commissioner, Sales Tax)
  • Specific overrides general: where it is not possible to give effect to both provisions harmoniously, collision may be avoided by holding that one section merely provides an exception or a specific rule different from the general rule in the other. A specific rule will override a general rule — generalia specialibus non derogant.
  • Limit on the harmonious rule: it can be adopted only where there is a real and not merely apparent conflict. Where the words on a reasonable construction admit of one meaning only, that natural meaning prevails and the court shall not attempt an interpretation based on equity and harmonious construction.
  • (4) The Rule in Heydon's Case / Mischief Rule — see the dedicated table below.
  • (5) Rule of Beneficial Construction: strictly not a rule but a method of interpreting a provision liberally so as to give effect to the declared intention of the legislation. Given to statutes bringing into effect provisions for improving the conditions of classes of people who are underprivileged or who have not been treated fairly in the past; in such cases an extended meaning may be given to words or clauses. But this can be done only when two constructions are reasonably possible and not when the words are quite unequivocal.
  • (6) Rule of Exceptional Construction: Maxwell goes to the extent of stating, "notwithstanding the general rule that full effect must be given to every word, yet if no sensible meaning can be given to a word or phrase, or if it would defeat the real object of the enactment, it may, or rather it should, be eliminated." This rule covers the treatment of "and"/"or" and "may"/"must"/"shall".
  • (7) Rule of Ejusdem Generis: "of the same kind or species" — where specific words pertaining to a class, category or genus are followed by general words, the general words shall be construed as limited to things of the same kind as those specified. It is not an absolute rule of law but part of a wider principle of construction, and has no application where the intention of the legislature is clear.

Heydon's Case — the Four Questions

In Heydon's Case (1584, 3 Co Rep 79 p. 637) the Barons of the Exchequer laid down that "for the true and sure interpretation of all Statutes in general, four things are to be discerned and considered":

#Question
1What was the law before the making of the Act?
2What was the defect, mischief, hardship caused by the earlier law (the mischief or defect for which the law did not provide)?
3How does the Act of Parliament seek to resolve or cure the mischief or deficiency (what is the remedy the Act has provided)?
4What are the true reasons for the remedy?
  • The courts shall then make such construction as will suppress the mischief and advance the remedy and suppress subtle inventions and evasions for the continuance of the mischief. Courts are bound to look at the state of the law at the time of passing the enactment — not only as it then stood, but under previous Statutes too.
  • Kanai Lal Paramnidhi, 1957 S.C.A. 1033 — the Supreme Court held that the observations of the Chief Baron and Barons of the Exchequer in Heydon's Case have been so frequently cited with approval by courts administering welfare enactments that they have attained the status of a classic on the subject and their validity cannot be challenged.
  • CIT v. Sodra Devi, 1957 SC 823 at 832–835 / (1957) 32 ITR 615 (SC) — the mischief rule can be applied only if there is ambiguity in the present law, i.e. only when the words used are reasonably capable of more than one meaning.
  • Even where the usual meaning of the language falls short of the whole object of the legislature, a more extended meaning may be attributed, provided the words are fairly susceptible of it. Where the object of an enactment is public safety, its working must be interpreted widely — thus in the case of the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923, the main object being provision of compensation to workmen, it was held the Act ought to be so construed, as far as possible, as to give effect to its primary provisions.

Ejusdem Generis — Conditions and Exceptions

Applies when (all five)Does NOT apply where (exceptions)
1. The statute contains an enumeration of specific words1. The preceding term is general, as well as that which follows
2. The subject of enumeration constitutes a class or category2. The particular words exhaust the whole genus
3. That class or category is not exhausted by the enumeration3. The specific objects enumerated are essentially diverse in character
4. General terms follow the enumeration4. There is an express intention of the legislature that the general term shall not be read ejusdem generis with the specific terms
5. There is no indication of a different legislative intent 

Companies Act illustration: the fifth ground contained in section 271(e) of the Companies Act, 2013 shall not be read ejusdem generis with the earlier five, although it is a general phrase following specific phrases — because the earlier grounds are essentially diverse in character.

Secondary Rules — Noscitur a Sociis and Contemporanea Expositio

  • Noscitur a Sociis: when two or more words susceptible of analogous meaning are coupled together, they are understood to be used in their cognate sense. They take their colour from each other — the meaning of the more general word being restricted to a sense analogous to that of the less general.
  • Contemporanea Expositio: a statute or document is to be interpreted by referring to the exposition it has received from contemporary authority. Contemporanea Expositio est optima et fortissinia in lege — "contemporaneous exposition is the best and strongest in the law", i.e. a law should be understood in the sense in which it was understood at the time when it was passed. Optima legum interpres est consuetudo — "Custom is the best interpreter of law". Caution: this maxim is to be applied for construing ancient statutes, but not to Acts that are comparatively modern. (However, contemporary official statements throwing light on the construction of a statute and statutory instruments made under it have been used as contemporanea expositio to interpret not only ancient but even recent statutes in India.)

"And"/"Or" and "May"/"Must"/"Shall"

  • "And" is a particle joining words and sentences expressing the relation of connection or addition — normally conjunctive, signifying that something follows in addition to that which precedes. "Or" is a disjunctive particle marking an alternative, generally corresponding to "either", as "either this or that".
  • Sometimes "and" is read as "or" and vice versa, to give effect to the manifest intention of the legislature as disclosed from the context. (Municipal Council v. Bishandas Nathumal, AIR 1969 MP 147) "And" may legitimately be construed as "or" when the intention of the legislature is clear and any other construction would tend to defeat that intention. (Amulya Chandra Roy v. Pashupathi Nath, AIR 1951 Cal 48) Where statements or stipulations are coupled by "and/or" they are to be read either disjunctively or conjunctively.
  • "May" signifies permission and implies discretion; "Shall" in the normal sense imports a command; "Must" is doubtlessly a word of command. All three should initially be deemed to have been used in their natural and ordinary sense, but in all cases the intention of the legislature guides the interpreter.
  • Where the normal significance of imperative and permissive terms leads to absurd, inconvenient or unreasonable results, they should be discarded.
  • "May" read as "shall": where "may" has been used as implying a requisite condition to be fulfilled, the court will and ought to exercise the powers which it should, and there "may" has compulsory force. Cotton, L.J. observed: "May can never mean 'must' so long as the English language retains its meaning; but it gives a power and then it may be a question, in what case, when any authority or body has a power given to it by the word 'may' it becomes its duty to exercise that power." [In re Baker, Nichols v. Baker (1890) 44 Ch. D. 262]
  • "Shall" read as "may": the use of "shall" does not always mean the enactment is obligatory or mandatory — it depends on the context and other circumstances. The employment of the auxiliary verb "shall" is inconclusive, and the mere absence of the imperative is not conclusive either.
  • Test for mandatory vs directory: decided not merely on any specific provision setting out the consequences of omission, but on the purpose for which the requirement was enacted, in the context of other provisions and the general scheme of the Act — including whether the requirement is insisted on as a protection for safeguarding the right or liberty of person or of property. If a provision gives a power coupled with a duty, it is mandatory; whether it is so depends on (i) the nature of the thing empowered to be done, (ii) the object for which it is done, and (iii) the person for whose benefit the power is to be exercised. Look to substance and not merely form — an enactment in mandatory form might substantially be directory and, conversely, a statute in directory form may in substance be mandatory.

"Subject to", "Notwithstanding" and "Without prejudice"

TermEffect
Subject toWhere the same subject matter is covered by that provision and by another provision/enactment subject to which it operates, and there is a conflict, the latter prevails over the former. The clause using "subject to" is subservient. This limitation cannot operate where the subject matter of the two provisions is not the same.
Notwithstanding (non-obstante)Makes the provision prevail over the other provision(s) mentioned therein.
Without prejudiceWhere particular provisions follow general provisions and are stated to be without prejudice to them, the particular provisions do not restrict or circumscribe the operation and generality of the preceding general provisions — they operate in addition to and not in derogation of the general provisions.

The Four Levels at which a Notwithstanding Clause Operates

ClauseEffectExample from the source
1. "Notwithstanding anything contained in another section or sub-section of that statute"Overrides such other section(s)/sub-section(s)Section 42(11), Companies Act, 2013: "(11) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (9) and sub-section (10), any private placement issue not made in compliance of the provisions of sub-section (2) shall be deemed to be a public offer and all the provisions of this Act and the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 shall be applicable."
2. "Notwithstanding anything contained in a statute"Overrides the entire enactmentSection 8(8), Companies Act, 2013: "(8) ……. amalgamated with another company registered under this section and having similar objects, then, notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in this Act, the Central Government may, by order, provide for such amalgamation to form a single company with such constitution……"
3. "Notwithstanding anything contained in other enactment"Prevails over the specific section(s)/sub-section(s) or all the provisions contained in another statute(i) Section 7A, Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956: "…and on such publication, the rules as approved by the Central Government shall be deemed to have been validly made notwithstanding anything contained in the Companies Act, 1956." (ii) Section 183, Companies Act, 2013: "183(1) The Board of Directors of any company or any person or authority exercising the powers of the Board of Directors of a company, or of the company in general meeting, may, notwithstanding anything contained in sections 180, 181 and section 182 or any other provision of this Act or in the memorandum, articles or any other instrument relating to the company, contribute such amount as it thinks fit to the National Defence Fund or any other Fund approved by the Central Government for the purpose of national defence."
4. "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force"Overrides all other laws(i) Section 8, Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956: "… the rules so made are amended shall, notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in the Companies Act, 1956, or in any other law for the time being in force, have effect…". (ii) Section 243(1B), Companies Act, 2013: "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of this Act, or any other law for the time being in force, or any contract, memorandum or articles, on the removal of a person from the officer of a director or any other officer connected with the conduct and management of the affairs of the company, that person shall not be entitled to, or be paid, any compensation for the loss or termination of officer."

Internal Aids to Interpretation

  • (a) Long Title: the Short Title merely identifies the enactment and is chosen for convenience; the Long Title describes the enactment and does not merely identify it. It is now settled that the Long Title is part of the Act and may be referred to for ascertaining the object, scope and purpose, and for throwing light on construction — although it cannot override the clear meaning of the enactment. [Aswini Kumar Ghose v. Arabinda Bose, AIR 1952 SC]
  • (b) Preamble: expresses the scope, object and purpose of the Act more comprehensively than the Long Title; may recite the ground and cause of making the statute and the evil sought to be remedied. It is part of the enactment and can legitimately be used for construing it, but does not over-ride the plain provision of the Act. It discloses the primary intention of the legislature but can be brought in as an aid to construction only if the language of the statute is not clear. If there is any conflict between the preamble and any provision of an Act, the provision prevails; a provision cannot be considered invalid merely because it does not accord with the preamble. Two situations where courts refer to the preamble: (1) where there is any ambiguity in the words of an enactment, to resolve the conflict; (2) where the words appear too general in scope or application, to determine the scope or limited application for which the words are meant.
  • (c) Heading and Title of a Chapter: headings/titles prefixed to sections or groups of sections can legitimately be referred to for construing the enactment or its parts, and can be used to determine the sense of any doubtful expression in a section ranged under a particular heading. They cannot control the plain meaning of the words, though they may be looked at in the light of the preamble if there is ambiguity. Headings may sometimes be referred to in order to know the scope of a section, in the same way as the preamble. But a heading cannot control or override a section. (Official Assignee v. Chuni Ram, AIR 1933 Bom 51)
  • (d) Marginal Notes: summaries/side notes at the side of a section or group of sections purporting to sum up their effect. They are not part of the enactment — they were not present when the Act was passed in Parliament but inserted after — hence they are not an aid to construction. In C.I.T. v. Ahmedbhai Umarbhai & Co. (AIR 1950 SC 134 at 141), Patanjali Shastri, J. declared: "Marginal notes in an Indian statute, as in an Act of Parliament, cannot be referred to for the purpose of construing the statute". Many cases show reference to marginal notes may be permissible in exceptional cases [Deewan Singh v. Rajendra Pd. Ardevi, (2007) 10 SCC; Sarabjit Rick Singh v. Union of India, (2008) 2 SCC]. However, marginal notes appended to Articles of the Constitution have been held to be part of the Constitution as passed by the Constituent Assembly and have therefore been used in construing the Articles.
  • (e) Definitional Sections / Interpretation Clauses: where a word is defined as having a particular meaning, that meaning alone must be given to it in interpreting a Section, unless there be anything repugnant in the context — an exhaustive definition. The Court cannot ignore an exhaustive statutory definition and extract what it considers the true meaning independently of it. Two-fold purpose: (i) to provide a key to the proper interpretation of the enactment; (ii) to shorten the language of the enacting part by avoiding repetition of the same words every time the legislature refers to those expressions.
  • (f) Illustrations: illustrations follow the text of the Sections and therefore do not form part of the Sections; they do form part of the statute and are of relevance and value in construing the text. However, illustrations cannot modify the language of the section and can neither curtail nor expand the ambit of the section.
  • (g) Proviso: its normal function is to except something out of the enactment or to qualify something stated in it which would be within its purview if the proviso were not there. Usually embedded in the main body of the section and an integral part of it; begins with "provided that". It qualifies the preceding enactment which is expressed in terms too general. Ordinarily a proviso is not interpreted as stating a general rule. A proviso or exception embraces only the field covered by the main provision — it carves out an exception to the main provision to which it has been enacted as a proviso and to no other. (Ram Narain Sons Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax, AIR 1955 SC 765)
  • (h) Explanation: appended to a section to explain the meaning of certain words or phrases used in it, or the purport of the section. It may be added to include something within the section or to exclude something from it. It should normally be read so as to harmonise with and clear up any ambiguity in the main section and should not be construed to widen the ambit of the section.
  • (i) Schedules: form part of an Act and must be read together with it for all purposes of construction. But the expressions in the Schedule cannot control or prevail over the expression in the enactment; if there appears to be any inconsistency, the enactment shall always prevail. Schedules often contain details and forms for working out the policy underlying the sections — for example the schedules appended to the Companies Act, 2013 and to the Constitution of India.
  • (j) Read the Statute as a Whole: construction is to be made of all its parts taken together and not of one part only. The deed/Act must be read as a whole, and the words of each clause interpreted so as to bring them into harmony with other provisions, if that does no violence to the meaning of which they are naturally susceptible. One of the safest guides to construing sweeping general words is to examine other words of like import in the same enactment or instrument to see what limitations must be imposed on them; if a number of such expressions have to be subjected to limitations and qualifications of the same nature, that is a strong argument for subjecting the disputed expression to a similar limitation.

Construction of Definitions — "Means", "Includes", "Deemed to include"

Wording in the definitionNature of the definition
"means"Prima facie restrictive and exhaustive — the meaning of the word must be restricted to that given in the definition section
"includes"Prima facie extensive — the word defined is not restricted to the meaning assigned but has an extensive meaning which also includes the assigned meaning
"means and includes"Exhaustive
"to apply to and include"Extensive
"is deemed to include"Inclusive/extensive — used to bring in, by a legal fiction, something within the word defined which according to its ordinary meaning is not included in it
  • Three headings for construing definitions: (i) restrictive and extensive definitions; (ii) ambiguous definitions; (iii) definitions subject to a contrary context.
  • Ambiguous definitions must be interpreted in the light of the other provisions of the Act and having regard to the ordinary meaning of the word defined; such a definition is not to be read in isolation but in the context of the phrase which it defines — the function of a definition is to give accuracy and certainty to a word which would otherwise be vague, not to contradict it or depose it altogether.
  • Definitions subject to a contrary context: where a word is defined to bear a number of inclusive meanings, the sense in which it is used in a particular provision must be ascertained from the context of the scheme of the Act, the language of the provision and the object intended to be served.
  • Universal principle: where an expression is defined in an Act, it must be taken to have throughout the Act the meaning assigned by the definition, unless doing so creates a repugnancy in the subject or context.

External Aids to Interpretation

  • (a) Historical Setting: the history of the external circumstances that led to the enactment is of much significance. All external/historical facts necessary to understand the subject matter, scope and object of the enactment may be used — history in general and Parliamentary History in particular, ancient statutes, contemporary or other authentic works and writings. One must also consider whether the statute was intended to alter the law or leave it where it stood before.
  • (b) Consolidating Statutes & Previous Law: where a Preamble contains expressions such as "An Act to consolidate" the previous law, courts may stick to the presumption that it is not intended to alter the law, and may solve doubtful points with the aid of that presumed intention, rejecting the literal construction.
  • (c) Usage: acts done under a statute often provide the key to the statute itself. Where the meaning of the language is doubtful, usage — how the language has been interpreted and acted upon over a long period — may determine its true meaning. Where a legislative measure of doubtful meaning has for several years received an interpretation generally acted upon by the public, the Courts should be very unwilling to change it unless they see cogent reasons. A uniform notorious practice under an old statute plus the inaction of the Legislature to amend it are important factors showing the practice was based on a correct understanding of the law; when usage receives judicial or legislative approval it gains additional weight.
  • (d) Earlier & Later Acts and Analogous Acts:
    • Exposition of one Act by the language of another: where different Statutes are in pari materia (an analogous case) — though made at different times, or even expired and not referring to each other — they shall be taken and construed together as one system and as explanatory of each other. If two Acts are read together, every part of each has to be construed as if contained in one composite Act; but a clear discrepancy may make it necessary to hold that the later Act (in point of time) modified the earlier one. This does not mean every word in the later Act is interpreted the same way as in the earlier Act.
    • Where the later of the two Acts provides that the earlier Act should, so far as consistent, be construed as one with it, then an enactment in the later statute that nothing therein should include debentures was held to exclude debentures from the earlier statute as well.
    • Where a single section of Act 'A' is incorporated into Act 'B', it must be read in the sense it bore in the original Act; it is legitimate to refer to all the rest of Act 'A' to ascertain what that section means, though only one section is incorporated into Act 'B'.
    • Earlier Act explained by the later Act: the later Act sometimes furnishes a legislative interpretation of the earlier one — if it is in pari materia and if, but only if, the provisions of the earlier Act are ambiguous. Where the earlier statute contained a negative provision and the later merely omits it, that cannot by itself amount to substantive affirmation; it is necessary to see how the law would have stood without the original provision and the terms in which the repealed sections are re-enacted.
    • Reference to a Repealed Act: a repealed part of an Act loses its operative force, but may still be taken into account for construing the un-repealed part, because it is part of the history of the new Act.
  • (e) Dictionary Definitions: first refer to the Act to see whether the word is defined in it; only where it is not defined may dictionaries be used to find the general sense in which the word is commonly understood. In selecting one out of several meanings, the context in which it is used in the Act must always be taken into account — meanings take their colour from the context. Judicial decisions laying down the meaning of words in construing statutes in pari materia carry greater weight than dictionary meanings; for technical terms, reference may be made to technical dictionaries.
  • (f) Use of Foreign Decisions: decisions of countries following the same system of jurisprudence as ours, given on laws similar to ours, can legitimately be used for construing our own Acts. But prime importance is always given to the language of the Indian statute, and where guidance can be obtained from Indian decisions, reference to foreign decisions may become unnecessary.

Rules of Interpretation of Deeds and Documents

  • Reasonable-man test: one has to find out what a reasonable man, who has taken care to inform himself of the surrounding circumstances of the deed/document and of its scope and intendments, would understand by the words used.
  • Read as a whole (Lord Watson): a deed must be read as a whole to ascertain the true meaning of its several clauses, and the words of each clause should be so interpreted as to bring them into harmony with other provisions, if that interpretation does no violence to the meaning of which they are naturally susceptible. The same approach applies with equal force to Acts and Rules.
  • Golden rule of construction of deeds: ascertain the intention of the parties to the instrument after considering all the words in their ordinary, natural sense; consider the relevant portion of the document as a whole and take into account the circumstances under which the particular words were used, as well as the status and training of the parties using the words. (Ramkishorelal v. Kamalnarayan, 1963 (Sup.) 2 S.C.R. 417 — it may not be reasonable to give the strict conveyancer's interpretation of a word when it is used by one not equally skilled in the art of conveyancing.)
  • No cross-reference between deeds: it is inexpedient to construe the terms of one deed by reference to the terms of another. (Nirmala Bala Ghose v. Balai Chand Ghose, (1965) 2 S.C.W.R. 988)
  • Same word, same meaning: the same word cannot have two different meanings in the same document, unless the context compels the adoption of such a course. (Kultar Singh v. Mukhtiar Singh, 1964, 7 S.C.R. 790)
  • Meaning that saves all clauses: where the same word understood in one sense gives effect to all the clauses in the deed, while in another sense it would render one or more clauses ineffective, the word should be understood in the former sense.
  • Conflict between clauses: an effort must be made to resolve the conflict by interpreting the clauses so that all are given effect. If that is not possible, the earlier clause overrides the latter. Likewise, where one part of the document conflicts with another, read the two harmoniously; if impossible, the earlier part prevails and the latter should be disregarded.

Examples (every example in the source)

  • Example 1 — What counts as a document: a writing is a document; any words printed or photographed are documents.
  • Example 2 — Betel leaves (Ramavtar v. Assistant Sales Tax Officer, AIR 1961 SC 1325): the question was whether the sale of betel leaves was subject to sales tax. Held: betel leaves could not be given the dictionary, technical or botanical meaning when the ordinary and natural meaning is clear and unambiguous. Being a word of everyday use, it must be understood in its popular sense by which people are conversant with it, as also the meaning the statute dealing with the matter would attribute to it. Therefore, the sale of betel leaves was liable to sales tax.
  • Technical words — "practice" (Ashwini Kumar Ghose v. Arabinda Bose, AIR 1952 SC 369): in construing the word "practice" in the Supreme Court Advocates Act, 1951, it was observed that practice of law generally involves the exercise of both the functions of acting and pleading on behalf of a litigant party. When the legislature confers on an advocate the right to practise in a court, that expression authorises him to appear and plead as well as to act on behalf of suitors in that court.
  • Example 3 — "Subject to" [Section 13(2), Companies Act, 2013]: "Any change in the name of a company shall be subject to the provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 4 and shall not have effect except with the approval of the Central Government in writing." Implication: any change in the name of the company has to be in accordance with the provisions of section 4(2) and section 4(3) of the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Example 4 — Notwithstanding clause at four levels: reproduced in full in the table above (sections 42(11), 8(8), 183 and 243(1B) of the Companies Act, 2013 and sections 7A and 8 of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956).
  • Example 5 — "Without prejudice" [Section 4(3), Companies Act, 2013]: "Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (2), a company shall not be registered with a name which contains……" Implication: while registering (and deciding) the name of the company as per section 4(3), the provisions of section 4(2) shall also be operative.
  • Example 6 — Prize Competition Act, 1955 (RMD Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India, AIR 1957 SC 628): section 2(d) defines "prize competition" as "any competition in which prizes are offered for the solution of any puzzle based upon the building up arrangement, combination or permutation of letters, words or figures". Issue: whether the Act applies to competitions involving substantial skill and not in the nature of gambling. The Supreme Court referred to the previous state of law, to the mischief that continued under that law, and to the resolutions of various States under Article 252(1) authorising Parliament to pass the Act, and held: "having regard to the history of the legislation, the declared object thereof and the wording of the statute, we are of opinion that the competitions which are sought to be controlled and regulated by the Act are only those competitions in which success does not depend on any substantial degree of skill."
  • Noscitur a Sociis Example — "Fresh orange juice is not a fruit juice" (Commissioners v. Savoy Hotel, (1966) 2 All E.R. 299): a Purchase Tax Act used the expression "manufactured beverages including fruit-juices and bottled waters and syrups". Held: the description "fruit juices" must be construed in the context of the preceding words, and orange-juice unsweetened and freshly pressed was not within the description.
  • Noscitur a Sociis Example — "Private dispensary of a doctor is not a commercial establishment" (Dr. Devendra M. Surti v. State of Gujarat, A.I.R. 1969 SC 63): section 2(4) of the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948 defines commercial establishment as "an establishment which carries on any business, trade or profession". Held: the word "profession" was construed with the associated words "business" and "trade", and a private dispensary of a doctor was not within the definition.
  • Contemporanea Expositio Example — Cox v. Leigh, 43 LJQB 123: the court was influenced in its construction of a statute of Anne by the fact that the construction contended for was the one that had been generally considered as the true one for one hundred and sixty years.
  • Example 7 — Long Title: the full title of the Supreme Court Advocates (Practice in High Courts) Act, 1951 specifies that this is an Act to authorise Advocates of the Supreme Court to practise as of right in any High Court.
  • Example 8 — Preamble and "may" (Gullipoli Sowria Raj v. Bandaru Pavani, (2009) 1 SCC 714): the word "may" in section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 — "a marriage may be solemnized between two Hindus….." — was construed as mandatory in the sense that both parties to the marriage must be Hindus as defined in section 2 of the Act. Held: a marriage between a Christian male and a Hindu female solemnised under the Hindu Marriage Act was void. The result was reached also having regard to the preamble, which reads: "An Act to amend and codify the law relating to marriage among Hindus".
  • Example 9 — "any" in a definition: the use of the word "any" in a definition connotes extension, for "any" is a word of very wide meaning and prima facie its use excludes limitation.
  • Example 10 — Inclusive definitions: (i) the inclusive definition of lease under section 2(16)(c) of the Stamp Act, 1899 has been widely construed to cover transactions for the purposes of the Stamp Act which may not amount to a lease under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. [State of Uttarakhand v. Harpal Singh Rawat, (2011) 4 SCC 575] (ii) Section 2(m) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 contains an inclusive definition of "person" — held to include a company although a company is not specifically named therein. [Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation v. Ashok Iron Works Pvt. Ltd., (2009) 3 SCC 240]
  • Example 11 — "Deemed to include": if A is deemed to be B, then compliance with A is in law compliance with B, and contravention of A is in law contravention of B.
  • Example 12 — Ambiguous definition, "retrenchment": termination of service of a seasonal worker after the work was over does not amount to retrenchment under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 [Anil Bapurao Karase v. Krishna Sahkari Sakhar Karkhana, AIR 1997 SC 2698]. But the termination of employment of a daily wager engaged in a project, on completion of the project, will amount to retrenchment if the worker had not been told when employed that his employment would end on completion of the project [S.M. Nilajkar v. Telecom District Manager, Karnataka, (2003) 4 SCC].
  • Example 13 — Illustrations cannot modify a section (Privy Council): in holding that section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 does not permit the award of interest as damages for mere detention of a debt, the Privy Council rejected the argument that the illustration given in the Act could be used to arrive at a contrary result. It was observed that nor can an illustration have the effect of modifying the language of the section, which alone forms the enactment.
  • Example 14 — Read the statute as a whole, "notice": if one section of an Act requires that "notice" should be given, then a verbal notice would generally be sufficient. But if another section provides that notice should be "served" on the person or "left" with him, or in a particular manner or place, then that would obviously indicate that a written notice was intended.
  • Earlier & later bye-laws — the chairman example: suppose the earlier bye-law limited the appointment of the chairman of an organisation to a person possessed of certain qualifications, and the later bye-law authorises the election of any person to be chairman. The later bye-law would be so construed as to harmonise and not conflict with the earlier one: "any person" in the later bye-law would be understood to mean only any eligible person having the requisite qualifications provided in the earlier bye-law.
  • Example — "Means" vs "Includes" in the Companies Act, 2013: Director [section 2(34)] — "Director means a director appointed to the board of a company"; the word "means" suggests an exhaustive definition. Whole-time director [section 2(94)] — "Whole-time director includes a director in the whole-time employment of the company"; the word "includes" suggests an extensive definition, so other directors may be included in the category of whole-time director.
  • Example — Gaurav Textile Company Limited (Descriptive Q.4): Gaurav Textile Company Limited has entered into a contract with a company and you are invited to read and interpret the contract document. Rules to apply: find what a reasonable man informed of the surrounding circumstances, scope and intendments would understand by the words; it is inexpedient to construe the terms of one deed by reference to another; the same word cannot have two different meanings in the same document unless the context compels it; apply the Golden Rule — ascertain the intention of the parties after considering all the words in their ordinary, natural sense, reading the relevant portions as a whole, taking into account the circumstances in which the words were used and the status and training of the parties; where the same word in one sense gives effect to all clauses and in another renders some ineffective, adopt the former sense; and where clauses conflict irreconcilably, the earlier clause overrides the latter.

Objects of an Explanation — Sundaram Pillai v. Pattabiraman

In Sundaram Pillai v. Pattabiraman, Fazal Ali, J. gathered the following objects of an explanation to a statutory provision:

  • Explain the meaning and intendment of the Act itself.
  • Clarify any obscurity and vagueness (if any) in the main enactment to make it consistent with the object.
  • Provide additional support to the object of the Act to make it meaningful and purposeful.
  • Fill up the gap which is relevant for the purpose of the explanation, to suppress the mischief and advance the object of the Act.
  • Cannot take away a statutory right.

However, it would be wrong to always construe an explanation as limited to the above objects — the meaning given to an explanation will really depend upon its terms and not on any theory of its purpose.

Proviso vs Exception vs Saving Clause

DeviceFunction
ProvisoUsed to remove special cases from the general enactment and provide for them specially
ExceptionIntended to restrain the enacting clause to particular cases
Saving clauseUsed to preserve from destruction certain rights, remedies or privileges already existing

Test Your Knowledge — MCQs with Answers

  • MCQ 1: The Rule in Heydon's case is also known as — (a) Purposive construction (b) Mischief Rule (c) Golden Rule (d) Exceptional Construction. Answer: (b) Mischief Rule.
  • MCQ 2: Pick the odd one out of the following aids to interpretation — (a) Preamble (b) Marginal Notes (c) Proviso (d) Usage. Answer: (d) Usage — the other three are internal aids, usage is an external aid.
  • MCQ 3: ______ is the cardinal rule of construction that words, sentences and phrases of a statute should be read in their ordinary, natural and grammatical meaning so that they may have effect in their widest amplitude — (a) Rule of Literal Construction (b) Rule of Harmonious Construction (c) Rule of Beneficial Construction (d) Rule of Exceptional Construction. Answer: (a) Rule of Literal Construction.
  • MCQ 4: An internal aid that may be added to include something within the section or to exclude something from it, is — (a) Proviso (b) Explanation (c) Schedule (d) Illustrations. Answer: (b) Explanation.
  • MCQ 5: When there is a conflict between two or more statutes or two or more parts of a statute, which rule is applicable — (a) Welfare construction (b) Strict construction (c) Harmonious construction (d) Mischief Rule. Answer: (c) Harmonious construction.

Grammatical Interpretation — Exceptions (Descriptive Q.7)

  • In all ordinary cases grammatical interpretation is the sole form allowable — the Court cannot take from, add to, or modify the letter of the law. Subject to two exceptions:
  • (i) Where the letter of the law is logically defective on account of ambiguity, inconsistency or incompleteness. As regards ambiguity, the Court is under a duty to travel beyond the letter of the law to determine from other sources the true intention of the legislature; where the statutory expression is defective on account of inconsistency, the court must ascertain the spirit of the law.
  • (ii) If the text leads to a result so unreasonable that it is self-evident the legislature could not mean what it says, the court may resolve the impasse by inferring logically the intention of the legislature.
  • Where there are two possible constructions of a clause, the courts may prefer the logical construction which emerges from the setting in which the clause appears, the circumstances in which it came to be enacted, and the words used.

Why It Matters / Application

Every reading of the Companies Act, 2013 turns on these rules. Whether a director's disclosure under section 102 must be full and frank (wide literal construction), whether section 42(11) overrides sub-sections (9) and (10) (non-obstante clause), whether a name change under section 13(2) must still satisfy sections 4(2) and 4(3) ("subject to"), whether section 4(3) operates in addition to section 4(2) ("without prejudice"), whether "Director" under section 2(34) is exhaustive while "whole-time director" under section 2(94) is extensive ("means" vs "includes"), and whether the fifth ground in section 271(e) is limited by the preceding grounds (ejusdem generis, held not applicable because the earlier grounds are essentially diverse) — each is decided by applying a specific rule of construction, not by intuition. The internal/external aids hierarchy also settles practical disputes: a Schedule to the Companies Act, 2013 cannot prevail over the enactment, a marginal note cannot be used to construe a section, and a heading cannot override a section. For deeds and contracts, the same discipline governs — the reasonable-man test, no cross-reference between deeds, and the earlier clause prevailing where clauses irreconcilably conflict.

Note — Exam Traps and Limits

Trap 1: Mischief Rule = Heydon's Rule, not the Golden Rule; the Golden Rule is the Rule of Reasonable Construction (ut res magis valeat quam pereat). Trap 2: the mischief rule applies only where the words are ambiguous and reasonably capable of more than one meaning (CIT v. Sodra Devi). Trap 3: Long Title and Preamble are part of the Act; marginal notes are not — except marginal notes to Articles of the Constitution, which are part of the Constitution and have been used in construing the Articles, and except exceptional cases (Deewan Singh; Sarabjit Rick Singh). Trap 4: illustrations do not form part of the Sections but do form part of the statute — and can neither curtail nor expand the ambit of the section (Example 13, section 73, Indian Contract Act, 1872). Trap 5: an Explanation may include or exclude, but must not widen the ambit of the section and cannot take away a statutory right. Trap 6: where the Schedule and the enactment are inconsistent, the enactment prevails; where the preamble and a provision conflict, the provision prevails. Trap 7: Contemporanea expositio is meant for ancient statutes, not comparatively modern Acts — though contemporary official statements and statutory instruments have been used to interpret even recent Indian statutes. Trap 8: beneficial construction is available only when two constructions are reasonably possible, never against unequivocal words. Trap 9: the departure from grammatical construction to avoid absurdity is permitted only to the extent it avoids the absurdity and no further, and never by conjecture or surmise. Trap 10: a proviso embraces only the field covered by the main provision to which it is attached and no other (Ram Narain Sons Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax, AIR 1955 SC 765).

Summary as given in the source

Enacted laws, Acts and Rules are drafted by legal experts and so it is expected that the language used will leave little room for interpretation or construction. Interpretation or construction of Statutes helps in finding the meaning of ambiguous words and expressions and in resolving inconsistency. If any provision of the statute is open to two interpretations, the Court has to choose that interpretation which represents the true intention of the legislature. The courts are the best interpreters; they strongly lean against a construction which reduces the statute to a futility. A statute or any enacting provision therein must be so construed as to make it effective and operative, on the principle expressed in the maxim ut res magis valeat quam pereat.

Other Laws · Chapter 3 — The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999

Source: 87786bos-aps2160-p2-ch3.pdf

Core Concept(s)

  • Why FEMA replaced FERA: Exchange control began with the Defence of India Rules imposed by the British in 1939; the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act was enacted in 1947 and replaced by the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 (FERA). After the 1991 liberalisation the Government permitted free movement of foreign exchange for trade receipts/payments and foreign investment, reserves rose substantially, and FEMA, 1999 was enacted — effective 1st June, 2000 vide Notification G.S.R. 371(E) dated 1.5.2000 — to manage rather than regulate foreign exchange.
  • Preamble objective: to consolidate and amend the law relating to foreign exchange for (i) facilitating external trade and payments, and (ii) promoting the orderly development and maintenance of the foreign exchange market in India.
  • Extra-territorial reach [Section 1]: FEMA extends to the whole of India, and also to all branches, offices and agencies outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India, and to any contravention committed outside India by any person to whom the Act applies. The emphasis on "owned or controlled" is what makes the scope wide.
  • The master rule of the Act: Current account transactions are freely permitted unless specifically prohibited; capital account transactions are prohibited unless specifically or generally permitted. Everything in the chapter flows from this asymmetry, which exists because the Indian Rupee is not yet fully convertible.
  • Accounting analogy: current account transactions correspond to profit-and-loss / revenue items; capital account transactions correspond to Balance Sheet / capital items. The two are intended to be mutually exclusive — Section 2(j) defines "current account transaction" negatively as anything that is not a capital account transaction.
  • Who controls what: RBI has overall control over foreign exchange transactions, but enforcement of FEMA is entrusted to a separate Directorate of Enforcement [Section 36]. Since 15th October 2019, capital account transactions in non-debt instruments are regulated by the Central Government and those in debt instruments by the RBI. Reasonable restrictions on current account transactions are imposed by the Central Government in consultation with RBI.
  • Reading hierarchy of FEMA: Act → Rules (notified by the Ministry of Finance) & Regulations (notified by the Reserve Bank of India) → Notifications & Circulars → Master Directions → FAQs.
  • Salient features: regulation of transactions between residents and non-residents; investments in India by non-residents and overseas investments by Indian residents; freely permissible current account transactions subject to reasonable restrictions; RBI and Central Government control over capital account transactions; compulsory realisation of export proceeds and repatriation to India; dealing in foreign exchange only through 'Authorised Persons' (Authorised Dealer / Money Changer / Off-shore banking unit); adjudication and compounding of offences; investigation by the Directorate of Enforcement; appeal to Special Director (Appeals) and the Appellate Tribunal.

Broad Structure of FEMA (7 Chapters)

ChapterMattersSections
IPreliminary1 – 2
IIRegulation and Management of Foreign Exchange3 – 9
IIIAuthorised Person10 – 12
IVContravention and Penalties13 – 15
VAdjudication and Appeal16 – 35
