VIIMiscellaneous39 – 49

Key Definitions / Terms [Section 2]

Authorised person [Section 2(c)]
An authorised dealer, money changer, off-shore banking unit or any other person for the time being authorised under Section 10(1) to deal in foreign exchange or foreign securities. Wherever a remittance is permitted (generally or specifically), the remitter must still obtain the foreign exchange from an Authorised Person.
Capital Account Transaction [Section 2(e)]
A transaction which alters the assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of persons resident in India, or assets or liabilities in India of persons resident outside India, and includes transactions referred to in Section 6(3). Note: for residents, even a change in contingent liabilities outside India is a capital account transaction. In plain terms: cross-border investments, loans, immovable property and transfer of assets.
Currency [Section 2(h)]
Includes all currency notes, postal notes, postal orders, money orders, cheques, drafts, travellers' cheques, letters of credit, bills of exchange and promissory notes, credit cards or such other similar instruments as may be notified by the Reserve Bank.
Currency Notes [Section 2(i)]
Means and includes cash in the form of coins and bank notes.
Current Account Transaction [Section 2(j)]
A transaction other than a capital account transaction; without prejudice to that generality it includes — (i) payments due in connection with foreign trade, other current business, services, and short-term banking and credit facilities in the ordinary course of business; (ii) payments due as interest on loans and as net income from investments; (iii) remittances for living expenses of parents, spouse and children residing abroad; and (iv) expenses in connection with foreign travel, education and medical care of parents, spouse and children.
Export [Section 2(l)]
(i) The taking out of India to a place outside India any goods; (ii) provision of services from India to any person outside India.
Import [Section 2(p)]
Bringing into India any goods or services.
Foreign Currency [Section 2(m)]
Any currency other than Indian currency.
Foreign Exchange [Section 2(n)]
Foreign currency, and includes — (i) deposits, credits and balances payable in any foreign currency; (ii) drafts, travellers' cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange expressed or drawn in Indian currency but payable in any foreign currency; (iii) drafts, travellers' cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange drawn by banks, institutions or persons outside India but payable in Indian currency.
Foreign Security [Section 2(o)]
Any security in the form of shares, stocks, bonds, debentures or any other instrument denominated or expressed in foreign currency, and includes securities expressed in foreign currency but where redemption or any form of return such as interest or dividend is payable in Indian currency.
Person [Section 2(u)]
Includes (i) an individual; (ii) a Hindu undivided family; (iii) a company; (iv) a firm; (v) an association of persons or a body of individuals, whether incorporated or not; (vi) every artificial juridical person not falling in the preceding sub-clauses; and (vii) any agency, office or branch owned or controlled by such person. Agencies, offices and branches have no independent status from their owners, yet FEMA treats them as separate "persons" — this is what allows a branch to be tested for residence in its own right.
Person resident in India [Section 2(v)]
(i) a person residing in India for more than 182 days during the course of the preceding financial year, but does not include — (A) a person who has gone out of India or stays outside India for or on taking up employment outside India, or for carrying on a business or vocation outside India, or for any other purpose in such circumstances as would indicate an intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period; (B) a person who has come to or stays in India otherwise than for employment in India, business or vocation in India, or any other purpose in circumstances indicating intention to stay in India for an uncertain period; (ii) any person or body corporate registered or incorporated in India; (iii) an office, branch or agency in India owned or controlled by a person resident outside India; (iv) an office, branch or agency outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India.
Person Resident Outside India [Section 2(w)]
A person who is not resident in India. (Purely residual — there is no independent test.)
Transfer [Section 2(ze)]
Includes sale, purchase, exchange, mortgage, pledge, gift, loan or any other form of transfer of right, title, possession or lien.
Resident but not permanently resident (Schedule III Explanation)
A person resident in India on account of employment or deputation of a specified duration (irrespective of length) or for a specific job or assignment whose duration does not exceed three years. Such a person, if a citizen of a foreign State other than Pakistan, or an Indian citizen on deputation to the office/branch/subsidiary/JV in India of a foreign company, may remit up to his net salary (after tax, provident fund and other deductions).
Transferable Development Rights (TDRs)
Certificates issued in respect of a category of land acquired for a public purpose by the Central or State Government, in consideration of surrender of land by the owner without monetary compensation, transferable in part or whole. Trading in TDRs is closed to persons resident outside India.

Residential Status — the three limbs [Section 2(v) read with Section 4]

  • First limb (the 182-day test): a person who was in India for more than 182 days in the preceding financial year is a Person Resident in India (PRII). One always looks backwards — status for FY 2021-22 is decided by the stay in FY 2020-21. Citizenship is irrelevant.
  • Second limb — clause (A), persons going OUT: even if the 182-day test is met, a person who goes out of / stays outside India for (i) taking up employment outside India, (ii) carrying on a business or vocation outside India, or (iii) any other purpose in circumstances indicating an intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period, becomes a Person Resident Outside India (PROI).
  • Third limb — clause (B), persons coming IN: a person who comes to or stays in India otherwise than for those same three purposes is not a PRII, even if he stayed in India for more than 182 days in the preceding year. The complexity arises because limb one says "but does not include" and limb three says "otherwise than" — two exceptions stacked on each other.
  • Status runs from a date, not for a year. Unlike the Income-tax Act, 1961 (where the previous year's income is taxed and a full year can be examined), FEMA is a regulatory law — one must know the person's status at the moment of the transaction. If status could be known only after the year ended, nobody could safely transact with a new arrival.
  • Limbs (A) and (B) apply only to individuals. An HUF, AOP or artificial juridical person cannot take up employment, cannot go out of or come to India, so they fall outside the second and third limbs; nor are they registered or incorporated like corporates. Legally the definition fails for HUF/AOP/BOI; practically, if the HUF or AOP is in India it is treated as an Indian resident.
  • Entities: any person or body corporate registered or incorporated in India is a PRII (again, this does not fit AOP/BOI).
  • Branches both ways: a branch/office/agency outside India owned or controlled by a PRII is itself a PRII — so one cannot set up an overseas branch to escape FEMA. A branch/office/agency in India owned or controlled by a PROI is also a PRII — this is deliberate, because Indian residents must be able to deal with such a branch without invoking FEMA at every step.
  • Students: although a student going abroad for a fixed course technically goes for a certain period (and so would remain a PRII), RBI's A.P. Circular No. 45 dated 8th December 2003 clarifies that students will be treated as non-residents, because they usually start working there to fund their stay and studies.

How It Works / Logic — Regulation and Management of Foreign Exchange

  • Dealing in foreign exchange [Section 3]: Save as otherwise provided in the Act or with the general or special permission of the RBI, no person shall — (a) deal in or transfer any foreign exchange or foreign security to any person not being an authorised person; (b) make any payment to or for the credit of any person resident outside India in any manner; (c) receive, otherwise than through an authorised person, any payment by order or on behalf of any person resident outside India. Explanation to (c): where a person in, or resident in, India receives a payment by order or on behalf of a PROI through any other person (including an authorised person) without a corresponding inward remittance from outside India, he is deemed to have received it otherwise than through an authorised person; (d) enter into any financial transaction in India as consideration for, or in association with, acquisition or creation or transfer of a right to acquire any asset outside India by any person.
  • "Financial transaction" (Explanation to Section 3): making any payment to, or for the credit of, any person; receiving any payment for, by order or on behalf of any person; drawing, issuing or negotiating any bill of exchange or promissory note; transferring any security; or acknowledging any debt. Section 3 imposes blanket restrictions and applies to both PRIIs and PROIs; its purpose is to channel inflow and outflow through authorised dealers.
  • Holding of foreign exchange [Section 4]: Except as provided in the Act, no person resident in India shall acquire, hold, own, possess or transfer any foreign exchange, foreign security or any immovable property situated outside India. Acquisition of such assets has since been permitted through separate notifications subject to conditions.
  • Current account transactions [Section 5]: Any person may sell or draw foreign exchange to or from an authorised person if such sale or drawal is a current account transaction. Proviso: the Central Government may, in public interest and in consultation with the RBI, impose reasonable restrictions — exercised through the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000, whose Schedules I, II and III set out the prohibited, Government-approval and RBI-approval lists. If a transaction is not listed in any of the three Schedules, it can be freely undertaken.
  • Why gifts are restricted even though they are current account: there is no restriction on current account transactions, only reasonable restrictions within them — otherwise people would export funds abroad under the garb of current account transactions.
  • Capital account transactions [Section 6(1)]: Subject to sub-section (2), any person may sell or draw foreign exchange to or from an authorised person for a capital account transaction.
  • Section 6(2): the Reserve Bank, in consultation with the Central Government, may specify (a) classes of capital account transactions involving debt instruments which are permissible, (b) the limit up to which foreign exchange is admissible, and (c) conditions. Proviso: neither the RBI nor the Central Government shall impose any restriction on drawal of foreign exchange for payment due on account of amortisation of loans or for depreciation of direct investments in the ordinary course of business.
  • Section 6(2A): the Central Government, in consultation with the RBI, may prescribe classes of capital account transactions not involving debt instruments which are permissible, the limits and the conditions. The Central Government issues the Non-debt Instruments notification; RBI issues the notification for mode of payment and reporting of non-debt instruments. Powers were transferred by the Finance Act 2015 but made effective only from 15th October 2019. For investment by Indian residents outside India, RBI continues to regulate both equity and debt.
  • Section 6(3): the old list of capital account transactions regulable by RBI stood deleted with effect from 15th October 2019.
  • Section 6(4): a PRII may hold, own, transfer or invest in foreign currency, foreign security or immovable property outside India if it was acquired, held or owned by him when he was resident outside India, or inherited from a person who was resident outside India.
  • RBI A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 90 dated 9th January, 2014 clarifies that Section 6(4) covers: (i) foreign currency accounts opened and maintained when the person was resident outside India; (ii) income earned from employment/business/vocation taken up outside India, or from investments made, or gift or inheritance received, while resident outside India; (iii) foreign exchange, and income/conversion/replacement/accrual thereon, held outside India by a PRII acquired by way of inheritance from a PROI; (iv) a PRII may freely utilise all eligible assets abroad, income on them and sale proceeds received after return to India for any payments or fresh investments abroad without RBI approval, provided the cost and subsequent payments are met exclusively out of funds forming part of those eligible assets and the transaction does not contravene extant FEMA provisions.
  • Section 6(5): the mirror image — a PROI may hold, own, transfer or invest in Indian currency, security or immovable property in India if it was acquired, held or owned by him when he was resident in India, or inherited from a person who was resident in India.
  • Section 6(6): the RBI may by regulation prohibit, restrict or regulate the establishment in India of a branch, office or other place of business by a PROI, for carrying on any activity relating to such branch/office/place of business.
  • Section 6(7): "debt instruments" means such instruments as may be determined by the Central Government in consultation with the RBI.
  • Realisation and repatriation: an Indian resident who acquires foreign funds abroad cannot simply hold on to them — he is required to bring them back to India as provided in Section 8.

Schedule I to the Current Account Transactions Rules, 2000 — Drawal PROHIBITED

  • Remittance out of lottery winnings.
  • Remittance of income from racing / riding, etc., or any other hobby.
  • Remittance for purchase of lottery tickets, banned/prescribed magazines, football pools, sweepstakes, etc.
  • Payment of commission on exports made towards equity investment in Joint Ventures / Wholly Owned Subsidiaries abroad of Indian companies.
  • Remittance of dividend by any company to which the requirement of dividend balancing is applicable.
  • Payment of commission on exports under Rupee State Credit Route, except commission up to 10% of invoice value of exports of tea and tobacco.
  • Payment related to "Call Back Services" of telephones.
  • Remittance of interest income on funds held in Non-resident Special Rupee Scheme account.

Schedule III — Prior approval of RBI required [Notification G.S.R. 426(E) dated 26th May 2015]

Para 1 — Facilities for individuals: individuals may avail foreign exchange for the following purposes within the limit of USD 250,000 only; any additional remittance in excess of that limit requires prior RBI approval:

#Purpose
(i)Private visits to any country (except Nepal and Bhutan)
(ii)Gift or donation
(iii)Going abroad for employment
(iv)Emigration
(v)Maintenance of close relatives abroad
(vi)Travel for business, attending a conference or specialised training, meeting medical expenses or check-up abroad, or accompanying as attendant a patient going abroad for medical treatment/check-up
(vii)Expenses in connection with medical treatment abroad
(viii)Studies abroad
(ix)Any other current account transaction
  • The three "estimate" exceptions: for items (iv) emigration, (vii) medical treatment and (viii) studies abroad, the individual may avail exchange in excess of the LRS limit (Regulation 4 of FEMA Notification 1/2000-RB dated 3rd May, 2000) without prior RBI approval if so required by the country of emigration, the medical institute offering treatment, or the university, respectively.
  • Set-off against LRS: if an individual remits any amount under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme in a financial year, the applicable Schedule III limit for that individual is reduced from USD 250,000 by the amount so remitted.
  • Resident but not permanently resident: may remit up to his net salary (after tax, provident fund and other deductions) — available to a citizen of a foreign State other than Pakistan, or an Indian citizen on deputation to the office/branch/subsidiary/JV in India of a foreign company, where the employment/deputation/assignment does not exceed three years.
  • A person other than an individual may also avail foreign exchange facility, mutatis mutandis, within the LRS limit for the above purposes.
  • Procedure (Para 3): drawal or remittance under Schedule III follows the same procedure as applicable for remitting under the LRS.

Para 2 — Facilities for persons OTHER than individuals (these remittances need prior RBI approval):

Donations for (a) creation of Chairs in reputed educational institutes, (b) contribution to funds (not being an investment fund) promoted by educational institutes, (c) contribution to a technical institution/body/association in the field of activity of the donor companyExceeding 1% of foreign exchange earnings during the previous three financial years or USD 5,000,000, whichever is less

Exemptions from the Schedule II / III approval requirement

  • RFC account: no approval is required where the remittance for a Schedule II or Schedule III transaction is made from a Resident Foreign Currency (RFC) account.
  • EEFC account: no approval is required where the remittance for a Schedule II or III transaction is made from an Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency (EEFC) account — except that approval is still required, even from an EEFC account, for: (a) remittance for membership of a P & I Club; (b) commission per transaction to agents abroad for sale of residential flats or commercial plots in India exceeding USD 25,000 or 5% of the inward remittance whichever is more; and (c) reimbursement of pre-incorporation expenses exceeding 5% of investment brought into India or USD 100,000 whichever is higher.
  • International Credit Card: a person on a visit abroad may incur the expenditure stated in Schedule III through an International credit card.

Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS)

  • All resident individuals, including minors, may freely remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year (April – March) for any permissible current or capital account transaction or a combination of both. This is inclusive of the foreign exchange facility under Para 1 of Schedule III of the FEM (CAT) Amendment Rules 2015 dated 26 May 2015.
  • Where the remitter is a minor, the LRS declaration form must be countersigned by the minor's natural guardian.
  • The Scheme is not available to corporates, partnership firms, HUF, Trusts, etc.
  • Consolidation: remittances under the Scheme may be consolidated in respect of family members, subject to each individual family member complying with its terms and conditions.
  • Exception to clubbing: clubbing by other family members is not permitted for capital account transactions such as opening a bank account / investment / purchase of property, if they are not co-owners / co-partners of the overseas bank account, investment or property.

Permissible Capital Account Transactions Regulations, 2000 [Notification No. FEMA 1/2000-RB dated 3rd May 2000]

Capital account transactions split into three buckets: (I) transactions permissible for persons resident in India and outside India; (II) transactions on which restrictions cannot be imposed; and (III) transactions which are prohibited.

Schedule I — permissible classes for persons RESIDENT IN INDIA:

  • (a) Investment by a person resident in India in foreign securities.
  • (b) Foreign currency loans raised in India and abroad by a person resident in India.
  • (c) Transfer of immovable property outside India by a person resident in India.
  • (d) Guarantees issued by a person resident in India in favour of a person resident outside India.
  • (e) Export, import and holding of currency / currency notes.
  • (f) Loans and overdrafts (borrowings) by a person resident in India from a person resident outside India.
  • (g) Maintenance of foreign currency accounts in India and outside India by a person resident in India.
  • (h) Taking out an insurance policy by a person resident in India from an insurance company outside India.
  • (i) Loans and overdrafts by a person resident in India to a person resident outside India.
  • (j) Remittance outside India of capital assets of a person resident in India.
  • (k) Undertaking derivative contracts.

Schedule II — permissible classes for persons RESIDENT OUTSIDE INDIA:

  • (a) Investment in India by a PROI — (i) issue of security by a body corporate or entity in India and investment therein by a PROI; and (ii) investment by way of contribution by a PROI to the capital of a firm, proprietorship concern or association of persons in India.
  • (b) Acquisition and transfer of immovable property in India by a PROI.
  • (c) Guarantee by a PROI in favour of, or on behalf of, a person resident in India.
  • (d) Import and export of currency / currency notes into/from India by a PROI.
  • (e) Deposits between a person resident in India and a person resident outside India.
  • (f) Foreign currency accounts in India of a person resident outside India.
  • (g) Remittance outside India of capital assets in India of a person resident outside India.
  • (h) Undertaking derivative contracts.

Transactions on which NO restriction can be imposed: (1) amortisation of loan; (2) depreciation of direct investments in the ordinary course of business. Restrictions also cannot be imposed where the drawal is for repayment of loan instalments.

Prohibited Capital Account Transactions

  • (a) General bar with the LRS carve-out: no person shall undertake, sell or draw foreign exchange to or from an authorised person for any capital account transaction — provided that a resident individual may draw from an authorised person foreign exchange not exceeding USD 250,000 per financial year (or such amount as RBI decides from time to time) for a capital account transaction specified in Schedule I. Explanation: drawal under item 1 of Schedule III of the Current Account Transactions Rules, 2000 is subsumed within this USD 250,000 limit.
  • Where drawal by a resident individual for a Schedule I capital account transaction exceeds USD 250,000 per financial year, the limit specified in the regulation relevant to that particular transaction applies to such drawal.
  • FATF bar: no part of the USD 250,000 drawn under the above proviso shall be used for remittance directly or indirectly to countries notified as non-co-operative countries and territories by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) and communicated by RBI to all concerned.
  • (b) Sectors closed to PROI investment: a person resident outside India is prohibited from investing in India, in any form, in any company, partnership firm, proprietary concern or entity (incorporated or not) which is engaged or proposes to engage in — (i) the business of chit fund; (ii) as a Nidhi company; (iii) agricultural or plantation activities; (iv) real estate business, or construction of farm houses; or (v) trading in Transferable Development Rights (TDRs).
    • Chit fund relaxation: the Registrar of Chits (or an officer authorised by the State Government), in consultation with the State Government concerned, may permit a chit fund to accept subscription from Non-resident Indians. NRIs may subscribe through banking channels and on a non-repatriation basis, without limit, subject to RBI conditions.
    • "Real estate business" Explanation: does not include development of townships, construction of residential/commercial premises, roads or bridges, and Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) registered and regulated under the SEBI (REITs) Regulations 2014.
  • (c) North Korea bar: no person resident in India shall undertake any capital account transaction which is not permissible in terms of Order S.O. 1549(E) dated April 21, 2017 of the Ministry of External Affairs with any citizen or resident of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, or an entity incorporated or otherwise in DPRK, until further orders, unless there is specific approval of the Central Government.
  • (d) Unwinding of existing DPRK exposure: existing investment transactions with such persons/entities, or any existing representative office or other assets possessed in DPRK by a person resident in India, which are impermissible under Order S.O. 1549(E), must be closed / liquidated / disposed / settled within 180 days from the date of issue of that Notification, unless the Central Government specifically approves continuance beyond that period.
  • Net effect: a capital account transaction is permitted only if specifically permitted under the regulations. If it is not stated as generally permitted, prior specific approval is required.

Examples — Residential Status

  • Example 1 (the basic 182-day rule): If a person resides in India for more than 182 days during FY 2020-21, then for FY 2021-22 he will be an Indian resident. For FY 2020-21 one must look at residence during FY 2019-20, and so on.
  • Clause (A) illustration — departure for employment: Continuing the above facts, if that person leaves India on 1st November 2021, he is a non-resident from 2nd November 2021 — even though his stay in FY 2020-21 exceeded 182 days. For FY 2021-22 he is a PRII till 1st November 2021 and a PROI thereafter; and from 1st April 2022 he continues to be a PROI so long as he stays out of India for employment. Likewise, a person who goes and stays outside India to carry on a business becomes a PROI from that date.
  • Clause (iii) illustration — the US green card: A green card entitles a person to stay in the USA and eventually become a US citizen. If a person goes abroad and starts staying in the USA on a green card, he is a non-resident from that date, because his stay abroad indicates he will stay there for an uncertain period.
  • Clause (B) illustration — visiting sick parents: A person comes to India on 1st June 2021 to visit his parents. His parents fall sick and he stays till 31st March 2022 and continues thereafter, but it is certain he will leave within the next 6 months when they recover. His stay is neither for employment, nor business, nor circumstances showing an uncertain stay. Hence even though he resided in India for more than 182 days in FY 2021-22, he continues to be a non-resident from 1st April 2022. (In FY 2021-22 he is in any case a PROI, having not resided in India for more than 182 days in FY 2020-21.)
  • Clause (B) contrast — arrival for employment: If a person comes to India on 1st June 2021 for employment, business, or in circumstances indicating an intention to stay for an uncertain period, he is a PRII from 1st June 2021 itself.
  • Illustration 1 — Mr. X: Mr. X resided in India during FY 2019-20 for less than 182 days. He came to India on April 1, 2020 for carrying on business, intends to leave the business on April 30, 2021 and leave India on June 30, 2021. Answer: Mr. X is a 'person resident in India' from 1st April 2020 (came for business). For FY 2021-22 he continues to be an Indian resident from 1st April 2021. If he leaves India for employment, business/vocation outside India, or any purpose indicating an intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period, he ceases to be a PRII from the date of his departure. Even if Mr. X is a foreign citizen, if he has not left India for any of these purposes he remains a 'person resident in India' during FY 2021-22. Thus it is the purpose of leaving India that decides his status from 1st July 2021.
  • Illustration 2 — Mr. Z (student in USA): Mr. Z resided in India during FY 2019-20 for more than 182 days, and left India on 1st August, 2020 for the United States to pursue higher studies for three years. Answer: He has not gone out for employment, business, or circumstances indicating an uncertain stay; accordingly on a strict reading he would be a 'person resident in India' during FY 2020-21 — but RBI's A.P. Circular No. 45 dated 8th December 2003 clarifies that students are treated as non-residents (they usually start working to fund their stay and studies). For FY 2021-22, he was not in India for more than 182 days in the preceding FY 2020-21, so he is not a person resident in India.
  • Illustration 3 — Toy Ltd. (Japanese company): Toy Ltd. is a Japanese company with business units worldwide; it has a robotic unit headquartered in Mumbai and a branch in Singapore, and the Mumbai headquarters controls the Singapore branch. Answer: Toy Ltd., being a Japanese company, is a person resident outside India [Section 2(w)]. Under Section 2(u) a 'person' includes any agency, office or branch owned or controlled by such person, so the Mumbai robotic unit is a 'person'. Under Section 2(v)(iii), an office/branch/agency in India owned or controlled by a PROI is a person resident in India — hence the Mumbai unit is a PRII. Since the Mumbai unit (a PRII) controls the Singapore branch, the Singapore branch is also a person resident in India.
  • Illustration 4 — Miss Alia (British Airways airhostess): She flies for 12 days a month and takes a break of 18 days, spent at her 'base'. Normally the base is the city where the airline is headquartered, but for security considerations she was based at Mumbai and was accommodated at Mumbai for more than 182 days in the financial year. Answer: She is employed in the UK. She has not come to India for employment, business or circumstances indicating an intention to stay for an uncertain period. Under Section 2(v)(B) such persons are not Indian residents even if their stay exceeds 182 days in the preceding year — so Miss Alia is not a Person Resident in India. However, if she had been employed at the Mumbai branch of British Airways, she would be a Person Resident in India.

Examples — Section 3 (Dealing in Foreign Exchange)

  • Clause (a) — dealing in foreign exchange: A PROI comes to India and wants to sell US$ 1,000 to his friend who is resident in India, the friend offering a better rate than the banks. This cannot be done — it would amount to dealing in foreign exchange with a person who is not an authorised person.
  • Clause (b) — payment for the credit of a non-resident: A PROI has an insurance policy in India and asks his brother in India to pay the premium. This is a payment for the credit of a non-resident and is not permitted.
  • Clause (c) — receipt otherwise than through an AP: A foreign tourist eats at an Indian restaurant and wants to pay US$ 20 in cash. The restaurant cannot accept the cash, as that would be a receipt otherwise than through an Authorised Person; it would have to take a money changer's licence to accept foreign currency.
  • Clause (d) — Hawala: An Indian resident gives ₹ 70,000 in cash to an Indian dealer; in exchange his brother in Dubai receives US$ 1,000 from a Dubai dealer, the two dealers settling between themselves later. Transactions of this kind are known as Hawala transactions and are not permitted.

Examples — Sections 4, 5 and 6 (Current vs Capital)

  • Example 2 (Section 4 — holding foreign exchange): An Indian resident receives a bank balance of US$ 10,000 from his uncle in London. He cannot hold on to the foreign funds — he is supposed to bring back the funds as provided in Section 8.
  • Example 3 (import of machinery, paid immediately): An Indian resident imports machinery from a UK vendor to install in his factory. Under accounting and income-tax law this is capital expenditure; but under FEMA it does not create an asset in India for the UK vendor, nor a liability of the Indian importer to the UK vendor. Once payment is made, neither party owns nor is owed anything in the other country. Hence it is a Current Account Transaction.
  • Example 4 (same import, on 3 months' credit): For the credit period of 3 months there is a liability of the Indian importer to the UK vendor, and technically a liability outside India under FEMA. However, Section 2(j)(i) treats "short-term banking and credit facilities in the ordinary course of business" as a current account transaction. Hence import of machinery on credit terms is a Current Account Transaction.
  • Example 5 (gift of US$ 1,000 to NRI brother): A PRII transfers US$ 1,000 from his Indian bank account to his NRI brother's bank account in New York as a gift. Under accounting/income-tax law a gift is a capital receipt; under FEMA, once the gift is accepted by the NRI nobody owns or owes anything to anyone in India or the USA — the transaction is over. Hence it is a Current Account Transaction.
  • Example 5, variant (a) — gift in India in Indian currency: If the PRII gives a PROI a gift in India in Indian currency, for the PROI it results in funds lying in India (alteration of an Indian asset); for the PRII there is no creation of asset or liability. Because it creates an asset in India for the PROI, it is a Capital Account Transaction.
  • Example 5, variant (b) — PROI gifting a PRII: If a PROI gifts a PRII by remitting funds into India, there is no restriction. But if the PROI gives the funds abroad, the resident cannot keep them abroad — he has to bring them into India.

Test Your Knowledge — MCQs (with answers)

  • MCQ 1 — Mr. Purshottam Saha (multiple drawals in FY 2021-22): In September 2021 he withdrew US$ 50,000 from State Bank of India, New Delhi for a month-long business trip to Atlanta, Athens, London and Berlin. In December 2021 he withdrew a further US$ 50,000 and remitted it to his son Raviyansh Saha studying in Toronto, Canada. In the first week of January 2022 he sent his ailing mother Mrs. Savita Saha with his wife Mrs. Rashmi Saha to Seattle for specialised treatment and asked SBI to remit US$ 75,000 to his green-card-holding brother Pranav Saha's Citibank, Seattle account for the treatment and to help Pranav meet increased expenses. In the last week of March 2022, on a Dubai trip, he withdrew a further US$ 35,000 for trip expenses and shopping with his daughter Devanshi Saha, whose 'destination marriage' at Zurich, Switzerland in August 2022 was estimated by the event manager at US$ 2,50,000. Answer: (a) — in respect of the withdrawals on various occasions from SBI and their remittance outside India during FY 2021-22, Mr. Purshottam Saha is not required to obtain any prior approval. (The rejected options were: (b) prior RBI approval needed for the US$ 35,000 Dubai drawal because the annual ceiling is US$ 1,75,000; (c) approval needed after US$ 1,00,000; (d) approval needed after US$ 50,000.)
  • MCQ 2 — M/s. Kedhar Sports Academy: A private coaching club providing cricket and football coaching pan-India organises, in its 25th year (2022), a T-20 format cricket tournament at Lancashire, England in the first half of April. Prize money is USD 40,000 for the winning team and USD 11,000 for the runner-up — a total remittance of USD 51,000. Answer: (c) — no prior permission from any authority is required and it can proceed with the remittance. (Schedule II requires Ministry of HRD, Department of Youth Affairs and Sports approval for remittance of sports prize money by a body other than an International/National/State level sports body only where the amount exceeds US$ 100,000; USD 51,000 is below that.)
  • MCQ 3 — Akash Ceramics Limited / M/s. Super Seller: Akash Ceramics Limited, an Indian company, sells a prime-location commercial plot in Chennai. The US-headquartered real estate broker M/s. Super Seller finds the buyer Glory Estate Inc. (based in the USA but controlled from India, hence a 'Person Resident in India' under FEMA). The deal is USD 600,000 (assume 1 USD = ₹ 70), and commission is 7% of the sale proceeds = USD 42,000, to be remitted in USD to Super Seller's US head office. Answer: (d) — prior RBI permission is mandatory for the entire commission of USD 42,000. (Schedule III Para 2(ii): the free limit is USD 25,000 or 5% of the inward remittance — here 5% of USD 600,000 = USD 30,000 — whichever is more, i.e. USD 30,000; USD 42,000 exceeds it, and approval is required for the whole remittance, not just the excess.)
  • MCQ 4 — Mohita Periodicals and Mags Publications Limited: The Chennai-registered company obtains consultancy services from an entity based in France to set up a software programme for its publications, payable in foreign currency; compliance officer Mrs. Ritika asks how much may be remitted without prior RBI approval. Answer: (d) — US$ 1,000,000. (This is not an infrastructure project, so the "other consultancy services" ceiling of USD 1,000,000 per project applies, not the USD 10,000,000 infrastructure ceiling.)
  • MCQ 5 — Mr. Umesh (return from USA + Minnesota branch): After five years in the USA, Mr. Umesh came to his paternal place in New Delhi on October 25, 2021 to conduct business with his younger brothers Rajesh and Somesh, contributing ₹ 10,00,000 as capital, and simultaneously started a proprietary business selling artistic brassware and jewellery procured from manufacturers at Moradabad. Within two months of arrival he established a branch of his proprietary business at Minnesota, USA. Answer: (c) — for FY 2022-23, Mr. Umesh and his Minnesota branch are both persons resident in India (he came to India for business, and a branch outside India owned or controlled by a PRII is itself a PRII under Section 2(v)(iv)).

Test Your Knowledge — Descriptive Questions (with answers)

  • Q1 — 'Printex Computer' (Singapore): A Singapore-based company with business units worldwide has a computer printer manufacturing unit headquartered in Pune and a Dubai branch controlled by the Pune headquarters. Answer: Printex Computer is a person resident outside India [Section 2(w)]. Under Section 2(u) a 'person' includes any agency, office or branch owned or controlled by such person, so the Pune unit is a 'person'. Under Section 2(v)(iii), an office/branch/agency in India owned or controlled by a PROI is a person resident in India, so the Pune unit is a PRII. The Dubai branch, though not owned, is controlled by the Pune unit (a PRII) — hence the Dubai branch is also a person resident in India.
  • Q2 — Mr. Sane (Indian National): (i) Remittance of US$ 50,000 out of lottery winnings — prohibited; it appears in the First Schedule to the FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000, so Mr. Sane cannot withdraw foreign exchange for this purpose. (ii) US$ 100,000 for sending a cultural troupe on a tour of the U.S.A. — permissible after obtaining permission from the Government of India, Ministry of Human Resources Development (Department of Education and Culture) as prescribed in the Second Schedule. In all cases where remittance is allowed, by general or specific permission, the remitter must obtain the foreign exchange from an Authorised Person as defined in Section 2(c).
  • Q3 — X (film star) and R (heart surgery): (i) X, a film star, wants to perform with associates in New York on Diwali for Indians residing there, requiring drawal of US$ 20,000. Answer: foreign exchange drawals for cultural tours require prior approval of the Ministry of Human Resources Development (Department of Education and Culture) irrespective of the amount — so X must seek that Ministry's permission. (ii) R wants heart surgery in the United Kingdom. Answer: individuals may avail foreign exchange within the limit of USD 2,50,000; any additional remittance normally requires RBI approval, however for medical treatment abroad no RBI approval is required — R can draw foreign exchange up to the amount estimated by the medical institute offering the treatment.
  • Q4 — M (transponders) and P (call back services): (i) M requires U.S. $ 5,000 for remittance towards hiring charges of transponders. Answer: it is a current account transaction for which approval of the Central Government is required for drawal (Schedule II). (ii) P requires U.S. $ 2,000 for payment related to call back services of telephones. Answer: this is a prohibited transaction (Schedule I) — Mr. P cannot obtain US $ 2,000 for that purpose.
  • Q5 — Suresh (Switzerland, biotechnology): Suresh resided in India during FY 2020-21 and left India on 15th July 2021 for Switzerland to pursue higher studies in Biotechnology for 2 years. He needs USD 25,000 per year for tuition fees and USD 30,000 per year for incidental and stay expenses. Answer on status: a student normally goes out for a certain period and so would remain resident, but per RBI A.P. Circular No. 45 dated 8th December 2003 students are treated as non-residents. Hence Mr. Suresh is a person resident in India for FY 2021-22 till 16th July 2021, and from 17th July 2021 a person resident outside India; for FY 2022-23 he is a person resident outside India as he left India on 15th July 2021. Answer on foreign exchange: under Para I of Schedule III to the FEM (Current Account Transactions) Amendment Rules, 2015 dated 26th May 2015, individuals may avail foreign exchange for studies abroad within USD 2,50,000; anything more needs prior RBI approval, though the further proviso permits remittances exceeding USD 2,50,000 without prior RBI approval based on the estimate received from the institution abroad. Here the requirement is only USD 55,000 per academic year, so RBI approval is not required.
  • Q6 — Mr. P (lottery) and Mr. Z (kidney transplant): (i) Mr. P won a big lottery and wants to remit US Dollar 20,000 out of his winnings to his son in the USA. Answer: such remittance is prohibited under the FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000 — Mr. P cannot withdraw foreign exchange for this purpose. (ii) Mr. Z is unwell and wants a kidney transplant in the USA. Answer: remittance for medical treatment abroad requires prior RBI approval only where the drawal exceeds USD 250,000; the Schedule also allows exchange in excess of the LRS limit if so required by the medical institute offering treatment. Therefore Mr. Z can draw foreign exchange up to USD 250,000 with no RBI approval, and beyond that limit authorised dealers may release foreign exchange based on the estimate from the doctor in India, or the hospital or doctor abroad.
  • Q7 — Mr. Rohan (Indian resident individual): (A) US$ 120,000 for studies abroad on the basis of estimates given by the foreign university. Answer: foreign exchange may be released for studies abroad up to US$ 250,000 without RBI permission; above that, prior RBI approval is required, though the further proviso to Para I of Schedule III allows remittances exceeding USD 250,000 based on the estimate received from the institution abroad. Since the drawal is only US$ 120,000, RBI permission is not required. (B) Gift remittance of US$ 10,000. Answer: gift remittance is a current account transaction; gift remittance exceeding US$ 250,000 needs prior RBI approval. As Mr. Rohan's gift is only USD 10,000, no RBI permission is needed.

Case Scenario 10 — Amit (FEMA)

  • Facts: Amit was an Indian resident during FY 2021-2022. On 15th July 2022 he left India to begin a two-year academic programme in Biotechnology in Switzerland. He needs USD 25,000 annually for tuition fees plus USD 30,000 annually for incidental and living expenses — a total of USD 55,000 per year.
  • Q1 — Residential status for FY 2022-2023: Answer (b) Non-Resident Indian (NRI) — a student abroad is treated as a non-resident per the RBI clarification.
  • Q2 — Residential status for FY 2023-2024: Answer (b) Non-Resident Indian (NRI) — he was not in India for more than 182 days in the preceding financial year.
  • Q3 — Maximum further amount remittable per financial year under LRS: Answer (b) USD 195,000 — the LRS ceiling of USD 250,000 less the USD 55,000 already required, i.e. USD 250,000 − USD 55,000 = USD 195,000. (Options rejected: USD 100,000, USD 200,000, USD 500,000.)

Why It Matters / Application

Every cross-border rupee-dollar decision an Indian entity or individual makes turns on two classifications that this chapter teaches: is the party a PRII or a PROI, and is the transaction current account or capital account. Get the first wrong and a company remits to the wrong person under the wrong regulation — Illustration 3 and the Printex question show that a Mumbai or Pune branch of a foreign parent is a resident, and its own overseas branch is also a resident, so a chain of ownership can pull a Singapore or Dubai establishment squarely inside FEMA. Get the second wrong and the wrong approval route is used: a gift remitted abroad is current account (freely permitted up to USD 250,000), while the same gift given in India in Indian currency to a non-resident is capital account and permitted only if specifically allowed. The Schedule tables are the practical checklist an authorised dealer applies before releasing funds — lottery remittances and call-back-service payments are refused outright; transponder hire and cultural tours go to a named Ministry; sports prize money above USD 100,000, agent commission above the higher of USD 25,000 / 5% of inward remittance, and non-infrastructure consultancy above USD 1,000,000 go to the RBI. Knowing that the LRS USD 250,000 limit is a single annual pool covering both current and capital account drawals, and that emigration, medical treatment and studies can break through it on the strength of a foreign institution's estimate, is what separates a correct answer from a wrong one in exactly the fact patterns used in MCQ 1, MCQ 3 and Case Scenario 10.

Note — Exceptions, Provisos and Exam Traps

  • Trap 1 — the "preceding financial year" trap. The 182-day count is always of the preceding financial year, never the current one, and the resulting status runs from a date, not for the whole year. That is why Mr. Suresh is a PRII till 16th July 2021 and a PROI from 17th July 2021 within one and the same financial year.
  • Trap 2 — purpose beats day-count. Miss Alia stayed in India for more than 182 days and is still a non-resident; Mr. X came on 1st April 2020 with under 182 days of prior stay and is a resident from that very day. Citizenship is never the test.
  • Trap 3 — students. On the bare wording of Section 2(v)(A), a student leaving for a fixed-duration course goes for a certain period and would remain a PRII. RBI A.P. Circular No. 45 dated 8th December 2003 overrides this and treats students as non-residents. Always cite the circular.
  • Trap 4 — whole amount vs excess. In the Akash Ceramics MCQ the answer is prior RBI approval for the entire USD 42,000, not merely for the excess over USD 30,000 — the option splitting the amount is deliberately wrong.
  • Trap 5 — "whichever is less" vs "whichever is more" vs "whichever is higher". Donations by non-individuals: 1% of last three years' forex earnings or USD 5,000,000, whichever is LESS. Agent commission on sale of flats/plots: USD 25,000 or 5% of inward remittance, whichever is MORE. Pre-incorporation expense reimbursement: 5% of investment brought in or USD 100,000, whichever is HIGHER. These three phrasings are frequently swapped in distractors.
  • Trap 6 — infrastructure vs other consultancy. USD 10,000,000 per project applies only to consultancy for infrastructure projects; everything else is capped at USD 1,000,000 per project (Mohita Periodicals).
  • Trap 7 — Nepal and Bhutan. The USD 250,000 private-visit facility is available for visits to any country except Nepal and Bhutan.
  • Trap 8 — the LRS is one pool. Drawal under item 1 of Schedule III is subsumed within the USD 250,000 capital account proviso, and any LRS remittance in a year reduces the Schedule III limit by that amount. Do not add the two limits together.
  • Trap 9 — the estimate exceptions are only three. Items (iv) emigration, (vii) medical treatment and (viii) studies abroad — and only these — may exceed the LRS limit without prior RBI approval, on the strength of a requirement from the country of emigration, the medical institute or the university respectively.
  • Trap 10 — EEFC is not a blanket exemption. Remitting from an RFC account exempts all Schedule II/III transactions, but remitting from an EEFC account still needs approval for P & I Club membership, agent commission on sale of flats/plots above the threshold, and pre-incorporation expense reimbursement above the threshold.
  • Amendment alert: Section 6(3) (the old RBI list of regulable capital account transactions) was deleted with effect from 15th October 2019 even though the definition in Section 2(e) still refers to it; and though the Finance Act 2015 transferred non-debt-instrument powers to the Central Government, the change took effect only from 15th October 2019.
  • Deemed receipt trap [Explanation to Section 3(c)]: receiving a payment on behalf of a non-resident through an authorised person is still a contravention if there is no corresponding inward remittance from outside India — the involvement of a bank does not cure a hawala-type settlement.
  • REITs and townships are not "real estate business": the prohibition on PROI investment in real estate business excludes development of townships, construction of residential/commercial premises, roads or bridges, and SEBI-registered REITs under the SEBI (REITs) Regulations 2014.
  • NRIs and chit funds: the general prohibition on PROI investment in chit funds is relaxed — NRIs may subscribe through banking channels, on a non-repatriation basis, without limit, if permitted by the Registrar of Chits in consultation with the State Government and subject to RBI conditions.
  • DPRK: existing impermissible investments, representative offices or assets in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea had to be closed/liquidated/disposed/settled within 180 days of the notification unless the Central Government approved continuance.
  • Note on the printed extract: the source PDF appends a common "Case Scenarios" booklet (pages CS.1–CS.24) after this chapter. Only Case Scenario 10 (Amit) is on FEMA; Case Scenarios 1–8 test the Companies Act, 2013 and the LLP Act, 2008 and Case Scenario 9 tests the General Clauses Act, 1897, and they belong with those chapters. Their answer keys as printed are: CS 1 — 1(d) 2(a) 3(c) 4(d) 5(b); CS 2 — 1(a) 2(d) 3(c) 4(d); CS 3 — 1(b) 2(d) 3(b) 4(c); CS 4 — 1(c) 2(b) 3(c) 4(b) 5(a); CS 5 — 1(c) 2(c) 3(c) 4(b); CS 6 — 1(c) 2(b) 3(b) 4(b) 5(d); CS 7 — 1(d) 2(a) 3(a); CS 8 — 1(c) 2(c) 3(b); CS 9 — 1(a) 2(c) 3(d) 4(b) 5(b).

Chapter Summary as printed

  • FEMA makes provisions in respect of dealings in foreign exchange.
  • FEMA regulates transactions between residents and non-residents.
  • Broadly, all current account transactions are free; however the Central Government can impose reasonable restrictions by issuing rules.
  • Capital account transactions are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Central Government.
  • FEMA envisages that the RBI will have a controlling role in the management of foreign exchange.
